doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL 1.8 Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Bank Format: Each item below gives a set of 2–3 statements/pairs. Determine how many are CORRECT: Only 1 / Only 2 / All 3 / None. Q1. Consider the following statements about hazard classification: (i) Heavy metals like Pb, Hg, As, Cd are classified as chemical hazards arising from environmental pollution. (ii) Hair and filth found in food are always classified as HACCP biological hazards. (iii) Food allergens are protein-derived chemical hazards under the Codex classification used in this syllabus. Answer: Only 1 is correct (statement i). • (i) TRUE — heavy metals are textbook chemical/environmental pollutant hazards. • (ii) FALSE — hair/filth are "undesirable defects," not HACCP hazards (Module 6 principle), and are NOT biological hazards by nature (hair is not a pathogen). • (iii) FALSE as phrased for this trap — in the hazard classification used, allergens are grouped as a distinct category alongside, not strictly "chemical hazards" in the narrow pesticide/pollutant sense (though some classifications do nest it there, this syllabus treats allergens as a 4th explicit category: Biological, Chemical, Physical, Allergens). Q2. Regarding Food Infection vs Intoxication: (i) Both are always accompanied by fever. (ii) Intoxication is not communicable from person to person. (iii) Infection incubation period is typically shorter than intoxication's incubation period. Answer: Only 1 is correct (statement ii). • (i) FALSE — fever is a more typical marker of infection, not necessarily intoxication. • (ii) TRUE. • (iii) FALSE — it is the REVERSE: infection has a longer incubation (hours-days) vs intoxication's shorter one (minutes-hours). Q3. On WHO Five Keys to Safer Food: (i) The five keys include "Keep Clean," "Separate Raw and Cooked," and "Cook Thoroughly." (ii) "Use Safe Water and Raw Materials" is one of the five keys. (iii) The WHO Five Keys mandate refrigeration below 0°C for all cooked food. Answer: Only 2 are correct (statements i and ii). • (i) TRUE. • (ii) TRUE. • (iii) FALSE — the guidance is to refrigerate promptly, preferably below 5°C, not 0°C; the "always/mandate" framing with an incorrect numeric threshold is a classic absolute-qualifier trap. Q4. On physical hazards: (i) Glass, wood, stones, and metal are all listed as physical hazard source materials. (ii) Insects can constitute both a macro-biological hazard AND a physical hazard depending on context. (iii) Physical hazards are defined as materials normally found in food in small amounts. Answer: Only 2 are correct (statements i and ii). • (i) TRUE — all four appear in the standard physical hazard table. • (ii) TRUE — insects are listed under both macro-biological hazards and as a physical hazard source (contamination/extraneous matter), a nuance often tested. • (iii) FALSE — physical hazards are explicitly defined as materials NOT normally found in food. FOODSAFE • 7

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Module 2: Additives & Plant Toxicants MODULE 2: FOOD ADDITIVES & PLANT-ORIGIN TOXICANTS 2.1 First-Principles: Why classify additives at all? Regulators do not ban "chemicals" per se — they distinguish between substances whose safety is self- evident from long traditional use and low toxicity even unrestricted (Class I) versus substances that are effective but carry a dose-dependent risk profile requiring a legal ceiling (Class II). This single idea — unrestricted vs quantity-capped — is the organizing logic behind nearly every additive question HPSC asks. FOOD PRESERVATIVES | ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ CLASS I CLASS II (natural, NOT restricted (chemical, RESTRICTED to in any food unless Rules specified foods, concentration say otherwise) capped per Rules) | | Common salt, sugar, Benzoic acid & salts, dextrose/glucose syrup, Sulphurous acid & sulphites, wood smoke, spices, Nitrites & nitrates, vinegar/acetic acid, honey Sorbic acid & salts [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Class I preservatives are permitted in UNLIMITED quantity in ALL foods." — Partially FALSE. Class I is "not restricted unless otherwise provided in the Rules" — a conditional, not an absolute, exemption. Always flag "unlimited/unrestricted/all" wording against the actual legal phrasing. 2.2 Additive Categories — Mechanism-First Walkthrough (a) Antioxidants Intuition: Fats and oils undergo autoxidation — a free-radical chain reaction with atmospheric oxygen that converts unsaturated fatty acids into aldehydes/ketones, producing rancid off-flavours, loss of colour, and destruction of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E) and essential fatty acids (e.g., linoleic acid). Unsaturated fatty acid + O2 (catalyzed by light, heat, metal, pigment) ↓ Lipid free radical (R•) ↓ (chain propagation) Peroxide → Aldehydes + Ketones → RANCID OFF-FLAVOUR An antioxidant works by donating a hydrogen atom to the lipid free radical, terminating the chain reaction before it propagates (free radical scavenging). Type Examples Notes Natural Tocopherols (Vitamin E family) Found in plant tissues; heat-labile — FOODSAFE • 8

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Type Examples Notes lost during refining, deodorizing, processing BHA is more effective in animal fats than vegetable oils; very effective for Synthetic BHA, BHT short-chain fatty acids (coconut, palm kernel oil) used in cereals/confectionery (b) Emulsifiers & Stabilizers Intuition: Oil and water naturally separate because they are chemically incompatible (one polar, one non- polar). An emulsifier is amphiphilic — it has both a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and a lipophilic (fat- loving) tail — allowing it to sit at the oil-water interface and stabilize what is naturally an unstable two- phase system. • HLB (Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance): a numeric scale describing the relative strength of hydrophilic vs lipophilic portions of an emulsifier molecule; determines whether the emulsifier favours oil-in-water or water-in-oil emulsions. • Most widely used emulsifier: monoglycerides; lecithin is another key natural emulsifier. (c) Clarifying Agents Used to remove chill haze (from tannins/proanthocyanidins/polyphenols) in beverages like beer, wine, fruit juices. • Gelatin — commonly used to clarify beverages. • PVP (polyvinylpyrrolidone) — synthetic resin with selective affinity for polyphenols. (d) Colorants FOOD COLORANTS ┌───────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ NATURAL NATURE-IDENTICAL ARTIFICIAL INORGANIC (carotenoid, SYNTHETIC (coal-tar dyes, (PROHIBITED except annatto, (lab-synthesized e.g. Indigocarmine) Titanium Dioxide, paprika, replicas of capped at 1% in saffron, natural colors) CHEWING GUM only) anthocyanin, caramel, chlorophyll, turmeric/curcumin) [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Titanium dioxide — 1% — chewing gum ONLY. This is a frequently tested exact numeric + exact food- category pair. Any MCQ substituting a different percentage (e.g., 2%) or a different food (e.g., "permitted in all confectionery") is a trap. The rule is narrowly scoped: PFA prohibits inorganic colors except titanium dioxide, and only in chewing gum, maximum 1%. (e) Flavour Enhancers & Sweeteners • MSG (Monosodium Glutamate): sodium salt of glutamic acid; does not itself possess a primary flavour but intensifies/synergizes flavours of other foods. FOODSAFE • 9

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL • 5′-ribonucleotides (from yeast): possess roughly 10× the flavour-enhancing property of MSG, and act synergistically with it (umami synergy). • Non-nutritive sweeteners: Saccharin (~300× sweeter than sucrose), cyclamate, aspartame, acesulfame-K — none perfectly replicates full sucrose taste profile. (f) Anticaking Agents • Function: absorb excess moisture, coat particles for water repellency, or act as an insoluble particulate diluent to maintain free-flow of hygroscopic powders. • Calcium silicate: used in baking powder and table salt, up to 2%. • Microcrystalline cellulose: prevents grated/shredded cheese from clumping. • Other agents: sodium silicon aluminate, tri-calcium phosphate, magnesium silicate, magnesium carbonate. (g) Antibiotics in Food — Nisin • Nisin: a polypeptide antibiotic produced by streptococci. • Permitted use: prevents outgrowth of Clostridium botulinum in high-moisture processed cheese. • Spectrum: active against Gram-positive organisms (spore-formers in particular). • Also used to prevent spoilage of condensed milk. Nisin's narrow Gram-positive spectrum is the key testable nuance — it does NOT control Gram-negative spoilage/pathogenic organisms. (h) Nitrites & Nitrates • Function: stabilize colour of cured meat after cooking (prevent green-brown discoloration of lean meat), impart flavour, and critically act as inhibitors of Clostridium botulinum (anti-botulism preservative function). • Lethal dose for humans is of the order of 1 gram. • US Code of Federal Regulations cap: nitrites permitted as preservatives in cured meat/poultry not exceeding 2000 ppm. 2.3 Class I vs Class II Preservatives — Master Table Class I (Natural, unrestricted*) Class II (Chemical, legally capped) Common salt Benzoic acid & its salts Sugar, dextrose/glucose syrup Sulphurous acid & its sulphites Wood smoke Nitrites & nitrates Spices Sorbic acid & its salts Vinegar / acetic acid Honey *unless otherwise provided in the Rules FOODSAFE • 10

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL 2.4 Endogenous Plant Toxicants & Anti-Nutrients — Deep Mechanistic Treatment (a) Glycoalkaloids — α-Chaconine & α-Solanine First principles: These are steroidal glycoalkaloids produced by Solanaceae plants (potato, tomato, nightshade) as a natural chemical defence against pests. They act on humans via cholinesterase inhibition and cell membrane disruption (saponin-like action). Parameter Detail All Solanaceous plants — potatoes most significant staple Source exposure Key compounds α-chaconine + α-solanine (summed) 200 mg/kg (potatoes), based on an estimated 300 g/day Maximum safety limit intake Variety, light exposure, irradiation, mechanical injury, Variability factors storage conditions Largely unaffected by common processing — baking, Thermal stability cooking, frying do NOT significantly reduce glycoalkaloid content Peeling is the most efficient method — outer layers are Detoxification richest in toxin; manual peeling can remove up to 60% of total content (varies with tuber size/variety) Tomatine (α-tomatine + dehydrotomatine mixture) is largely degraded as the fruit ripens — tomatoes are Tomato-specific note therefore much safer than potatoes regarding glycoalkaloid exposure [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Cooking/boiling/frying completely detoxifies glycoalkaloids." — FALSE. Glycoalkaloids are thermally stable; peeling (not heat) is the primary mitigation, and even peeling removes only up to ~60%, not 100%. (b) Cyanogenic Glycosides Mechanism — enzymatic HCN release: Cyanogenic glycoside (intact, non-toxic while compartmentalized) │ tissue damage (chopping/chewing/grinding) brings │ substrate and enzyme into contact ▼ β-glycosidase (endogenous plant enzyme) ▼ Hydrolysis releases cyanohydrin → spontaneously decomposes ▼ Hydrogen Cyanide (HCN) — the toxic agent Source Crop Cyanogenic Glycoside Cassava Linamarin (main cyanogen) Stone fruit pits (e.g., apricot, peach, almond kernels) Amygdalin FOODSAFE • 11

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Traditional detoxification practices (cassava, Africa/South America): chopping, grinding, soaking in running water, fermentation, cooking — these physically disrupt plant tissue, allow HCN to volatilize/leach out, and denature enzymes. Amygdalin risk specifically arises when heat-processed products made from stone fruits retain the seeds/pits — consumers may be unknowingly exposed to HCN from unremoved seeds. (c) Lectins (Haemagglutinins) • Chemical nature: carbohydrate-binding glycoproteins, ubiquitous in nature. • Dietary relevance: present in most commonly eaten plant foods, especially legumes — consumed daily in appreciable quantities. • Key toxicological feature: high stability — survive gastrointestinal digestion, binding to gut mucosal carbohydrate receptors and causing gastric upset / mucosal damage via disruption of nutrient absorption and gut lining integrity. (d) Pyrrolizidine Alkaloids • Large group — ~350 distinct chemicals. • Toxicological classification: shown carcinogenic in animals; classified as potential human carcinogens (hepatotoxic mechanism — liver injury). • Exposure routes: (i) contamination of food supply by seeds containing these alkaloids, (ii) presence in traditional remedies/dietary supplements. (e) Anti-Nutrient Overview Table Toxicant Plant Family Glucosinolates Cruciferae (cabbage family) Cucurbitacins Cucurbitaceae (gourd family) Proteinase inhibitors Leguminosae Coumarins Leguminosae, Rubiaceae, Umbelliferae Cyanogenic glycosides Leguminosae, Gramineae, Rosaceae Glycoalkaloids Solanaceae Lectins Leguminosae Furocoumarins Umbelliferae, Rutaceae Family-mnemonic: Solanaceae → Glyco-ALKALoids (potato/tomato); Cruciferae → GlucoSINOlates (cabbage/mustard); Cucurbitaceae → CucurbitaCINS (gourds); Leguminosae → Lectins + Proteinase inhibitors + Coumarins (legumes carry the heaviest anti-nutrient burden). FOODSAFE • 12

Detail the naturally occurring toxicants found in plant horticultural foods, their toxic mechanisms, and processing methods for detoxification." Answer architecture (~15 marks, 3–4 pages): 1. Introduction (1 mark): Define food additive and preservative; justify classification logic (unrestricted traditional vs restricted chemical). 2. Regarding preservative classification: (i) Sorbic acid and its salts belong to Class II. (ii) Honey is classified under Class I. (iii) Benzoic acid belongs to Class I because it occurs naturally in some fruits. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (i) TRUE. • (ii) TRUE. • (iii) FALSE — despite natural occurrence trace amounts, benzoic acid & its salts are statutorily classified as Class II (restricted), a classic "natural origin ≠ unrestricted class" trap. Q2. On glycoalkaloids: (i) The combined maximum safety limit for α-chaconine and α-solanine in potatoes is 200 mg/kg. (ii) Peeling can remove up to 60% of glycoalkaloid content. (iii) Titanium dioxide is permitted in all bakery products. doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Module 3: Microbiology & Spoilage MODULE 3: MICROBIOLOGICAL PRINCIPLES & SPOILAGE CRITERIA 3.1 First-Principles: The Three-Lever Control Model Every microorganism needs three things to grow: suitable temperature, suitable pH, and available water. Food preservation technology is fundamentally the science of pushing one or more of these three levers outside the microbial comfort zone. This module is organized around those three levers, in the exact order the syllabus tests them: Temperature → pH → Water Activity. MICROBIAL GROWTH REQUIRES: ┌─────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┐ │ TEMPERATURE │ pH │ WATER ACTIVITY│ │ (°C) │ (H+ conc.) │ (aw) │ └─────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘ Push any lever outside tolerance → growth slows/stops 3.2 Cardinal Parameter 1: Temperature Domains Microbial Group Growth Range Optimal Growth Temperature Psychrotrophs Grow well at ≤7°C 20–30°C Mesophiles Grow well between 20–45°C 30–40°C Thermophiles Grow well at ≥45°C 55–65°C Key nuance: Psychrotrophs' optimal growth is NOT at refrigeration temperature — it is at 20–30°C. Their defining feature is that they can still grow, albeit slowly, at 7°C or below — this is precisely why refrigeration only extends shelf life (by increasing lag phase) rather than fully halting spoilage. Reducing temperature increases microbial lag time, which is the biochemical basis for chilling as a preservation method. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Refrigeration completely stops microbial growth." — FALSE. It only slows growth (extended lag phase) — psychrotrophs remain active at chill temperatures, hence refrigerated shelf life is finite, not infinite. 3.3 Cardinal Parameter 2: pH (Hydrogen-Ion Activity) Intuition Most microorganisms are physiologically "happiest" near neutral pH (~7.0). As the environment becomes more acidic, enzymatic machinery inside the cell is disrupted, and most pathogens cannot sustain growth. FOODSAFE • 15

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL But not all organisms have the same acid tolerance — this differential tolerance is exploited for both food safety classification and spoilage control. Organism / Food Type pH Tolerance Most microorganisms (general optimum) Close to pH 7.0 A few organisms Can grow below pH 4.0 Lactic acid bacteria (spoilage group) Can grow as low as pH 2.0 Clostridium botulinum Cannot grow below pH 4.6 THE Critical Public Health Threshold: pH 4.6 pH 4.6 is THE single most important numeric threshold in this entire module. Because of Clostridium botulinum's pathogenic potential (producer of the lethal botulinum neurotoxin) and its inability to grow/sporulate-outgrow below pH 4.6, this value is used as the universal legal/technical cutoff differentiating: - Low-acid foods: pH > 4.6 (require more stringent thermal processing — e.g., full retort sterilization — because C. botulinum CAN grow) - Acid / high-acid foods: pH ≤ 4.6 (safer from C. botulinum outgrowth; can often be processed with milder heat treatments) Nuance: The minimum pH tolerated by a given organism also depends on which acid is used — citric, hydrochloric, phosphoric, and tartaric acids permit growth of certain lactobacilli at lower pH values than acetic and lactic acids. This means pH value alone is not the complete story — the identity of the acidulant modulates antimicrobial efficacy (undissociated acid molecules of weaker organic acids like acetic/lactic penetrate cell membranes more effectively, giving them superior antimicrobial action at a given pH compared to strong mineral acids). [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "All bacteria are more pH-sensitive than filamentous fungi and yeasts." — Broadly TRUE as a generalization (bacteria tend to be more pH-sensitive than fungi/yeasts), but the trap variant "pathogenic bacteria tolerate LOWER pH than spoilage bacteria" is FALSE — it is the reverse: pathogenic bacteria are MORE pH-sensitive (narrower tolerance) than spoilage organisms like lactic acid bacteria. 3.4 Cardinal Parameter 3: Water Activity (aw) Intuition Total moisture content is not what matters to a microbial cell — what matters is how much of that water is metabolically available (not bound to solutes/structures). Water activity (aw) quantifies this available fraction, scaled 0 (no available water) to 1.0 (pure water). Food / Organism Type Water Activity Threshold Fresh produce aw exceeds 0.99 Spoilage bacteria (most) Grow at aw above 0.91 FOODSAFE • 16

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Food / Organism Type Water Activity Threshold Filamentous fungi / moulds Can grow at aw as low as 0.80 Gram-positive vs Gram-negative generalization: Bacteria generally need HIGHER water activity than fungi; Gram-negative bacteria need higher aw than Gram-positive bacteria. This ordering (Gram- negative bacteria > Gram-positive bacteria > fungi, in terms of minimum aw required) is a testable hierarchy. Mechanism of control: Lowering aw below the organism's optimum increases lag phase and reduces growth rate — this induced stress is called osmotic stress. This is the biochemical basis for preservation by salting, sugaring, and drying. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Numeric trap: Do not swap the thresholds. Spoilage bacteria: >0.91. Filamentous fungi: as low as 0.80. Fresh produce: >0.99. If an MCQ states "most filamentous fungi require aw above 0.91 to grow," this is FALSE — fungi are notably MORE tolerant of low water activity than bacteria, growing down to 0.80. 3.5 Microbiological Spoilage Patterns (a) Bacterial Spoilage • Only specific bacterial groups cause spoilage despite many bacteria being capable of growing in food. • Governing factors: storage temperature, oxygen availability, food composition, pH, thermal treatment, competing microbiota. • Classic manifestation in horticultural produce: bacterial soft rot. (b) Yeast Spoilage • Yeasts are unicellular eukaryotic organisms. • They gain a competitive advantage over bacteria specifically in foods with: high sugar or salt content, low pH, or other selective conditions. • Mechanism: produce extracellular enzymes (proteases, lipases, amylases, pectinases) and volatile/non-volatile metabolites that spoil flavour and texture. • Key genera: Saccharomyces, Candida, Zygosaccharomyces, Debaryomyces, Rhodotorula, Pichia. • Especially important in fruit/vegetable spoilage due to environmental exposure and minimal processing; low pH of these foods also limits competing bacterial growth, giving yeasts a competitive field. (c) Filamentous Fungi Spoilage • Grow on a very wide range of foods: grains, meats, milk, fruits, vegetables, seeds, high-fat products. • Manifestations: discoloration, off-flavours, loss of structure/texture, visible mycelium formation, volatile compound production. FOODSAFE • 17

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL • Fungi are obligate aerobes, capable of growing across a WIDE range of pH, temperature, and water activity — their metabolic flexibility is precisely why they are the dominant spoilage organism at low aw (0.80) where bacteria cannot compete. Spoilage Comparison Summary Organism Group Cell Type Competitive Niche Key Genera/Examples Neutral pH, moderate-high Bacteria Prokaryote Soft rot bacteria aw Yeasts Eukaryote (unicellular) High sugar/salt, low pH Zygosaccharomyces, Candida Eukaryote Low aw (down to 0.80), wide Filamentous fungi Various moulds (multicellular/mycelial) pH/temp tolerance 3.6 Controlling Microbiological Spoilage — General Strategy CONTROL STRATEGY | ┌─────┼─────────┬──────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Prevent Remove Inhibit Inactivate access cells/ growth (thermal / (barrier)spores (manipulate non-thermal (wash/ T, pH, aw) methods) filter) 3.7 Stage 2 Model Answer Framework (10 Marks) Question: "Explain the significance of intrinsic factors (specifically pH and water activity) in controlling foodborne pathogens. Why is pH 4.6 universally designated as a critical food safety threshold?" Answer architecture (~10 marks, 2 pages): 1. Intrinsic vs extrinsic factors (1 mark): Define intrinsic (food-inherent: pH, aw, redox potential, nutrient composition) vs extrinsic (environment-imposed: storage temperature, atmosphere, packaging). 2. pH section (3 marks): General microbial optimum near 7.0; differential tolerance (lactic acid bacteria down to pH 2.0 vs C. botulinum blocked below 4.6); acid-identity nuance (citric/HCl/phosphoric/tartaric vs acetic/lactic). 3. Why pH 4.6 (3 marks): Explicit explanation — Clostridium botulinum cannot grow/produce toxin below this threshold; hence pH 4.6 is used worldwide to classify foods as low-acid (>4.6, requiring full retort sterilization to destroy C. botulinum spores) vs acid/high-acid (≤4.6, safer, can use milder thermal processing). Link to practical canning regulation (e.g., GMP requirement that acid/acidified foods be monitored and maintained at pH 4.6 or below). 4. Water activity section (2 marks): Define aw; give thresholds for fresh produce (>0.99), spoilage bacteria (>0.91), fungi (0.80); explain osmotic stress mechanism. 5. Integration/Conclusion (1 mark): Both factors are manipulated together industrially (e.g., pickling = low pH + reduced aw) for synergistic pathogen control — hurdle technology concept. FOODSAFE • 18

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL 3.8 Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Bank Q1. Regarding temperature domains: (i) Psychrotrophs have an optimal growth temperature range of 20–30°C. (ii) Mesophiles grow well between 20–45°C with optimum at 30–40°C. (iii) Thermophiles have optimal growth below 45°C. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — thermophiles grow well AT OR ABOVE 45°C, with optimum 55–65°C; the statement reverses the threshold direction. Q2. On pH and Clostridium botulinum: (i) C. botulinum cannot grow below pH 4.6. (ii) pH 4.6 is used to differentiate low-acid from high-acid/acid foods. (iii) Lactic acid bacteria can tolerate pH as low as 2.0. Answer: All 3 are correct. • All three statements are directly supported by the source material. Q3. On water activity thresholds: (i) Most spoilage bacteria require aw above 0.91. (ii) Filamentous fungi can grow at aw as low as 0.80. (iii) Fresh fruits and vegetables typically have aw below 0.80. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — fresh produce has aw exceeding 0.99, not below 0.80; this is a scope-reversal trap. Q4. On spoilage organisms: (i) Yeasts gain competitive advantage in high-sugar, low-pH foods. (ii) Zygosaccharomyces and Candida are key spoilage yeast genera. (iii) Filamentous fungi are strict anaerobes. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — filamentous fungi are obligate aerobes, the exact opposite. Q5. On acid identity and microbial growth: (i) Citric, hydrochloric, phosphoric and tartaric acids enable lactobacilli growth at lower pH than acetic/lactic acid. (ii) All acids have identical antimicrobial efficacy at the same pH value. (iii) Acetic and lactic acids are generally MORE inhibitory per unit pH than mineral acids due to undissociated acid effects. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and iii — note these are consistent, not contradictory; ii is false). • (ii) FALSE — different acids have different antimicrobial efficacy at the same measured pH, which is precisely why this nuance is tested. FOODSAFE • 19

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Module 4: Post-Harvest Adulteration MODULE 4: POST-HARVEST ADULTERATION & CHEMICAL TREATMENTS 4.1 First-Principles: Why does post-harvest malpractice exist? Consumers judge produce primarily by appearance — colour, size, shine, perceived ripeness/sweetness — at the point of purchase, before any taste or safety assessment is possible. This appearance-based buying heuristic creates a profit incentive for unscrupulous traders to manipulate the visible signal without manipulating the underlying quality — i.e., fake the signal (colour, size, apparent ripeness) rather than deliver the substance (genuine nutrient/flavour maturity). Every malpractice in this module follows this exact logic: cheap chemical trick → false visual/sensory signal → consumer deception → health risk. True quality driver (slow, costly, requires time) ──X── bypassed by trader │ Fast/cheap chemical shortcut │ False visual/sensory signal │ Consumer deceived + potential health hazard 4.2 Artificial Ripening Agents (a) Calcium Carbide ("Masala") — STRICTLY BANNED Reaction mechanism: Calcium Carbide (CaC2) + Moisture (H2O) ↓ Acetylene gas (C2H2) + Calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2) ↓ Acetylene is structurally/functionally ANALOGOUS to ethylene (C2H4) ↓ Triggers surface-level ripening signalling in fruit Why it is banned under FSSA, 2006 — multi-factor reasoning (exam gold): 1. Acidic nature of the compound/by-products — contributes to tissue damage; chronic consumption linked to ulcers, kidney and liver damage. 2. Trace contamination with arsenic and phosphorus hydride — industrial-grade calcium carbide (the commonly available/cheap form) is contaminated with arsenic and phosphorus compounds, which are themselves toxic. 3. Superficial colouration without internal ripening — acetylene changes ONLY the surface colour of the fruit; the interior remains unripened — a cosmetic fraud rather than genuine ripening. This is functionally and texturally inferior to ethylene-based ripening. 4. Carcinogenic property attributed to calcium carbide with prolonged exposure. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Calcium carbide ripens fruit exactly like ethylene, just faster." — FALSE. It mimics ethylene's effect only at the surface — internal ripening (sugar development, aroma compounds, FOODSAFE • 20

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Rationale for waxing: replaces natural wax lost during primary processing (washing etc.), reduces water loss, surface abrasion, controls internal gas composition, provides shiny/attractive appearance, extends shelf life. Preferred over: petroleum-based waxes (which may contain wood rosins or solvent residues). Typical waxed commodities: breadfruit, passion fruit, coconut, carambola, grapefruit, guava, mango, lime, lemon, orange, papaya, avocado, tangerine, pineapple (fruits); melon, bitter gourd, cassava, eggplant, peppers, sweet potato, tomato, pumpkin, yam, cucumber, asparagus, turnip, brinjal, okra, parsnip, sweet peppers (vegetables). Mandatory Label Declarations for Waxed Produce Under FSSA, 2006, fresh fruits/vegetables coated with wax (bees or carnauba) MUST have a clear label declaration stating: 1. Origin of the wax — animal-based (e.g., beeswax, shellac) vs vegetable-based (e.g., carnauba) — with food-grade certification. 2. Presence of known allergens that may be present in coating ingredients — e.g., milk, soybeans, fish, peanuts, nuts, wheat. 3. Post-harvest antimicrobial coatings/substances — their application must be indicated on each shipping container. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "All waxes and mineral oils are permitted on fruits and vegetables under GMP." — FALSE. No mineral oil and no colour is permitted at all on fresh fruits/vegetables per Indian regulatory bodies; only the THREE named food-grade waxes (carnauba, beeswax, shellac) are permitted, strictly under GMP, with mandatory labelling. Nutrient absorption caveat: Wax coating can form an insoluble layer that reduces nutrient absorption in the intestine — hence the practical consumer advice to wash fruits thoroughly / boil vegetables briefly before consumption, acknowledging that negative impact cannot be fully eliminated by washing alone. 4.5 Regulatory Residue/Tolerance Summary Substance Tolerance/Limit Status Permitted per GMP as food additives, with mandatory label Approved waxes (carnauba/beeswax/shellac) declaration Strictly prohibited — NO tolerance limit at all under Calcium carbide (ripening agent) FSSA, 2006 Mineral oil / any colour on fresh F&V NOT ALLOWED — no tolerance limit assigned Allowed up to tolerable limits prescribed under FSSA, Heavy metals 2006 — must not exceed assigned value Must not exceed maximum limit per FSSAI/FDA Naturally occurring toxic substances/anti-nutrients specifications FOODSAFE • 23

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Module 5: Packaging & Labelling Law MODULE 5: PACKAGING & LABELLING STATUTORY STANDARDS 5.1 First-Principles: Why does the label matter legally? A food label is a legally binding representation to the consumer — it is the primary (often only) information bridge between a manufacturer's internal quality/safety processes and the buyer's informed choice. Every mandatory declaration exists to answer one of three consumer questions: (1) Is this food safe for me right now? (2) What exactly am I eating? (3) Who is accountable if something goes wrong? Organize your memorization around these three questions. LABEL ANSWERS THREE QUESTIONS: ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────┐ │ IS IT SAFE NOW? │ WHAT AM I EATING? │ WHO IS ACCOUNTABLE? │ │ (dates, veg/non- │ (ingredients, │ (manufacturer │ │ veg, allergens) │ nutrition facts) │ address, batch, │ │ │ │ country of origin)│ └─────────────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────┘ 5.2 Statutory Date Markings — Precise Definitions "Date of Manufacture" vs "Date of Packaging" Term Definition The date on which the food becomes the product as Date of manufacture described (i.e., the food's identity/composition is finalized) The date on which the food is placed in the immediate Date of packaging container in which it will ultimately be sold These are conceptually distinct steps — a food can be manufactured on Day 1 and packaged on Day 3; both dates may be legally relevant depending on the product category. "Best Before" vs "Use By / Expiry Date" — THE critical distinction PRODUCT TIMELINE Manufacture ──► "Best Before" ──► "Use By / Expiry" (quality marker) (safety marker) │ │ Food MAY still be Food shall NOT perfectly safe to be sold — safety consume past this threshold passed date, though quality may have diminished (BUT: food shall not be sold if it becomes unsafe at ANY stage) FOODSAFE • 25

Signifies the end of the estimated period, under stated storage "Use-by date" / "Recommended last conditions, after which the food The food SHALL NOT be sold after consumption date" / "Expiry date" probably will not have the quality this date — absolute safety/sale cutoff and safety attributes normally expected. On date markings: (i) "Best before" signifies the food must never be sold after that date under any circumstance. (ii) "Use by"/"Expiry date" signifies the food shall not be sold after that date. doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Module 6: HACCP System MODULE 6: THE HACCP SYSTEM & QUALITY ASSURANCE 6.1 First-Principles: Why HACCP replaced end-product testing The core insight that birthed HACCP: if you only test the FINISHED product for safety, you can never achieve near-100% assurance, because (a) you'd have to destructively test almost every unit to be statistically confident, leaving nothing left to sell, and (b) by the time a defect is found, the unsafe batch may already be shipped. HACCP's genius is to shift control upstream, into the process itself — identify exactly WHERE in the process a hazard could enter or fail to be controlled, and build real-time monitoring AT THAT POINT, so you catch failures before the product is even finished, let alone shipped. OLD MODEL: Raw material → Process → Process → Process → [TEST FINISHED PRODUCT] (if contaminated, discovered too late / insufficient sampling) HACCP MODEL: Raw material → [MONITOR CCP1] → Process → [MONITOR CCP2] → Process → Product (hazard caught in real time, AT the exact point of risk) 6.2 Historical Foundations Milestone Detail Pillsbury Company, pioneered application of HACCP Origin concept to food production in the early 1960s Supplying food for the U.S. space program (NASA) — existing QC (end-product testing) could not provide Driving need adequate contamination assurance; extensive end-testing would consume so much product that little food would remain available for space flights 1985 — NACMCF (National Advisory Committee on Formalization Microbiological Criteria for Foods) formulated the HACCP principles [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Date-pairing trap: Pillsbury origin = early 1960s (the practical invention); NACMCF formal principles = 1985 (the codification). Do not swap these two dates — a question may ask "In which year were the 7 HACCP principles formulated?" and offer "1960s" as a distractor; the correct year for the formal 7- principle codification is 1985. 6.3 Hazard vs Undesirable Defect — THE scope-defining distinction In HACCP terminology, "hazard" has a narrower, more precise meaning than in everyday food safety usage. It refers ONLY to conditions/contaminants that can cause illness or injury. FOODSAFE • 31

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Documentation & Verification Corrective Record-Keeping Procedures Actions Principle 1: Conduct Hazard Analysis • HACCP team bears initial responsibility to decide which hazards are significant and must be addressed. • Safety concerns must be explicitly differentiated from quality concerns (quality issues are NOT the subject of HACCP control). • Tool: hazard identification and evaluation worksheet — organizes the process step (Column 1), identified hazard (Column 2), hazard evaluation result (Column 3), and justification for accepting/rejecting the hazard (Column 4). Principle 2: Determine Critical Control Points (CCPs) • For every significant hazard identified in Principle 1, there must be one or more CCPs where the hazard is controlled. • A CCP = a specific point in the process flow where applying a control measure effectively prevents, eliminates, or reduces the hazard to an acceptable level. • Determined using decision tree logic — a structured sequence of questions applied at each process step to test whether that step qualifies as a CCP. Principle 3: Establish Critical Limits • A critical limit = the boundary/boundaries used to ensure a process produces safe product at a given CCP. • Each CCP may require one or more critical limits, one per associated food-safety hazard. • Deviation from a critical limit → mandatory corrective action. • If exact critical limit data is unavailable: gather from scientific publications, regulatory guidelines, experts, or experimental studies; if still unavailable, select a conservative value. The rationale/reference becomes part of the HACCP plan's support documentation. Principle 4: Establish CCP Monitoring Procedures Monitoring must define four elements: Element Meaning What characteristic will be monitored (e.g., temperature, What pH, line speed) How How the critical limit/control measure will be measured Frequency How often monitoring is performed Who Who is responsible for performing the monitoring Purpose: accurate monitoring reveals loss of control at a CCP and deviation from a critical limit in real time; also creates records proving compliant production (feeds into Principle 7 and Principle 6 verification). Principle 5: Establish Corrective Actions When a critical limit is violated, pre-determined, documented corrective actions must be instituted. Effective corrective action plans must: FOODSAFE • 33

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL 1. Correct and eliminate the cause of non-compliance, restoring the CCP to control. 2. Segregate, assess, and determine disposition of the non-compliant product. Options: isolate/hold product for safety evaluation; divert affected product to a non-critical line; reprocess; destroy product. Principle 6: Establish Verification Procedures • Verification = collecting and evaluating scientific/technical information to confirm the HACCP plan, if properly implemented, will effectively control hazards. • Validation = a component of verification performed BEFORE the plan is implemented — substantiates that the plan, if followed, is sufficient to control the likely food-safety hazards; provides objective evidence that all elements have a scientific basis. • Approaches to validation: incorporation of fundamental scientific principles, use of scientific data, reliance on expert opinion, or in-plant observation/testing. Validation vs ongoing verification: Validation happens once, UP FRONT (before operation). Verification (in the broader sense, including scheduled audits) is ongoing, confirming the system continues to function as validated. Principle 7: Establish Documentation and Record-Keeping Procedures Accurate record-keeping is essential — provides documentation that critical limits were met OR appropriate corrective action was taken when exceeded. Four record categories: 1. HACCP-plan support documents 2. Monitoring records 3. Corrective action records 4. Verification records 6.5 CCP vs Prerequisite Programme (PRP) — The Critical Distinction Feature CCP (Critical Control Point) PRP (Prerequisite Programme) General, plant-wide foundational A specific point in the process flow practices (e.g., GMP, GHP, sanitation, Scope directly controlling a significant, pest control, personnel hygiene) that identified hazard create the environment in which the HACCP plan can function Decision tree logic, applied per Applied broadly, NOT hazard-specific; Determined by process step, tied to a specific hazard baseline operational conditions Failure typically requires general corrective maintenance, not Direct, immediate food-safety risk necessarily an immediate product- Failure consequence requiring corrective action under disposition decision (though severe Principle 5 PRP failure can elevate a step to CCP status) Continuous/frequent, tied to a Periodic inspection/audit (e.g., Monitoring measurable critical limit sanitation checklists) Cook temperature/time for a specific Water potability programme; pest Examples pasteurization step; metal detector at control programme; personnel hygiene FOODSAFE • 34

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL Feature CCP (Critical Control Point) PRP (Prerequisite Programme) training; equipment calibration packaging schedule Decision tree logic for identifying a CCP (conceptual sequence): Step 1: Does a control measure exist at this step for the identified hazard? │ NO ──┴── YES │ │ Modify Step 2: Is control at this step NECESSARY for safety? step/ │ process NO ──┴── YES → NOT a CCP (not necessary for safety) │ Step 3: Is the hazard likely to occur above acceptable level, OR could it increase to an unacceptable level, at this step? │ NO ──┴── YES │ │ NOT a CCP Step 4: Will a SUBSEQUENT step eliminate or reduce the hazard to an acceptable level? │ YES ─┴─ NO │ │ NOT a CCP THIS STEP IS A CCP [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Every step that controls a hazard is automatically a CCP." — FALSE. If a LATER step in the process will adequately eliminate/reduce the SAME hazard to an acceptable level, the EARLIER step is not designated a CCP — the decision tree explicitly tests for this downstream-elimination possibility before confirming CCP status. 6.6 Stage 2 Model Answer Framework (15 Marks) Question: "Elaborate the 7 Principles of Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP). Explain how a Critical Control Point (CCP) is determined and distinguished from a Prerequisite Programme (PRP)." Answer architecture (~15 marks, 3–4 pages): 1. Introduction (1 mark): Brief history — Pillsbury/NASA origin (1960s), NACMCF formalization (1985); define HACCP as a preventive (not reactive) system. 2. The 7 Principles — full elaboration (9 marks, ~1.3 marks each): Walk through Principles 1–7 exactly as detailed above, naming the key deliverable/tool at each stage (hazard analysis worksheet, decision tree, critical limits, monitoring's 4 W's, corrective action disposition options, validation vs verification, 4 record types). 3. CCP determination via decision tree (3 marks): Explain the sequential logic — is control necessary? is the hazard likely to occur/increase? will a later step eliminate it? — concluding in CCP designation only when all conditions align. 4. CCP vs PRP distinction (2 marks): Reproduce the comparison table — CCP is hazard-specific and point-specific with a measurable critical limit; PRP is a general plant-wide foundational practice (GMP/GHP) that enables the HACCP system to function, but is not itself tied to a single measurable critical limit at a single process point. FOODSAFE • 35

doc: HPSC FSO Master Study Manual — Hazards & Foodborne Illness
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MASTER STUDY MANUAL 6.7 Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Bank Q1. On HACCP origins: (i) HACCP originated at the Pillsbury Company in connection with the NASA space programme. (ii) The 7 HACCP principles were formulated by NACMCF in 1985. (iii) HACCP was developed in the early 1960s as a reactive, end-product-testing-based system. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — HACCP was developed specifically because end-product testing (reactive) was found inadequate; HACCP is explicitly a preventive, not reactive, system — the exact reverse characterization. Q2. On HACCP hazard scope: (i) Hair and filth are automatically classified as HACCP hazards. (ii) Economic fraud is excluded from the HACCP hazard definition unless directly tied to illness/injury. (iii) A hazard in HACCP terms must have the potential to cause an adverse health effect. Answer: Only 2 are correct (ii and iii). • (i) FALSE — hair and filth are "undesirable defects," not automatically HACCP hazards, unless a direct injury/illness link is shown. Q3. On the 7 principles, consider this set relating to Principle 4 (Monitoring): (i) Monitoring must specify "what," "how," "frequency," and "who." (ii) Monitoring is only required at the END of the production line. (iii) Monitoring records support verification under Principle 6. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and iii). • (ii) FALSE — monitoring occurs AT each CCP throughout the process, not solely at the end; this contradicts HACCP's core preventive, real-time logic. Q4. On CCP vs PRP: (i) A CCP is always hazard-specific and tied to a measurable critical limit. (ii) A PRP (e.g., GMP/GHP/sanitation programme) is plant-wide and foundational, not hazard-point-specific. (iii) Every PRP failure automatically qualifies as a critical-limit deviation requiring product disposition under Principle 5. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — PRP failures are generally managed through general corrective maintenance, not necessarily triggering the formal CCP critical-limit deviation/product-disposition process (unless the PRP failure is severe enough to compromise an actual CCP). Q5. On validation vs verification: (i) Validation occurs before the HACCP plan is implemented. (ii) Verification is the same process as validation and occurs only once. (iii) Verification includes collecting and evaluating scientific/technical information to confirm the plan will effectively control hazards. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and iii). • (ii) FALSE — validation is a one-time, pre-implementation component; verification (in the broader sense) is an ONGOING activity, not identical to or synonymous with a single one-time validation event. FOODSAFE • 36

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Rules of engagement for Stage 1 1. Never answer a count-based pair by instinct. Write c1, c2, c3 in the margin for each statement (1 if correct, 0 if wrong), then compute N = c1 + c2 + c3 and match it to the option. This single discipline removes the majority of negative-marking losses. 2. Treat every absolute qualifier as a red flag. "EVOH is always the best barrier" is wrong because EVOH fails at high humidity. "Recycled plastics are completely banned" is wrong after the FSSAI certified food- grade recycled PET exception. 3. Distinguish look-alike pairs on sight: PVC versus PVDC, LDPE versus LLDPE, FAAS versus GFAAS, ECD versus FID, C-enamel versus R-enamel, overall migration versus specific migration, active versus intelligent packaging, time-temperature indicator versus freshness indicator. Rules of engagement for Stage 2 1. Open with a one-line definition or statutory citation (regulation name, year, schedule). 2. Give a mechanism (what happens at the molecular or instrumental level) before giving the application. 3. Add one labelled schematic (described in words if you cannot draw) and one comparative table; examiners award marks for structure. 4. Close with a regulatory or public-health linkage, since the post is Food Safety Officer, not Food Technologist. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Number Fact 1.25 percent H2SO4 then 1.25 percent NaOH, 30 min each Crude fibre digestion 40 to 60 °C Boiling range of petroleum ether used in Soxhlet 253.7 nm Mercury resonance line used in cold vapour AAS 6000 to 10000 K Argon plasma temperature in ICP-MS 27.12 MHz Usual RF frequency of the ICP load coil First ionisation energy of argon; elements below this ionise 15.76 eV efficiently in the plasma 70 eV Standard electron ionisation energy in GC-MS 63Ni Beta source of the electron capture detector 365 nm excitation, about 435 to 450 nm emission Fluorescence detection of aflatoxins 0.5 µg/kg FSSAI limit for aflatoxin M1 in milk FSSAI default maximum residue limit for pesticides not 0.01 mg/kg specifically listed FSSAI ceiling on trans fatty acids in fats and oils (from 1 2 percent January 2022) 0.25 Negative marking per wrong answer in HPSC Stage 1 ...is quantified by HPLC after pre-column derivatisation, because histamine itself has no useful chromophore: dansyl chloride gives a UV-absorbing (254 nm) derivative, while o-phthalaldehyde (OPA) with a thiol gives a fluorescent isoindole derivative (excitation 340 nm, emission 450 nm) read on a fluorescence detector at microgram-per-kilogram sensitivity. The FSSAI limit for histamine in fish and fishery products is 200 mg/kg (the Codex guideline is 100 mg/kg as the average of nine sample units, with 200 mg/kg as the hygiene limit for any single unit). The hazard is scombroid poisoning: temperature- abused tuna, mackerel, sardine and mahi-mahi allow bacterial histidine decarboxylase (Morganella morganii, Klebsiella, Hafnia) to convert free histidine to histamine, which is heat stable and survives canning and cooking, so the Food Safety Officer must enforce time-temperature control at landing rather than rely on processing. 4.1.6 Remaining HPLC notes: separation science you must be able to write • Reversed-phase versus normal-phase: in reversed-phase HPLC the stationary phase is non-polar (octadecylsilane, C18, bonded to 3 to 5 µm silica) and the mobile phase is polar (water with methanol or acetonitrile, often buffered); polar analytes elute first, and increasing the organic fraction shortens retention. Normal-phase HPLC uses bare silica or amino-bonded silica with a non-polar mobile phase (hexane with isopropanol); non-polar analytes elute first. About 80 percent of food methods are reversed-phase. • Isocratic versus gradient elution: isocratic keeps mobile-phase composition constant (simple, compatible with the refractive index detector); gradient elution raises the organic fraction during the run to elute strongly retained compounds with sharp peaks (required for mixed vitamin or multi-colour screens, incompatible with the refractive index detector because the baseline drifts with composition). • Column efficiency: the van Deemter equation H = A + B/u + C·u relates plate height H to linear velocity u; A is eddy diffusion (particle size and packing), B is longitudinal diffusion, C is resistance to mass transfer. Smaller particles reduce A and C, which is why ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) uses sub-2 µm particles at pressures up to 1000 to 1500 bar to give ten times faster runs with higher resolution. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Typical Gradient Food Detector Principle Selectivity sensitivity compatible applications Multi-residue pesticides, Universal and veterinary drugs, Mass Mass-to-charge structurally pg to fg Yes mycotoxins, spectrometer ratio of ions specific melamine, acrylamide (Section 4.3) 4.1.7 Core HPLC applications in FSSAI enforcement 1. Vitamins: fat-soluble vitamins A (retinol, 325 nm), D (265 nm), E (tocopherols, 292 nm UV or fluorescence) and K after saponification and hexane extraction, reversed-phase C18 with methanol; water-soluble vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B6, B9, C) by ion-pair reversed-phase with UV or fluorescence detection; vitamin C by reversed-phase on a C18 column at 245 nm with metaphosphoric acid stabilisation. Needed to verify fortification claims (FSS (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, 2018, for example vitamin A and D in edible oil and milk, iron, folic acid and B12 in wheat flour and rice). 2. Synthetic food colours: extraction of the dye on wool or on a polyamide or C18 solid-phase cartridge, reversed-phase gradient with ammonium acetate buffer and methanol, PDA detection. India permits only eight synthetic colours (tartrazine, sunset yellow FCF, carmoisine, ponceau 4R, erythrosine, indigo carmine, brilliant blue FCF, fast green FCF) at a maximum of 100 mg/kg singly or in combination (200 mg/kg in a few categories), so the method must separate and identify non-permitted dyes such as metanil yellow, rhodamine B, orange II, auramine and Sudan dyes, which are a prosecutable offence. 3. Aflatoxins B1, B2, G1 and G2: extraction with methanol-water, immunoaffinity column clean-up, reversed-phase C18 with water-methanol-acetonitrile, fluorescence detection. Aflatoxins B1 and G1 fluoresce weakly in aqueous mobile phases, so post-column derivatisation is applied: electrochemically generated bromine (Kobra cell), iodine solution added by a second pump, trifluoroacetic acid pre- column, or a photochemical reactor (UV lamp) that hydrates the terminal furan double bond into the strongly fluorescent hemiacetal. FSSAI limits (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations, 2011, as amended): total aflatoxins 15 µg/kg and aflatoxin B1 10 µg/kg in cereals, nuts and oilseeds, 30 µg/kg total in certain spices such as chillies and nutmeg, and aflatoxin M1 0.5 µg/kg in milk. 4. Sugar profiling: aminopropyl (NH2) column, acetonitrile-water 75:25 isocratic, refractive index detection; separation order fructose, glucose, sucrose, maltose, lactose; used to detect added sucrose in honey and fruit juices and to verify sugar-free claims. High-performance anion-exchange chromatography with pulsed amperometric detection gives higher sensitivity. 5. Other routine targets: preservatives (benzoate, sorbate, propionate), artificial sweeteners (saccharin, aspartame, acesulfame-K, sucralose by ELSD), caffeine in energy drinks (FSSAI ceiling 300 mg/L), melamine screening, polyphenols and curcumin content in turmeric, capsaicin in chilli, patulin in apple juice (50 µg/kg limit). HPSC EXAM TRAP: detector matching Refractive index detection is universal but insensitive and cannot be used with gradient elution; fluorescence is the most sensitive but only for fluorescent molecules or their derivatives; the photodiode array is the detector that confirms identity by spectrum. Aflatoxins are measured by fluorescence after post-column derivatisation, not by refractive index; sugars are measured by refractive index, not by UV (they have no chromophore). text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Part 1. Packaging Materials & Barrier Properties PART 1: FOOD PACKAGING MATERIALS AND BARRIER PROPERTIES 1.0 Why packaging exists: the four functions 1. Containment: holding the product in a defined unit. 2. Protection: against physical (shock, compression), chemical (oxygen, moisture, light, odour) and biological (microbes, insects, rodents) hazards; this is where barrier science lives. 3. Convenience: portioning, opening, reclosing, microwaveability, retortability. 4. Communication: labelling, traceability, tamper evidence; this is where the Food Safety Officer meets the Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020. 1.1 Barrier science from first principles A polymer film is not a wall; it is a solvent. Gas or vapour transport follows the solution-diffusion model: 1. The permeant dissolves in the polymer surface (governed by the solubility coefficient S). 2. It diffuses down a concentration gradient (governed by the diffusion coefficient D). 3. It desorbs on the other side. Permeability coefficient P = D × S, and the steady-state transmission rate is proportional to P × area × partial-pressure difference divided by thickness. Everything in packaging barrier design manipulates D or S. Factor Effect on barrier Reason Crystallites are impermeable; Higher crystallinity gives lower permeant must take a tortuous path Crystallinity permeability through amorphous regions (HDPE beats LDPE) Polar polymers (EVOH, nylon) resist "Like dissolves like": solubility S is high non-polar oxygen but absorb water; Polarity match when permeant and polymer have non-polar polyolefins resist water but similar polarity pass oxygen Biaxial orientation (BOPP, BOPET, Strain-induced crystallisation and Orientation OPA) improves barrier, stiffness and chain alignment clarity Arrhenius relationship; retort Temperature Permeability rises with temperature conditions temporarily open the structure Hydrophilic polymers (EVOH, nylon, Water plasticises the hydrogen-bonded Relative humidity cellophane) lose barrier at high RH network, increasing free volume and D Transmission rate inversely Thickness Longer diffusion path proportional to thickness Inorganic layers have essentially no Metallisation or foil Approaches zero transmission free volume; limited only by pinholes and cracks Standard units and test methods: FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 6

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS • WVTR (water vapour transmission rate): g/m²·day at 38 °C and 90 percent RH (ASTM E96 gravimetric cup; ASTM F1249 infrared sensor). • OTR (oxygen transmission rate): cm³/m²·day·atm at 23 °C, usually 0 or 50 percent RH (ASTM D3985 coulometric sensor). EVOH must always be quoted with its RH because its OTR can rise ten to a hundred fold at 90 percent RH. HPSC EXAM TRAP: the barrier paradox No single homopolymer is excellent against both oxygen and water. Polyolefins (PE, PP) are good moisture barriers and poor oxygen barriers; EVOH and nylon are the reverse. PVDC is the only common polymer that is good against both, and aluminium foil is the only material that is essentially total against both plus light. Any statement that EVOH or nylon is a "good moisture barrier" is wrong. 1.2 Glass Composition (soda-lime-silica container glass) Constituent Raw material Approximate percent Role Network former; gives Silica, SiO2 Sand 70 to 74 rigidity and chemical inertness Flux; lowers melting Soda, Na2O Soda ash, Na2CO3 12 to 16 temperature from about 1700 °C to about 1500 °C Stabiliser; without it soda Lime, CaO Limestone, CaCO3 10 to 13 glass is water-soluble (water glass) Chemical durability, reduces Alumina, Al2O3 Feldspar 1 to 3 devitrification Lowers melting energy; Cullet (recycled glass) Crushed glass 30 to 60 of batch infinitely recyclable Amber absorbs ultraviolet Iron oxides and chromium below about 450 nm, Colourants (green); carbon and sulfur trace protecting beer, edible oil (amber) and milk from light-induced oxidation Properties • Chemical inertness: attacked only by hydrofluoric acid and hot concentrated alkali; no migration of organic substances, which is why glass is the reference inert material. Minor alkali (sodium) leaching into acidic or pharmaceutical products is controlled by hydrolytic resistance classes. • Absolute barrier to gases, vapours, micro-organisms and odours; transparent (consumer appeal but light sensitivity); rigid, stackable, reclosable, microwave compatible, fully recyclable. • Drawbacks: heavy (density about 2.5 g/cm³), brittle, fracture hazard (glass fragments are a critical physical hazard in HACCP plans), poor thermal shock resistance. Thermal shock resistance Glass fails under sudden temperature change because the outer surface contracts or expands before the interior, generating tensile stress. Soda-lime container glass survives a sudden differential of only about 40 to 50 °C (hot filling into a cold jar, or cold water on a hot jar, is a classic breakage cause), which is why hot- fill lines pre-warm containers and retort processes raise and lower temperature gradually. Borosilicate FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 7

doc: Modern Food Packaging, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Analysis
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS glass (about 12 percent B2O3; laboratory and ovenware) has a coefficient of thermal expansion of about 3.3 × 10^-6 per kelvin versus about 9 × 10^-6 for soda-lime glass, so it tolerates differentials well above 100 °C. Annealing After forming (blow-and-blow for narrow-neck bottles, press-and-blow for jars on the IS machine) the container cools unevenly and locks in internal stresses. It passes through an annealing lehr held at about 550 to 600 °C (near the annealing point, above the strain point) and is then cooled slowly under control. Un-annealed glass can shatter spontaneously or under minimal impact. Annealing quality is checked with a polariscope (strain viewer). Surface coatings and treatments • Hot-end coating: tin tetrachloride or titanium tetrachloride vapour applied at about 500 °C, forming a thin SnO2 or TiO2 film that heals surface micro-cracks and anchors the cold-end coating. • Cold-end coating: polyethylene wax or stearate emulsion applied at about 100 °C for lubricity, so bottles do not scratch each other on filling lines (surface scratches cut glass strength by up to 60 percent). • Interior surface treatment (dealkalisation): sulfur dioxide or ammonium sulfate introduced at the hot end converts surface sodium to sodium sulfate, which is washed away, leaving a silica-rich inner skin with improved hydrolytic resistance. This is the "interior coating" concept in the syllabus; it reduces alkali extraction into acidic beverages and pharmaceuticals. • Closures: crown cork (beer, carbonated drinks), lug cap with plastisol liner (vacuum-sealed jars; the safety button indicates loss of vacuum), roll-on pilfer-proof (ROPP) aluminium caps. Statutory note: FSS (Packaging) Regulations, 2018, Schedule II covers glass containers, requiring conformity to the listed Indian Standards and freedom from defects that could lead to breakage or fragments. 1.3 Metal packaging 1.3.1 Tinplate Tinplate is low-carbon mild steel (about 0.15 to 0.5 mm) electrolytically coated with tin. From the steel outwards the structure is: 1. Steel base: strength and formability. 2. Iron-tin alloy layer (FeSn2): formed during reflow melting of the electrodeposited tin; improves corrosion resistance. 3. Free tin layer: sacrificial and corrosion resistant. 4. Passivation film: chromium oxide produced by cathodic treatment in sodium dichromate solution (the common "311" passivation); prevents tin oxide growth and sulfide staining, and improves lacquer adhesion. 5. Oil film: dioctyl sebacate (DOS) or similar, a few mg/m², for lubrication during handling and forming. Electrolytic tinplate (ETP) replaced hot-dipped tinplate from the 1930s and allows differential coating (different tin mass on inside and outside). Coating mass ranges from 2.8 to 11.2 g/m² per side (grades such as E2.8/2.8, E5.6/2.8, E11.2/5.6). Heavier tin is used for unlacquered (plain) cans of acidic fruit products. Why plain tin cans work for some fruits: in de-aerated acidic fruit packs tin is anodic to steel, so tin dissolves slowly and sacrificially, protecting the steel from pitting; the slight tin pickup is harmless below the FSSAI limit of 250 mg/kg and even preserves colour by reducing anthocyanin oxidation. In the presence of residual oxygen, nitrates or certain pigments the polarity can reverse and rapid detinning or hydrogen swell follows. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 8

Can construction: three-piece cans (body with welded side seam plus two ends; lead solder is banned) and two-piece cans (drawn and wall-ironed, DWI, for beverages; drawn and redrawn, DRD, for food). text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS • Two-piece DWI beverage cans with stay-on-tab easy-open ends; non-magnetic, so separation at recycling uses eddy-current separators. • Aluminium foil: rolled to 6 to 200 µm; food foil is annealed (soft temper); it has dead-fold (keeps a crease), is opaque (total light barrier), heat-stable, and when pinhole-free offers essentially zero OTR and WVTR. The foil thickness to pinhole relationship: pinholes arise from rolling inclusions and double rolling of thin gauges. Below about 15 µm (some references say 17 µm) the pinhole count rises steeply; a 9 µm foil may carry several hundred pinholes per square metre, a 7 µm foil even more. Hence: 1. Foil above 15 µm (for example 20 µm semi-rigid trays, household foil) can be used alone as a near- absolute barrier. 2. Foil of 6 to 12 µm is always laminated to plastic films (PET on the outside, polyolefin on the inside); the polymer layers bridge pinholes so the laminate behaves as a near-total barrier even though the foil itself is not. 3. The retort pouch uses 9 to 12 µm foil for exactly this reason. HPSC EXAM TRAP: foil and "100 percent barrier" A thin foil is a 100 percent barrier only in the laminate, not on its own. The correct statement is: "aluminium foil below 15 µm is prone to pinholes and is therefore laminated". 1.4 Food polymers and plastics Master comparative table Polymer Oxygen Water vapour Melting or Typical food (recycling Chemistry Density, g/cm³ barrier barrier softening uses code) High-pressure Bread bags, free-radical frozen food polyethylene, bags, heat-seal Tm 105 to 115 LDPE (4) long-chain 0.910 to 0.925 Poor Good layer, squeeze °C branched, 40 bottles, milk to 50 percent pouches crystalline (blend) Ziegler-Natta Stretch wrap, or metallocene heavy-duty copolymer sacks, tougher with butene, Tm 120 to 125 seal layers, LLDPE (4) 0.915 to 0.925 Poor Good hexene or °C Indian milk octene; short- pouches chain (LLDPE branches blends) Low-pressure Very good Milk jugs, Ziegler-Natta, Poor to (about four Tm 130 to 135 edible oil cans, HDPE (2) linear, 70 to 90 0.941 to 0.965 moderate times better °C crates, caps, percent than LDPE) boil-in-bag crystalline Isotactic Yoghurt cups, polypropylene; retort trays, Tm 160 to 170 BOPP is 0.90 to 0.91 caps, BOPP PP (5) Poor Very good °C (retortable, biaxially (lightest) snack films, hot-fillable) oriented; CPP CPP retort seal is cast layer FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 10

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS heat-sealability (wide sealing window, seals through light contamination), but poor oxygen, aroma and grease barrier. • LLDPE is made at low pressure with Ziegler-Natta or metallocene catalysts by copolymerising ethylene with an alpha-olefin, so branches are short and uniform. It has similar density to LDPE but higher tensile, puncture and tear strength and a higher melting point, giving down-gauging (thinner films with the same strength) and hot-tack strength for form-fill-seal machines. It is slightly hazier and harder to process than LDPE, so LDPE and LLDPE are commonly blended. • HDPE is linear with almost no branching; chains pack tightly, giving the highest density, stiffness, melting point and the best moisture barrier of the three, but translucency rather than clarity. It is environmentally stress-cracking sensitive with surfactants unless high molecular weight grades are used. HPSC EXAM TRAP: density ordering Correct ascending order of density: PP (0.90) < LDPE and LLDPE (0.91 to 0.925) < HDPE (0.94 to 0.965) < EVOH (1.12 to 1.20) < PET (1.33 to 1.40) < PVC (1.35 to 1.45) < PVDC (1.6 to 1.7). Polyolefins float in water; PET, PVC and PVDC sink. 1.4.2 Polypropylene: PP, BOPP, CPP Isotactic PP (all methyl groups on one side, Ziegler-Natta catalysed) crystallises to a stiff, glossy polymer with the lowest density and the highest melting point of the common polyolefins. Consequences: • Retortable and hot-fillable (Tm 160 to 170 °C) whereas PE deforms at 121 °C. • Poor low-temperature impact: homopolymer PP becomes brittle below about 0 °C, so frozen-food and retort grades use ethylene-propylene random or block copolymers. • BOPP (biaxially oriented, tenter frame) gives high clarity, stiffness, twist retention and improved moisture barrier; metallised BOPP is the standard snack-food film; acrylic or PVDC coatings add sealability and barrier. • CPP (cast polypropylene, chill-roll cast, unoriented) is soft, tough, clear and heat-sealable at 150 to 170 °C, and is the inner food-contact sealant layer of retort pouches because it survives 121 to 135 °C sterilisation without delaminating or losing seal strength. Random copolymer CPP (ethylene-modified) is preferred for low-temperature toughness. 1.4.3 Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) PET is a condensation polyester of purified terephthalic acid (or dimethyl terephthalate) and ethylene glycol, usually polymerised with an antimony trioxide catalyst (hence the antimony specific migration limit of 0.04 mg/kg). Bottles are injection moulded as preforms, reheated to about 100 °C (above Tg) and stretch-blow moulded; biaxial stretching induces strain crystallisation, giving high strength, clarity and the gas barrier that holds 3 to 4 volumes of carbon dioxide in carbonated soft drinks for several months. Heat-set PET tolerates hot filling at 85 to 90 °C; crystallised CPET trays are oven and microwave stable. Acetaldehyde and why a scavenger is needed: during melt processing at 270 to 290 °C PET undergoes thermal chain scission to vinyl ester end groups, which rearrange to release acetaldehyde (CH3CHO). Acetaldehyde dissolves in the bottle wall and slowly migrates into the contents, giving a fruity, sweetish off-flavour detectable in still water at about 10 to 20 µg/L (it is masked in flavoured colas but obvious in packaged drinking water). Control measures: low-acetaldehyde resin grades, solid-state polycondensation, careful melt temperature and residence time, and acetaldehyde scavengers such as anthranilamide (2- aminobenzamide), added at a few hundred mg/kg, which reacts with acetaldehyde to form a non-volatile quinazolinone. The Bureau of Indian Standards specification for PET bottles for packaged drinking water prescribes acetaldehyde control for this reason. Barrier enhancement for oxygen-sensitive beverages (beer, juice): multilayer PET/EVOH/PET or PET/MXD6 nylon, plasma coatings of silicon oxide (SiOx) or diamond-like carbon on the inner surface, and oxygen- scavenging resins (cobalt-catalysed MXD6). text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS 1.4.4 PVC and PVDC PVC: polymer of vinyl chloride monomer (VCM is a confirmed human carcinogen; residual VCM in packaging is restricted to 1 mg/kg and non-detectable migration under EU rules). Unplasticised PVC (uPVC) is rigid and clear and was widely used for mineral water and edible oil bottles in India before PET displaced it; it has good oil and grease resistance, moderate oxygen barrier, and only moderate moisture barrier. Plasticised PVC (30 to 40 percent plasticiser such as DEHP, DOA, DINP) gives cling film with self- adhesion and high oxygen permeability (useful for fresh meat bloom), but plasticiser migration into fatty foods is the chief regulatory concern (Part 3). PVC softens at about 80 °C (not retortable) and liberates hydrogen chloride and dioxins on uncontrolled incineration. PVDC: polyvinylidene chloride copolymerised with vinyl chloride or methyl acrylate (Saran, Dow, 1933). Its high chlorine content and high crystallinity give an outstanding barrier to oxygen, water vapour and aromas, and unlike EVOH its barrier does not deteriorate with humidity. Because pure PVDC is hard to process (it degrades near its melting point, releasing HCl), it is mostly used as a thin coating (K-coating) on cellophane, BOPP, PET and nylon, as a shrink film for cheese and processed meat, and as chub-pack film. Drawbacks: yellowing on ageing, chlorine content (environmental objection), not suitable for high- temperature retorting as a monolayer. HPSC EXAM TRAP: PVC is not PVDC PVC = one chlorine per repeat unit, moderate barrier, plasticiser migration issue. PVDC = two chlorines per repeat unit, excellent dual barrier, used as a coating. A statement "PVC offers excellent oxygen and moisture barrier" is false; the same sentence about PVDC is true. 1.4.5 Ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) EVOH is made by hydrolysing ethylene-vinyl acetate copolymer (pure polyvinyl alcohol cannot be melt- processed and is water-soluble, so ethylene is copolymerised in). The dense hydrogen bonding between hydroxyl groups and the high crystallinity give the lowest oxygen permeability of any melt-processable polymer (dry OTR of the order of 0.1 to 1 cm³/m²·day for a 25 µm film, two to three orders of magnitude better than PET). Trade-offs: • Lower ethylene content (27 to 32 mol percent): best gas barrier, worst moisture sensitivity, harder to process. • Higher ethylene content (44 to 48 mol percent): better processability and humidity tolerance, poorer barrier. • At relative humidity above about 75 percent, water plasticises the hydroxyl network and OTR rises ten to a hundred fold; after retorting the laminate suffers "retort shock" (temporary barrier loss) that recovers as the layer dries. Therefore EVOH is never used alone: it is co-extruded as a thin core between polyolefin skins with maleic- anhydride-grafted tie layers (for example PP/tie/EVOH/tie/PP), where the hydrophobic skins keep the core dry. Applications: squeezable ketchup and mayonnaise bottles, retortable transparent trays and pouches (foil replacement for microwaveable products), cheese and processed meat films, modified atmosphere trays. 1.5 Retort pouches Definition and origin A retort pouch is a flexible, heat-sealable, hermetically sealed laminate container capable of withstanding thermal sterilisation at 115 to 135 °C (commonly 121 °C for 20 to 40 minutes, delivering commercial sterility expressed as an F0 value) so that low-acid foods are shelf stable at ambient temperature without refrigeration. It was developed in the 1960s and 1970s by the United States Army Natick Laboratories with FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 13

Layers are bonded by adhesive lamination with two-component polyurethane adhesives, which must be fully cured before filling to avoid primary aromatic amine migration (Part 3). Transparent and microwaveable retort pouches replace foil with PET/SiOx, PET/AlOx or EVOH-based barrier layers at some sacrifice of shelf life. Heat penetration dynamics versus the cylindrical tinplate can Thermal sterilisation of a conduction-heating food is unsteady-state conduction, and the time for the slowest-heating point (cold spot) to reach a target temperature scales with the square of the characteristic conduction distance. A 307 × 409 can (73 mm diameter, 115 mm height) has a cold-spot conduction path of about 36 mm; a filled retort pouch is a thin slab 15 to 25 mm thick, with a half-thickness of only 8 to 12 mm. Consequences: 1. Process time at the same retort temperature is cut by 30 to 50 percent for the same F0, because the whole pouch heats almost uniformly. 2. Less overcooking of the surface layers while waiting for the centre: better retention of thiamine, vitamin C, colour, texture and flavour; the product tastes closer to freshly cooked. 3. Lower energy per unit, faster cooling, lower steam and water consumption. 4. Requirements that cans do not impose: the pouch must be processed in an overpressure retort (steam- air or water immersion or spray) because internal vapour pressure at 121 °C would otherwise burst the seals; pouches are held flat in racks to control thickness; residual air must be minimised (under about 10 mL, by vacuum or steam-flush sealing) since trapped air insulates, floats the pouch and promotes oxidation; seal areas must be clean, and seals are tested for strength, burst pressure and leakage. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Part 2. Active, Intelligent & Atmosphere Packaging PART 2: ACTIVE, INTELLIGENT AND MODIFIED ATMOSPHERE PACKAGING 2.0 Definitions that examiners quote • Active packaging: packaging in which the package, the product and the environment interact deliberately to extend shelf life, improve safety or sensory quality, while maintaining quality; the EU definition (Regulation (EC) 1935/2004 and Regulation (EC) 450/2009) is that active materials "deliberately incorporate components that would release or absorb substances into or from the packaged food or the environment surrounding the food". Active packaging acts. • Intelligent (smart) packaging: materials and articles that monitor the condition of packaged food or the environment surrounding the food and communicate that information. Intelligent packaging informs; it does not change the food. • Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): replacement of the air in the package with a defined gas mixture at the time of packing, after which the atmosphere is not controlled (distinguish from controlled atmosphere storage, where gas composition is actively maintained in a store). Feature Active packaging Intelligent packaging Change the internal environment or Sense and report the state of the food, Purpose the food to extend shelf life the package or its history Absorbs or releases substances No substance exchange intended; Interaction (oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene, optical, chemical or electronic signal moisture, antimicrobials, flavours) Oxygen scavenger sachet, ethylene Time-temperature indicator, freshness absorber, antimicrobial film, desiccant, Examples indicator, leak (integrity) indicator, carbon dioxide emitter, ethanol RFID tag, barcode, biosensor emitter Migration of the active substance into Indicator chemicals must not migrate; Regulatory issue food (must be permitted substances; label information must not mislead sachets must not be ingested) 2.1 Oxygen scavengers Oxygen drives lipid oxidation (rancidity, loss of essential fatty acids and vitamins A, C, E), oxidative browning and pigment loss, and growth of aerobic spoilage organisms including moulds. Vacuum and gas flushing leave 0.5 to 2 percent residual oxygen; a scavenger drives headspace oxygen below 0.01 percent (100 ppm) and keeps absorbing oxygen that permeates through the film during storage. Iron-based sachets (Ageless by Mitsubishi Gas Chemical, 1977; FreshPax, Oxy-Guard) Finely divided reduced iron powder with an electrolyte (sodium chloride) and a moisture donor, packed in an oxygen-permeable but food-grade sachet. The reaction is electrochemical rusting: 4Fe + 3O2 + 6H2O → 4Fe(OH)3 Stoichiometry: 4 moles of iron (about 223 g) consume 3 moles of oxygen (about 67 L at standard conditions), so 1 g of iron absorbs roughly 300 mL of oxygen; sachets are graded by capacity (for example 100 or 200 mL oxygen). Moisture-dependent types need a food water activity above about 0.65; self- reacting types carry their own moisture and work in dry foods. Advantages: cheap, high capacity, rapid. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 16

Removing it from the package or store extends shelf life. Potassium permanganate system: KMnO4 (4 to 6 percent) impregnated on a porous inert carrier (alumina, silica gel, zeolite, vermiculite, perlite) oxidises ethylene stepwise to acetaldehyde, then acetic acid, then carbon dioxide and water; the overall reaction can be written 3C2H4 + 12KMnO4 → 12MnO2 + 12KOH + 6CO2 + 6H2O. The colour change from purple (permanganate) to brown (manganese dioxide) indicates exhaustion. Because permanganate is toxic and strongly oxidising it is never incorporated in food-contact film; it is used only in sachets, blankets or filters in cartons and cold stores. Other absorbers: activated carbon with palladium catalyst, zeolite- or clay-loaded polyethylene films (sold in Japan and Korea, limited capacity), and ethylene-oxidising catalysts in ripening rooms. Note that 1-methylcyclopropene (SmartFresh) is a ripening inhibitor applied as a gas treatment, not a packaging absorber. 2.4 Antimicrobial packaging Antimicrobial agents are either released from the package to the food surface (migrating systems, suitable where surface contamination governs spoilage, such as sliced meat and cheese) or immobilised on the film surface (non-migrating, contact-active systems).
