A CO2 emitter compensates: • Sodium bicarbonate with citric or ascorbic acid, activated by product moisture: NaHCO3 + H+ → Na+ + CO2 + H2O. Used in pads under fresh meat, poultry and fish. • Dual-function sachets (iron oxygen scavenger with ferrous carbonate or ascorbate plus bicarbonate, for example Ageless G) absorb oxygen and emit an equal volume of carbon dioxide to keep the pack full. Carbon dioxide absorbers: freshly roasted coffee releases carbon dioxide for days and would burst a hermetic pack; calcium hydroxide sachets absorb it, Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O; the alternative is a one-way degassing valve in the pack. Absorbers are also used for kimchi and other fermenting foods. 2.6 Modified atmosphere packaging and vacuum packaging Gases used: oxygen (maintains the cherry-red oxymyoglobin of fresh meat, allows respiration of produce, prevents anaerobic growth), carbon dioxide (antimicrobial, soluble), nitrogen (inert filler preventing collapse, displaces oxygen in snacks), and in some countries carbon monoxide (colour fixation of meat; not permitted in India and the EU) and argon. Vacuum packaging removes air without replacing it and depends on an oxygen-barrier film (PA/PE, PVDC-coated) and refrigeration. 2.7 Intelligent packaging systems 2.7.1 Time-temperature indicators (TTIs) A TTI is a device whose irreversible, visible response integrates the temperature history (full-history TTI) or signals only that a threshold was crossed (critical temperature indicator, partial history). The reaction rate follows Arrhenius kinetics; a TTI is matched to a food when its activation energy is within about 25 kJ/mol of the activation energy of the food's deterioration (for example microbial growth in chilled fish, about 60 to 90 kJ/mol). text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Type Commercial example Mechanism Reading Gold nanoparticle Colour change on Nanoparticle Experimental aggregation systems aggregation Uses: cold-chain monitoring of vaccines, chilled and frozen foods, milk, seafood exports; supports first- expired-first-out instead of first-in-first-out logistics. 2.7.2 Freshness and spoilage indicators These respond to metabolites of spoilage rather than to temperature history. • Volatile amines: spoilage of fish and meat releases trimethylamine (from trimethylamine oxide by Shewanella and Photobacterium), dimethylamine, ammonia and biogenic amines, collectively measured as total volatile basic nitrogen (TVB-N). Amines are alkaline and raise headspace pH; indicator films containing bromocresol green, bromophenol blue, bromothymol blue, methyl red, chlorophenol red or natural anthocyanins change colour (COX Technologies FreshTag for fish; many anthocyanin-based research films). • Hydrogen sulfide: poultry spoilage indicators using myoglobin-based pigments that convert to sulfmyoglobin (green). • Carbon dioxide: bromothymol-blue or methyl-red based indicators for kimchi and MAP integrity. • Aroma: RipeSense (New Zealand) senses aromatic volatiles from ripening pears and changes from red to orange to yellow. • Pathogen or toxin biosensors: antibody-based labels (for example FoodSentinel barcode that becomes unreadable when a target pathogen binds) remain largely developmental. 2.7.3 Integrity (leak) indicators: oxygen indicators based on redox dyes The classic oxygen indicator tablet (Ageless Eye, Mitsubishi) contains methylene blue, a reducing sugar (glucose) and an alkali in a gel. In an oxygen-free pack (below about 0.1 percent oxygen) the dye is in its reduced leuco form and appears pink; when oxygen enters through a pinhole or a failed seal (above about 0.5 percent) methylene blue is re-oxidised and turns blue, usually within minutes. It is used inside packs with oxygen scavengers and in modified atmosphere packs to show seal failure, and it reverts if oxygen is scavenged again, which is a limitation for tamper evidence. Related systems use ultraviolet-activated titanium dioxide and methylene blue in printed inks for irreversible indication. 2.7.4 Data carriers: barcodes and RFID • Barcodes: linear EAN-13 (the 13-digit code on retail packs, administered in India by GS1 India, prefix 890) carry only an identifier; two-dimensional GS1 DataMatrix and QR codes carry batch, expiry and serial numbers and support consumer access to FSSAI licence details and recall information. • RFID (radio-frequency identification): a tag (microchip plus antenna) is read without line of sight; passive tags are powered by the reader field, active tags carry a battery. Frequencies: low frequency about 125 kHz (short range, animal identification), high frequency 13.56 MHz (near-field communication, smart phones, library and item level), ultra-high frequency 860 to 960 MHz (pallet and case level, several metres read range). Benefits: automatic traceability (one step back, one step forward as required by FSSAI licensing conditions and Codex), cold-chain data when combined with temperature sensors, rapid recall, anti-counterfeiting. Limitations: cost per tag, interference from metals and liquids, data privacy. HPSC EXAM TRAP: active versus intelligent A time-temperature indicator, a freshness indicator and an oxygen leak indicator are intelligent packaging (they inform). An oxygen scavenger, an ethylene absorber and an antimicrobial film are active packaging (they act). Statements that classify a scavenger as intelligent, or an indicator as active, FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 21

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Part 3. Migration Chemistry & FSSAI Packaging Regulations 2018 PART 3: MIGRATION CHEMISTRY AND FSS (PACKAGING) REGULATIONS, 2018 3.1 Migration from first principles Migration is the mass transfer of substances from a food contact material into the food (or a simulant) by diffusion. The migrating substances are starting substances (monomers, catalysts such as antimony), additives (plasticisers, antioxidants, slip agents, colourants), processing aids, adhesive and ink components, and non-intentionally added substances (NIAS) such as oligomers, degradation products and impurities. Kinetics: migration obeys Fick's second law; early migration grows with the square root of contact time and later approaches equilibrium set by the partition coefficient between polymer and food. Migration increases with temperature (retorting, microwaving, hot filling), contact time, fat content of the food (lipophilic migrants partition into oil), decreasing molecular weight of the migrant (substances above about 1000 Da are considered not to be absorbed from the gut and are exempt from toxicological evaluation), and polymer mobility (polyolefins have high diffusivity, PET and polystyrene low). Migration also occurs through the gas phase (volatile ink components and mineral oil from paperboard) and by set- off (printed outer surface transferring ink to the food-contact side in a reel or stack). Functional barrier concept: a layer (for example aluminium foil or thick PET) that reduces migration from layers behind it to below the detection limit allows the use of non-approved substances behind it, subject to a no-carcinogen rule. 3.2 Overall migration versus specific migration Criterion Overall migration (OM) Specific migration (SM) Total mass of all non-volatile substances transferred from the Amount of a single named substance What is measured material into a food simulant, (monomer, additive, metal) transferred irrespective of identity Toxicology: the specific migration limit Inertness of the material (a general Basis of the limit (SML) is derived from the tolerable quality criterion), not toxicology daily intake Gravimetric: evaporate the simulant to Instrumental: HPLC, GC-MS, LC-MS/MS, How measured dryness and weigh the residue (or AAS or ICP-MS for the specific analyte extract from oil by solvent and weigh) mg/dm² of contact surface or mg/kg of mg/kg of food or simulant (occasionally Units food or simulant mg/dm²) Substance specific, for example DEHP 60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm² (FSSAI 2018 Statutory ceiling 1.5 mg/kg, antimony 0.04 mg/kg, zinc Schedule IV; EU Regulation 10/2011) 25 mg/kg SML (specific migration limit); also QM (maximum residual quantity in the Abbreviation OML (overall migration limit) material) where migration cannot be measured FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 23

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS The arithmetic link examiners love: regulators assume a 60 kg adult eats 1 kg of food per day that has been in contact with 6 dm² of packaging (a cube of 1 litre volume has 6 dm² of surface). Therefore 10 mg/dm² × 6 dm²/kg = 60 mg/kg. Both figures express the same ceiling; for small containers (below 500 mL) and sheet materials the surface-based figure is used, for larger containers the mass-based figure. HPSC EXAM TRAP: overall migration is not a toxicological limit Passing the overall migration test does not prove safety; a material can be below 60 mg/kg overall and still exceed the SML of a potent migrant such as BPA or a primary aromatic amine. Conversely a high overall migration (for example from a plasticised PVC) can occur with every individual SML met. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Statutory migration limits (Schedule IV, plastics) Parameter Limit 60 mg/kg of food or simulant, or 10 mg/dm² of contact Overall migration limit surface, tested per IS 9845 Barium 1.0 mg/kg Cobalt 0.05 mg/kg Copper 5.0 mg/kg Iron 48 mg/kg Lithium 0.6 mg/kg Manganese 0.6 mg/kg Zinc 25 mg/kg Antimony 0.04 mg/kg Phthalic acid, bis(2-ethylhexyl) ester (DEHP) 1.5 mg/kg Heavy metals of toxicological concern (lead, cadmium, mercury, hexavalent chromium) are controlled at source: colourants and pigments must meet IS 9833 purity limits, lead solder is prohibited, and the FSS (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011 set limits in the food itself (for example lead in milk 0.02 mg/kg, tin in canned foods 250 mg/kg, mercury in fish 0.5 mg/kg and 1.0 mg/kg in predatory species). The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive 94/62/EC sets a benchmark of 100 mg/kg for the sum of lead, cadmium, mercury and hexavalent chromium in packaging material; migration of lead from plastics under the EU specific limits is at the 0.01 to 1 mg/kg level depending on the article class. Candidates should quote the Gazette text of Schedule IV in the descriptive paper and avoid inventing figures. Absolute prohibitions and their scientific basis 1. Newspaper and similar printed materials shall not be used for wrapping, packing or serving food (FSSAI advisory of 2016 incorporated in Regulation 3). Basis: newspaper inks contain mineral oil hydrocarbons, solvents, pigments with lead and other metals and sometimes chemical driers; the paper is handled unhygienically and carries microbial load; lipophilic ink components migrate readily into fried and oily street foods. The common sight of pakoras drained on newspaper is therefore a punishable violation. 2. Recycled plastics and products made of recycled plastics (including carry bags) shall not be used for packaging, storing, carrying or dispensing food. Basis: unknown prior use, contamination with non-food chemicals, degradation products and unapproved additives. Exception: FSSAI's subsequent amendment framework and Bureau of Indian Standards IS 17899 T (2022) allow recycled PET and other recycled plastics for food contact only when produced by an FSSAI-approved or certified food-grade recycling process with decontamination challenge testing, in line with Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules; recycled material used behind a functional barrier is treated separately. In an examination answer: "prohibited, except certified food-grade recycled plastic produced under FSSAI-recognised processes". 3. Printed surface of packaging shall not come in direct contact with food, so printed recycled paper, printed carry bags and reverse-printed films where the print faces inward are not acceptable; printing inks must conform to IS 15495. 4. Packaging must not impart undesirable odour, colour or taste, and must not transfer substances harmful to health; this is the general safety clause under which any novel migrant can be acted upon. 5. Plastics in contact with food must be made only of listed polymers conforming to listed Indian Standards; carbon black and pigments only per IS 9833. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 28

HPSC EXAM TRAP: absolute-qualifier phrasing on prohibitions "Newspaper may be used for wrapping dry foods if clean": false, the prohibition is absolute. "Recycled plastics are permitted for food contact": false as a general statement, but "recycled plastics are permitted only when certified food-grade under FSSAI-recognised processes" is true. "The overall migration limit applies to glass": false, it applies to plastics (glass is treated as inert and controlled by specification). "The 2018 Packaging Regulations also cover labelling": false, labelling is in the 2020 Labelling and Display Regulations. Migration testing workflow a Food Safety Officer should be able to describe 1. Identify the packaging material, layer structure and intended use (food type, contact time, temperature). 2. Select simulants from the food classification (aqueous, acidic, alcoholic, fatty, dry) and the time- temperature condition matching the worst foreseeable use. 3. Expose a known surface area (for example 1 dm²) to a known volume of simulant (for example 100 mL, giving 6 dm² per kg convention) by total immersion, pouch filling or cell method. 4. Overall migration: evaporate the aqueous simulant to dryness, weigh the residue, correct for blank, express as mg/dm² and convert to mg/kg; for oil, determine the weight loss of the specimen corrected for oil uptake. 5. Specific migration: analyse the simulant by HPLC-UV or LC-MS/MS (phthalates, BPA, PAAs, benzophenone), GC-MS (volatiles, styrene, vinyl chloride), ICP-MS or AAS (metals). 6. Compare against the OML and SMLs, issue the NABL certificate of conformity, and in enforcement draw samples under Section 38 of the Act for referral to the Food Analyst. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 29

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Part 4A. Instrumental Food Analysis PART 4A: INSTRUMENTAL FOOD ANALYSIS 4.0 Chromatography from first principles Chromatography separates components of a mixture by their differential partitioning between a stationary phase and a mobile phase that moves past it. Key quantities: • Retention factor k = (tR − t0)/t0, where tR is the retention time of the analyte and t0 the hold-up time of an unretained compound. • Selectivity α = k2/k1 for two adjacent peaks. • Column efficiency as number of theoretical plates N = 16 (tR/W)², where W is the baseline peak width; plate height H = L/N. • Resolution Rs = 2 (tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2); Rs of 1.5 is baseline separation. • Van Deemter equation H = A + B/u + C·u: A is eddy diffusion (multiple flow paths through packed particles), B/u is longitudinal diffusion (dominant at low linear velocity u), C·u is resistance to mass transfer (dominant at high velocity). Open-tubular capillary GC columns have no A term (Golay equation), which is why they are far more efficient than packed columns; in HPLC, smaller particles (sub-2 µm in UHPLC) shrink A and C, raising efficiency at the price of back-pressure above 600 bar. The practical rule for choosing a technique: volatile and thermally stable analytes (fatty acid esters, pesticides, flavour volatiles, solvents) go to GC; non-volatile, polar or thermolabile analytes (vitamins, colours, mycotoxins, sugars, antibiotics, carbamate pesticides, acrylamide) go to HPLC or LC-MS/MS; elements go to AAS or ICP-MS. 4.1 High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) Instrumentation 1. Solvent reservoirs and degasser: HPLC-grade solvents (water, acetonitrile, methanol, buffers), filtered through 0.45 or 0.22 µm membranes and degassed (helium sparging or vacuum degasser) to prevent bubbles in the pump and detector. 2. Pump: dual-piston reciprocating pump delivering 0.1 to 10 mL/min against 100 to 400 bar (up to 1200 bar in UHPLC) with pulse dampening; isocratic elution (constant composition) or gradient elution (composition changed with time to elute strongly retained compounds faster) using low-pressure (proportioning valve before one pump) or high-pressure (two pumps) mixing. 3. Injector: six-port rotary valve (Rheodyne) with a fixed loop of 5 to 100 µL, loaded at atmospheric pressure and switched into the high-pressure stream; autosamplers automate this. 4. Column: stainless steel tube, typically 150 to 250 mm long and 4.6 mm internal diameter, packed with 3 to 5 µm porous silica particles chemically bonded with the stationary phase. Reversed-phase columns carry octadecylsilane (ODS, C18) non-polar chains and are used with polar aqueous mobile phases; less polar analytes are retained longer. Normal-phase (bare silica, amino, cyano) retains polar compounds; ion-exchange, size-exclusion, HILIC and chiral phases serve special needs. A guard column protects the analytical column; a column oven (25 to 60 °C) stabilises retention. 5. Detector (see table), data system for integration and quantitation by external standard, internal standard or standard addition. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 30

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Applications Vitamins: fat-soluble vitamins (A as retinol, D2 and D3, E as tocopherols, K1) are released by alkaline saponification (ethanolic KOH with pyrogallol or BHT antioxidant), extracted into hexane or diethyl ether and determined by reversed-phase HPLC with UV or fluorescence detection; water-soluble B vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B6, folate, B12) are extracted by acid and enzymatic (takadiastase, phosphatase) hydrolysis and separated by ion-pair reversed-phase HPLC with UV, fluorescence (B1 after oxidation to thiochrome, B2 native) or MS detection; vitamin C is extracted in metaphosphoric acid and measured at about 245 nm, with dithiothreitol reduction to include dehydroascorbic acid. Relevant for verifying nutrition labels under the Labelling and Display Regulations and fortification claims under the Fortification Regulations. Synthetic food colours: India permits eight synthetic colours (Ponceau 4R, Carmoisine, Erythrosine, Tartrazine, Sunset Yellow FCF, Indigo Carmine, Brilliant Blue FCF and Fast Green FCF) with a general ceiling of 100 mg/kg (200 mg/kg in specified products such as certain canned fruits and sweets) singly or in combination, only in listed foods. Non-permitted colours (Metanil Yellow, Rhodamine B, Orange II, Sudan dyes, Auramine, Malachite Green) are frequent adulterants of sweets, spices and beverages. Colours are extracted by adsorption on wool or polyamide, or by solid-phase extraction, and separated by reversed- phase ion-pair HPLC with PDA detection; each colour is identified by retention time plus its visible spectrum, allowing a single run to screen permitted and non-permitted dyes. Screening methods: thin- layer chromatography and spot tests under the FSSAI manual. Aflatoxins: aflatoxins B1, B2, G1 and G2 (Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus in groundnuts, maize, chillies, nuts, copra) and M1 (hydroxylated metabolite of B1 secreted in milk) are extracted with methanol- water or acetonitrile-water, cleaned up on immunoaffinity columns bearing anti-aflatoxin antibodies, eluted with methanol and separated on a C18 column with water-methanol-acetonitrile. B2 and G2 fluoresce strongly in aqueous mobile phase, but B1 and G1 (with a terminal double bond in the dihydrofuran ring) show quenched fluorescence; so post-column derivatisation is applied: reaction with iodine in a heated reactor, electrochemically generated bromine (Kobra cell), or a photochemical reactor (ultraviolet irradiation forming hydrated derivatives), each of which saturates the double bond and restores fluorescence; pre-column trifluoroacetic acid derivatisation is the alternative. Detection: Ex 365 nm, Em 435 to 450 nm. FSSAI limits (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations as amended): total aflatoxins 15 µg/kg and aflatoxin B1 10 µg/kg in cereals, nuts and oilseeds; aflatoxin M1 0.5 µg/kg in milk. Confirmation and multi-mycotoxin work (ochratoxin A, deoxynivalenol, zearalenone, fumonisins, patulin in apple juice) move to LC-MS/MS. Sugar profiling: sugars have no chromophore, so they are separated on amino-bonded (NH2) columns with acetonitrile-water (about 75:25) and detected by RID, or on cation-exchange (calcium or lead form) columns with water at 80 °C, or on anion-exchange columns at high pH with pulsed amperometric detection (HPAEC-PAD) for trace sugars and oligosaccharides. Applications: honey authenticity (fructose, glucose, sucrose ratios; detection of added high-fructose syrup), lactose in lactose-free milk, sucrose in fruit juice adulteration, sugar declarations for the nutrition panel and the Indian sugar-content thresholds for high-fat, sugar and salt labelling. Other routine HPLC targets: preservatives (benzoic and sorbic acid; FSSAI class II preservative limits), sweeteners (saccharin, aspartame, acesulfame-K, sucralose by HPLC-UV or ELSD), caffeine in beverages (FSSAI 145 ppm cap in carbonated beverages, 320 ppm in energy drinks), melamine (HPLC-UV screening, LC-MS/MS confirmation), histamine in fish (fluorescence after derivatisation; relevant to sc FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 32

GC, GC-MS, LC-MS/MS & Atomic Spectroscopy PART 4B: GAS CHROMATOGRAPHY, TANDEM MASS SPECTROMETRY AND ATOMIC SPECTROSCOPY 4.2 Gas chromatography (GC and GC-MS) 4.2.1 First principles Gas chromatography separates volatile and thermally stable analytes (boiling point generally below about 400 °C, molecular mass below about 600 Da) by partitioning them between an inert gaseous mobile phase, which merely carries the analyte and does not interact with it, and a liquid stationary phase coated on the inner wall of a capillary column. Retention is governed by the vapour pressure of the analyte at the column temperature (hence boiling-point order on non-polar columns) and by the polarity match between analyte and stationary phase. Because retention depends exponentially on temperature, temperature programming (for example 60 °C held 2 minutes, then 10 °C per minute to 300 °C) is used to elute both light and heavy components with good peak shape in one run. Non-volatile analytes (fatty acids, sugars, amino acids, sterols) are first converted to volatile derivatives (methylation, silylation, acylation). 4.2.2 Carrier gas selection Optimum linear Carrier gas Efficiency and speed Cost and safety Comment velocity Default for GC-MS Good efficiency, fast (ionisation potential Expensive, supply Helium 20 to 40 cm/s analyses, flat van of 24.6 eV, no shortages, inert Deemter curve interference) and for most capillary work Cheap (generated on site by electrolysis), Increasingly used Fastest analyses, flammable (explosive with FID and modern Hydrogen 40 to 60 cm/s flattest curve, lowest 4 to 75 percent in air), MS systems with leak viscosity can hydrogenate sensors some analytes in the injector Common with packed columns and FID in Highest efficiency but Indian laboratories; only at a slow Nitrogen 10 to 15 cm/s Cheapest, safe unsuitable for MS velocity, long run because of lower times pumping efficiency and ion source effects Carrier gas purity must be at least 99.999 percent with oxygen and moisture traps, because oxygen oxidises the stationary phase at high temperature (column bleed), and electron capture detectors require oxygen-free gas. A statement that ECD responds to all organic compounds, or that FID is used for organochlorine residue screening at µg/kg, is wrong. 4.2.6 GC-MS fundamentals • Interface: the capillary column runs directly into the ion source held under vacuum (10^-5 to 10^-6 torr) maintained by a turbomolecular pump; helium is pumped away. • Electron ionisation (EI): a heated tungsten or rhenium filament emits electrons accelerated through 70 V; collision ejects an electron from the analyte, M + e- → M+• + 2e-, producing the molecular ion, which fragments into characteristic ions. 70 eV is used because ionisation efficiency reaches a plateau there, so small fluctuations do not alter the spectrum and spectra are reproducible between instruments and comparable with libraries (NIST, Wiley, with more than 300000 spectra). Fragmentation follows predictable rules (alpha-cleavage, McLafferty rearrangement, tropylium ion at m/z 91 for benzyl compounds). • Chemical ionisation (CI) with methane, isobutane or ammonia reagent gas is a soft technique giving the protonated molecule [M+H]+ when the molecular ion is absent under EI. • Analysers: single quadrupole (most common), ion trap, time-of-flight (high resolution, exact mass), triple quadrupole GC-MS/MS for pesticide residues with MRM as described for LC-MS/MS. • Acquisition modes: full scan (for identification, library search of unknowns) and selected ion monitoring (SIM, where the quadrupole dwells on two to four characteristic ions per analyte, raising sensitivity 10 to 100 fold; one quantifier ion and qualifier ions whose ratios must match the standard within the tolerances of the EU SANTE pesticide guidance, usually within 30 percent relative). 4.2.7 Derivatisation: fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) Triglycerides are non-volatile and free fatty acids tail badly on GC columns because of hydrogen bonding, so lipids are converted to volatile fatty acid methyl esters by transesterification. Two official routes: 1. Boron trifluoride-methanol (AOAC 969.33, IS 548 Part 3, AOCS Ce 2-66): the fat is first saponified by refluxing with 0.5 N methanolic sodium hydroxide (triglyceride + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3RCOONa), then 12 to 14 percent BF3 in methanol is added and the mixture refluxed at 100 °C for 2 to 5 minutes; the Lewis acid catalyses esterification, RCOOH + CH3OH → RCOOCH3 + H2O, giving quantitative methylation of all acids including free acids and phospholipid acids. Esters are extracted into heptane or hexane after adding saturated sodium chloride solution. 2. Methanolic potassium hydroxide (ISO 12966-2, IUPAC 2.301, rapid cold method): 2 N KOH in methanol is shaken with the oil dissolved in heptane at room temperature for 1 to 2 minutes; base-catalysed transesterification, RCOOR' + CH3OH → RCOOCH3 + R'OH, proceeds via the methoxide ion. It is fast and avoids heating (no isomerisation of conjugated or polyunsaturated acids) but does not methylate free fatty acids and fails for oils with high acidity. Alternatives: 2 percent sulfuric acid in methanol (acid catalysed, slow), sodium methoxide, trimethylsulfonium hydroxide (one-step in the injector). Analysis: 100 m biscyanopropyl polysiloxane column, FID, hydrogen or helium carrier, oven 140 to 240 °C programme, split injection, internal standard C17:0 or C23:0 methyl ester, identification by comparison with a 37-component FAME mix; results expressed as percent of total fatty acids. On the polar column, elution within each carbon number is saturated, then trans, then cis isomers, so elaidic acid (C18:1 trans-9) elutes before oleic acid (C18:1 cis-9), and the sum of the trans peaks gives total trans fatty acids. Regulatory linkage: FSSAI limits industrially produced trans fatty acids to 2 percent by weight of total fats in all fats and oils and in foods containing fats and oils (effective 1 January 2022, down from 5 percent in 2021 and 10 percent earlier); a trans fat free claim requires not more than 0.2 g per 100 g or 100 mL. The same FAME profile detects adulteration (for example argemone-free but cheaper palm olein in groundnut oil, lard in ghee by Reichert-Meissl and butyric acid C4:0 content, which only milk fat contains at about 3 to 4 percent) and verifies omega-3 claims. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS 4.2.8 Pesticide residue screening by GC Sample preparation uses the QuEChERS method (quick, easy, cheap, effective, rugged, safe; AOAC 2007.01, EN 15662): 10 g homogenised produce is shaken with 10 mL acetonitrile, salted out with anhydrous magnesium sulfate and sodium chloride (or citrate buffers), and the extract is cleaned by dispersive solid- phase extraction with primary secondary amine (PSA) sorbent, which removes fatty acids and sugars, plus C18 for fat and graphitised carbon black for chlorophyll. Organochlorines are screened by GC-ECD, organophosphates by GC-NPD or FPD, and all are confirmed by GC-MS or GC-MS/MS. The FSSAI default maximum residue limit for any pesticide not specifically listed in the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations is 0.01 mg/kg, and DDT, endosulfan, lindane and many organochlorines are banned or restricted under the Insecticides Act, 1968, so their presence at any level is an enforcement issue. 4.3 Tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) 4.3.1 Why LC-MS/MS exists Most veterinary drugs, mycotoxins, modern pesticides, acrylamide and melamine are polar, thermally labile or non-volatile, so they are unsuited to GC without derivatisation, and in complex food matrices a UV detector cannot distinguish a residue at 1 µg/kg from co-eluting matrix. Coupling HPLC to a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer solves both problems: the liquid chromatograph handles polar molecules, and two stages of mass filtering give selectivity so high that clean-up can be minimal while sensitivity reaches sub-µg/kg. 4.3.2 Atmospheric pressure ionisation: ESI versus APCI The challenge is to convert ions in a liquid flowing at 0.2 to 1 mL per minute into gas-phase ions at atmospheric pressure, then sample them into the vacuum. Electrospray ionisation (ESI, John Fenn, Nobel Prize 2002): the eluent passes through a stainless steel capillary held at 3 to 5 kV relative to the counter electrode; the field charges the liquid surface, draws it into a Taylor cone and sprays a fine mist of highly charged droplets, assisted by a coaxial nitrogen nebulising gas. Heated drying gas evaporates solvent, droplets shrink until charge repulsion exceeds surface tension (the Rayleigh limit) and they undergo repeated Coulomb fission; finally ions leave the droplets (ion evaporation model for small molecules; charged residue model for proteins). Ionisation happens in solution, so ESI favours compounds that are already ionic or readily protonated or deprotonated: acids, bases, zwitterions, polar drugs, peptides, proteins (which acquire multiple charges). Positive mode gives [M+H]+ (or [M+Na]+, [M+NH4]+), negative mode gives [M-H]-. ESI is the softest ionisation (no fragmentation, intact molecular information) but is prone to matrix effects: co-eluting matrix components compete for charge and suppress (or enhance) the analyte signal, which is why isotope-labelled internal standards (13C or deuterium) and matrix-matched calibration are mandatory in residue methods. Atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI): the eluent is nebulised and vaporised in a heated tube at 350 to 500 °C; a corona discharge needle (about 3 kV) ionises solvent and nitrogen to form reagent ions (H3O+, CH3OH2+), which transfer a proton to the analyte in the gas phase (M + H3O+ → [M+H]+ + H2O). Because ionisation occurs in the gas phase, APCI suits neutral, moderately polar to non-polar, thermally stable molecules of low to medium mass (below about 1500 Da) and gives only singly charged ions; it tolerates higher flow rates and non-polar mobile phases and is less affected by matrix suppression, but cannot be used for thermolabile or very polar or large molecules. Atmospheric pressure photoionisation (APPI, krypton lamp 10 eV) extends the range to non-polar compounds such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and vitamins D and K. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 38

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Criterion ESI APCI In the gas phase, by proton transfer Where ionisation occurs In solution, within charged droplets from reagent ions Corona discharge needle after thermal Energy source High voltage on the spray capillary vaporisation Polar, ionic, basic or acidic, thermally Neutral, less polar, thermally stable, labile, high mass (proteins, peptides, low mass (steroids, triglycerides, Best analytes tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, carbamates, some mycotoxins, glyphosate) vitamins) Charge state Multiple charges possible Singly charged Flow rate tolerance nL to 1 mL per minute 0.2 to 2 mL per minute Matrix effect High (ion suppression) Lower Minimal, slightly more thermal Fragmentation Minimal (softest) breakdown Share of food residue methods About 80 to 90 percent 10 to 20 percent 4.3.3 Triple quadrupole (QqQ) architecture A quadrupole is four parallel metal rods to which a direct current voltage and a radio-frequency voltage are applied; for a given voltage ratio only ions of one mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) have stable trajectories and pass through, while others strike the rods (described by the Mathieu equations). Scanning the voltages sweeps the transmitted mass. The triple quadrupole arranges three such devices in line: 1. Q1 (first mass filter): set to transmit only the precursor ion of the target analyte, for example [M+H]+ at m/z 445 for tetracycline. Everything else from the ion source, including matrix ions of other masses, is rejected here. 2. q2 (collision cell): a radio-frequency-only quadrupole or hexapole (no mass filtering; lower-case q) filled with argon or nitrogen at about 1 to 5 millitorr. The precursor ion is accelerated into the gas (collision energy 5 to 50 eV) and undergoes collision-induced dissociation (CID): kinetic energy is converted to internal energy and the ion breaks at its weakest bonds into product ions and neutral fragments. 3. Q3 (second mass filter): set to transmit only a specific product ion, for example m/z 410 (loss of ammonia and water from tetracycline). Only an ion that had the correct precursor mass and also produced the correct fragment reaches the detector (electron multiplier), so chemical noise is almost eliminated. Scan modes derived from this architecture: product ion scan (Q1 fixed, Q3 scanned; used for method development and structure elucidation), precursor ion scan (Q3 fixed, Q1 scanned; finds all compounds giving a common fragment, for example all glucuronides), neutral loss scan (both scanned with a fixed offset), and multiple reaction monitoring. HPSC EXAM TRAP: q2 is not a mass analyser In a triple quadrupole the precursor is selected in Q1, fragmented in the collision cell q2 (which only transmits ions and does no mass selection), and the product is selected in Q3. A statement that the collision cell selects the precursor or product ion is wrong. 4.3.4 Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM, also called selected reaction monitoring) In MRM both Q1 and Q3 are fixed on a precursor-product pair called a transition, with a dwell time of 5 to 100 milliseconds, then switched to the next transition; a modern instrument monitors several hundred transitions in one run using retention-time windows (scheduled MRM). For each analyte at least two transitions are acquired: the most intense (quantifier) for calibration and a second (qualifier) whose ratio FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 39

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Ionisation and typical Target Why it matters Statutory reference transitions (m/z) Mycotoxins (aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, Multi-mycotoxin methods ESI positive and negative FSSAI mycotoxin limits as in deoxynivalenol, replace single HPLC-FLD switching, aflatoxin B1 313 Section 4.1 zearalenone, fumonisins, methods → 285 and 313 → 241 patulin) 4.4 Atomic spectroscopy for heavy metals 4.4.1 First principles Atomic absorption relies on free, gaseous, ground-state atoms absorbing light at a resonance wavelength characteristic of the element (lead 283.3 nm, cadmium 228.8 nm, arsenic 193.7 nm, mercury 253.7 nm, copper 324.8 nm, zinc 213.9 nm). According to the Boltzmann distribution, at flame temperatures (2000 to 3000 K) more than 99.9 percent of atoms of most elements are in the ground state, so absorption is far more sensitive and matrix independent than flame emission for all but the easily excited alkali metals (sodium, potassium, lithium, measured by flame photometry). The instrument comprises a hollow cathode lamp of the same element as the analyte (emitting a very narrow line, which is why one lamp per element is needed and AAS is sequential), an atomiser (flame, furnace, quartz cell), a monochromator to isolate the resonance line, a photomultiplier detector, and a background corrector (deuterium continuum lamp or Zeeman effect using a strong magnetic field to split the absorption line). Absorbance follows the Beer- Lambert law, A = ε·b·c, and quantitation uses external calibration, standard addition for difficult matrices, and certified reference materials for validation. Sample preparation is common to all techniques and is the usual source of error. Wet digestion with concentrated nitric acid and hydrogen peroxide in closed-vessel microwave digesters (180 to 200 °C) is the method of choice because it is fast and retains volatile elements; dry ashing at 450 to 550 °C followed by dissolution in dilute nitric acid is cheaper but loses mercury entirely and partly loses arsenic, cadmium, lead and selenium by volatilisation and retention in silica. All glassware is acid-washed; reagent blanks are run with every batch. 4.4.2 Flame AAS (FAAS) The sample solution is drawn by a pneumatic nebuliser into a spray chamber, where only the finest 5 to 10 percent of the aerosol reaches the burner; the rest drains to waste. An air-acetylene flame (about 2300 °C) through a 10 cm slot burner atomises most elements; the hotter nitrous oxide-acetylene flame (about 2900 °C) is needed for refractory, oxide-forming elements (aluminium, calcium at high concentration, silicon, titanium, vanadium). Atom residence time in the light path is only a few milliseconds. Consequences: detection limits in the mg/L (ppm) to high µg/L range (lead about 0.02 mg/L, cadmium about 0.002 mg/L), precision of 0.5 to 1 percent, analysis in 10 seconds per element, low cost, robust. Interferences: chemical (phosphate or sulfate forming refractory calcium compounds, overcome by adding lanthanum chloride as a releasing agent), ionisation (alkali and alkaline earth metals ionise in hot flames, suppressed by adding excess caesium or potassium), spectral (rare, because lines are narrow), and background absorption or scatter from salts (corrected by the deuterium lamp). FAAS is adequate for nutrients and additives (iron, zinc, copper, calcium, sodium, potassium in fortified foods, tin in canned foods at 250 mg/kg) but usually too insensitive for lead, cadmium and arsenic at the µg/kg limits now set for foods. 4.4.3 Graphite furnace AAS (GFAAS, electrothermal AAS, ETAAS) A 10 to 50 µL aliquot is pipetted onto a L'vov platform inside a pyrolytically coated graphite tube, which is heated electrically under an argon purge (argon prevents the tube from burning) through a programme: FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 41

doc: Modern Food Packaging, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Analysis
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS drying at 100 to 120 °C (30 seconds) to evaporate solvent; pyrolysis or ashing at 400 to 1200 °C to destroy organic matter and volatilise matrix salts without losing the analyte; atomisation at 1800 to 2800 °C within 1 to 2 seconds, with gas flow stopped so the atom cloud is confined in the light path; and a clean-out step at 2600 °C. Matrix modifiers are added to allow a higher pyrolysis temperature: palladium with magnesium nitrate stabilises arsenic, selenium and lead; ammonium dihydrogen phosphate converts volatile cadmium and lead chlorides to less volatile phosphates. Because the entire sample is atomised into a confined volume and atoms reside for seconds rather than milliseconds, sensitivity improves 100 to 1000 fold: detection limits of 0.01 to 1 µg/L (ppb), for example lead 0.05 µg/L and cadmium 0.002 µg/L. Drawbacks: slow (2 to 3 minutes per determination, single element), strong background from matrix smoke requiring Zeeman correction, more chemical interference, higher cost, limited linear range, and need for the stabilised temperature platform furnace (STPF) protocol for reliable results. GFAAS is the workhorse for lead, cadmium and chromium in FSSAI contaminant testing where ICP-MS is unavailable. These elements form volatile covalent hydrides when their lower oxidation states are reduced by sodium borohydride in hydrochloric acid: NaBH4 + 3H2O + HCl → H3BO3 + NaCl + 8H (nascent hydrogen) As3+ + 3H → AsH3 (arsine); Se4+ + 4H → SeH2 (hydrogen selenide); Sb3+ + 3H → SbH3 (stibine) The gaseous hydride is swept by argon from the reaction vessel (or a continuous-flow manifold with a gas- liquid separator) into a quartz tube held at 900 to 1000 °C in the light path, where it decomposes to free atoms (2AsH3 → 2As + 3H2). Because the analyte is separated from the digest matrix and introduced as a gas with near 100 percent efficiency, sensitivity improves 10 to 100 fold over FAAS, with detection limits of 0.01 to 0.1 µg/L. Two chemistry points are routinely examined: the analyte must be in the lower oxidation state, so arsenic(V) is pre-reduced to arsenic(III) with potassium iodide and ascorbic acid, and selenium(VI) is pre-reduced to selenium(IV) by heating in 6 M hydrochloric acid; and transition metals (copper, nickel) interfere by consuming borohydride or decomposing the hydride, controlled by masking agents or dilution. HGAAS after digestion gives total inorganic arsenic; it does not respond to arsenobetaine, the dominant and non-toxic arsenic form in fish and shrimp, so a low HGAAS result on seafood is not a FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 42

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS contradiction of a high total arsenic by ICP-MS. Arsenic speciation (arsenite, arsenate, methylated forms) requires HPLC coupled to ICP-MS and is relevant for rice, where FSSAI and Codex limit inorganic arsenic (Codex 0.2 mg/kg in polished rice, 0.35 mg/kg in husked rice) and drinking water is limited to 0.01 mg/L under IS 10500. 4.4.5 Cold vapour AAS (CVAAS) for mercury Mercury is unique among metals in having an appreciable vapour pressure of the free monatomic element at room temperature, so no flame or furnace is required. After oxidative digestion (nitric and sulfuric acids with potassium permanganate or persulfate, in closed vessels to prevent loss, with excess oxidant destroyed by hydroxylamine hydrochloride just before measurement), mercury(II) is reduced to the metal with acidic stannous chloride: Hg2+ + Sn2+ → Hg0 + Sn4+ (alternatively with sodium borohydride: Hg2+ + 2BH4- + 6H2O → Hg0 + 2H3BO3 + 7H2) A stream of argon or air sweeps the mercury vapour through a drying tube into a long-path quartz absorption cell at room temperature, where absorbance is measured at the 253.7 nm resonance line from a mercury hollow cathode or electrodeless discharge lamp. Detection limits are 0.01 to 0.1 µg/L, improved a further 10 to 100 fold by pre-concentrating the vapour on a gold trap (amalgamation) and releasing it by heating. Cold vapour atomic fluorescence (CVAFS) is even more sensitive. Precautions: mercury adsorbs on surfaces and is lost on dry ashing or open-vessel heating; samples with high chloride can lose mercury as volatile chlorides; the technique measures total mercury, while the toxicologically relevant species in fish is methylmercury (about 90 percent of fish mercury, determined by GC-ECD, GC-AFS or LC-ICP-MS). FSSAI limits mercury in fish and fishery products at 0.5 mg/kg (1.0 mg/kg in listed predatory fish such as tuna, shark and swordfish) and methylmercury at 0.25 mg/kg, and mercury in other foods at 1.0 mg/kg under the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations, 2011, as amended. 4.4.6 Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) Components and mechanism: 1. Sample introduction: a peristaltic pump feeds the digested solution (total dissolved solids kept below 0.2 percent) to a concentric or cross-flow nebuliser; a spray chamber passes only the finest aerosol (1 to 2 percent) to the plasma. 2. Torch and plasma: three concentric quartz tubes carry argon as plasma (outer, cooling) gas at 12 to 17 L per minute, auxiliary gas and nebuliser gas. A two- or three-turn copper load coil around the torch is driven by a radio-frequency generator at 27.12 MHz (some instruments use 40.68 MHz) at 1.0 to 1.6 kW. A Tesla spark seeds free electrons; the oscillating magnetic field accelerates them, their collisions ionise argon, and the resulting eddy currents sustain a self-heating, electrodeless plasma at 6000 to 10000 K (the analytical zone is about 6500 to 8000 K). The aerosol is desolvated, vaporised, atomised and ionised within a few milliseconds. Because the first ionisation energy of argon is 15.76 eV, every element with a lower first ionisation energy is ionised efficiently, more than 90 percent for most metals; only helium, neon and fluorine are not ionised, and elements with high ionisation energies (arsenic 9.8 eV, mercury 10.4 eV, selenium 9.75 eV) are ionised 30 to 50 percent, which still allows ng/L detection. 3. Interface: the plasma, at atmospheric pressure, is sampled through a water-cooled nickel or platinum sampler cone (orifice about 1 mm) into a region at a few torr, then through a skimmer cone (orifice about 0.4 mm) into the high vacuum; the supersonic expansion freezes the ion population. 4. Ion optics and collision-reaction cell: electrostatic lenses focus the ions and remove photons and neutrals; a collision-reaction cell filled with helium (kinetic energy discrimination) or a reactive gas (hydrogen, ammonia, oxygen) removes polyatomic interferences formed from argon, water and acids. 5. Mass analyser and detector: a quadrupole scans the full mass range 2 to 260 in less than a second, so all elements are determined simultaneously (quasi-simultaneously by fast sequential scanning); high- resolution sector field and triple quadrupole ICP-MS/MS variants resolve the most difficult interferences. A dual-mode electron multiplier covers nine orders of magnitude, from ng/L to hundreds of mg/L. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 43

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Performance: detection limits of 0.001 to 0.1 µg/L (sub-ppt to ppt) for lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, uranium and the rare earths; 70 or more elements in two to three minutes; isotope ratio measurement (lead isotopes for source attribution, enriched stable isotopes for bioavailability studies); and coupling to HPLC or GC for speciation (inorganic arsenic in rice, methylmercury in fish, chromium(VI)). Internal standards (rhodium, indium, bismuth, germanium) correct for drift and matrix suppression. Interferences the examiner expects you to name: isobaric overlaps (114Sn on 114Cd, 204Hg on 204Pb, corrected by equations or alternative isotopes 111Cd and 208Pb) and polyatomic ions (40Ar35Cl+ on 75As, the classic problem in high-chloride seafood digests; 40Ar12C+ on 52Cr; 40Ar16O+ on 56Fe; 40Ar40Ar+ on 80Se; 35Cl16O+ on 51V), removed by the collision cell or by using hydrogen as reaction gas. Mercury shows a memory effect from adsorption in the sample path, controlled by adding gold (which forms a soluble mercury-gold complex) to all solutions. Limitations: capital and running cost (argon consumption about 15 to 20 L per minute), dissolved solids limit, the need for clean-room practices because the sensitivity makes laboratory contamination the dominant error. For comparison, ICP optical emission spectrometry (ICP- OES) uses the same plasma but measures emitted light, with detection limits in the µg/L range, suited to nutrient minerals rather than ultra-trace contaminants. Proximate Analysis (AOAC/FSSAI Methods) PART 5: OFFICIAL PROXIMATE ANALYSIS PROTOCOLS (AOAC AND FSSAI MANUAL METHODS) 5.0 The Weende system Proximate analysis, developed at the Weende Experiment Station (Henneberg and Stohmann, 1860s), partitions a food into six fractions: moisture, crude protein, crude fat (ether extract), total ash, crude fibre, and nitrogen-free extract (NFE, the digestible carbohydrate estimated by difference). The word crude signals that each fraction is defined by the method, not by chemistry: crude protein is nitrogen times a factor, crude fat is whatever the solvent dissolves, crude fibre is whatever survives acid and alkali. These are the methods cited in the FSSAI Manual of Methods of Analysis of Foods and in AOAC Official Methods, and they underpin nutrition labelling under the Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020, as well as standards of identity (for example minimum protein in milk powder, maximum moisture in spices and cereals). NFE (percent) = 100 − (moisture + crude protein + crude fat + total ash + crude fibre), so every error in the five measured fractions accumulates in NFE. 5.1 Moisture Moisture controls microbial stability (through water activity), texture, economic value (water sold at the price of food) and compliance with standards (for example not more than 14 percent in wheat flour, 12 percent in most spice powders, 5 percent in milk powder). It measures total nitrogen (organic nitrogen plus ammonium, but not nitrate, nitrite, azo or nitro nitrogen without modification) and converts it to protein by a factor. Step 1: Digestion (oxidation of organic matter and conversion of nitrogen to ammonium sulfate) About 1 g of sample is heated with 15 to 25 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid, 10 to 15 g of potassium sulfate and a catalyst (0.3 to 1 g of copper sulfate, or copper with titanium dioxide, or selenium; mercuric oxide was the original catalyst but is now avoided for toxicity and because it binds ammonia, needing thiosulfate release) in a long-necked Kjeldahl flask or block digester at 380 to 420 °C for 1 to 3 hours, until the black charred liquid becomes clear and pale blue-green. Organic nitrogen (in protein, R-NH2) + H2SO4 (with catalyst, heat) → (NH4)2SO4 + CO2 + SO2 + H2O Roles of the reagents: sulfuric acid oxidises carbon and hydrogen and converts amino nitrogen to ammonium; potassium sulfate raises the boiling point of the acid from about 338 °C to about 380 to 400 °C, speeding digestion (too much salt and the temperature exceeds 410 °C, at which ammonia is lost); the copper catalyst accelerates oxidation of refractory nitrogen compounds (heterocyclic nitrogen in tryptophan, histidine, nicotinic acid digests slowly and incompletely without it). FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 47

doc: Modern Food Packaging, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Analysis
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Step 2: Neutralisation and steam distillation (liberation of ammonia) The cooled digest is diluted with water and made strongly alkaline with 40 to 50 percent sodium hydroxide (excess, since the acid must be fully neutralised and the ammonium converted to free ammonia), then steam distilled. (NH4)2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2NH3 (gas) + 2H2O The ammonia is absorbed in a receiving flask containing 4 percent boric acid (about 25 to 50 mL) with a mixed indicator (methyl red and bromocresol green, or methyl red and methylene blue). Ammonia forms the ammonium-borate ion pair: NH3 + H3BO3 → NH4+ + H2BO3− The indicator turns from pinkish-red (acid) to green as ammonia is absorbed. Boric acid is a weak acid (pKa 9.2) that holds the ammonia but does not itself consume the titrant, which is the elegance of the method: no standardised receiving acid is needed and there is no back-titration. The older alternative collects ammonia in a measured excess of standard sulfuric or hydrochloric acid and back-titrates the unreacted acid with standard sodium hydroxide. Step 3: Titration The borate formed is titrated with standard 0.1 N hydrochloric acid (or sulfuric acid) until the indicator returns from green to the original pink end point: H2BO3− + H+ (from HCl) → H3BO3 One mole of hydrochloric acid corresponds to one mole of ammonia and therefore to one mole of nitrogen (14.007 g). Calculation Nitrogen (percent) = [(V sample − V blank) × N × 1.4007] ÷ W where V is the titre in mL, N the normality of the acid, 1.4007 the milliequivalent weight of nitrogen (14.007) multiplied by 100 and divided by 1000, and W the sample weight in grams. Crude protein (percent) = Nitrogen (percent) × F Worked example: 1.000 g of wheat flour, titre 10.50 mL of 0.1 N HCl, blank 0.20 mL. Nitrogen = (10.50 − 0.20) × 0.1 × 1.4007 ÷ 1.000 = 1.443 percent. Protein with the general factor = 1.443 × 6.25 = 9.02 percent; with the wheat factor = 1.443 × 5.70 = 8.22 percent. The difference of 0.8 percentage points is why FSSAI standards specify the factor. Nitrogen-to-protein conversion factors Food Factor Basis General (meat, eggs, pulses, mixed Assumes proteins contain 16 percent 6.25 foods) nitrogen: 100 ÷ 16 = 6.25 Milk proteins (casein, whey) contain Milk and milk products 6.38 about 15.67 percent nitrogen: 100 ÷ 15.67 = 6.38 Wheat proteins (gliadin, glutenin) Wheat and wheat products (whole contain about 17.5 percent nitrogen 5.70 wheat, flour, bread) because of high glutamine and proline content: 100 ÷ 17.54 = 5.70 Rice proteins contain about 16.8 Rice 5.95 percent nitrogen FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 48

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Food Factor Basis Soybean 5.71 High glutamine content Gelatin 5.55 Glycine-rich Almonds 5.18; other nuts and seeds 5.30 to 5.46 Arginine-rich storage proteins Maize, barley, oats 6.25 (maize), 5.83 (barley, oats, rye) Prolamin content HPSC EXAM TRAP: Kjeldahl measures nitrogen, not protein Any nitrogen source raises the apparent protein: urea (46.6 percent N), ammonium salts, and melamine (66.6 percent N), the adulterant of the 2008 Chinese infant formula and pet food scandals. FSSAI therefore detects urea in milk by the dimethylaminobenzaldehyde (DMAB) or urease test and melamine by LC-MS/MS; the Dumas combustion method (AOAC 992.15; sample burnt at 900 to 1000 °C in oxygen, nitrogen oxides reduced to N2 over copper and measured by a thermal conductivity detector) is a faster, reagent-free alternative that is equally fooled by non-protein nitrogen. True protein requires precipitation (trichloroacetic acid or copper hydroxide) before nitrogen determination, or amino acid analysis. Note also that the factor for milk (6.38) is higher than 6.25 and the factor for wheat (5.70) is lower; reversing them is a common MCQ trap. 5.3 Crude fat: Soxhlet solvent extraction Devised by Franz von Soxhlet (1879) for milk fat and adopted as AOAC 920.39 (cereals), 960.39 (meat), 948.22 (nuts); IS 4684. Apparatus and operation The apparatus has three parts: a boiling flask containing the solvent, a central extraction chamber holding a cellulose thimble with 2 to 5 g of dried, finely ground sample (plugged with fat-free cotton), and a reflux condenser above. Solvent vapour rises through the side tube, condenses and drips onto the sample; the chamber fills with solvent, dissolving lipid; when the liquid reaches the top of the siphon arm, the entire contents siphon back into the flask. Each cycle (5 to 6 per hour) bathes the sample in fresh, distilled solvent, while the dissolved fat accumulates in the flask. This semi-continuous extraction runs for 6 to 16 hours (4 hours at 5 to 6 drops per second for most foods). The solvent is then recovered by distillation, the flask dried at 100 to 105 °C for 1 hour, cooled in a desiccator and weighed. Crude fat (percent) = [(W flask with fat − W empty flask) ÷ W sample] × 100 Solvent choice Solvent Boiling range Advantages Disadvantages Cheaper, non-hygroscopic, does not dissolve sugars or water-soluble material, lower peroxide risk, more Petroleum ether (light selective for true lipids Does not extract polar lipids 40 to 60 °C petroleum, hexane fraction) (triglycerides, free fatty (phospholipids, glycolipids) acids, sterols, carotenoids, waxes); the solvent prescribed in most FSSAI and AOAC food methods FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 49

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Solvent Boiling range Advantages Disadvantages Absorbs up to 2 percent Extracts a wider range water, which then co- including some extracts sugars and urea, Diethyl ether 34.6 °C phospholipids; historical inflating results; forms Weende solvent (hence explosive peroxides on ether extract) storage; very flammable; hygroscopic Chloroform-methanol gives Hexane, chloroform- total lipid including bound methanol (Folch and Bligh- 69 °C; mixed Toxic solvents, not routine and polar lipids for research Dyer) and labelling Conditions and limitations • The sample must be dried first (moisture blocks penetration of the non-polar solvent and water would be co-extracted) and finely ground to expose lipid; cereals and oilseeds are usually ground to pass a 1 mm sieve. • Soxhlet measures free lipid only. Bound lipids in bakery products, dairy products and processed foods (lipoproteins, starch-lipid complexes, fat enclosed in intact cells) are released by acid hydrolysis before extraction (Weibull-Stoldt, AOAC 922.06: boiling with 3 N hydrochloric acid, filtering, drying, then Soxhlet), or by the Rose-Gottlieb alkaline (ammonia) ethanol-ether method for milk and infant formula (AOAC 905.02, Mojonnier flask), or the Gerber butyrometer method for milk (sulfuric acid digests protein, amyl alcohol aids separation, centrifugation reads fat directly; the field method of the Food Safety Officer). • Automated Soxtec (submersion then rinsing) and accelerated solvent extraction reduce time to under one hour. • Thermally labile lipids can oxidise during long extraction; the result is reported as crude fat or ether extract, never as triglyceride content. 5.4 Total ash and acid-insoluble ash Total ash (dry ashing, AOAC 923.03, 942.05; IS 1155) Ash is the inorganic residue after complete combustion of organic matter and is a measure of total mineral content (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, iron, trace metals present as oxides, carbonates, phosphates, chlorides, sulfates). Procedure: 2 to 5 g of sample in a tared silica, porcelain or platinum crucible is first charred gently over a flame or hot plate until smoking ceases (to prevent loss by spattering and foaming), then ignited in a muffle furnace at 550 °C (a range of 525 to 600 °C is specified by different methods) for 4 to 6 hours or overnight, until the ash is white or light grey and free of carbon. The crucible is cooled in a desiccator and weighed to constant weight. Total ash (percent) = [(W crucible with ash − W empty crucible) ÷ W sample] × 100 Why 550 °C: high enough to burn carbon completely within hours, low enough to limit volatilisation of chlorides, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and of mercury, arsenic, selenium, cadmium and lead, and to limit fusion of the ash with the crucible. Black specks of unburnt carbon are treated by wetting the ash with water or dilute nitric acid, drying and re-ashing. Where sodium chloride is high (pickles, butter), 500 °C is used. Wet ashing (nitric, sulfuric and perchloric acids) and microwave digestion are preferred when the ash is to be analysed for individual metals (Part 4B). Sulfated ash (treatment with sulfuric acid before ignition, converting all cations to stable sulfates) is used for food additives and colours. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 50

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Acid-insoluble ash (AIA) The total ash is boiled with 25 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid (about 10 percent, 1 part concentrated acid to 2.5 parts water) for 5 minutes; the soluble mineral salts dissolve, the solution is filtered through ashless filter paper, the residue is washed free of chloride with hot water, and the paper with residue is ignited again at 550 °C and weighed. The acid-insoluble ash is almost entirely silica: sand, soil, dust and grit. It is the statutory index of extraneous mineral adulteration in spices, flours and tea, and of poor washing of grains. Commodity (FSS Food Products Acid-insoluble ash maximum, Standards and Food Additives Total ash maximum, percent percent Regulations, 2011) Atta (whole wheat flour) 2.0 (on dry basis) 0.1 Maida (refined wheat flour) 1.0 0.1 Besan (Bengal gram flour) 5.0 0.5 Turmeric powder 9.0 1.5 Chilli powder 8.0 1.25 Coriander powder 9.0 1.5 Black pepper (whole) 7.0 1.5 4.0 to 8.0 (with water-soluble ash not Tea 1.0 less than 45 percent of total ash) not more than 9.3 (whole), 11 not specified; ash is a purity index for Milk powder (skimmed) dairy Related ash indices: water-soluble ash and alkalinity of water-soluble ash (tea, where low values indicate exhausted tea leaves), ash insoluble in water, and the ash content of sugar and honey as purity measures. 5.5 Crude fibre: the Weende method Crude fibre is the organic residue that resists sequential boiling in dilute acid (simulating gastric digestion) and dilute alkali (simulating intestinal digestion) and is then lost on ignition (AOAC 962.09, 978.10; IS 10226). Procedure 1. Weigh about 2 g of dried, fat-free sample (the Soxhlet residue is ideal; fat above 1 percent must be removed or it coats particles and interferes). 2. Acid digestion: boil gently with 200 mL of 1.25 percent (0.255 N) sulfuric acid under reflux for exactly 30 minutes, keeping the volume constant with hot water; filter through a linen cloth, Buchner funnel or fritted crucible, and wash with boiling water until the washings are no longer acid. 3. Alkali digestion: transfer the residue to 200 mL of 1.25 percent (0.313 N) sodium hydroxide and boil for exactly 30 minutes; filter and wash with boiling water until free of alkali, then with 25 mL of 1.25 percent sulfuric acid, three times with water, and finally with 25 mL of ethanol (and petroleum ether if fat remains). 4. Dry the residue in a crucible at 130 °C for 2 hours (or 100 to 105 °C overnight), cool in a desiccator and weigh (W1). 5. Ignite in a muffle furnace at 550 °C for 30 minutes (or until carbon free), cool and weigh (W2). Crude fibre (percent) = [(W1 − W2) ÷ W sample] × 100 FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 51

doc: Modern Food Packaging, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Analysis
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS The loss on ignition is the crude fibre; the ash remaining (W2) is subtracted so that mineral matter trapped in the residue is not counted as fibre. Exact timing, acid and alkali concentrations and boiling intensity must be standardised because the result is purely operational. What crude fibre is and is not Crude fibre recovers 50 to 80 percent of the cellulose, only 10 to 50 percent of the lignin and under 20 percent of the hemicellulose, and none of the pectins, gums, beta-glucans or resistant starch; it therefore underestimates total dietary fibre by a factor of 2 to 5, and the ratio varies with the food. Crude fibre remains a legal standard of identity for spices, flours and animal feeds (for example FSSAI maximum crude fibre values in chilli powder and coriander powder, bran content in atta), but the nutrition label value for dietary fibre must come from the enzymatic-gravimetric method (AOAC 985.29 or 991.43, the Prosky method: digestion with heat-stable alpha-amylase, protease and amyloglucosidase, precipitation of soluble fibre with four volumes of ethanol, weighing of the residue corrected for its protein and ash) or AOAC 2009.01 and 2011.25 for total dietary fibre including resistant starch and low-molecular-weight oligosaccharides. For feeds, the Van Soest detergent system (neutral detergent fibre, acid detergent fibre, acid detergent lignin) is used. 5.6 Summary table of the proximate scheme Key reagents and Fraction Official principle Reports Classic error conditions 100 to 105 °C air oven; 70 °C vacuum oven Water and volatiles Volatile oils counted Loss on drying or Karl for sugary foods; Moisture (oven) or water only as moisture; sugar Fischer iodine-sulfur dioxide- (Karl Fischer) decomposition base-methanol reagent Concentrated sulfuric acid, potassium sulfate, copper sulfate; 40 percent Non-protein nitrogen sodium hydroxide; 4 Kjeldahl: digestion, (urea, melamine) Crude protein percent boric acid Total nitrogen × factor distillation, titration counted as protein; with mixed indicator; wrong factor standard 0.1 N hydrochloric acid; factor 6.25 (6.38 milk, 5.70 wheat) Petroleum ether 40 to Bound lipid missed; Soxhlet continuous 60 °C (or diethyl Free lipid soluble in Crude fat moisture in sample solvent extraction ether), 4 to 16 hours, the solvent co-extracts sugars dried sample Loss of volatile elements and Muffle furnace 550 °C Total minerals as Total ash Dry ashing chlorides at higher to white or grey ash oxides and salts temperatures; unburnt carbon Ash boiled in dilute 10 percent HCl, Silica, sand, dirt Incomplete washing Acid-insoluble ash hydrochloric acid, ashless filter paper, (adulteration index) of chloride residue ignited 550 °C FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 52

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Part 6. Stage 1 Revision Bank (Count-Based Pairs) PART 6: STAGE 1 REVISION BANK, COUNT-BASED PAIR QUESTIONS Method for every question: assign c1, c2, c3 = 1 for a correct statement and 0 for an incorrect statement; compute N = c1 + c2 + c3; map N = 0 to None, N = 1 to Only one, N = 2 to Only two, N = 3 to All three. Never pick an option until N is written down. With 0.25 negative marking, a guessed count question has an expected value of zero; a verified one is a full mark. Question 1: Packaging polymers and retort pouches Consider the following statements: 1. High-density polyethylene has a lower density but a higher degree of crystallinity than low-density polyethylene, which is why it is a better moisture barrier. 2. In a four-ply retort pouch the biaxially oriented nylon (OPA) layer is positioned between the aluminium foil and the inner cast polypropylene sealant layer to provide puncture and flex-crack resistance. 3. Ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer retains its exceptional oxygen barrier at all relative humidities and is therefore used as a monolayer retort film. How many of the above statements are correct? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None Step-by-step verification: • Statement 1: HDPE has higher crystallinity (70 to 90 percent versus 40 to 50 percent) and therefore higher density (0.941 to 0.965 g/cm³ versus 0.910 to 0.925 g/cm³), not lower; the barrier conclusion is right but the density clause is wrong, so the statement as a whole is wrong. c1 = 0. • Statement 2: The four-ply construction is PET (12 µm) / aluminium foil (9 to 12 µm) / OPA (15 µm) / CPP (70 to 100 µm); nylon sits between foil and sealant to protect the foil from cracking. c2 = 1. • Statement 3: EVOH is hygroscopic; above about 75 percent RH its oxygen transmission rate rises ten to a hundred fold and it suffers retort shock; it is always buried as a core layer between polyolefin skins and never used as a monolayer. The absolute qualifier at all relative humidities is the trap. c3 = 0. N = c1 + c2 + c3 = 0 + 1 + 0 = 1. Answer: (a) Only one. Question 2: Active and intelligent packaging systems Consider the following statements: 1. A methylene blue oxygen indicator inside a pack is pink in the absence of oxygen and turns blue when oxygen enters through a leaking seal. 2. A potassium permanganate ethylene absorber changes colour from purple to brown as permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide, indicating exhaustion. 3. A polymerisation-based time-temperature indicator such as the Lifelines Fresh-Check label is classified as active packaging because it reacts chemically with temperature. How many of the above statements are correct? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None Step-by-step verification: • Statement 1: In the reduced (leuco) state in an oxygen-free pack the tablet is pink; oxygen re-oxidises methylene blue to its blue form. c1 = 1. • Statement 2: KMnO4 (purple) oxidises ethylene and is itself reduced to MnO2 (brown); the colour change signals that capacity is spent. c2 = 1. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 54

doc: Modern Food Packaging, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Analysis
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS • Statement 3: A TTI monitors and communicates the temperature history; it does not act on the food or the headspace, so it is intelligent packaging regardless of the chemistry inside the label. The reasoning (reacts chemically) is a distractor. c3 = 0. N = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Answer: (b) Only two. Question 3: FSSAI migration regulations Consider the following statements with reference to the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018: 1. The overall migration limit for plastic food contact materials is 60 mg/kg of food or simulant, equivalently 10 mg/dm² of contact surface. 2. Food simulant B, 3 percent (w/v) acetic acid in water, represents acidic aqueous foods with a pH below 4.5 such as fruit juices, pickles and tomato products. 3. Newspapers and similar printed materials are prohibited for storing, wrapping or packaging food. How many of the above statements are correct? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None Step-by-step verification: • Statement 1: Schedule IV sets the overall migration limit at 60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm², identical to EU Regulation 10/2011; the two figures are linked by the convention of 6 dm² of packaging per kilogram of food (10 × 6 = 60). c1 = 1. • Statement 2: Simulant B is the only acidic simulant, 3 percent acetic acid, assigned to foods below pH 4.5. c2 = 1. • Statement 3: Regulation 4 of the 2018 Regulations prohibits newspaper and similar materials for storing and wrapping food, and also requires that the printed surface of any packaging must not come into direct contact with food; FSSAI had issued the same advisory in 2016. c3 = 1. N = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Answer: (c) All three. Question 4: Instrumental analysis and proximate methods Consider the following statements: 1. Flame atomic absorption spectrometry achieves lower (better) detection limits than graphite furnace atomic absorption spectrometry because the flame atomises the whole sample continuously. 2. The Kjeldahl nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor for milk and milk products is 5.70. 3. The electron capture detector gives a response proportional to the number of carbon atoms in every organic compound and is therefore the universal detector for gas chromatography. How many of the above statements are correct? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None Step-by-step verification: • Statement 1: The reverse is true: the flame wastes 90 to 95 percent of the sample in the spray chamber and atoms reside only milliseconds in the beam, so FAAS works at mg/L; the graphite furnace atomises the whole 10 to 50 µL aliquot into a confined volume and reaches µg/L, 100 to 1000 times better. c1 = 0. • Statement 2: The milk factor is 6.38 (15.67 percent nitrogen in milk proteins); 5.70 is the wheat factor. c2 = 0. • Statement 3: Equal-carbon response and universality describe the flame ionisation detector; the electron capture detector with its 63Ni beta source responds selectively to electronegative, chiefly halogenated, compounds and barely responds to hydrocarbons. c3 = 0. N = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0. Answer: (d) None. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 55

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS Absolute-qualifier mini-bank (mark each true or false before reading the key) 1. Aluminium foil is always a 100 percent barrier. False: below 15 µm pinholes make it a barrier only within a laminate. 2. All recycled plastics are banned for food contact in India. False: certified food-grade recycled PET from approved recyclers is permitted after the amendment framework that followed the 2018 Regulations. 3. Passing the overall migration test proves the material is toxicologically safe. False: specific migration limits must also be met. 4. Mercury is determined by hydride generation AAS. False: cold vapour AAS at 253.7 nm. 5. Only Simulant E is a solid. True: Tenax, poly(2,6-diphenyl-p-phenylene oxide), for dry foods. 6. C-enamel is never used for acid fruit packs. True: zinc oxide would be extracted; R-enamel or plain heavy-tin cans are used. 7. The refractive index detector can be used with gradient elution. False. 8. Crude fibre never equals dietary fibre. True in practice: crude fibre underestimates dietary fibre by a factor of 2 to 5. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 56

Stage 2 Descriptive Model Answers PART 7: STAGE 2 DESCRIPTIVE MODEL ANSWERS 10-Mark Model Answer Question: Explain the architecture, material composition, and advantages of retort pouches over conventional tinplate cans in food preservation. Suggested marking scheme: definition and context 1 mark; layer-by-layer architecture with gauges and functions 3 marks; heat-penetration mechanism 2 marks; comparative advantages 2 marks; limitations and process requirements 1 mark; regulatory and quality-control linkage 1 mark. Target length: 400 to 450 words, one labelled schematic, one table. Model answer 1. Definition and context A retort pouch is a flexible, heat-sealable, hermetically closed laminate container that withstands thermal sterilisation at 115 to 135 °C (typically 121 °C for 20 to 40 minutes, delivering the required F0 value) so that low-acid foods become commercially sterile and shelf stable at ambient temperature. It was developed by the United States Army Natick Laboratories with Reynolds Metals and Continental Flexible Packaging in the 1960s and 1970s for military rations and is now used for ready-to-eat curries, rice, tuna, soups and pet food. It is the flexible-packaging alternative to the three-piece tinplate can developed from Appert and Durand (1810). 1. Architecture and material composition Schematic (outside to inside, food contact at the bottom): Layer Material and gauge Function Reverse-printable surface, tensile and Biaxially oriented polyethylene 1. Outer abrasion strength, heat resistance terephthalate (BOPET), 12 µm against sealing jaws Essentially total barrier to oxygen, water vapour, light and aroma once Soft-annealed aluminium foil, 9 to 12 laminated (foil below 15 µm has 2. Barrier µm pinholes on its own, bridged by the adjacent polymer layers); provides 18 to 36 months shelf life Puncture, flex-crack and abuse 3. Toughness (four-ply only) Biaxially oriented nylon 6 (OPA), 15 µm resistance; protects the foil in bony or sharp products Food-contact layer; heat seals at about Cast polypropylene (CPP), often 160 °C, survives 121 to 135 °C without 4. Inner sealant ethylene-modified random copolymer, delamination or seal loss, inert and 70 to 100 µm low taint; thick enough to bridge seal- area contamination The three-ply pouch is PET / Al / CPP; the four-ply pouch is PET / Al / OPA / CPP. Layers are bonded by two- component polyurethane adhesives that must be fully cured before use to prevent migration of primary aromatic amines. Transparent, microwaveable variants replace foil with PET-SiOx, PET-AlOx or EVOH barrier layers at some sacrifice of shelf life. FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 57

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS 1. Heat-penetration mechanism Sterilisation of conduction-heating foods is unsteady-state conduction, and the time for the cold spot to reach process temperature scales with the square of the conduction distance. A 307 × 409 can has a cold- spot path of about 36 mm, whereas a filled pouch is a slab 15 to 25 mm thick with a half-thickness of 8 to 12 mm. The pouch therefore reaches the same F0 in 30 to 50 percent less time at the same retort temperature, and because the entire slab heats almost uniformly the surface layers are not overcooked while the centre catches up. 1. Advantages over the tinplate can Aspect Retort pouch Tinplate can 30 to 50 percent shorter; less steam, Process time and energy Long; surface overcooking water and cooling Better retention of thiamine, vitamin C, Nutrient and sensory quality Lower colour, texture, flavour Light; flat when empty, saving about Weight and storage Heavy and bulky 85 percent storage space Tear-notch opening, boil-in-bag and Convenience Opener required; not microwaveable microwave reheating (foil-free types) Tin and iron pickup in plain cans (FSSAI tin limit 250 mg/kg); lacquer Metal pickup None (polymer contact) migration (bisphenol A from epoxy coatings) Lower mass, but multilayer laminate is Disposal Readily recycled magnetically hard to recycle 1. Limitations and process requirements The pouch must be processed in an overpressure retort (steam-air or water immersion) because internal vapour pressure at 121 °C would otherwise burst seals; pouches are racked flat to control thickness; residual air must be kept below about 10 mL by vacuum or steam-flush sealing; seals must be clean and are tested for strength, burst pressure and leaks; filling is slower and unit cost higher than canning; and the pouch needs a carton for distribution. 1. Regulatory linkage The laminate materials must conform to Schedule IV of the FSS (Packaging) Regulations, 2018 (overall migration not more than 60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm² by IS 9845, and specific migration limits for metals and DEHP), and the product must meet FSSAI commercial sterility requirements, verified by incubation at 37 °C for 10 days (and 55 °C for thermophiles). The Food Safety Officer inspects seal integrity, residual air, retort records (F0, come-up time, overpressure) and incubation results. Conclusion: the retort pouch delivers can-equivalent sterility with a thinner geometry, giving faster, gentler processing and higher product quality, at the cost of stricter seal and process control. 15-Mark Model Answer Question: Examine the statutory framework of Food Packaging under FSSAI Regulations (2018). Detail the food simulants used for migration testing, the difference between overall and specific migration limits, and the statutory prohibitions on packaging materials. Suggested marking scheme: legal basis and structure of the Regulations 3 marks; general requirements 2 marks; food simulants with compositions and food classes 3 marks; overall versus specific migration with FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 58
