text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | MODERN PACKAGING & INSTRUMENTAL ANALYSIS the statutory numbers 3 marks; prohibitions 2 marks; enforcement, testing and conclusion 2 marks. Target length: 650 to 750 words, two tables, one callout for the number link. Model answer 1. Legal basis and structure Section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 empowers the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India to make regulations, and Section 16 charges it with specifying standards for packaging. The Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018 were notified on 24 December 2018 and came into force on 1 July 2019, separating packaging from the earlier combined Packaging and Labelling Regulations, 2011 (labelling now sits in the Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020). The Regulations contain general requirements, specific requirements, and schedules: Schedule I (paper and board), Schedule II (glass), Schedule III (metals and alloys: tinplate, tin-free steel, aluminium, stainless steel), Schedule IV (plastics, with overall and specific migration limits and the Indian Standards for each polymer, for example IS 10146 polyethylene, IS 10910 polypropylene, IS 12252 PET, IS 10151 PVC, IS 12247 nylon, IS 13601 polycarbonate), and an indicative list of suggested packaging materials for food categories (dairy, fats and oils, cereals, meat and fish, fruits and vegetables, beverages, water, spices). The Regulations are to be read with the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations (limits for metals and migrants in food) and with the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. 1. General requirements • Packaging materials must be of food grade and must not transfer their constituents to food in quantities that could endanger human health, change the composition of the food unacceptably, or deteriorate its organoleptic properties (the inertness principle shared with EU Regulation 1935/2004). • Materials must conform to the Indian Standards listed in the Schedules; the food business operator must obtain a certificate of conformity from an NABL-accredited laboratory. • Packaging must be suitable for the type of food and its storage and processing conditions (hot fill, retort, frozen, microwave). • Pigments and colourants in plastics must comply with IS 9833; the printed surface must not contact food. • Containers must be free of defects: no rust, improper seaming, dents or leakage in cans; glass free of flaws that could cause breakage; paper free of harmful dyes and loading materials. 1. Food simulants for migration testing Foods are too variable to test directly, so standardised liquids and solids that mimic the extractive power of food classes are used (EU Regulation 10/2011 Annex III; the same logic underlies IS 9845 referenced by Schedule IV). Simulant Composition Food class represented Aqueous foods, pH above 4.5 (milk- A 10 percent ethanol (v/v) in water free, non-acidic beverages, vegetables) Acidic aqueous foods, pH below 4.5 B 3 percent acetic acid (w/v) in water (fruit juices, pickles, tomato products, soft drinks) Alcoholic foods up to 20 percent C 20 percent ethanol (v/v) alcohol; foods with lipophilic ingredients Alcoholic foods above 20 percent; oil- D1 50 percent ethanol (v/v) in-water emulsions; milk and dairy products Vegetable oil (refined olive or sunflower, less than 1 percent free Fatty foods with free surface fat (oils, D2 fatty acids; substitutes 95 percent ghee, butter, fried snacks) ethanol or iso-octane) FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 59

The material is exposed on one side at a defined surface-to-volume ratio and the simulant is analysed. 1. Overall migration versus specific migration Criterion Overall migration limit (OML) Specific migration limit (SML) Total non-volatile matter transferred, A named substance (monomer, Measures regardless of identity additive, catalyst residue, metal) Toxicology: derived from tolerable Basis Inertness, a quality criterion daily intake Gravimetric residue after evaporating HPLC, GC-MS, LC-MS/MS, AAS or ICP- Method the simulant (IS 9845) MS Barium 1 mg/kg; cobalt 0.05; copper 5; iron 48; lithium 0.6; manganese 0.6; 60 mg/kg of food or simulant, or 10 zinc 25; antimony 0.04; arsenic, Statutory value under Schedule IV mg/dm² of contact surface cadmium, chromium, lead and mercury 0.01 each; bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) 1.5 The two overall figures express one ceiling: regulators assume a 60 kg adult eats 1 kg of food per day that contacted 6 dm² of packaging (a 1 litre cube has 6 dm² of surface), so 10 mg/dm² × 6 dm²/kg = 60 mg/kg. The surface-based figure is applied to sheet materials and small containers; the mass-based figure to larger containers. Passing the overall test does not prove safety: a material can be under 60 mg/kg overall and still exceed the SML of a potent migrant such as bisphenol A or a primary aromatic amine, so both tests are required. Where a syllabus source quotes lead at 1 mg/kg, write the Schedule IV value (0.01 mg/kg) and note that 1 mg/kg is the barium limit. 1. Statutory prohibitions • Newspaper and similar printed materials shall not be used for storing, wrapping or packaging food; printing inks carry lead, benzophenone, mineral oil hydrocarbons and primary aromatic amines, and the paper carries microbial load. • The printed surface of any packaging material shall not come into direct contact with food (reverse printing or an unprinted inner layer is required). • Recycled plastics shall not be used for packaging, storing, carrying or dispensing food, except that food- grade recycled PET produced by recyclers registered and certified under the subsequent FSSAI and Central Pollution Control Board framework (consistent with the amended Plastic Waste Management Rules) may be used for direct food contact; recycled paper and board bearing print or of unknown origin remain unsuitable for direct contact. • Plastics not listed with an Indian Standard in Schedule IV, and pigments or colourants outside IS 9833, are not permitted; non-food-grade, rusted, dented or previously used containers, and lead-soldered cans, are prohibited. • Packaging must not be used for a food category for which it is unsuitable (for example non-retortable films for sterilised products, or unlacquered cans for sulfur-rich foods). 1. Enforcement and testing linkage The Food Safety Officer may draw samples of packaging along with food under Section 38 of the Act; overall migration is tested gravimetrically by IS 9845, metals by AAS or ICP-MS (lead and cadmium by graphite furnace or ICP-MS at 0.01 mg/kg), DEHP by GC-MS, bisphenol A by LC-MS/MS, and PET bottles for FOODSAFE STUDY NOTES • 60

Non-conformity attracts penalties under Sections 50 to 66 for sub-standard, unsafe or misbranded food. Conclusion: the 2018 Regulations convert the inertness principle into enforceable numbers (60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm² overall; substance-specific SMLs), standardised simulants, Indian Standard conformity, and clear prohibitions (newspaper, printed contact surfaces, uncertified recycled plastics), while the certified food- grade recycled PET exception shows the framework evolving towards circular packaging without compromising migration safety. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Part 1A: Legume Toxicants PART 1A: LEGUME TOXICANTS AND ANTINUTRITIONAL FACTORS First-principles orientation Legumes are seeds. A seed must survive insects, fungi and predators until germination, so it stores chemical defences: neurotoxic amino acids, cyanide-releasing glycosides, pro-oxidant glycosides, carbohydrate- binding proteins, protease inhibitors and phosphorus locked as phytate. Human processing (soaking, germination, fermentation, moist heat) is essentially a set of counter-strategies against these defences. Every toxicant below is best understood by asking three questions: what is the molecule, what does it hit in the human body, and which processing step breaks it. 1. Lathyrism and Khesari Dal (Lathyrus sativus) 1.1 Botany and epidemiology • Lathyrus sativus is called khesari, kesari dal, teora, chickling vetch or grass pea. It is drought-hardy and cheap, so it dominates the diet of the poorest cultivators in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Odisha and Maharashtra in drought years. • Neurolathyrism appears when khesari supplies more than about 30 percent of dietary energy for 2 to 6 months, typically in young adult males aged 15 to 45, often during famine when it is eaten unprocessed as roasted seeds or coarse flour. • Historical context: Sleeman (1844) described it in Central India; the Lathyrism Enquiry Field Unit of the Indian Council of Medical Research worked at Rewa in the 1950s and 1960s. 1.2 The molecule • Toxin: beta-N-oxalyl-L-alpha,beta-diaminopropionic acid, abbreviated BOAA, also called ODAP (3-N- oxalyl-L-2,3-diaminopropanoic acid). • Structure: a non-protein amino acid in which the beta-amino group of L-2,3-diaminopropionic acid is acylated by oxalic acid. Two isomers exist: beta-ODAP (the neurotoxic form, about 95 percent of the total) and alpha-ODAP (far less toxic); heating can interconvert them. • Content: 0.1 to 2.5 percent of seed dry weight depending on variety and drought stress. Low-toxin lines (ODAP below 0.1 percent) such as Pusa 24 and Ratan have been bred. • It is water-soluble, which is the entire basis of the detoxification chemistry. 1.3 Mechanism of neurotoxicity BOAA / ODAP (structural analogue of glutamate) | v Agonist at AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors on motor neurons | v Sustained sodium and calcium influx (excitotoxicity) | v Mitochondrial complex I inhibition, reactive oxygen species, glutathione depletion, inhibition of glutamate uptake by astrocytes | FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 4

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS v Selective degeneration of Betz cells and the lateral corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts supplying the lower limbs | v Irreversible spastic paraparesis • Why lower limbs: the longest corticospinal axons, those to the legs, are most vulnerable to energy failure. • Synergistic risk factors: low intake of sulphur amino acids (methionine and cysteine deplete glutathione), zinc deficiency, hard physical labour, and febrile illness. 1.4 Clinical pathology Stage Presentation Calf cramps, heaviness of legs, nocturnal spasms after a heavy Prodrome khesari meal Latent (no-stick) stage Spastic gait but walks unaided Needs one stick; scissoring gait, crossed adductor spasm, toe- One-stick stage walking Two-stick stage Needs two sticks or crutches Crawler stage Cannot stand; moves on all fours • Upper motor neuron signs: hypertonia, exaggerated knee and ankle jerks, ankle clonus, extensor plantar response (Babinski sign). Sensation, bladder and intellect are usually spared. • The lesion is irreversible; there is no antidote. Prevention is entirely dietary and regulatory. 1.5 Processing detoxification (all exploit water solubility) Method Procedure Removal of ODAP Soak dehusked dal in 2 to 3 volumes of Steeping in hot water water at 60 to 70 degrees Celsius for 1 hour, 70 to 80 percent discard water, wash Soak overnight, steam or boil in excess Parboiling water for 15 to 20 minutes, discard water, 80 to 90 percent sun-dry Soak in 1 to 2 percent calcium hydroxide Lime soaking (lime water) for several hours, wash; alkaline Up to 90 percent pH hydrolyses the oxalyl amide bond Lactic fermentation (as in idli or dhokla Fermentation Partial, variable batter) Little or no removal; dry heat does not Dry roasting or frying Negligible remove a water-soluble toxin The examiner's favourite pairing: the method must be a wet method with discarding of the soak water. Any question stating that roasting detoxifies khesari is false. 1.6 Statutory position • The Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules (Rule 44A, 1961) prohibited the sale of khesari gram and its products in any form. • This continues under the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011, which prohibit the sale of kesari gram (Lathyrus sativus), kesari dal, kesari flour and any admixture of kesari with other grams, dal or flour. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 5

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS • In 2016 the FSSAI scientific panel reviewed lifting the ban in view of low-toxin varieties, but the sale prohibition remains the examinable legal position; a notification lifting it has not been finalised. • Analytical detection in adulterated dal: khesari dal is wedge-shaped with a square truncated end, unlike the rounder lentil or red gram; the chemical test is the 50 percent hydrochloric acid test (pink colour on heating with the dal in dilute hydrochloric acid indicates khesari). [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Neurolathyrism (from Lathyrus sativus, BOAA) must not be confused with osteolathyrism (from Lathyrus odoratus, sweet pea, caused by beta-aminopropionitrile, which inhibits lysyl oxidase and weakens collagen). A pair that assigns BOAA to skeletal deformity is false. 2. Cyanogenic Glycosides 2.1 The molecules and their sources Glycoside Aglycone type Sugar Main foods Final hydrolysis products Bitter almonds, Gentiobiose (two apricot, peach, plum Benzaldehyde + HCN + 2 Amygdalin Mandelonitrile (aromatic) glucose) and cherry kernels, glucose apple seeds Intermediate in Prunasin Mandelonitrile Glucose amygdalin breakdown; Benzaldehyde + HCN wild cherry Cassava (tapioca), lima Linamarin Acetone cyanohydrin (aliphatic) Glucose Acetone + HCN beans, flax Cassava (minor), lima Lotaustralin Methyl ethyl ketone cyanohydrin Glucose Butanone + HCN beans Sorghum (jowar), Dhurrin p-Hydroxymandelonitrile Glucose especially young p-Hydroxybenzaldehyde + HCN shoots • The intact glycoside is non-toxic. The plant stores it in the vacuole and keeps the hydrolysing enzyme in a separate compartment (cell wall or cytoplasm). Chewing, grating, grinding or insect damage breaks the compartments. 2.2 Enzymatic hydrolysis Cyanogenic glycoside | beta-glucosidase (linamarase in cassava, emulsin in almonds) v Sugar + cyanohydrin (alpha-hydroxynitrile) | hydroxynitrile lyase, or spontaneous at pH above 5 and warm temperature v Carbonyl compound (benzaldehyde, acetone) + hydrogen cyanide (HCN) • Gut bacteria also possess beta-glucosidases, so swallowed intact glycoside can still release cyanide in the colon. This is why 'eat it raw without chewing' is not safe. 2.3 Mechanism of cyanide toxicity • Cyanide ion binds the ferric iron (Fe3+) of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in the mitochondrial electron transport chain. • Electron transfer to oxygen stops; oxidative phosphorylation ceases; cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acidosis. • Result is histotoxic hypoxia: arterial blood stays bright red and oxygen-saturated, but tissues cannot use it. Venous blood is also bright red, a classical sign. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 6

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS • Detoxification in the body: the mitochondrial enzyme rhodanese transfers sulphur from thiosulphate to cyanide, forming the far less toxic thiocyanate, which is excreted in urine. This is why sodium thiosulphate is an antidote and why chronic cassava eaters have high urinary thiocyanate (and secondary goitre, because thiocyanate blocks iodide uptake). 2.4 Clinical pathology Form Picture Headache, dizziness, bitter-almond odour, tachypnoea then respiratory depression, convulsions, coma, death within minutes to Acute poisoning hours; lethal oral dose of HCN about 0.5 to 3.5 mg/kg body weight (50 to 200 mg in an adult) Abrupt, permanent, symmetrical spastic paraparesis in cassava- dependent populations of Central and East Africa during drought, Konzo linked to inadequately processed bitter cassava plus protein (sulphur amino acid) deficiency Chronic sensory ataxia, optic atrophy, deafness in long-term low- Tropical ataxic neuropathy dose cassava eaters (Nigeria) Thiocyanate competes with iodide at the thyroid sodium-iodide Endemic goitre and cretinism symporter • Antidotes: hydroxocobalamin (binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin), sodium nitrite (induces methaemoglobin, which scavenges cyanide), sodium thiosulphate (substrate for rhodanese), and 100 percent oxygen. 2.5 Detoxification by processing Each step either frees the HCN (by letting the enzyme act) or removes it (HCN is volatile, boiling point 26 degrees Celsius, and water-soluble). Step Chemistry Note Peel of bitter cassava carries most of the Peeling First step, large reduction linamarin Ruptures compartments so linamarase Grating or crushing Essential to liberate HCN before heating meets linamarin Hydrolysis plus leaching of soluble glycoside Soaking in water (3 to 5 days, retting) Discard the water and cyanide into water Slow drying allows enzyme hydrolysis then Sun-drying after wetting ('wetting method') Rapid drying traps intact glycoside volatilisation of HCN Lactic bacteria and endogenous enzymes complete hydrolysis; acid pH keeps Fermentation (gari, fufu, lafun) Gari limit 2 mg/kg HCN (Codex) cyanohydrin stable so a later heating step is needed Volatilises HCN and destroys enzyme; must follow grating, because boiling first Boiling in excess water Order of operations matters inactivates the enzyme and locks the glycoside inside • Statutory and Codex ceilings: sweet cassava 50 mg/kg total HCN; cassava flour 10 mg/kg; gari 2 mg/kg. Bitter cassava carries more than 100 mg/kg and up to 1,000 mg/kg fresh weight. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Boiling intact chunks of bitter cassava without grating is less effective than grating followed by soaking, because the enzyme that liberates HCN is itself denatured by heat. Sun-drying is only effective if the tissue is first crushed or kept moist long enough for hydrolysis. Also note that amygdalin is wrongly marketed as 'vitamin B17' or laetrile; it has no vitamin status and causes cyanide poisoning. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 7

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 3. Favism and Faba Beans (Vicia faba) 3.1 The molecules • Vicine and convicine are pyrimidine beta-glucosides concentrated in the cotyledons of faba (broad) beans at 0.5 to 1.0 percent dry weight. • Hydrolysis by beta-glucosidase (in the bean, in gut bacteria and in the intestinal mucosa) removes glucose to give the aglycones divicine (from vicine) and isouramil (from convicine). • Divicine and isouramil are unstable 2,6-diaminopyrimidine-diols that autoxidise rapidly, generating hydrogen peroxide and superoxide radicals and oxidising reduced glutathione (GSH) to oxidised glutathione (GSSG). 3.2 The genetic lesion: G6PD deficiency Glucose-6-phosphate | glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), first step of the pentose phosphate pathway v 6-Phosphogluconolactone + NADPH | v NADPH is the only source of reducing power in the mature red cell | v Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate GSH from GSSG • The red blood cell has no mitochondria and no nucleus; the pentose phosphate pathway is its sole NADPH source. • In G6PD deficiency (X-linked, hence mainly affecting males; common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, African and Indian populations, including Parsis and some tribal groups), NADPH supply fails under oxidant stress. • Divicine and isouramil deplete GSH faster than it can be regenerated; haemoglobin is oxidised to methaemoglobin and denatured into Heinz bodies that precipitate on the membrane; the spleen removes damaged cells (extravascular haemolysis) and some cells lyse in circulation (intravascular haemolysis). 3.3 Clinical pathology • Acute haemolytic anaemia 24 to 48 hours after eating fresh or dried faba beans (or inhaling pollen in sensitive children): pallor, jaundice, dark red-brown urine (haemoglobinuria), fever, back and abdominal pain, tachycardia; severe cases progress to acute kidney injury and death. • Laboratory: fall in haemoglobin, raised unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, reduced haptoglobin, Heinz bodies on supravital stain, 'bite cells' on the smear, reticulocytosis after recovery. • Children aged 1 to 5 years are most affected. The same oxidant mechanism is triggered by primaquine, sulphonamides, naphthalene mothballs and infections, so favism is one member of a wider family of G6PD haemolytic crises. 3.4 Control • Vicine and convicine are heat-stable, so ordinary cooking does not protect a G6PD-deficient person; soaking removes only part because the glycosides are only moderately water-soluble. • Low-vicine faba bean genotypes (vc minus gene) carry less than 10 percent of normal levels. • Dietary avoidance by affected individuals and neonatal G6PD screening are the practical controls. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Favism is not an allergy and not a cyanide poisoning. The bean is harmless to people with normal G6PD. A statement that 'faba beans are toxic to all consumers' is false; a statement that 'cooking abolishes favism' is also false. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 8

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 4. Phytohaemagglutinins (Lectins) 4.1 Nature • Lectins are carbohydrate-binding (glyco)proteins. The kidney bean lectin phytohaemagglutinin (PHA) of Phaseolus vulgaris (rajma, red kidney bean, also white kidney bean and cannellini) is a tetrameric protein of about 120 kilodaltons with two subunit types, PHA-E (erythroagglutinating) and PHA-L (leucoagglutinating). • Raw red kidney beans contain 20,000 to 70,000 haemagglutinating units (hau) per gram; a properly boiled bean contains 200 to 400 hau. As few as 4 or 5 raw beans can cause illness. • Related lectins: concanavalin A (jack bean), soybean agglutinin, ricin (castor bean; a ribosome- inactivating lectin, not a food lectin but the examiner's favourite comparator). 4.2 Mechanism Ingested PHA survives gastric acid and proteolysis | v Binds oligosaccharide receptors (N-acetylgalactosamine, galactose-rich glycans) on the brush border of enterocytes | v Disrupts microvilli, increases permeability, stimulates hyperplastic crypt changes, impairs disaccharidase and transporter function | v Malabsorption, bacterial overgrowth, fluid secretion, endocytosis of lectin into the circulation (haemagglutination in vitro) | v Nausea, vomiting within 1 to 3 hours, diarrhoea and abdominal pain within hours; recovery usually in 3 to 4 hours, rarely needs hospitalisation • Chronic feeding of raw beans to animals causes growth depression, loss of nitrogen, pancreatic and intestinal hypertrophy. 4.3 Thermal destruction and the slow-cooker paradox • Lectins are proteins and are denatured by moist heat at 100 degrees Celsius: soak dry beans at least 5 hours, discard the water, then boil vigorously for at least 10 minutes (30 minutes is the conservative recommendation). Pressure cooking is fully effective. • Why slow cooking at sub-boiling temperatures (slow cookers at 70 to 80 degrees Celsius) increases toxicity: partial heating at these temperatures does not unfold PHA but increases its extraction and activity, so the cooked bean can show up to five times the haemagglutinating activity of the raw bean. Dry heat (roasting) and microwave heating of dry beans are also unreliable. • Outbreaks in the United Kingdom were traced to raw or slow-cooked beans in salads and casseroles; canned kidney beans are already retorted and safe. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] 'Any heating reduces lectin activity' is false. Only temperatures at or above boiling for an adequate time denature PHA; sub-boiling heating increases it. Also, lectin toxicity is a pure protein effect; it is not a cyanide effect and not an allergy. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 9

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 5. Enzyme Inhibitors: Trypsin and Chymotrypsin Inhibitors 5.1 The two soybean inhibitor families Property Kunitz trypsin inhibitor (KTI) Bowman-Birk inhibitor (BBI) Molecular mass About 20 to 21 kilodaltons (181 amino acids) About 8 kilodaltons (71 amino acids) Disulphide bonds 2 7 (very compact) Single-headed: one site, inhibits trypsin Double-headed: one site for trypsin (lysine Reactive sites mainly (arginine 63 to isoleucine 64) 16), one for chymotrypsin (leucine 43) More stable; needs longer heating; survives Heat stability Less stable; destroyed by moist heat dry heat Acid and digestive stability Partly degraded Resistant to gastric acid and pepsin Share of soy trypsin inhibitor activity About 80 percent About 20 percent • Other legumes (chickpea, pigeon pea, kidney bean, lima bean, groundnut) contain mostly Bowman- Birk type inhibitors; potatoes and cereals contain other serine protease inhibitors. 5.2 Mechanism and pancreatic hypertrophy Inhibitor forms a tight, slow-dissociating complex with trypsin in the duodenum | v Free trypsin falls; protein digestion falls | v Loss of trypsin-mediated negative feedback on the intestinal CCK-releasing peptide (monitor peptide / luminal CCK-releasing factor) | v More cholecystokinin (CCK) released from duodenal I cells | v Pancreatic acinar cells chronically stimulated: hypersecretion of trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen; acinar hypertrophy and hyperplasia (rodents); loss of sulphur amino acids in secreted enzymes; growth depression • Because pancreatic enzymes are rich in cysteine and methionine, inhibitor-induced hypersecretion drains the limiting sulphur amino acids from a legume diet, aggravating protein deficiency. • Rodents respond with pancreatic hypertrophy; humans and larger animals show hypersecretion but little hypertrophy, so the examiner expects the qualified statement. 5.3 Thermal inactivation dynamics • Inactivation is first order in time and strongly moisture dependent: moist heat at 100 degrees Celsius for 15 to 20 minutes destroys 80 to 90 percent of soybean trypsin inhibitor activity; autoclaving at 120 degrees Celsius for 15 to 30 minutes removes virtually all. Dry roasting at the same temperature is far less effective. • Over-heating causes Maillard loss of lysine, so toasting conditions are optimised to leave a small residual activity (about 10 to 20 percent of raw) while protecting protein quality. • Analytical control: Trypsin Inhibitor Activity assay (benzoyl-DL-arginine-p-nitroanilide substrate), and the indirect urease activity test (change in pH of 0.05 to 0.30 units indicates adequately heated soy meal, because urease and trypsin inhibitor have similar heat sensitivity). FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 10

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 6. Mineral Chelators: Phytic Acid 6.1 The molecule • Phytic acid is myo-inositol 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexakis(dihydrogen phosphate), abbreviated IP6, with six phosphate groups carrying up to 12 negative charges at intestinal pH. • It is the principal phosphorus store of seeds: 1 to 5 percent of cereals, legumes, oilseeds and nuts by dry weight; in wheat and rice it is concentrated in the aleurone layer and bran, in legumes in the cotyledons, and in maize in the germ. Milling of wheat removes much of it; dehulling of legumes removes less. 6.2 Chelation mechanism Phytate (12 negative charges) + divalent and trivalent cations (Zn2+, Fe2+ / Fe3+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cu2+) | at the near-neutral pH of the small intestine v Insoluble metal-phytate and protein-metal-phytate ternary complexes | v Minerals are not released at the mucosal surface; excreted in faeces • Humans lack sufficient intestinal phytase, so the complexes pass unabsorbed. Zinc is the most affected mineral, iron next, then calcium and magnesium. • Useful predictive ratios: a phytate-to-zinc molar ratio above 15 markedly impairs zinc absorption; a phytate-to-iron molar ratio above 1 impairs non-haem iron absorption; a calcium-times-phytate-to- zinc ratio above 200 is also inhibitory, because calcium potentiates zinc-phytate precipitation. • Phytate also binds proteins (reducing digestibility) and starch, and inhibits alpha-amylase, trypsin and pepsin. 6.3 Degradation by phytase • Phytase (myo-inositol hexakisphosphate phosphohydrolase) sequentially removes phosphate groups to give IP5, IP4, IP3 and ultimately inositol plus inorganic phosphate; only IP6 and IP5 are strongly inhibitory, so even partial dephosphorylation helps. • Plant phytases are 6-phytases (cereals); microbial phytases are mostly 3-phytases (Aspergillus niger). Optimum pH 4.5 to 5.5, optimum temperature 45 to 55 degrees Celsius. Process Mechanism Typical reduction of phytate Leaching and activation of endogenous Soaking 20 to 50 percent phytase Strong synthesis and activation of phytase Germination (sprouting) 50 to 80 percent as the seed mobilises phosphorus Fermentation (idli, dosa, dhokla, sourdough, Microbial phytase plus acid pH optimum 50 to 90 percent tempeh) Phytate is heat-stable; little reduction unless Cooking Low combined with soaking Milling Physical removal of bran and germ Large in wheat (80 percent in refined flour) • Enhancers that counter phytate: ascorbic acid, citric acid and meat factors improve iron absorption even in the presence of phytate. • Health note: phytate also has antioxidant and anti-carcinogenic properties in the colon, so a balanced answer mentions that complete elimination is not the goal in a mixed diet. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Phytic acid is an antinutrient, not a toxin; the harm is deficiency of zinc, iron and calcium, not direct injury. 'Cooking destroys phytate' is false; 'germination and fermentation reduce phytate' is true. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 11

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Part 1B: Other Botanical Toxicants PART 1B: OTHER BOTANICAL TOXICANTS 1. Solanine and Chaconine: Glycoalkaloids of the Solanaceae 1.1 Chemistry and sources • The two major potato (Solanum tuberosum) glycoalkaloids share the same steroidal aglycone, solanidine (a C27 cholestane-type alkaloid with a nitrogen-containing indolizidine ring). They differ in the trisaccharide at carbon 3: ◦ alpha-Solanine: solatriose (glucose, galactose, rhamnose). ◦ alpha-Chaconine: chacotriose (glucose and two rhamnose units). • alpha-Chaconine is roughly 60 percent of the total and is the more toxic of the two; the pair act synergistically. • Tomato contains alpha-tomatine (aglycone tomatidine), high in green fruit and degraded on ripening; brinjal contains solasonine and solamargine; nightshade berries contain solanine. • Distribution in the potato: concentrated in the peel (30 to 80 percent of the total), in sprouts, eyes and green tissue; a normal tuber contains 20 to 100 mg/kg, a green, sprouted or damaged tuber may exceed 1,000 mg/kg. • Greening is chlorophyll formation under light; the same light also stimulates glycoalkaloid synthesis, so greening is a marker, not the toxin itself. 1.2 Mechanism Glycoalkaloid | +--> Inhibits acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (reversible) | -> acetylcholine accumulates -> salivation, cramps, bradycardia, | confusion, in severe cases respiratory depression | +--> Sugar side chain complexes with membrane 3-beta-hydroxysterols (cholesterol) -> membrane disruption, leakage -> gastrointestinal mucosal damage, haemolysis in vitro • Absorption from the gut is poor, which is why gastrointestinal effects dominate and systemic cholinergic effects appear only at higher doses. 1.3 Clinical pathology • Onset 8 to 12 hours (sometimes 30 minutes to 24 hours): nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, burning throat, headache, fever; severe cases show drowsiness, hallucinations, bradycardia, hypotension, dilated pupils, respiratory failure. • Toxic dose: 2 to 5 mg/kg body weight; potentially lethal at 3 to 6 mg/kg. Classic outbreak: 78 London schoolboys in 1979 from stored potatoes containing about 250 to 300 mg/kg. 1.4 Thermal stability and control • Glycoalkaloids decompose only above 170 degrees Celsius (melting with decomposition near 260 degrees Celsius); boiling, baking and microwaving change them little, since they are not leached in quantity and not destroyed. Deep frying at 170 degrees Celsius or above reduces them partly because of thermal degradation and loss into oil. • Practical control: store tubers in the dark, cool and dry; discard green, sprouted, bitter or damaged tubers; peel thickly (removes 30 to 80 percent); cut out eyes and sprouts. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 12

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS • Safe ceiling: 200 mg total glycoalkaloids per kg fresh weight (20 mg/100 g), the value used by most regulators and plant breeders (new varieties exceeding it are not released); bitterness is detectable at about 140 mg/kg, burning at 200 mg/kg. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] 'Boiling detoxifies green potatoes' is false. 'Peeling reduces glycoalkaloids' is true. 'The limit is 200 mg/kg for each of solanine and chaconine' is false: 200 mg/kg is the total. 2. Goitrogens and Glucosinolates (Brassica family) 2.1 Chemistry • Glucosinolates are beta-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulphates: a glucose attached through sulphur to a carbon that carries a variable side chain (R) and an N-O-sulphate group. More than 120 occur in the Brassicaceae (Cruciferae): cabbage, cauliflower, mustard, rapeseed, turnip, radish, kale, broccoli. Glucosinolate Side chain Source Hydrolysis product of concern Rapeseed, turnip, rutabaga, Goitrin (5-vinyl-oxazolidine-2- Progoitrin 2-Hydroxy-3-butenyl cabbage thione) Black mustard, cabbage, Allyl isothiocyanate (pungency); Sinigrin Allyl (2-propenyl) horseradish thiocyanate ion Indole-3-carbinol and Glucobrassicin Indol-3-ylmethyl Cabbage, broccoli thiocyanate ion Sinalbin p-Hydroxybenzyl White mustard p-Hydroxybenzyl isothiocyanate 2.2 Myrosinase hydrolysis Glucosinolate (in vacuole) + myrosinase (thioglucosidase, in separate 'myrosin' cells) | tissue disruption by chopping, chewing or insect attack v Glucose + unstable thiohydroximate-O-sulphonate aglycone | +-- neutral pH -----> isothiocyanate (R-N=C=S) +-- acid pH, Fe2+ --> nitrile (R-C=N) and sulphur +-- indole or hydroxybenzyl side chain --> thiocyanate ion (SCN-) +-- 2-hydroxy side chain (progoitrin) --> isothiocyanate cyclises spontaneously to goitrin (oxazolidine-2-thione) • Cooking inactivates myrosinase, but intact glucosinolates reaching the colon are hydrolysed by gut bacteria, so cooked cabbage is still mildly goitrogenic. 2.3 Two different antithyroid mechanisms (the examiner's distinction) Agent Site Mechanism Overcome by extra iodine? Competitive inhibition of iodide uptake, which the user's syllabus Thiocyanate ion (SCN-) and other Sodium-iodide symporter of the Yes, high iodine intake restores describes as competitive anions thyroid follicular cell uptake inhibition of thyroidal iodine uptake Blocks organification (iodination No, iodine supplementation does Goitrin (oxazolidine-2-thione) of tyrosyl residues of not reverse it (thiourea-like Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and related thiones thyroglobulin) and coupling, so action, similar to thyroxine synthesis falls propylthiouracil) FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 13

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS • Consequences: lowered thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine, raised thyroid stimulating hormone, follicular hyperplasia and goitre. Human goitre from Brassica alone is rare; it becomes significant where iodine intake is marginal (the 'cabbage goitre' of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan belts, and the cassava-thiocyanate goitre of Central Africa). • Rapeseed meal for animals is limited to about 30 micromoles glucosinolate per gram; low- glucosinolate 'double-zero' canola (low erucic acid, low glucosinolate) was bred for this reason. • Processing: blanching in boiling water leaches soluble glucosinolates (30 to 60 percent into the water) and inactivates myrosinase; fermentation (sauerkraut) hydrolyses them; adequate dietary iodine is the public-health control. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Goitrin is formed from progoitrin, not from sinigrin. Sinigrin gives allyl isothiocyanate (the hot taste of mustard). A pair that writes 'sinigrin to goitrin' is false. 3. Oxalates 3.1 Forms and sources • Oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid, HOOC-COOH) occurs as soluble sodium and potassium oxalate in cell sap, and as insoluble calcium oxalate crystals (raphides, needle-shaped bundles; druses; crystal sand). Food Approximate oxalate (mg/100 g fresh) Predominant form Spinach (palak) 600 to 1,300 Mainly soluble Amaranth (chaulai) 500 to 1,000 Mainly soluble Rhubarb (leaves far higher than stalks) 500 to 1,300 in stalks; leaves are poisonous Both Beet greens 600 to 900 Soluble Colocasia (arbi, taro) leaves and corms 200 to 500, plus raphides Insoluble raphides cause acridity Tea (dry leaf), cocoa, nuts, star fruit High Soluble 3.2 Mechanism of harm Soluble oxalate absorbed (2 to 15 percent of intake) | v Binds ionised calcium in blood -> hypocalcaemia (acute, high dose only) -> tetany, convulsions, cardiac arrhythmia | v Filtered by kidney, precipitates as calcium oxalate monohydrate (whewellite) in tubules -> acute oxalate nephropathy; chronically, nucleation of calcium oxalate renal calculi (about 75 percent of all kidney stones) Insoluble calcium oxalate (raphides) in colocasia and dieffenbachia | v Needles pierce oral mucosa, with proteolytic enzyme co-released -> burning, itching, oedema of lips and tongue (acridity), rarely airway oedema • In the gut, dietary oxalate binds calcium and lowers calcium absorption (antinutrient effect); conversely, dietary calcium taken with an oxalate-rich meal binds oxalate in the lumen and reduces oxalate absorption, which is why spinach with paneer or yoghurt is nutritionally rational. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS • Acute lethal dose of oxalic acid is about 15 to 30 g in adults (not achievable from spinach, but achievable from rhubarb leaves or industrial oxalic acid, the classical 'salt of sorrel' poison). 3.3 Processing • Boiling leaves in a large volume of water and discarding it removes 30 to 90 percent of soluble oxalate (depends on surface area and water volume); steaming removes less; frying removes almost none because there is no aqueous phase. • Cooking colocasia with tamarind, lime or amchur (acid) and with calcium-rich ingredients reduces acridity; adequate boiling softens raphides. • Stone patients are advised to limit high-oxalate foods, drink ample water and not to restrict dietary calcium. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Spinach is not a good calcium source despite its high calcium content, because the calcium is largely locked as oxalate. Rhubarb stalks are edible; rhubarb leaves are toxic. 'Frying removes oxalate' is false. 4. Argemone mexicana and Epidemic Dropsy 4.1 The adulterant • Argemone mexicana (prickly poppy, satyanashi, pili kateli, Mexican poppy) grows as a weed in mustard fields. Its seeds resemble black mustard (Brassica nigra) seeds in size and colour and are harvested with the crop or added deliberately because the seed oil is cheap. • Argemone seeds contain 30 to 35 percent of a pale yellow oil rich in the benzophenanthridine (isoquinoline) alkaloids sanguinarine (about 0.3 percent of oil) and its reduced form dihydrosanguinarine (about 1 percent); the seed also contains protopine and berberine. Dihydrosanguinarine is converted to sanguinarine in the body. • Dangerous level: oil containing about 1 percent argemone oil (0.01 percent sanguinarine) causes disease; outbreaks occur with 2 to 10 percent adulteration. 4.2 Mechanism Sanguinarine (a quaternary benzophenanthridine cation) | +--> Inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase (ouabain-like) in vascular endothelium | and cardiac muscle -> endothelial swelling, increased capillary | permeability, plasma leakage | +--> Inhibits pyruvate oxidation and glucose-6-phosphatase, depletes | hepatic glycogen; oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation | +--> Dilates capillaries and arterioles; pooling of blood | v Non-inflammatory, bilateral pitting oedema of the legs, hypoproteinaemia, high-output cardiac failure, retinal vascular dilatation and haemorrhages, raised intra-ocular pressure (glaucoma) 4.3 Clinical pathology (epidemic dropsy) • Onset 1 to 3 weeks after eating the adulterated oil; whole households fall ill together, which distinguishes it from cardiac or renal dropsy. • Gastrointestinal prodrome: diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of appetite. • Dropsy: bilateral pitting oedema of the lower limbs that spreads upwards, with erythema, tenderness and a sensation of heat; dilated superficial veins; sarcoid-like skin nodules; hair loss. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 15

can cause blindness. • Others: mild anaemia, fever, breathlessness, proteinuria, hepatomegaly. • Major outbreaks: Calcutta 1877 (first description); Delhi 1998 (about 3,000 cases, more than 60 deaths, which triggered the ban on loose sale of edible oil); recurring episodes in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gwalior 2000 and 2012. • Treatment is supportive (diuretics, calcium, antioxidants, management of glaucoma); removal of the oil from the diet is curative in survivors. 4.4 Analytical identification Test Principle Procedure Sensitivity Shake 5 mL oil with 5 mL Sanguinarine forms a coloured concentrated nitric acid in a test Nitric acid test (Hofmann test, Detects about 0.25 percent and (red to orange-red) complex with tube; comparison of Rf with ultraviolet authentic sanguinarine Thin-layer chromatography and Quantitative estimation of Silica gel plate or reversed-phase Quantitative confirmation, high-performance liquid sanguinarine and column, fluorescence or microgram levels chromatography dihydrosanguinarine ultraviolet detection Argemone seed is black, rough, with a reticulated (net-like) surface, slightly larger than Physical examination of seed mustard, bitter, and shows a Hand lens and crushing test Field screening white kernel inside when crushed; mustard seed is smooth with a yellowish kernel 4.5 Statutory position • Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, standard for mustard oil and all edible oils: the test for argemone oil shall be negative; argemone oil is a prohibited adulterant with nil tolerance. • Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011: prohibition on sale of edible oil adulterated with argemone oil and, since 1998, restriction on sale of loose edible oil (packaged oil must carry the manufacturer's identification). • Under the Act, argemone adulteration that causes injury is treated as unsafe food attracting the severest penalties (Section 59, up to life imprisonment where death results). [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Epidemic dropsy is not a nutritional oedema (not protein-energy malnutrition) and not a cardiac disease of the individual; it is a poisoning that affects a whole family. The screening test is nitric acid (0.25 percent); the confirmatory and most sensitive test is paper chromatography (0.0001 percent). A pair reversing these sensitivities is false. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Part 2: Marine & Animal Biotoxins PART 2: MARINE AND ANIMAL BIOTOXINS First-principles orientation Most marine biotoxins are made not by the animal eaten but by microscopic planktonic algae (dinoflagellates and diatoms) or by bacteria. Filter-feeding bivalves (mussels, clams, oysters, scallops) concentrate the algae; reef fish concentrate algal toxins through the food chain; pufferfish concentrate bacterial toxin. Nearly all of these toxins are small, water-soluble or lipid-soluble molecules that are heat-stable, tasteless and odourless, so cooking is useless and the only control is monitoring of harvesting waters and the product. The majority act on ion channels or signalling enzymes of nerve and muscle, which is why the clinical pictures are neurological. Shared background: the voltage-gated sodium channel • Nerve conduction and muscle contraction depend on the rapid opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav). Toxins bind at numbered receptor sites: ◦ Site 1 (outer pore mouth): saxitoxin and tetrodotoxin plug the pore and block sodium entry; the nerve cannot fire; result is flaccid paralysis. ◦ Site 5 (transmembrane segments): brevetoxins and ciguatoxins bind, shift activation to more negative potentials and prevent inactivation; the channel opens persistently; result is repetitive firing, paraesthesiae and the temperature-reversal sensation. 1. Shellfish Poisoning Syndromes 1.1 Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning (PSP) Feature Detail Saxitoxin (STX) and more than 50 analogues (gonyautoxins, neosaxitoxin, decarbamoyl and sulphocarbamoyl derivatives); Toxins saxitoxin is a tricyclic tetrahydropurine with two guanidinium groups, water-soluble, heat-stable, acid-stable, destroyed by alkali Marine dinoflagellates Alexandrium (catenella, tamarense, minutum; formerly Gonyaulax), Gymnodinium catenatum, Producers Pyrodinium bahamense; also freshwater cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Aphanizomenon) Mussels, clams, oysters, scallops, cockles; also crabs, lobsters, Vectors gastropods that feed on contaminated bivalves Reversible, high-affinity block of site 1 of the voltage-gated sodium channel of nerve and skeletal muscle; conduction fails; Mechanism neuromuscular transmission and respiratory muscle contraction stop; cardiac muscle is relatively spared One of the most potent known non-protein toxins: lethal oral dose Potency about 1 to 4 mg (about 10 to 20 micrograms per kg); 5 to 30 micrograms per kg causes symptoms Onset 5 to 30 minutes, up to 2 hours: tingling and numbness of lips, tongue and face spreading to limbs; floating sensation, headache, dizziness, incoordination, dysarthria; in severe cases muscle Clinical picture weakness progressing to respiratory paralysis within 2 to 12 hours; consciousness preserved; mortality 1 to 15 percent, mainly within 12 hours if ventilation is not provided; survivors recover fully Treatment No antidote; mechanical ventilation, gastric lavage, activated FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 17

heat-stable Diatoms, not dinoflagellates: Pseudo-nitzschia (multiseries, Producer australis, pungens); also the red alga Chondria armata (from which it was first isolated as an anthelmintic in Japan) Mussels, razor clams, scallops, crabs; also anchovies and sardines, Vectors through which sea lions and sea birds are poisoned Potent agonist at ionotropic glutamate receptors, particularly kainate and AMPA receptors; sustained excitation, calcium overload and excitotoxic neuronal death, concentrated in the hippocampus Mechanism (CA1 and CA3 regions) and amygdala, the brain regions responsible for forming new memories; the blood-brain barrier is crossed poorly, so the very young and the elderly with leakier barriers are most affected Onset 15 minutes to 38 hours: vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; then headache, confusion, disorientation, seizures, coma; survivors show permanent anterograde amnesia (loss of short-term Clinical picture memory), peripheral neuropathy and seizures; first recognised in the Prince Edward Island (Canada) outbreak of 1987 from blue mussels: 107 cases, 3 deaths, 12 with lasting memory loss 20 mg domoic acid per kg (20 micrograms per gram) of shellfish Regulatory limit meat, Codex and worldwide High-performance liquid chromatography with ultraviolet detection at 242 nm (the AOAC reference method), liquid chromatography- Analysis mass spectrometry, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; the mouse bioassay is insensitive [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Three traps in one table: (1) ASP is from a diatom, the other three are from dinoflagellates; (2) saxitoxin blocks the sodium channel, brevetoxin opens it; (3) okadaic acid does not act on an ion channel at all, it inhibits protein phosphatases. A fourth: PSP and ASP limits are both expressed per mass but in different units, 80 micrograms per 100 g versus 20 mg per kg. 2. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Feature Detail between 35 degrees north and 35 degrees south latitude Gambierdiscus produces gambiertoxins; herbivorous reef fish (surgeonfish, parrotfish) graze the algae; carnivorous reef fish eat the herbivores; toxins are oxidised in the fish liver into more potent Bioaccumulation chain ciguatoxins and biomagnified; the largest, oldest predators are most toxic: barracuda, grouper, red snapper, amberjack, moray eel, Spanish mackerel, coral trout; viscera (liver, roe) carry most toxin Ciguatoxin binds site 5 of the voltage-gated sodium channel (same site as brevetoxin but with higher affinity), causing persistent activation at resting potential, spontaneous and repetitive action Mechanism potentials in sensory nerves and swelling of nodes of Ranvier; maitotoxin activates non-selective cation channels and calcium entry, causing calcium-dependent cell damage Onset 1 to 24 hours (usually 2 to 6 hours). Gastrointestinal phase: vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps. Neurological phase: circumoral and extremity paraesthesiae, pruritus, myalgia, arthralgia, and the pathognomonic temperature reversal dysaesthesia or cold allodynia (cold objects feel hot or burning and hot feels cold, Clinical picture because persistently activated cold-sensitive fibres misfire); metallic taste, dental pain, blurred vision. Cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension. Symptoms persist for weeks to months and may be reactivated by alcohol, nuts or fish; mortality below 0.5 percent; ciguatera is the commonest non-bacterial fish-borne illness worldwide (10,000 to 50,000 cases per year) Toxins are heat-stable, freeze-stable, tasteless and not removed by drying, salting or smoking; no visual or sensory test; avoid large predatory reef fish and their viscera; mouse bioassay, receptor- Control binding assay, cytotoxicity assay and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry; United States guidance level 0.01 micrograms P- CTX-1 equivalents per kg fish; intravenous mannitol has been used empirically for neurological symptoms 2.2 Scombroid (Histamine) Poisoning Feature Detail Dark-fleshed, fast-swimming fish with high free histidine in muscle: family Scombridae (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack, seer fish) and Fish involved non-scombroid species such as sardine, anchovy, mahi-mahi (dolphin fish), bluefish, herring, marlin Free L-histidine is decarboxylated to histamine by bacterial histidine decarboxylase (a pyridoxal-phosphate dependent enzyme); the bacteria are normal gut and gill flora, mainly Gram-negative enteric organisms: Morganella morganii (the strongest producer), Chemistry Klebsiella pneumoniae, Hafnia alvei, Enterobacter aerogenes, Proteus, Raoultella; also Photobacterium at low temperature; fastest at 20 to 30 degrees Celsius; production is negligible below 4 degrees Celsius but, once formed, histamine and the enzyme persist Histamine acts directly on H1 and H2 receptors of blood vessels, bronchi, gut and skin, reproducing the picture of an immunoglobulin E mediated allergic reaction without any antibody; it occurs in people with no fish allergy, affects several people eating Why it is a 'pseudo-allergy' the same fish, and responds to antihistamines; co-amines in spoiled fish (cadaverine, putrescine) inhibit intestinal diamine oxidase and potentiate histamine; this is why gut-wall inactivation fails and why patients on isoniazid or monoamine oxidase inhibitors are more sensitive Onset 10 minutes to 2 hours: flushing of face and neck, urticaria, pruritus, headache, palpitations, burning or peppery taste, oral Clinical picture tingling, nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, hypotension, bronchospasm; resolves within 12 to 24 hours; rarely fatal; treated with antihistamines (H1 and H2 blockers) FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 20

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Part 3A: Heavy Metals PART 3A: HEAVY METALS AND TOXIC TRACE ELEMENTS First-principles orientation Heavy metals are not metabolised and not destroyed by cooking; the body can only excrete them slowly. Harm therefore depends on cumulative body burden, on the chemical species (ionic, organic, valence) that determines absorption and target organ, and on the age of the consumer (children absorb more lead, foetuses are more sensitive to methylmercury). Three mechanisms recur: (1) binding to sulphydryl groups of enzymes, (2) displacement of essential metals (lead for calcium and zinc, cadmium for zinc and calcium, arsenate for phosphate), and (3) oxidative stress. The analytical backbone is the same for all: acid digestion (microwave) followed by atomic absorption spectrometry (flame, graphite furnace, hydride generation for arsenic, cold vapour for mercury) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Statutory framework • Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011, Regulation 2.1 (Metal Contaminants), as harmonised with Codex by the 2018 to 2020 amendments: commodity- specific maximum limits in mg/kg (parts per million) for lead, cadmium, mercury, methylmercury, arsenic, tin, copper, zinc, nickel and chromium. • Section 3(1)(zz) of the Act: food is unsafe if it contains contaminants beyond specified limits. • Codex General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995) is the international reference; JECFA sets Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intakes (PTWI) or Provisional Tolerable Monthly Intakes (PTMI). 1. Lead (Pb) 1.1 Sources in food • Leaded petrol (historical), lead-based paints, lead-soldered cans, lead-glazed ceramics (acidic foods such as pickles, fruit juices and curd leach lead), brass and bronze utensils, lead water pipes, contaminated soil and irrigation water near smelters and battery recycling, lead chromate adulteration of turmeric and spices, calcium supplements from bone meal, and dust deposition on leafy vegetables grown by roadsides. • Children absorb 40 to 50 percent of ingested lead; adults 10 to 15 percent; absorption rises with iron, calcium and zinc deficiency and with fasting. 1.2 Mechanism: the haem synthesis block Succinyl-CoA + glycine | delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (mitochondria) v Delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) <-- accumulates and spills into urine (neurotoxic itself) | delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD), a zinc enzyme | *** INHIBITED BY LEAD (lead displaces zinc from the active-site cysteines) *** v Porphobilinogen -> ... -> coproporphyrinogen III (coproporphyrin rises in urine) | v Protoporphyrin IX | ferrochelatase (mitochondrial, inserts Fe2+) | *** INHIBITED BY LEAD *** FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 23

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS v Haem <-- falls; zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP) and free erythrocyte protoporphyrin rise • Result: microcytic hypochromic anaemia (haem synthesis fails despite adequate iron), shortened red cell survival, and basophilic stippling of red cells (lead inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA fragments persist). • ALAD inhibition is the most sensitive biochemical marker; zinc protoporphyrin is the screening marker; blood lead is the definitive measure. 1.3 Neurological and other toxicity • Lead mimics calcium: it enters neurons through calcium channels, interferes with neurotransmitter release, activates protein kinase C, and disrupts the blood-brain barrier. • Children: irreversible loss of intelligence quotient (about 1 to 3 points per 10 micrograms per decilitre at low levels), behavioural problems, hearing loss, growth retardation; acute encephalopathy with cerebral oedema and convulsions above about 70 micrograms per decilitre. No threshold is considered safe; the United States reference value for action is 3.5 micrograms per decilitre. • Adults: peripheral motor neuropathy (wrist drop, foot drop), lead colic (abdominal pain, constipation), Burton's blue line on the gums, nephropathy (proximal tubular damage, gout, chronic kidney disease), hypertension, reduced fertility, and in pregnancy, miscarriage and low birth weight; lead stored in bone is mobilised during pregnancy and lactation. • JECFA withdrew the PTWI of 25 micrograms per kg body weight in 2010 because no safe level could be identified. • Treatment: remove the source; chelation with calcium disodium edetate, dimercaprol or succimer (dimercaptosuccinic acid) in symptomatic or high-level cases. 1.4 Representative FSSAI limits for lead (mg/kg) Food category Limit Milk; infant formula and infant foods 0.02 Cereal grains; pulses 0.2 Fruits; fruiting and root vegetables 0.1 Leafy vegetables (brassicas) 0.3 Edible fats and oils 0.1 Fish 0.3 Crustaceans 0.5 Bivalve molluscs; cephalopods 1.0 (cephalopods) and 1.5 (bivalves) Fruit juices and nectars 0.05 Table salt (iodised and iron-fortified) 2.0 Tea; turmeric (whole and powder); spices (dried) 10 Packaged drinking water and natural mineral water 0.01 mg/L Foods not otherwise specified 2.5 (older general ceiling; verify current status) FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 24

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 2. Cadmium (Cd) 2.1 Sources • Phosphate fertilisers (cadmium is a natural contaminant of rock phosphate), sewage sludge, zinc and lead smelting and mining effluent, electroplating, nickel-cadmium batteries, cigarette smoke (1 to 2 micrograms per cigarette; smokers have double the body burden). • Plants take up cadmium readily: rice (especially in flooded paddies irrigated with contaminated water), wheat, leafy vegetables, potatoes; the richest animal sources are kidney and liver, and the hepatopancreas of crustaceans and cephalopods (crab brown meat, squid), and oysters and mussels. Cocoa and chocolate are also notable. 2.2 Mechanism Ingested Cd2+ (absorption 3 to 5 percent, higher with iron deficiency, as cadmium uses the divalent metal transporter DMT1) | v Liver synthesises metallothionein (cysteine-rich, binds Cd as Cd-MT) | v Cd-MT released into blood, freely filtered by the glomerulus, reabsorbed by proximal tubular cells, degraded in lysosomes, releasing free Cd2+ | v When tubular metallothionein capacity is exceeded (renal cortex above about 200 micrograms per gram), free Cd2+ binds sulphydryl enzymes, generates oxidative stress and triggers apoptosis of proximal tubular cells | v Irreversible proximal tubular dysfunction: low-molecular-weight proteinuria (beta-2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein), glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, calciuria (a Fanconi-like syndrome) | v Loss of phosphate and calcium, reduced renal activation of vitamin D (1-alpha-hydroxylase), plus direct cadmium inhibition of osteoblasts and substitution for calcium in bone mineral | v Osteomalacia and osteoporosis, bone demineralisation, multiple pseudofractures • Biological half-life is 10 to 30 years; the kidney and liver hold about half the body burden; the critical organ is the renal cortex. • Cadmium is classified as a Group 1 human carcinogen (lung, prostate, kidney) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. • JECFA PTMI: 25 micrograms per kg body weight per month (set in 2010, replacing the PTWI of 7 micrograms per kg per week). 2.3 Itai-Itai disease • 'Itai-itai' means 'ouch-ouch', from the cries of pain of patients. Occurred in the Jinzu River basin, Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from the 1910s and recognised in 1955 to 1968; caused by cadmium discharged from the Mitsui Mining and Smelting zinc mine at Kamioka into irrigation water, concentrated in rice. • Victims were mainly post-menopausal multiparous women with low calcium and vitamin D status: severe bone pain, waddling gait, spontaneous fractures of ribs and pelvis, skeletal deformity, height loss, renal tubular dysfunction, anaemia; many were bedridden. lowest in sardine, anchovy, pomfret, small mackerel, shrimp, salmon, tilapia 3.3 Mechanism • Methylmercury has extreme affinity for sulphydryl groups; it binds tubulin and disrupts microtubules (so neuronal migration in the foetal brain fails), inhibits protein synthesis, depletes glutathione, causes oxidative damage and disturbs calcium homeostasis and neurotransmitter release. • The adult brain lesion is focal (cerebellar granule cells, calcarine visual cortex, dorsal root ganglia); the foetal lesion is diffuse because migration is disrupted everywhere. 3.4 Clinical pathology and Minamata disease • Adult methylmercury poisoning (Hunter-Russell syndrome, 1940): paraesthesiae of lips and fingers, constriction of visual fields (tunnel vision), cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, deafness, tremor, cognitive decline; latency weeks to months, dose-dependent. • Minamata disease: Minamata Bay, Kumamoto, Japan; the Chisso Corporation's acetaldehyde plant used mercuric sulphate as catalyst and discharged methylmercury in effluent from 1932 to 1968; fish and shellfish in the bay accumulated it; the disease was recognised in 1956 (cats 'dancing' and dying first); more than 2,200 officially certified patients, more than 1,700 deaths, and thousands more affected; a second outbreak at Niigata (Agano River, Showa Denko) in 1965. • Congenital (foetal) Minamata disease: mothers with little or no symptoms gave birth to children with cerebral palsy-like syndromes, microcephaly, mental retardation, seizures, blindness and deafness, proving that the foetus is far more sensitive than the mother; this is the basis of fish-consumption advisories for pregnant women. • JECFA PTWI for methylmercury: 1.6 micrograms per kg body weight per week (foetal protection); for total mercury 4 micrograms per kg per week. • Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013, in force 2017; India ratified in 2018) phases out mercury products and controls emissions. 3.5 Representative FSSAI limits for mercury (mg/kg) Food category Limit Fish (general) 0.5 total mercury Large predatory fish (shark, swordfish, tuna, marlin, pike) 1.0 methylmercury Other foods (general, older ceiling) 1.0 (verify current specification) Packaged drinking water 0.001 mg/L Table salt and food additives 0.1 (as specified in individual standards) 4. also in rice highly toxic acid) Fish and shellfish (this is why total arsenic in fish is high but harmless, and why limits for Arsenobetaine and arsenosugars Essentially non-toxic, excreted unchanged seafood refer to inorganic arsenic or are set higher) • Groundwater: the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta is the world's largest arsenic calamity: West Bengal (Murshidabad, Nadia, North and South 24 Parganas), Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Jharkhand and Bangladesh, where shallow tube wells tap arsenic-rich alluvial aquifers (geogenic release from iron oxyhydroxides under reducing conditions). • Rice: grown in flooded (anaerobic) paddies, which keep arsenic in the mobile As(III) form; rice roots take up arsenite through the silicon transporters Lsi1 and Lsi2, so rice accumulates ten times more arsenic than other cereals; bran and husk contain the most, so brown rice has more than polished rice; cooking in excess arsenic-free water and discarding it removes 30 to 60 percent, but cooking in arsenic-contaminated water adds arsenic. 4.2 Mechanism Arsenite, As(III) | binds vicinal (paired) sulphydryl groups of dihydrolipoamide in the | pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes v Blocks entry of pyruvate into the citric acid cycle; ATP production falls; also binds keratin (hair, nails, skin), inhibits glutathione reductase and thioredoxin reductase, generates reactive oxygen species, inhibits DNA repair Arsenate, As(V) | chemically mimics phosphate (PO4 3-) v Substitutes for phosphate in glycolysis (1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate forms instead of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and hydrolyses spontaneously: 'arsenolysis'), uncoupling ATP synthesis; is reduced in vivo to arsenite • Hepatic methylation (arsenic methyltransferase, using S-adenosylmethionine) was once considered detoxification; trivalent methylated intermediates are now known to be genotoxic and to inhibit enzymes more strongly than arsenite. 4.3 Clinical pathology • Acute poisoning (rare from food): garlic odour, severe cholera-like watery diarrhoea (rice-water stools), vomiting, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmia (QT prolongation), haemolysis, delirium, death; lethal dose of arsenic trioxide about 100 to 300 mg; delayed peripheral neuropathy in survivors; Mees' lines (transverse white bands) on nails 4 to 6 weeks later. • Chronic arsenicosis (the public health problem): raindrop pigmentation (hyper- and hypopigmented spots on trunk), palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, Bowen's disease, skin cancer (squamous and basal cell), lung and bladder cancer (Group 1 carcinogen), peripheral neuropathy, blackfoot disease (gangrene of toes from peripheral vascular disease, Taiwan), hepatomegaly and portal fibrosis, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, reduced intelligence in children. • JECFA withdrew the PTWI of 15 micrograms per kg in 2010; the benchmark dose lower limit for 0.5 percent increased lung cancer is 3 micrograms per kg per day, within the range of dietary exposures in affected regions. • Treatment: dimercaprol or succimer for acute poisoning; for chronic exposure, provision of arsenic- free water (deep aquifers, surface water, arsenic removal plants using iron co-precipitation and adsorption) is the only effective measure. Tin (Sn) 5.1 Why tin appears in food • Tinplate is steel coated with a thin layer of tin, used for cans because tin is corrosion-resistant and non-toxic at low levels. Inorganic tin is poorly absorbed (less than 5 percent) and has low systemic toxicity, but high concentrations irritate the gut. • Detinning (dissolution of tin into the food) is accelerated by: acidic foods (fruit juices, tomato products, pineapple, rhubarb, pickles; pH below 4), nitrate in the food (from fertilised vegetables and water; nitrate acts as a cathodic depolariser and is the single most important accelerator), oxidising agents, residual oxygen in the headspace, sulphur-containing foods, long storage at high temperature, and opened cans left in the refrigerator (air enters and corrosion accelerates sharply). Acid + nitrate + dissolved oxygen in canned food | v Anodic dissolution of the tin coating: Sn -> Sn2+ + 2 electrons (tin sacrificially protects the underlying steel, which is cathodic) | v Stannous ions in the food, rising with storage time and temperature; hydrogen gas from steel exposure can swell the can ('hydrogen swell', a non-microbial swell to be distinguished from microbial spoilage) • Control: internal lacquering (epoxy-phenolic, vinyl, polyester enamel) of cans for acidic and nitrate- rich foods, low-nitrate raw materials, exclusion of oxygen (hot filling, vacuum closing), cool storage, and transfer of opened can contents to glass or plastic. 5.2 Toxicity • Acute gastrointestinal irritation (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, headache) within 30 minutes to 2 hours when food contains more than about 200 mg/kg tin; recovery is rapid; no chronic effect from inorganic tin at dietary levels; organotins (tributyltin, used as antifouling paint) are far more toxic and are a separate environmental issue. • JECFA PTWI for inorganic tin: 14 mg per kg body weight per week. 5.3 Statutory ceilings Food category Limit Canned foods (processed and canned products, general) 250 mg/kg (FSSAI, aligned with Codex) FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 29

Pesticide Classes 1.1 Organochlorines Compound Status in India Note Metabolites DDE and DDD; half-life in soil 2 Banned for agriculture since 1989; to 15 years; eggshell thinning in raptors; DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) permitted only for public health vector Stockholm Convention persistent organic control (malaria, kala-azar) pollutant BHC or HCH (hexachlorocyclohexane; the Technical HCH banned 1997; lindane Classic contaminant of milk, butter and gamma isomer is lindane) banned 2013 ghee in Indian surveys Banned by Supreme Court order 2011, Endosulfan Kasaragod (Kerala) aerial spraying tragedy phased out Aldrin, dieldrin, chlordane, heptachlor, endrin, All Stockholm Convention persistent Banned toxaphene organic pollutants • Properties: highly lipophilic, chemically stable, resistant to biodegradation, hence persistent in soil and water, bioaccumulate in adipose tissue and biomagnify through the food chain; excreted in milk, so they contaminate dairy fat and breast milk. • Mechanism: DDT holds the voltage-gated sodium channel open (repetitive firing, tremor, convulsions); cyclodienes (aldrin, dieldrin, endosulfan) and lindane antagonise the GABA-A chloride channel (loss of inhibition, seizures). Chronic effects: endocrine disruption (DDE is anti-androgenic), liver enzyme induction, suspected carcinogenicity (DDT Group 2A, lindane Group 1). • Analysis: fat extraction, clean-up by gel permeation or florisil, gas chromatography with electron capture detector. 1.2 Organophosphates Compound Note Low mammalian toxicity because mammalian carboxylesterases Malathion hydrolyse it; used for grain storage and public health Widely used; neurodevelopmental concerns; European Union Chlorpyrifos withdrew approval 2020; MRLs reduced Highly toxic (Class I); monocrotophos caused the Bihar mid-day Monocrotophos, methyl parathion, phorate, phosphamidon meal deaths of 2013 (23 children) Dimethoate, quinalphos, profenofos, acephate Common on vegetables and fruits in Indian monitoring • Mechanism of acetylcholinesterase inhibition: Organophosphate (phosphorothioate, P=S) | hepatic cytochrome P450 oxidative desulphuration (bioactivation) v Oxon (P=O), the active inhibitor | v Phosphorylates the serine hydroxyl of the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase (covalent, initially reversible by oximes) FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 31

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS | v 'Ageing': loss of an alkyl group from the phosphorylated enzyme within hours to days (minutes for soman, 24 to 48 hours for most insecticides); the bond becomes irreversible; recovery needs new enzyme synthesis (weeks) | v Acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses • Clinical picture: muscarinic (DUMBELS: diarrhoea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation; bradycardia), nicotinic (fasciculations, weakness, respiratory muscle paralysis, tachycardia), central (anxiety, confusion, seizures, coma). Death from respiratory failure. Intermediate syndrome (proximal weakness 1 to 4 days later) and organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy (2 to 3 weeks later, from inhibition of neuropathy target esterase). • Treatment: decontamination, atropine (muscarinic antagonist, titrated to drying of secretions), pralidoxime (2-PAM; reactivates the enzyme if given before ageing), diazepam for seizures. • Biomarker: red cell cholinesterase (true acetylcholinesterase) and plasma pseudocholinesterase depression. • Analysis: QuEChERS extraction (quick, easy, cheap, effective, rugged, safe), gas chromatography with flame photometric or nitrogen-phosphorus detector, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. 1.3 Carbamates • Examples: carbofuran, carbaryl, aldicarb (the most toxic; the 'Temik' poisoning of watermelons, California 1985), methomyl, propoxur, thiodicarb, carbosulfan. • Mechanism: carbamylate the same serine of acetylcholinesterase, but the carbamyl-enzyme bond hydrolyses spontaneously within minutes to hours; no ageing; so inhibition is reversible and short- lived, symptoms are similar but briefer, central effects are less (poor blood-brain barrier penetration). • Treatment: atropine; pralidoxime is not generally recommended (and was historically thought to worsen carbaryl toxicity) because the enzyme recovers on its own. • Environmental fate: not persistent, water-soluble, do not bioaccumulate; carbofuran is highly toxic to birds and was banned in the European Union. 1.4 Synthetic pyrethroids • Derived from natural pyrethrins of Chrysanthemum cinerariaefolium but with photostable structures: Type I (no alpha-cyano group): permethrin, allethrin, bifenthrin; Type II (alpha-cyano group): cypermethrin, deltamethrin, fenvalerate, lambda-cyhalothrin. • Mechanism: prolong the open state of voltage-gated sodium channels in insect nerve (Type I: repetitive firing and tremor, T-syndrome; Type II: persistent depolarisation, choreoathetosis and salivation, CS-syndrome); Type II also act on chloride channels. • Mammalian safety: rapidly hydrolysed by esterases and oxidised by cytochrome P450, poorly absorbed through skin, so acute mammalian toxicity is low (selectivity ratio insect to mammal about 1,000); the main human effect is paraesthesia of exposed skin; highly toxic to fish and bees. Piperonyl butoxide synergist inhibits insect P450. 1.5 Neonicotinoids and others (for completeness) • Imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, acetamiprid: agonists of insect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors; systemic in plants; implicated in bee decline; low mammalian toxicity. • Fungicides (mancozeb, carbendazim), herbicides (glyphosate, paraquat; paraquat has no antidote and causes pulmonary fibrosis) and fumigants (aluminium phosphide, phosphine, the commonest fatal poisoning in rural India; methyl bromide, phased out) are other residue classes with MRLs. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Term Definition Who sets it Provisional Tolerable Weekly or Monthly Intake, the equivalent of ADI for cumulative PTWI and PTMI JECFA contaminants (lead, cadmium, mercury) that are not deliberately added 0.01 mg/kg for any pesticide on any commodity for which no MRL has been fixed Tolerance or Default MRL FSSAI (FSSAI, 2018 amendment), functioning as the limit of determination 2.2 Worked derivation • Suppose the rat two-year NOAEL for a pesticide is 2.5 mg per kg body weight per day. ADI = 2.5 / 100 = 0.025 mg per kg per day. For a 60 kg adult, acceptable intake = 1.5 mg per day. • Suppose supervised trials under GAP on brinjal give highest residues of 0.4 mg/kg; the MRL is set at 0.5 mg/kg (rounded to the next standard level). If an Indian adult eats 100 g brinjal per day, the intake from brinjal at the MRL is 0.05 mg per day, which is 3.3 percent of the ADI; summing over all commodities on which the pesticide is registered gives the Theoretical Maximum Daily Intake, which must stay below the ADI or the GAP is revised. 2.3 The chain in one diagram Animal toxicology ---> NOAEL ---> divide by safety factor (100) ---> ADI | Field trials under GAP ---> residue data ---> MRL proposed | | | v v Dietary intake check: TMDI must be below ADI | v MRL notified by FSSAI (Reg 2.3.1) 2.4 Legal architecture in India • Insecticides Act, 1968 and Insecticides Rules, 1971: registration (Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee), labelling (colour triangle: red for extremely toxic, yellow for highly toxic, blue for moderately toxic, green for slightly toxic), bans and restrictions. • Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, Section 19 and Section 20 read with the Contaminants Regulations: no insecticide may be used directly on food except fumigants registered for the purpose; MRLs in Regulation 2.3.1 (Table with over 200 pesticides and commodities); the 0.01 mg/kg default; the Monitoring of Pesticide Residues at National Level scheme (Ministry of Agriculture) generates the surveillance data. • A few representative MRLs (mg/kg; verify against the current table): DDT in milk and milk products 0.05 on a fat basis (older value 1.25 on fat), in fish 7.0 (older); HCH in milk 0.05 on fat; malathion in cereals 4.0, in vegetables 3.0; chlorpyrifos in cereals 0.05, in vegetables 0.2, in cottonseed 0.05; cypermethrin in vegetables 0.5; carbaryl in vegetables 5.0; carbofuran in vegetables 0.1. 3. Veterinary Drug Residues and Antibiotics 3.1 Why residues occur • Antibiotics are used in livestock, poultry, aquaculture and dairy for treatment, prophylaxis and (historically) growth promotion. Residues appear in milk, meat, eggs, honey and shrimp when the withdrawal period (time between the last dose and slaughter or milking) is not observed, when doses are excessive, or when prohibited drugs are used. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS humans through food, water, direct contact and manure on crops | v Treatment failure in human infections; resistance genes transfer to human pathogens (for example, colistin resistance gene mcr-1 from pigs to people) • Policy response: FSSAI Regulation 2.3.2 (2018) with a table of MRLs for about 103 antibiotics and pharmacologically active substances in meat, milk, eggs and aquaculture, plus an annexed list of substances prohibited for use in any food-producing animal (chloramphenicol, nitrofurans, nitroimidazoles, chlorpromazine, colchicine, dapsone, diethylstilbestrol, fluoroquinolones in aquaculture, glycopeptides, sulphonamides in shrimp, and others); the Coastal Aquaculture Authority list of 20 banned antibiotics for shrimp farming; National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (2017); Drugs and Cosmetics Rules amendment (2020) requiring withdrawal period on veterinary drug labels. • Analysis: screening by microbial inhibition tests (Delvotest, Charm) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, confirmation by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Chloramphenicol is not 'restricted to an MRL'; it is prohibited with zero tolerance because aplastic anaemia has no dose threshold. Penicillin residues matter at micrograms per kg because of allergy, not because of general toxicity. A pair claiming that 'cooking destroys all antibiotic residues' is false: tetracyclines and sulphonamides are partly heat-stable, and chloramphenicol survives boiling. 4. Process-Induced Chemical Contaminants 4.1 Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) • Chemistry: fused aromatic ring compounds formed by incomplete combustion and pyrolysis of organic matter above about 350 to 400 degrees Celsius. Benzo[a]pyrene (five rings) is the marker compound; the European Union 'PAH4' group adds benz[a]anthracene, benzo[b]fluoranthene and chrysene. Sixteen PAHs are prioritised by the United States Environmental Protection Agency. • Formation in food: Charcoal grilling, barbecuing, tandoor: fat drips onto the fire, pyrolyses, and PAH-laden smoke redeposits on the meat surface; direct flame contact charring; higher with fattier meat, closer flame, longer time + Smoking of fish, meat and cheese: wood smoke (hardwood above 400 degrees Celsius) carries PAHs; traditional direct smoking far worse than liquid smoke or indirect smoking with filtered smoke + Drying of cereals, oilseeds and cocoa beans by direct combustion gases; roasting of coffee; refined oils (coconut oil from copra dried over fires is the classic high-PAH oil) • Mechanism of carcinogenesis: Benzo[a]pyrene (inert procarcinogen) | cytochrome P450 1A1 and 1B1 (induced by PAHs themselves via the | aryl hydrocarbon receptor), then epoxide hydrolase, then P450 again v Benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-epoxide (BPDE), the ultimate carcinogen | v Covalent bulky adducts at the N2 position of guanine in DNA | v If not repaired by nucleotide excision repair, replication across the adduct FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 36
