text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS causes G to T transversions; the characteristic mutation at codon 157 of the TP53 tumour suppressor gene in smokers' lung cancer is the molecular signature | v Initiation of carcinogenesis (Group 1 human carcinogen: lung, skin, bladder; dietary association with gastrointestinal cancers) • Limits: European Union: benzo[a]pyrene 2 micrograms per kg and PAH4 12 micrograms per kg in smoked meat and fish (previously 5 micrograms per kg benzo[a]pyrene); 2 micrograms per kg benzo[a]pyrene and 10 PAH4 in oils and fats; 1 microgram per kg benzo[a]pyrene in infant foods. Codex has a code of practice for reducing PAH in smoking and drying. FSSAI has adopted benzo[a]pyrene ceilings in edible oils and smoked products in the harmonised amendments (verify the exact figures). • Mitigation: indirect smoking, filtered or liquid smoke, lower temperature, remove charred parts, marinate, pre-cook and finish briefly on the grill, keep food away from flames, avoid fat dripping, dry cereals with indirect heat. • Analysis: saponification or extraction, clean-up on silica or solid-phase extraction, high-performance liquid chromatography with fluorescence detection or gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. 4.2 Acrylamide • Discovery: Swedish National Food Administration, April 2002, after tunnel workers exposed to acrylamide grout were found to have no higher adduct levels than unexposed people who ate fried foods. • Formation: Free asparagine (amino acid abundant in potato, wheat, rye, coffee beans) + Reducing sugar carbonyl (glucose, fructose) | Maillard reaction, above about 120 degrees Celsius, low moisture, | maximal 160 to 180 degrees Celsius v Schiff base -> decarboxylated Amadori product (via Strecker-type chemistry) | v Acrylamide (CH2=CH-CO-NH2): the carbon skeleton comes from asparagine, the sugar carbonyl is the catalyst; minor routes from acrolein and acrylic acid • Foods: French fries and potato chips (highest, hundreds to thousands of micrograms per kg), biscuits, crispbread, breakfast cereals, roasted coffee (and coffee substitutes), toasted bread crust, roasted nuts; not formed in boiled or steamed foods (water keeps temperature at 100 degrees Celsius). • Toxicology: absorbed, distributed widely, metabolised by cytochrome P450 2E1 to glycidamide (an epoxide), which forms DNA adducts (N7-guanine); acrylamide itself binds sulphydryls and causes peripheral neuropathy (occupational), reproductive toxicity in rats; carcinogenic in rodents at multiple sites; Group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans); haemoglobin adducts are the exposure biomarker. • Management: no legal maximum limits in most jurisdictions; European Union Regulation 2017/2158 sets benchmark levels (French fries 500 micrograms per kg, potato crisps 750, soft bread 50, breakfast cereals 150 to 300, roasted coffee 400, instant coffee 850) and mandatory mitigation measures; Codex Code of Practice (2009). • Mitigation: choose low-sugar potato varieties, store potatoes above 6 degrees Celsius (cold storage causes 'cold sweetening' and raises reducing sugars), blanch or soak cut potatoes (removes sugar and asparagine), add asparaginase enzyme to dough, lower frying temperature (below 175 degrees Celsius), fry to golden yellow not brown, add calcium or citric acid, shorter roasting of coffee. • Analysis: liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry or gas chromatography-mass spectrometry after bromination; isotope dilution with carbon-13 labelled acrylamide. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 4.3 Ethyl Carbamate (Urethane) • Chemistry: NH2-CO-O-C2H5, the ethyl ester of carbamic acid; a natural trace constituent of all fermented foods and beverages; once used as a medicine and as a co-solvent, banned when found carcinogenic in 1943. • Formation routes: Route 1 (wine, sake, yoghurt, bread, soy sauce): yeast metabolises arginine (arginase) releasing urea; urea + ethanol -> ethyl carbamate + ammonia, accelerated by heat and storage time; citrulline from lactic acid bacteria (arginine deiminase pathway) is a second precursor via carbamyl phosphate Route 2 (stone-fruit spirits: kirsch, slivovitz, apricot and plum brandies): cyanogenic glycosides in pits release hydrogen cyanide; cyanide is oxidised (copper and light catalysed) to cyanate; cyanate + ethanol -> ethyl carbamate; this is why distilled stone-fruit spirits have the highest levels Route 3: diethyl pyrocarbonate (a former wine preservative) + ammonia -> ethyl carbamate; the preservative was banned in 1972 for this reason • Toxicology: metabolised by cytochrome P450 2E1 to vinyl carbamate and its epoxide, which forms DNA adducts; multisite carcinogen in rodents (lung, liver, lymphoma, mammary); Group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans); JECFA margin of exposure for heavy consumers of stone-fruit spirits is of concern. • Typical levels: wines 1 to 30 micrograms per L; sake and sherry higher; stone-fruit brandies up to several mg per L; bread and yoghurt a few micrograms per kg. • Limits: Canada (the first regulator, 1985): table wine 30 micrograms per L, fortified wine 100, distilled spirits 150, fruit brandies 400, sake 200; United States voluntary targets (wine 15 micrograms per L); Codex Code of Practice (2011) for stone-fruit distillates; European Union target 1 mg per L in stone- fruit spirits. • Mitigation: low-urea yeast strains, acid urease addition to wine and sake, limiting arginine (vineyard nitrogen management), removing pits before mashing, copper catalysts in stills to remove cyanide, storing spirits in the dark, controlled distillation cuts. • Analysis: extraction, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with selected ion monitoring; Dedicated [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Compendium Trap 1: Neurolathyrism (BOAA, Lathyrus sativus, spastic paraparesis) versus osteolathyrism (beta- aminopropionitrile, Lathyrus odoratus, skeletal collagen defect). Trap 2: Linamarin is cassava; amygdalin is bitter almond and apricot kernel; dhurrin is sorghum. Boiling intact bitter cassava is less effective than grating followed by soaking because heat inactivates linamarase before it can free the cyanide. Trap 3: Favism affects only G6PD-deficient individuals; the glycosides are heat-stable; the mechanism is oxidative haemolysis, not cyanide and not allergy. Trap 4: Slow cooking of kidney beans at 70 to 80 degrees Celsius increases lectin activity up to five-fold; only boiling destroys it. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 41

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Trap 5: Kunitz inhibitor is single-headed (trypsin) and heat-labile; Bowman-Birk is double-headed (trypsin and chymotrypsin) and heat-stable. Trap 6: Glycoalkaloid limit 200 mg/kg is for the total of solanine plus chaconine; they survive boiling and frying; peeling is the remedy. Trap 7: Goitrin (from progoitrin) blocks thyroid peroxidase and is not overcome by iodine; thiocyanate (from indole and other glucosinolates, and from cassava) blocks the iodide symporter and is overcome by iodine. Sinigrin gives allyl isothiocyanate, not goitrin. Trap 8: Argemone: nitric acid test is the screening test (0.25 percent); paper chromatography is the confirmatory, most sensitive test (0.0001 percent); the alkaloid is sanguinarine; the statutory tolerance is nil. Trap 9: ASP is from a diatom (Pseudo-nitzschia); PSP, DSP and NSP are from dinoflagellates. Saxitoxin and tetrodotoxin block sodium channels; brevetoxin and ciguatoxin activate them; okadaic acid inhibits phosphatases, not channels. Trap 10: Scombroid poisoning is not an allergy, is not destroyed by cooking or canning, and is prevented by rapid chilling below 4 degrees Celsius after catch. Trap 11: Lead inhibits ALAD and ferrochelatase (anaemia with normal iron), cadmium causes Itai-itai (Toyama, Japan), methylmercury causes Minamata (Kumamoto, Japan), arsenic causes blackfoot disease (Taiwan) and arsenicosis (West Bengal). Do not cross-match the place names. Trap 12: ADI = NOAEL / 100 (not multiplied). MRL is a Good Agricultural Practice trading standard, not a toxicological threshold; the default MRL where none exists is 0.01 mg/kg. Trap 13: Carbamate acetylcholinesterase inhibition is reversible without ageing; pralidoxime is for organophosphates. Chloramphenicol has zero tolerance (aplastic anaemia has no threshold); penicillin's milk MRL is 4 micrograms per kg because of allergy. Trap 14: Acrylamide needs asparagine plus reducing sugar above 120 degrees Celsius and is absent from boiled food; benzo[a]pyrene comes from pyrolysis above 350 to 400 degrees Celsius and smoke; ethyl carbamate comes from urea or cyanate plus ethanol in fermented and distilled products. 5. Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Questions (exactly 4) Instruction: For each question, three statements are given. Determine how many are correct and choose Only 1 / Only 2 / All 3 / None. Verification uses N = c1 + c2 + c3, where c = 1 for a correct pair and c = 0 for an incorrect pair. Question 1: Legume toxicants • (i) BOAA, the neurotoxin of Lathyrus sativus, acts as an agonist at AMPA-type glutamate receptors. • (ii) Amygdalin is the principal cyanogenic glycoside of cassava (tapioca). • (iii) The Kunitz inhibitor of soybean inhibits chymotrypsin more strongly than trypsin. Step-by-step verification: • (i): BOAA is a glutamate analogue and AMPA receptor agonist causing excitotoxic degeneration of corticospinal tracts. Correct. c1 = 1. • (ii): The cassava glycoside is linamarin (with minor lotaustralin); amygdalin is in bitter almond and apricot kernels. Incorrect. c2 = 0. • (iii): Kunitz inhibitor is single-headed and inhibits trypsin primarily; chymotrypsin inhibition is a feature of the double-headed Bowman-Birk inhibitor. Incorrect. c3 = 0. • N = c1 + c2 + c3 = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. • Answer: Only 1. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 42

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Question 2: Marine biotoxins • (i) Saxitoxin causes paralysis by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels at the neuromuscular junction. • (ii) Domoic acid, the amnesic shellfish poison, is produced by the dinoflagellate Alexandrium. • (iii) Brevetoxins of Karenia brevis act by activating (opening) voltage-gated sodium channels. Step-by-step verification: • (i): Saxitoxin plugs site 1 of the sodium channel; nerve conduction fails; respiratory paralysis follows. Correct. c1 = 1. • (ii): Domoic acid is produced by the diatom Pseudo-nitzschia, not by a dinoflagellate; Alexandrium produces saxitoxin. Incorrect. c2 = 0. • (iii): Brevetoxins bind site 5 and keep the channel open, causing persistent depolarisation. Correct. c3 = 1. • N = c1 + c2 + c3 = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. • Answer: Only 2. Question 3: Heavy metals • (i) Lead causes anaemia by inhibiting delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase. • (ii) Itai-itai disease of the Jinzu River basin in Japan was caused by chronic cadmium exposure through rice. • (iii) The statutory ceiling for tin in canned foods is 250 mg/kg. Step-by-step verification: • (i): Lead displaces zinc from ALAD and inhibits ferrochelatase, blocking haem synthesis; zinc protoporphyrin accumulates. Correct. c1 = 1. • (ii): Cadmium from the Kamioka mine contaminated irrigation water and rice, causing renal tubular damage and osteomalacia. Correct. c2 = 1. • (iii): FSSAI, in line with Codex, sets 250 mg/kg for canned foods (150 mg/kg for canned beverages). Correct. c3 = 1. • N = c1 + c2 + c3 = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. • Answer: All 3. Question 4: Residues and toxicological parameters • (i) Carbamate insecticides cause irreversible 'ageing' of phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase, so pralidoxime is essential in their treatment. • (ii) Chloramphenicol has a defined Maximum Residue Limit in milk under the FSSAI Contaminants Regulations. • (iii) The Acceptable Daily Intake is obtained by multiplying the NOAEL by the safety factor of 100. Step-by-step verification: • (i): Carbamates carbamylate the enzyme reversibly; the bond hydrolyses spontaneously; there is no ageing; pralidoxime is not routinely indicated. Incorrect. c1 = 0. • (ii): Chloramphenicol is on the prohibited (zero-tolerance) list for all food-producing animals because aplastic anaemia has no threshold; no MRL exists. Incorrect. c2 = 0. • (iii): ADI = NOAEL divided by the safety factor (NOAEL / 100), not multiplied. Incorrect. c3 = 0. • N = c1 + c2 + c3 = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0. • Answer: None. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 43

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS 6. Stage 2 Model Answer (10 Marks) Question: Detail the biochemical etiology, clinical symptoms, and processing detoxification methods for Neurolathyrism and Epidemic Dropsy. Introduction (1 mark) Neurolathyrism and epidemic dropsy are the two classical Indian food toxicoses of plant origin: the first arises from an inherent neurotoxic amino acid in a legume consumed as a famine staple; the second arises from adulteration of mustard oil with the seed oil of a weed. Both are entirely preventable by processing or regulatory control, and both remain statutory concerns under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Part A: Neurolathyrism (4.5 marks) Etiology. Khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) contains 0.1 to 2.5 percent of beta-N-oxalyl-L-alpha,beta- diaminopropionic acid (BOAA or ODAP), a water-soluble non-protein amino acid in which oxalic acid is amide- linked to the beta-amino group of diaminopropionic acid. BOAA is a structural analogue of glutamate and acts as an agonist at AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors on motor neurons. Sustained receptor activation causes sodium and calcium influx (excitotoxicity), inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, oxidative stress and glutathione depletion, leading to selective degeneration of Betz cells and the long corticospinal axons to the lower limbs. Disease follows consumption of khesari as more than about 30 percent of the diet for 2 to 6 months, mainly in young men doing hard labour, and is aggravated by deficiency of sulphur amino acids and zinc. Clinical features. Prodromal calf cramps and heaviness of the legs are followed by a spastic gait with scissoring and toe-walking. The disease is staged as no-stick, one-stick, two-stick and crawler stages. Examination shows hypertonia, exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, clonus and an extensor plantar response, with sensation, sphincters and intellect spared. The paraparesis is permanent; there is no antidote. Detoxification. Because BOAA is water-soluble, every effective method is a wet method with discarding of the soak water: (1) steeping dehusked dal in hot water at 60 to 70 degrees Celsius for one hour removes 70 to 80 percent; (2) parboiling (soaking, boiling or steaming, discarding water, sun-drying) removes 80 to 90 percent; (3) soaking in 1 to 2 percent lime water (calcium hydroxide) hydrolyses the oxalyl amide bond and removes up to 90 percent; (4) lactic fermentation gives partial removal. Dry roasting and frying are ineffective. Low- toxin cultivars (ODAP below 0.1 percent) are a breeding solution. Statutorily, the sale of kesari gram, kesari dal, kesari flour and their admixtures is prohibited under the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011 (continuing Rule 44A of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules). Part B: Epidemic Dropsy (4 marks) Etiology. Seeds of Argemone mexicana (prickly poppy, satyanashi), a mustard-field weed, resemble mustard seeds and contaminate or are deliberately added to mustard oil. Argemone oil contains the benzophenanthridine alkaloids sanguinarine (about 0.3 percent) and dihydrosanguinarine (about 1 percent), the latter converted to sanguinarine in the body. Sanguinarine inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase in vascular endothelium and cardiac muscle, increases capillary permeability, dilates capillaries, inhibits pyruvate oxidation and glucose-6-phosphatase, and causes oxidative stress. The result is plasma leakage into tissues, pooling of blood and high-output cardiac strain. Oil with about 1 percent argemone oil is sufficient to cause disease. Clinical features. Whole families fall ill 1 to 3 weeks after consuming the oil. After a gastrointestinal prodrome there is bilateral, pitting, non-inflammatory oedema of the legs with erythema and tenderness, dilated veins and skin nodules; tachycardia, cardiomegaly and congestive heart failure (the main cause of death, about 5 percent); and raised intra-ocular pressure causing glaucoma, with retinal haemorrhages and possible blindness. Anaemia, fever, hepatomegaly and proteinuria also occur. The Delhi outbreak of 1998 (about 3,000 cases and more than 60 deaths) led to the restriction on sale of loose edible oils. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 44

doc: Food Toxicology, Inherent Toxicants, Contaminants & Residues
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Detection and control. There is no detoxification; the control is prevention of adulteration, supported by analysis: the nitric acid test (5 mL oil shaken with 5 mL concentrated nitric acid gives a red to orange-red colour; sensitivity about 0.25 percent), the ferric chloride test (orange-brown precipitate on heating; about 1 percent), and the confirmatory paper chromatography of the alcoholic extract, in which sanguinarine fluoresces orange-yellow under ultraviolet light and is detectable to 0.0001 percent; thin-layer and high- performance liquid chromatography quantify the alkaloids. The standard for all edible oils requires the argemone test to be negative (nil tolerance), and adulteration causing injury is punishable under Section 59 of the Act. Conclusion (0.5 mark) Neurolathyrism is an inherent-toxicant problem solved by wet processing and sale prohibition; epidemic dropsy is an adulteration problem solved by analytical surveillance and packaged-oil regulation. The Food Safety Officer's role is to enforce both: seize khesari admixtures in the dal trade and sample mustard oil for the argemone test. 18. Stage 2 Model Answer: 15 Marks Question Examine the classification, physiological mechanisms and statutory regulatory framework governing heavy metals and agrochemical residues in food. Model answer Heavy metals and agrochemical residues are chemical hazards that may enter food through soil, water, industrial activity, agricultural practices, veterinary treatment, processing equipment and environmental deposition. Their risk depends on chemical form, dose, duration, bioavailability and consumer susceptibility. Classification Important toxic elements include lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic and tin. • Lead is a neurotoxic and haematotoxic metal. • Cadmium is a cumulative renal and skeletal toxicant. • Mercury exists as elemental, inorganic and methylmercury forms. • Arsenic occurs as trivalent, pentavalent and organic compounds; inorganic arsenic is the major food- safety concern. • Tin may leach from food cans, particularly into acidic foods. Agrochemical residues include organochlorine pesticides, organophosphates, carbamates and synthetic pyrethroids. Veterinary residues include beta-lactams, tetracyclines, sulfonamides and prohibited substances such as chloramphenicol. Physiological mechanisms Lead Lead inhibits delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase, thereby impairing haem synthesis and causing anaemia. It also disrupts calcium signalling and neurotransmitter function. Children may suffer impaired cognition, developmental delay and behavioural changes. FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 45

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD TOXICOLOGY & CONTAMINANTS Cadmium Cadmium induces metallothionein and accumulates in proximal renal tubules. Chronic exposure produces tubular proteinuria, reduced renal function, bone demineralisation and osteomalacia. Severe chronic exposure is associated with Itai-Itai disease. Mercury Methylmercury is absorbed efficiently from fish, crosses the blood–brain and placental barriers and causes neurological and developmental toxicity. Bioaccumulation and biomagnification make large predatory fish important exposure sources. Minamata disease is the classical example. Arsenic Trivalent arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and inhibits enzymes. Pentavalent arsenic can interfere with phosphate-dependent metabolism. Chronic exposure causes skin lesions, neuropathy, vascular disease and cancer. Contaminated groundwater and rice are important exposure pathways in affected areas. Tin Inorganic tin leached from cans may cause gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea at high concentrations. Organophosphate pesticides Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase and cause accumulation of acetylcholine. Muscarinic, nicotinic and central nervous system symptoms may occur, including salivation, bronchospasm, fasciculations, convulsions and respiratory failure. Carbamates Carbamates reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase and produce a similar but generally shorter-lived cholinergic syndrome. Organochlorines Organochlorines are persistent, lipophilic and bioaccumulative. They may cause neurotoxicity, endocrine effects, reproductive effects and chronic organ toxicity. Synthetic pyrethroids Pyrethroids prolong sodium-channel opening and may cause paraesthesia, tremor and seizures in severe exposure. Veterinary drugs Residues can cause allergy, direct toxicity, disruption of gut flora, antimicrobial resistance and treatment failure. Chloramphenicol is prohibited because of the risk of aplastic anaemia. Regulatory framework The statutory framework is based on the Food Safety and Standards legislation and the applicable regulations relating to contaminants, toxins and residues. Maximum limits for heavy metals are generally commodity-specific. Separate standards may apply to milk, cereals, pulses, vegetables, spices, meat, fish, canned foods and rice. Therefore, a universal lead, cadmium, mercury or arsenic limit should not be quoted without identifying the food category. Tin has a commonly examined statutory ceiling of 250 milligrams per kilogram in canned food. For arsenic, the distinction between total arsenic and inorganic arsenic is essential. Fish standards may distinguish total mercury from methylmercury or apply species-specific controls. Pesticide maximum residue limits are individual pesticide–commodity combinations. A residue below the maximum residue limit is legally acceptable for that combination, whereas the acceptable daily intake is a FOODSAFE • HPSC FSO STUDY NOTES | Page 46

The no observed adverse effect level is used in risk assessment, and a safety factor accounts for uncertainty and biological variability. Veterinary drugs are regulated through permitted residue limits, withdrawal periods and prohibitions. Chloramphenicol is treated as a prohibited residue and is not governed by an ordinary positive tolerance level. Monitoring and enforcement Food control requires: 1. Risk-based sampling 2. Representative collection 3. Validated extraction 4. Atomic absorption or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry for metals 5. Gas chromatography or liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry for pesticide and veterinary residues 6. Screening followed by confirmatory testing 7. Calibration, recovery and uncertainty assessment 8. Comparison with the current notified legal limit 9. Traceability and recall when violations are confirmed Conclusion Heavy metals cause toxicity through enzyme inhibition, oxidative stress, renal accumulation, neurotoxicity and interference with mineral or haem metabolism. Agrochemical residues cause acute cholinergic toxicity, chronic neurological or endocrine effects and antimicrobial resistance. Effective regulation requires commodity-specific maximum limits, scientifically derived acceptable daily intakes, withdrawal periods, prohibition of dangerous substances and reliable laboratory surveillance. 19. How to use this handout This handout teaches each commodity from first principles in a fixed order: physical-chemical nature of the raw material → engineering unit operation → machinery parameters → biochemical transformation → diagnostic quality defect → statutory or trade limit → descriptive answer skeleton. Three labels recur throughout: • Principle: a physical, chemical or biological law that will not change between editions of a textbook. • Convention: a widely taught number or range that varies slightly between references (for example 8–10 percent bran versus 5–8 percent bran in paddy). Learn the ordering and the magnitude; quote the figure used by the examiner's likely source. • Standard: a regulatory or grading figure (FSSR, BIS, USDA, EU). Verify against the currently notified text before quoting it as law. 2. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Freezing point depression, not specific gravity, is the reference method for added water, because sugar or salt added by an adulterator can restore the lactometer reading but every added solute changes the freezing point in a predictable way. A pair stating that cryoscopy detects skimming is wrong; cryoscopy detects water. 1.2 Centrifugal separation and Stokes' law Principle: Fat globules are less dense (about 0.92 g/mL) than skim milk (about 1.036 g/mL), so they rise. The rate of rise of a single globule under gravity is given by Stokes' law: $$v = \frac{d^2 (\rho_s - \rho_f) g}{18 \eta}$$ where $d$ is globule diameter, $\rho_s$ is serum density, $\rho_f$ is fat density, $g$ is gravitational acceleration and $\eta$ is viscosity. Doubling the diameter quadruples the creaming rate; cooling raises viscosity and slows creaming; in raw cold milk the cryoglobulin (IgM)-mediated clustering of globules accelerates creaming far beyond the single-globule prediction. In a centrifugal separator $g$ is replaced by $\omega^2 r$ (angular velocity squared times radius), giving separation forces of 5,000–10,000 g at 6,000–8,000 rpm. The disc-bowl separator stacks conical discs 0.4–0.6 mm apart so that each globule travels only a short distance before reaching a disc surface. Warm milk (40– 55 °C) is separated because fat is fully liquid and viscosity is low. Outputs: cream (35–40 percent fat for butter, 20–25 percent for table cream) and skim milk (0.05–0.1 percent fat). Separation efficiency is judged by skim-milk fat; above 0.1 percent indicates worn discs, excessive throughput or cold milk. A clarifier is the same machine without a cream outlet; a bactofuge removes bacteria and spores by density difference at higher g. Standardisation by the Pearson square Worked example: Prepare 1,000 kg of 3.0 percent fat milk from whole milk at 6.0 percent and skim milk at 0.1 percent. Whole 6.0 ──────┐ ┌── parts whole = 3.0 − 0.1 = 2.9 │ target │ ├── 3.0 ────┤ │ │ Skim 0.1 ──────┘ └── parts skim = 6.0 − 3.0 = 3.0 Total parts = 2.9 + 3.0 = 5.9. Whole milk = 1,000 × 2.9/5.9 = 491.5 kg; skim milk = 508.5 kg. Check: (491.5 × 6.0 + 508.5 × 0.1)/1,000 = (2,949 + 50.9)/1,000 = 3.0 percent. The rule: each component's parts equal the difference between the target and the other component's value, taken across the diagonal. 1.3 Homogenisation engineering Principle: Creaming cannot be stopped by chemistry alone; it is stopped by making the fat globules so small that Stokes' velocity becomes negligible. Reducing mean diameter from 3–4 µm to below 1 µm (practically all below 2 µm) cuts the creaming rate by more than a factor of ten while increasing the total fat surface area 6–10 fold. Mechanical or thermal vapour recompression lowers steam use further. Spray-drying sequence 1. Concentrate is pumped to the atomiser at the top of a tall cylindrical chamber. 2. Atomisation converts the liquid into droplets of 10–200 µm, creating enormous surface area. 3. Hot air (inlet 180–220 °C) contacts the droplets; evaporation is so fast that the droplet surface stays near the wet-bulb temperature (about 50 °C) during the constant-rate period, protecting proteins. 4. Above the glass-transition temperature (Tg) the matrix softens; about 10–20 °C above Tg the particles become sticky and adhere to walls and to each other. Tg of dry amorphous lactose is about 100 °C but falls steeply as moisture rises (water is a plasticiser), so a powder at 5 percent moisture can become sticky at 40–50 °C. A pair stating that high solubility index indicates good solubility is wrong. Roller-dried powder has lower solubility (higher index) because the film is heat-denatured on the drum at 130–150 °C. 1.7 Butter technology Principle (phase inversion): Cream is an oil-in-water emulsion. Churning subjects it to air incorporation and mechanical shock; fat globules are driven to the air bubble surfaces, their membranes are stripped, partially crystalline fat spreads over the bubbles, and when the foam collapses the bare globules coalesce into butter grains. The serum (buttermilk) is expelled and the continuous phase becomes fat: a water-in-oil emulsion with 16 percent water dispersed as droplets of 1–10 µm. Process sequence 1. Cream separation to 35–40 percent fat; neutralisation if acidity is high (to protect fat from hydrolysis during pasteurisation). 2. Pasteurisation of cream at 85–95 °C (higher than milk because fat protects microbes and lipase must be destroyed); vacreation removes feed flavours. 3. Ripening (optional, cultured butter) with Lactococcus lactis subsp. cremoris and Leuconostoc (diacetyl producers) to 0.4–0.5 percent acidity. 4. Ageing at 4–7 °C for 12–16 hours to crystallise fat; the ratio of solid to liquid fat (about 50 percent solid at churning) governs grain formation; the Alnarp tempering program (cold-warm-cold) adjusts spreadability. 5. Churning at 8–14 °C (lower in summer, higher in winter) in a batch churn at 20–30 rpm for 30–45 minutes, or in a continuous Fritz-Eisenreich machine with a high-speed beater (1,000–1,400 rpm) followed by working sections. Break point occurs when grains the size of wheat appear. 6. Draining buttermilk; washing grains with chilled water to remove curd and serum. 7. Salting (salt not more than 3 percent in table butter) and working: kneading disperses moisture into fine droplets (most below 10 µm) so that microbial growth is confined to isolated droplets, removes free water, and gives a uniform close texture. Over-working causes greasy, leaky butter; under-working causes mottled, free-moisture butter. 8. Packaging and cold storage at −20 to −25 °C for long storage. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Part 2: Cereals, Pulses & Grain Technology Part 2. Cereal, Pulse and Grain Technology 2.1 Rice (Oryza sativa) processing Anatomy of paddy Principle: Milling is the mechanical separation of the layers of the grain. Every yield figure in rice milling follows from the proportion of each layer. Share of paddy weight Layer Composition and function Removed at (convention) Silica-rich, inedible, Husk (hull: lemma and 20–22 percent abrasive; used as fuel and Dehusking (shelling) palea) for furfural Fat 15–20 percent, protein, Bran (pericarp, seed coat, 5–10 percent (commonly fibre, B-vitamins, minerals; Whitening and polishing nucellus, aleurone) quoted 8–10) aleurone carries lipase Germ (embryo) 2–3 percent Fat and protein rich Comes off with bran Starch (90 percent of endosperm dry matter; Endosperm About 70 percent amylose 15–30 percent), This is the milled rice protein 7–8 percent (glutelin oryzenin) Theoretical yields: brown rice 78–80 percent of paddy; milled (white) rice 68–72 percent of paddy. Raw paddy milling in India often yields only 62–65 percent, mainly because of breakage. Milling flow sheet 1. Cleaning: sieves, aspirators and destoners remove straw, stones, dust, immature grains. 2. Dehusking (shelling): Rubber roll sheller — two rubber-covered rolls rotating in opposite directions at different speeds (differential about 25 percent; for example 1,100 and 850 rpm) with a gap of about 0.5–0.8 mm; the shear between rolls splits the husk off with minimal breakage; 85– 90 percent shelling efficiency per pass. Older Engelberg (huller) and disc (emery) shellers cause heavy breakage and bran loss and are discouraged. Husk is aspirated off; the mixture of brown rice and unshelled paddy goes to a paddy separator (tray or compartment type, using differences in density, size and surface friction) and unshelled paddy is returned. 3. Whitening (bran removal): (a) abrasive whiteners (Satake vertical cone): a rotating emery cone inside a perforated screen grinds the bran off; low pressure, suitable for hard parboiled rice and the first pass; (b) friction whiteners (horizontal): grains rub against each other and against a ribbed steel rotor at higher pressure; the bran peels off; gives a smoother surface, better for raw rice and the final passes. Modern mills use multi-pass abrasive followed by friction, with bran aspiration to keep the grain cool. 4. Polishing: a soft leather or cloth-lined cone or water-mist polisher removes adhering bran dust and gives gloss (mist polishing). Over-polishing lowers yield and nutrients. 5. Grading: indented cylinders or plan-sifters separate head rice, large brokens, small brokens (brewers) and bran. Food Commodity Processing • 14

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Key milling indices • Head rice yield (HRY): weight of whole kernels (length ≥ three-quarters of the intact kernel) as a percentage of paddy; the single most important economic index because brokens sell at half price. Raw rice HRY 50–60 percent; parboiled rice 65–70 percent. • Degree of milling (DOM) / degree of polishing: percentage of bran removed relative to brown rice weight; 8–10 percent is full milling; under-milled 4–6 percent. Measured by weight loss, surface lipid content, or whiteness meter. Higher DOM lowers thiamine (about 80 percent of thiamine is in the bran and germ) and fat. • Milling recovery: total milled rice as a percentage of paddy. • Breakage is caused by fissures (sun-cracks from rapid field drying, moisture re-adsorption), chalky kernels, immature grain and high milling pressure; optimum paddy moisture for milling is 13–14 percent. Parboiling: hydrothermal processing Principle: Soaking, steaming and drying paddy before milling gelatinises the starch inside the husk. On drying, the starch re-solidifies as a hard, translucent, fissure-free mass, so the grain resists breakage and the bran is held more tightly, while soluble nutrients migrate inward. Conditions (CFTRI hot-soaking Step Purpose method) Hot water 65–70 °C for 3–4 hours (raises paddy moisture to about 30 Cleaning and soaking percent); traditional cold soaking takes Hydrate the endosperm uniformly 2–3 days and causes fermentation odour Saturated steam at 100 °C Gelatinise starch (gelatinisation Steaming (atmospheric) for 5–10 minutes, or temperature 60–75 °C), kill fungi and pressure parboiling at 1–2 kg/cm² insects, inactivate enzymes Sun or mechanical drying to 12–14 Re-solidify starch, allow safe storage Drying percent moisture, ideally in two stages and milling with tempering to avoid stress cracks As raw rice but with higher whitening Bran comes off in larger flakes, Milling pressure (harder grain) preferred for bran-oil extraction Biochemical changes: starch gelatinisation and partial retrogradation on drying; amylose-lipid complex formation (lowers glycemic index, reduces cooking loss and stickiness); migration of thiamine, niacin and minerals from the aleurone into the endosperm (thiamine retention 70–80 percent in parboiled milled rice against 20–30 percent in raw milled rice; this is why parboiling protected rice-eating populations from beriberi); protein denaturation and surface protein film, which reduces solids loss in cooking water; inactivation of lipase (preventing hydrolytic rancidity of the bran, so parboiled bran keeps better and gives better oil); sealing of fissures and hardening (HRY rises to 65–70 percent); husk loosening; colour change to amber-yellow from Maillard reactions and diffusion of husk pigments; development of a characteristic parboiled flavour; insect resistance from hardness and lower free sugars. Advantages Disadvantages Higher head rice yield (less breakage) Colour darkening and off-flavour if soaking is prolonged Higher thiamine and mineral retention Longer cooking time (more energy) Lipase inactivation; better bran oil Extra capital, fuel and water; effluent Lower cooking loss, non-sticky grains, higher swelling Bran is harder to remove; consumes more whitening energy Better storage and insect resistance Vitamin losses from heat if over-processed Easier husk removal Mould growth and fermentation in traditional cold soaking Food Commodity Processing • 15

A pair stating that parboiling removes bran is wrong: bran removal is milling. Parboiling increases, not decreases, the B-vitamin content of milled rice. 2.2 Wheat milling Wheat kernel Bran (pericarp, testa, aleurone) about 14–15 percent; endosperm about 83 percent (starch 70 percent, protein 10–12 percent as gluten-forming gliadin and glutenin); germ 2–3 percent (fat 10 percent, enzymes, vitamin E). Hard wheat (Triticum aestivum hard varieties) has strong adhesion between starch and protein and fractures along cell walls to give gritty flour and strong gluten for bread; soft wheat gives fine, weak-gluten flour for biscuits and cakes. Cleaning Magnetic separator (iron), milling separator (sieves and aspiration for straw, dust), destoner (gravity table), disc or cylinder separator (seeds of other crops, by length), scourer (removes beeswing and surface dirt), washer-whizzer (optional). Cleaning is called the screen room. Conditioning and tempering Principle: The miller wants the bran to come off as large, tough, unbroken flakes and the endosperm to crumble easily. Water does both: it toughens the bran (plasticises the fibrous pericarp so it does not shatter into fine specks that contaminate the flour) and mellows the endosperm (weakens the protein- starch bond). Wheat type Target moisture Resting (tempering) time 18–24 hours (water must diffuse to the Hard wheat 15.5–16.5 percent centre) Soft wheat 14.0–15.0 percent 6–12 hours Durum for semolina 16.0–17.0 percent 12–24 hours (very hard, long diffusion) Warm conditioning (water at 45 °C) shortens tempering; hot conditioning above 60 °C damages gluten. Over-wetting makes the mill choke and the flour mouldy; under-wetting gives bran powder in the flour and high ash. Roller milling: the gradual reduction system Principle: The mill does not grind wheat in one stroke. It opens the grain, scrapes endosperm from the bran in stages (break system), classifies the stock by size and purity (sifting and purifying), and only then grinds the clean endosperm particles (semolina, middlings) into flour (reduction system). Each pair of rolls is followed by a sifter. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Maize kernel: endosperm 82 percent (starch 70 percent of kernel, protein zein and glutelin), germ 11–12 percent (fat 33 percent; source of corn oil), pericarp (bran) 5–6 percent, tip cap 1 percent. Flow sheet 1. Cleaning: remove cob pieces, dust, stones, other seeds. 2. Steeping: kernels soaked in counter-current steep tanks at 48–52 °C for 30–48 hours in water containing 0.1–0.2 percent sulphur dioxide (as sulphurous acid) and lactic acid (produced by Lactobacillus during steeping, about 1–2 percent). Functions of SO2: (a) cleaves disulphide bonds of the protein matrix (zein and glutelin) surrounding starch granules, loosening the granules; (b) suppresses putrefactive and spore-forming bacteria while permitting lactic fermentation; (c) prevents enzymatic browning; (d) softens the kernel to 45 percent moisture. Steepwater is drawn off, concentrated to 50 percent solids as corn steep liquor (CSL) — rich in soluble protein, lactic acid, B-vitamins and minerals; used as a fermentation nutrient (penicillin, citric acid production) and in gluten feed. 3. First grinding (degermination): coarse attrition (Bauer) mills tear the softened kernel open without breaking the oil-rich germ. 4. Germ separation: in hydrocyclones (formerly flotation tanks), the oil-rich germ (specific gravity below 1.0) rises in the starch slurry (specific gravity about 1.08) and is removed overhead. Germ is washed, dried and pressed or solvent-extracted for corn oil (crude, then refined; high in linoleic acid and tocopherols); the germ cake goes to feed. 5. Fine grinding and fibre screening: the degermed slurry is ground finely in impact or attrition mills; fibre (bran) is screened off on fine bend screens (DSM) and washed counter-currently; fibre plus CSL becomes corn gluten feed (21 percent protein). 6. Starch-gluten separation: the mill starch (starch + gluten protein) is sent to continuous centrifuges (primary separators). Gluten protein (specific gravity about 1.1) is lighter than starch (1.5) and comes off as the overflow; it is thickened, dewatered and dried to corn gluten meal (60 percent protein, rich in xanthophyll; poultry feed pigment). 7. Starch washing: the starch underflow is washed in 8–14 stages of hydrocyclones to remove residual protein (below 0.3 percent) and solubles. 8. Starch finishing: dewatered on vacuum filters and flash-dried to 12 percent moisture (native starch), or modified (acid-thinned, cross-linked, oxidised, pre-gelatinised), or converted to sweeteners. Yield per 100 kg maize (dry basis, approximate): starch 66–68 kg, gluten feed 20 kg, gluten meal 5–6 kg, oil 3–4 kg. Steeping uses sulphur dioxide, not sodium hydroxide; the alkaline process (nixtamalisation with lime) is a different, food-use treatment of maize for tortillas that improves niacin availability. 2.4 Pulse processing and milling Principle: A pulse grain is two cotyledons (85–90 percent of grain) wrapped in a seed coat (husk, 10–15 percent) that is attached by a layer of gums and mucilage, strongest in pigeon pea (arhar) and weakest in chickpea and lentil. Dal milling must loosen this gummy bond before the husk can be removed without crushing the cotyledons. Loosening is done by water, oil and heat; removal is done by abrasion; splitting of the cotyledons follows naturally once the husk is gone. Why dehull? Removes the fibrous, tannin-rich seed coat (improves digestibility, cooking time, appearance and reduces polyphenol antinutrients), and splitting shortens cooking. Dehulling does not remove trypsin inhibitors or oligosaccharides (raffinose, stachyose, verbascose: flatulence factors) — these need soaking, cooking or germination. Meat, Poultry, Fish and Egg Processing 3.1 Muscle biology Principle: Meat is skeletal muscle whose living machinery (contraction, energy supply, oxygen transport) has stopped. Everything that happens after slaughter is the running down of that machinery without a blood supply; tenderness, colour and water-holding capacity are the visible results. Structural hierarchy Muscle → bundles (fasciculi, wrapped in perimysium) → fibres (cells, wrapped in endomysium, 10–100 µm diameter) → myofibrils (1–2 µm) → sarcomeres (repeating units between Z-lines, 2–3 µm in resting muscle) → thick filaments (myosin) and thin filaments (actin with tropomyosin and troponin). The whole muscle is sheathed in epimysium (connective tissue) continuous with tendon. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 3.2 Post-mortem physiology Glycolysis without oxygen After exsanguination, oxygen delivery stops. The muscle continues to need ATP to maintain ion gradients and to keep the actin-myosin cross-bridges relaxed. Creatine phosphate regenerates ATP for a few minutes; thereafter the only route is anaerobic glycolysis of stored glycogen (0.5–1.3 percent of muscle): $$\text{Glycogen} \rightarrow \text{Glucose-1-phosphate} \rightarrow \ldots \rightarrow \text{Pyruvate} \rightarrow \text{Lactic acid} + \text{ATP}$$ Because there is no circulation, lactic acid accumulates and pH falls from about 7.0–7.2 in living muscle to an ultimate pH (pHu) of 5.4–5.8 in normal beef, pork and lamb within 18–24 hours (beef) or 6–8 hours (pork), and 2–4 hours in poultry breast. Glycolysis stops when glycogen is exhausted or when the pH inactivates phosphofructokinase, whichever comes first. The lower the pH, the closer proteins are to their isoelectric point (about 5.1–5.3 for myofibrillar proteins), the lower the net charge and the lower the water-holding capacity (WHC). The pH decline is also what makes fresh meat microbiologically more stable than live tissue and what gives cooked meat its typical flavour profile. Fish also carry trimethylamine oxide (TMAO) as an osmolyte, which bacteria convert to the fishy-smelling trimethylamine. Post-harvest autolysis cascade Fish rigor begins within minutes to a few hours (faster if struggled on the hook or stored warm) and resolves within 1–3 days on ice. Nucleotide degradation runs in parallel: ATP ──► ADP ──► AMP ──► IMP ──► HxR (inosine) ──► Hx (hypoxanthine) (ATPase) (myokinase) (AMP deaminase) (5'-nucleotidase, endogenous) (nucleoside phosphorylase, mainly bacterial) • ATP, ADP and AMP disappear within about 24 hours. • IMP (inosine monophosphate) is responsible for the pleasant fresh-fish umami flavour; its accumulation is the peak of eating quality (1–3 days on ice). • Inosine is flavourless; hypoxanthine is bitter and signals spoilage. The IMP → inosine step is autolytic; the inosine → hypoxanthine step is accelerated by bacteria, so the ratio tracks both autolysis and microbial activity. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Deterioration chemistry during storage 1. Carbon dioxide loss through pores: albumen pH rises from 7.6 at lay to 9.0–9.5 within a few days at room temperature (yolk pH rises from 6.0 to 6.4–6.8). This is the primary trigger of all other changes; it is slowed by cool storage, oiling the shell (mineral oil seals pores), coating, or storage in CO2-enriched atmospheres. 2. Thinning of thick albumen: at high pH the ovomucin-lysozyme electrostatic complex dissociates and the ovomucin gel network breaks (β-ovomucin loses carbohydrate), so thick white becomes thin, watery white; Haugh unit falls; the yolk moves freely and the outline becomes visible on candling. 3. Water migration: water moves from the white into the yolk by osmosis; the yolk enlarges and flattens; the vitelline membrane stretches and weakens (yolk index falls); the yolk becomes easier to break and more accessible to any bacteria that penetrate the white. 4. Air-cell enlargement: water loss (0.5–1 percent weight loss per week at ambient) enlarges the air cell; the egg floats in brine when stale (specific gravity below 1.06). 5. Chemical flavour changes: off-flavours from lipid oxidation, absorption of odours through pores, conversion of ovalbumin to S-ovalbumin (poorer foaming and gel strength). 6. Microbial rots: bacteria enter via pores when the cuticle is damaged or the egg is wet (thermal contraction draws contaminated water in, so eggs must not be washed in water cooler than the egg). The albumen's defences (lysozyme, ovotransferrin, avidin, high pH) are overcome by certain Gram-negative bacteria, and the yolk, once reached, supports rapid growth. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Part 4: Horticultural Processing Part 4. Horticultural Processing (Fruits and Vegetables) 4.1 Post-harvest physiology Principle: A harvested fruit or vegetable is alive. It continues to respire, transpire, ripen and senesce using its own stored reserves, because it has been cut off from the plant's supply of water, sugars and minerals. Post-harvest technology is the management of this living tissue to slow its metabolism without killing it. Respiration $$\text{C}6\text{H}{12}\text{O}6 + 6\,\text{O}2 \rightarrow 6\,\text{CO}2 + 6\,\text{H}2\text{O} + \text{energy (about 2,816 kJ, i.e. 673 kcal per mole of glucose)}$$ About 40 percent of the energy is captured as ATP; the remainder is released as vital heat (heat of respiration), which must be removed by the cold store refrigeration load. Vital heat is proportional to respiration rate: leafy vegetables, broccoli, asparagus, mushrooms and berries (high respiration, 20–60 mg CO2/kg/h at 5 °C) are highly perishable and generate much heat; apples, citrus, onions, potatoes and nuts (low respiration, 1–10 mg CO2/kg/h) store for months. • Respiratory quotient (RQ) = CO2 evolved / O2 consumed: about 1.0 for carbohydrate substrate, below 1 for lipids (avocado), above 1 when organic acids are oxidised or when fermentation begins (anaerobic conditions, RQ rises sharply with ethanol and acetaldehyde accumulation). • Temperature coefficient Q10 = (rate at T + 10 °C) / (rate at T). For most produce Q10 is 2–3 in the 5–25 °C range (and higher, up to 4–7, between 0 and 10 °C). Consequence: each 10 °C reduction halves to thirds the respiration rate and roughly doubles or triples the storage life. Pre-cooling immediately after harvest (hydrocooling, forced-air cooling, vacuum cooling for leafy crops, package icing) removes field heat and gives the largest single gain in shelf life. • Chilling injury: tropical and subtropical produce (banana below 13 °C, mango below 10 °C, tomato below 10–12 °C, cucumber and capsicum below 7 °C) suffers membrane phase change at low but non-freezing temperature, with pitting, uneven ripening, browning and decay. Each commodity therefore has a lowest safe temperature. Transpiration Water loss by evaporation from the surface, driven by the vapour pressure deficit between the saturated intercellular air of the tissue and the storage air. Rate is governed by surface-to-volume ratio (leafy vegetables lose fastest), surface structure (cuticle thickness, waxiness, stomata, lenticels, wounds), temperature and relative humidity, and air velocity. A loss of 5–10 percent of fresh weight produces visible wilting, shrivelling and loss of crispness and saleable weight. Control: high RH (85–95 percent; 95– 100 percent for leafy crops), low temperature (lowers vapour pressure), reduced air movement once cooled, waxing (carnauba, shellac on citrus, apple, cucumber), film packaging and liners, curing of root crops (healing of wounds). Climacteric versus non-climacteric fruits Feature Climacteric Non-climacteric After a pre-climacteric minimum, Respiration declines gradually with no respiration rises sharply to a Respiration pattern peak; ripening changes are slow and climacteric peak that coincides with continuous ripening, then declines in senescence Food Commodity Processing • 33

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 4.3 Thermal canning (appertisation) Principle: Canning destroys spoilage and pathogenic microorganisms by heat inside a hermetically sealed container so that re-contamination cannot occur. The severity of the heat process is set by the most heat- resistant pathogen capable of growing in the product, and that depends on pH: Clostridium botulinum cannot grow at pH 4.6 or below, so acid foods need only 100 °C, while low-acid foods (pH above 4.6, aw above 0.85) must receive a botulinum cook at 121 °C. Unit-operation sequence 1. Selection and preparation: sound, uniform maturity (peas at tenderometer reading, mango firm- ripe); washing (chlorinated water 25–50 ppm); sorting, grading; peeling (hand, steam, lye at 1–2 percent NaOH at 95–100 °C for 1–3 minutes for peaches and tomatoes, abrasive for root crops); cutting, coring, pitting. 2. Blanching: short heat treatment in hot water (85–100 °C, 1–5 minutes) or steam, followed by cooling (except before hot filling). Purposes: inactivate enzymes that would otherwise cause off- flavour and colour changes during the come-up time and in any under-processed cold spot (lipoxygenase, polyphenol oxidase, pectin methylesterase, catalase, peroxidase); expel intercellular gases (reduces can corrosion, improves vacuum and prevents floating); wilt and soften tissue for filling; fix colour (chlorophyll) and remove raw flavour; reduce microbial load; aid skin removal. Peroxidase test: peroxidase is the most heat-resistant of the quality-related plant enzymes and is easily measured (guaiacol plus hydrogen peroxide turns brown within 1–3 minutes if peroxidase survives), so its absence proves that all other relevant enzymes are also inactivated; catalase is used as an alternative, less stringent indicator. Over-blanching leaches sugars, vitamins (ascorbic acid losses 10–40 percent) and minerals and softens texture; calcium chloride (0.1–0.5 percent) is added to blanch water for firmness of tomatoes and beans. 3. Filling: hand or machine; syrup (20–40 °Brix for fruits; grades light, medium, heavy) or brine (1–2 percent salt for vegetables); fill weight and headspace (6–9 mm) controlled; drained weight is a standard. 4. Exhausting: heating the filled, open can in a hot-water or steam exhaust box so that the centre reaches 80–85 °C (some references 82–90 °C for 5–10 minutes), or hot filling at above 80 °C, or mechanical vacuum closing. Purposes: expel air from the headspace and tissue so that, after sealing and cooling, a partial vacuum (250–400 mm Hg) forms inside the can; the vacuum prevents bulging during processing and at altitude, minimises oxidation (discolouration, vitamin C loss), reduces internal corrosion and strain on seams, and lets the ends stay concave as a visible indicator of soundness. Vacuum is a consequence of exhausting, not of the retort. 5. Sealing (double seaming): the can lid (end) is mechanically interlocked with the body flange in two operations: the first-operation roll curls the end hook under the body hook; the second- operation roll flattens and tightens the hooks together with the sealing compound (rubber-based) in the end curl, giving a hermetic seam of five thicknesses of metal (three from the end, two from the body). Seam quality is checked by body hook, cover hook, overlap, tightness and seam thickness; glass jars use lug or vacuum caps. 6. Cooling is to 38–40 °C, not to room temperature, so that the can dries. 4.4 Freezing Principle: Freezing preserves by converting water to ice (removing it as a solvent and lowering water activity) and by low temperature slowing all reactions. It does not sterilise: most bacteria survive, some are killed, and enzymes remain partly active, which is why vegetables are blanched before freezing and why frozen fruits are packed with sugar or ascorbic acid. • Ice crystal size and quality: slow freezing (hours; home freezer) forms large extracellular crystals that rupture cell walls, draw water out of cells, and cause heavy drip loss, mushiness and nutrient leaching on thawing. Fast freezing (minutes; passing the critical zone of −1 to −5 °C, where 70–80 percent of water freezes, in under 30 minutes) forms many small intracellular crystals that preserve structure. Recrystallisation (growth of large crystals at the expense of small ones) occurs during temperature fluctuation in storage, so a constant −18 °C or lower is needed. • Individual quick freezing (IQF): each piece (pea, corn kernel, berry, shrimp, diced carrot, mango cube) is frozen separately, so the pack is free-flowing and the consumer can take out a portion. Achieved in fluidised-bed freezers (cold air at −30 to −40 °C blown upward through a perforated belt at a velocity that suspends the pieces; freezing time 3–10 minutes), belt tunnel freezers, impingement freezers, or cryogenic freezers (liquid nitrogen at −196 °C, or solid CO2 at −78 °C; freezing in seconds to a few minutes; least drip loss, highest cost; used for shrimp, berries, cut fruit). IQF requires blanched vegetables and firm fruit; glazing (spraying water to form an ice coat) protects IQF shrimp and fish from freezer burn. Food Commodity Processing • 38

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER • Other freezers: air-blast (batch rooms and tunnels, −30 to −40 °C, 3–5 m/s), plate (contact, for rectangular blocks of spinach or fish), immersion (brine or glycol for packaged products), scraped- surface (for juices). • Freezer burn: sublimation of ice from the surface of unprotected product in dry freezer air, leaving a dry, white, spongy, toughened surface; prevented by vapour-tight packaging, glazing and full packs. • Thawing should be slow at refrigeration temperature or in the cooking step (vegetables cooked from frozen) to limit drip and microbial growth. 4.5 Dehydration Principle: Drying removes water until water activity falls below about 0.6 (microbial growth stops below 0.6; enzymes and non-enzymatic browning are minimal around 0.2–0.4). The engineering problem is to remove water fast enough to prevent spoilage and slow enough to avoid damaging the product. Drying kinetics • Constant-rate period: the surface is wet; water evaporates at the wet-bulb temperature as fast as the air can carry it away; rate depends on air temperature, humidity and velocity, not on the product. • Critical moisture content: the point at which the surface is no longer saturated. • Falling-rate period(s): water must diffuse from the interior to the surface; the rate depends on product thickness, structure and temperature; the product temperature rises toward the air temperature, so heat damage is most likely late in drying. Most of the drying time is spent here. • Equilibrium moisture content: the moisture at which the product is in equilibrium with the drying air; the lowest achievable at that temperature and humidity (reason for finishing in a lower-humidity bin). Case hardening If the initial drying is too fast (very hot, very dry air on a sugar- or starch-rich product such as fruit slices or potato), the surface dries and shrinks into a hard, dense, impermeable skin while the interior is still wet. Sugars and dissolved solids carried to the surface by capillary flow crystallise or form a glassy film; proteins and pectins denature and gel at the surface. The skin seals in moisture: internal water can no longer diffuse out, the drying rate collapses, the centre remains moist and later spoils (mould) or the product cracks and splits as the interior finally shrinks. Prevention: moderate initial air temperature and higher initial humidity (or a two-stage schedule: humid-warm then dry-hot), thinner and uniform slices, adequate pretreatment (sulphuring, blanching) and dipping in alkaline emulsions (dipping grapes in ethyl oleate-potassium carbonate removes the waxy cuticle to speed drying uniformly). Stage 1 count-based pair bank (exactly four items) Protocol: score each pair $c_i \in \{0, 1\}$, compute $N = c_1 + c_2 + c_3$, map $N$ to None / Only 1 / Only 2 / All 3. Item 1 — Thermal processing of milk Consider the following process–condition pairs: 1. HTST pasteurisation — 72 °C for 15 seconds 2. LTLT pasteurisation — 63 °C for 15 seconds 3. UHT processing — 135–150 °C for 1–4 seconds How many pairs are correctly matched? Verification: • Pair 1: HTST is 72 °C (71.7 °C in Indian practice) for 15 seconds in a plate heat exchanger with holding tube. Correct. $c_1 = 1$. • Pair 2: LTLT (holder) is 63 °C for 30 minutes, not 15 seconds; the unit has been changed from minutes to seconds. Incorrect. $c_2 = 0$. • Pair 3: UHT is 135–150 °C for 1–4 seconds followed by aseptic packaging. Correct. $c_3 = 1$. • $N = c_1 + c_2 + c_3 = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2$. Answer: Only 2. The trap is the unit substitution in pair 2; the temperature was left correct to lure a careless reader. Item 2 — Wheat roller milling Consider the following pairs: 1. Break rolls — corrugated surface with a speed differential of about 2.5 : 1 2. Reduction rolls — corrugated surface with a speed differential of about 1.25 : 1 3. Maida (straight-grade refined flour) — extraction rate of 70–72 percent How many pairs are correctly matched? Verification: • Pair 1: Break rolls are fluted (corrugated) and run at the high differential of about 2.5 : 1 to shear the kernel open. Correct. $c_1 = 1$. • Pair 2: Reduction rolls have a smooth surface; the differential of 1.25 : 1 is correct but the surface description is wrong, and one wrong attribute makes the pair wrong. Incorrect. $c_2 = 0$. • Pair 3: Maida extraction is 70–72 percent; atta is 95–100 percent; patent flour 40–60 percent. Correct. $c_3 = 1$. • $N = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2$. Answer: Only 2. Note the half-truth design of pair 2: a correct number attached to an incorrect attribute. Item 3 — Post-mortem muscle biochemistry Consider the following pairs: 1. PSE meat — results from chronic pre-slaughter stress that exhausts muscle glycogen 2. DFD meat — ultimate pH above 6.2 and a dark, dry cut surface 3. Resolution of rigor mortis — actin–myosin cross-bridges are released because ATP is resynthesised after 24 hours Food Commodity Processing • 42

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER B. Stage 2 model answer — 10 marks Question Detail the step-by-step industrial sequence of wheat roller milling. Contrast the mechanical actions and extraction products of break rolls versus reduction rolls. Model answer (about 11 minutes; 450–550 words plus one table and one flow sheet) Introduction and principle. Wheat roller milling is a gradual-reduction process whose objective is to separate the starchy endosperm (about 83 percent of the kernel) from the bran (14–15 percent) and germ (2–3 percent) as completely as possible, and then to reduce the endosperm to flour of the required particle size with minimum bran contamination (measured as ash) and controlled starch damage. The process relies on the fact that properly conditioned bran is tough and tears into large flakes, while the endosperm is friable and crumbles. Step-wise industrial sequence. 1. Receiving and cleaning (screen room): magnetic separators remove iron; milling separators (sieves plus aspiration) remove straw, dust and chaff; destoners remove stones by specific gravity; disc or cylinder separators remove other seeds by length; scourers remove surface dirt and beeswing. 2. Conditioning and tempering: water is added to raise moisture to 14–15 percent for soft wheat and 15.5–16.5 percent for hard wheat, and the grain rests in tempering bins for 12–24 hours (shorter for soft wheat). Water toughens the bran so that it does not shatter into specks and mellows the endosperm so that it separates cleanly from the bran and grinds easily. 3. Break system (B1–B5): the tempered wheat passes through four to six pairs of corrugated (fluted) rolls running at a speed differential of about 2.5 : 1. The fast roll shears the kernel open against the slow roll and scrapes the endosperm off the bran in progressively finer stages; flutes increase from about 10–12 per inch on B1 to 26–28 per inch on B5, and roll gaps narrow at each stage. After each break the stock is sifted. 4. Sifting (plansifters): stacked sieves separate each break product into overtails (bran with adhering endosperm, sent to the next break), coarse semolina and fine middlings (sent to purifiers), and a small amount of break flour. 5. Purification: the purifier is an oscillating sieve deck with an upward air current. Light bran chips of the same size as semolina particles are lifted off by aspiration while the denser endosperm particles pass through the graded sieves. This step is what makes low-ash white flour possible. 6. Sizing and reduction system (C1–C12): purified semolina and middlings pass through eight to twelve pairs of smooth rolls at a differential of about 1.25 : 1. The particles are crushed, not sheared, into flour; the germ, being oily and plastic, is flattened into flakes and sifted out; residual fine bran (shorts) is removed as tailings. 7. Flour collection, treatment and packing: flour streams are blended into patent, straight-grade (maida, 70–72 percent extraction) and clear grades; treated with permitted improvers (ascorbic acid, enzymes, fortification with iron, folic acid and vitamin B12); and packed. Whole-wheat atta (95–100 percent extraction) is produced by recombining bran and germ with the flour or by stone (chakki) milling. Flow sheet (in words): Wheat → cleaning → conditioning (14–16.5 percent moisture, 12–24 h) → Break 1 → sifter → Break 2 … Break 5 → bran out; semolina and middlings → purifiers → sizing rolls → reduction rolls C1 … C12 with sifters → flour streams → blending and treatment → maida, patent flour, suji, bran, shorts, germ. Contrast of break and reduction rolls. Food Commodity Processing • 44

Stage 2 model answer — 15 marks Question Examine the post-mortem biochemical changes occurring in muscle tissue from slaughter to the resolution of rigor mortis. Explain the aetiology of PSE and DFD meat defects and evaluate strategies to mitigate them. Model answer (about 16–17 minutes; 750–900 words with two tables) Introduction and principle. Conversion of muscle to meat is the running-down of living muscle metabolism after the blood supply stops. Three linked processes determine meat quality: anaerobic glycolysis and pH decline, ATP depletion leading to rigor mortis, and proteolytic resolution of rigor during conditioning. Abnormalities in the rate or extent of the first process produce the PSE and DFD defects. 1. Immediate post-slaughter phase (0–30 minutes). Exsanguination removes oxygen delivery. Muscle keeps consuming ATP to maintain ion gradients and relaxation. Creatine phosphate regenerates ATP briefly; thereafter the only ATP source is anaerobic glycolysis of muscle glycogen (0.5–1.3 percent). 2. Post-mortem glycolysis and pH decline (30 minutes to 24 hours). Glycogen is converted via glucose-1- phosphate and the Embden–Meyerhof pathway to pyruvate and then to lactic acid, yielding two or three ATP per glucose unit. Without circulation, lactic acid accumulates and pH falls from about 7.0–7.2 to an ultimate pH of 5.4–5.8 within 6–8 hours in pork, 2–4 hours in poultry breast and 18–24 hours in beef. Glycolysis stops when glycogen is exhausted or when low pH inactivates phosphofructokinase. Consequences of the pH fall: proteins approach their isoelectric point (about 5.1–5.3), net charge and water-holding capacity (WHC) fall, the muscle structure opens and scatters more light (paler colour), oxymyoglobin bloom develops on cutting, flavour precursors form, and the meat becomes microbiologically more stable than living tissue. 3. Rigor mortis (onset 1–12 hours; full rigor 3–24 hours). When ATP falls below about 1 µmol/g, the sarcoplasmic reticulum can no longer pump calcium; calcium leaks into the sarcoplasm, myosin heads Food Commodity Processing • 45

The muscle loses extensibility and becomes stiff; WHC reaches its minimum. The degree of sarcomere shortening depends on temperature at ATP exhaustion: cold shortening occurs if pre-rigor muscle is chilled below 10 °C (calcium pump failure in the cold, contraction up to 40 percent, severe toughness), and heat shortening at above 35 °C; thaw rigor follows thawing of pre-rigor frozen muscle. 4. Resolution of rigor: conditioning or ageing (1–21 days). The actomyosin bonds are not reversed. Instead, endogenous proteases weaken the structural scaffold around them. Calpains (µ- and m-calpain, calcium-activated neutral proteases most active early post-mortem at pH 6–7 and regulated by calpastatin) degrade titin, nebulin, desmin and troponin-T, loosening the Z-line and the myofibril–membrane linkages. Cathepsins (lysosomal acid proteases B, D, H and L) are released as pH falls and contribute during longer ageing. The result is progressive tenderisation, partial recovery of WHC and development of aged flavour over 7–21 days at 1–4 °C for beef, 3–5 days for pork and about one day for poultry. Electrical stimulation of carcasses accelerates glycolysis so that rigor is complete before chilling, preventing cold shortening and speeding ageing. 5. Aetiology of PSE and DFD. PSE is the product of too fast a fall while the muscle is warm; DFD is the product of too little fall because glycogen was consumed by chronic stress. First principle: why lipids behave differently from sugars A sugar molecule presents many groups that interact favourably with water. A triacylglycerol presents three long hydrocarbon chains and relatively few polar groups. Water therefore does not dissolve bulk fat readily. Uploaded-source finding: The textbook classifies lipids primarily through their hydrophobic character and solubility in organic solvents, rather than through one universal structural feature. Some lipids are amphiphilic: they contain both water-compatible and water-incompatible regions. Functions in food and nutrition • Supply approximately nine kilocalories per gram. • Supply essential fatty acids and carry fat-soluble vitamins. • Contribute body, tenderness, texture and mouthfeel. • Carry or generate characteristic flavour compounds. • Contribute to satiety. • Participate in emulsions and biological membranes when amphiphilic. Why polyunsaturated fatty acids are oxidation-sensitive Hydrogen abstraction is favoured at positions that form resonance-stabilised radicals. Bis-allylic positions between double bonds are particularly vulnerable. This explains why additional unsaturation generally increases susceptibility to autoxidation under comparable conditions. A practical comparison must still account for antioxidants, oxygen exposure, temperature, metals and the food matrix. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Every unsaturated oil oxidises faster than every saturated fat under all conditions” is too absolute. Molecular susceptibility and actual storage stability are not identical. 5.4. Squalene and vitamin-related distinctions • Squalene has thirty carbon atoms, not forty. • The textbook reports squalene at approximately one to seven grams per kilogram in olive oil and approximately 3.3 grams per kilogram in rice oil. • Cholesterol participates in steroid and bile-acid biosynthesis. • Irradiation of ergosterol produces ergocalciferol, vitamin D2. • Photochemical conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol produces cholecalciferol, vitamin D3. • The fortification compendium nevertheless specifies plant-source vitamin D for the oil and milk vehicles covered by its tables. Source: Lesson 8, pages 50–52; fortification Schedule I. 5.6. Autoxidation: the free-radical chain reaction Intuitive opening A radical is a species containing an unpaired electron. Once a lipid radical reacts with oxygen, the resulting peroxyl radical can remove hydrogen from another lipid molecule. One initiation event can therefore sustain many propagation steps. Let RH represent an oxidisable lipid and R• its carbon-centred radical. INITIATION RH + initiating radical --> R• + hydrogenated initiator PROPAGATION R• + O2 --> ROO• ROO• + RH --> ROOH + R• TERMINATION FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 9

Hydrolytic and ketonic rancidity Hydrolytic rancidity Water breaks ester linkages; lipases accelerate the reaction in suitable conditions. Triacylglycerol + water --> diacylglycerol + free fatty acid Diacylglycerol + water --> monoacylglycerol + free fatty acid Monoacylglycerol + water --> glycerol + free fatty acid The complete net hydrolysis consumes three water molecules per triacylglycerol. Consequences: • Increased acidity and acid value. • Objectionable flavour when sufficient short-chain fatty acids are released. • Reduced smoke point in frying oil. • Desirable flavour development when carefully controlled during certain cheese-ripening processes. At deep-frying temperatures, substantial hydrolysis does not require survival of the original food lipase; heat and food-derived water are sufficient contributors. Certain fungi can convert fatty acids through incomplete beta-oxidative pathways into beta-keto acids. Decarboxylation produces methyl ketones. Related methyl-ketone formation can be desirable in blue-cheese flavour, while uncontrolled formation elsewhere is a defect. A high value is not inherently good or bad: its meaning depends on what is measured. How much steam-volatile, water- Millilitres of 0.1 normal alkali for the Polenske value insoluble fatty acid is recovered under defined five-gram fat sample the prescribed method? A. Saponification value Definition: Milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to saponify one gram of fat under the prescribed conditions. Principle: Reflux the fat with a known excess of alcoholic potassium hydroxide. Back-titrate unused alkali with standard acid. A reagent blank measures the initial alkali available. Triacylglycerol + 3 KOH --> glycerol + 3 potassium fatty acid salts $$Saponification\ value = \frac{56.1(B-S)N}{m}$$ Where: • B is the blank acid titre in millilitres. • S is the sample acid titre in millilitres. • N is the acid normality. • m is sample mass in grams. • 56.1 is the relevant potassium hydroxide mass-conversion factor. For an ideal pure triacylglycerol: $$Saponification\ value \approx \frac{168300}{M}$$ Here M is its molar mass in grams per mole. Three ester bonds account for the factor of three. Interpretation: Shorter average fatty acid chains generally mean more triacylglycerol molecules per gram and therefore a higher saponification value. Qualification: Free fatty acids, unsaponifiable matter and degradation products affect the relationship. It is not a direct chain-length ruler for every degraded or mixed sample. Hypothetical worked example: Blank titre 25.0 millilitres; sample titre 10.0 millilitres; acid normality 0.5; fat mass 2.0 grams. $$Saponification\ value = \frac{56.1(25.0-10.0)(0.5)}{2.0} = 210.375$$ Report approximately 210.4 milligrams of potassium hydroxide per gram. B. Iodine value Definition: Grams of iodine absorbed, expressed as iodine equivalent, by one hundred grams of fat under the prescribed method. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 12

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY Principle: Halogen reagent reacts with carbon–carbon double bonds. The unreacted reagent is determined iodometrically. Method Characteristic reagent Wijs Iodine monochloride in acetic acid Hanus Iodine monobromide in acetic acid $$Iodine\ value = \frac{12.69(B-S)N}{m}$$ Here the titres are thiosulphate titres in millilitres, N is thiosulphate normality and m is sample mass in grams. Interpretation: Greater double-bond content per unit mass generally gives a higher iodine value. The fatty acid chain length and sample composition also influence the result. Frying connection: Oxidative and polymerisation reactions consume or alter unsaturation, so iodine value commonly decreases. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Iodine value measures a bulk unsaturation-related property; it does not identify the omega family or distinguish every cis and trans isomer. C. Peroxide value Definition: A primary oxidation index conventionally expressed as milliequivalents of active oxygen per kilogram of fat. Principle: Peroxide-related oxidants liberate iodine from iodide under the method conditions. Titrate the liberated iodine with sodium thiosulphate. ROOH + 2 I- + 2 H+ --> ROH + I2 + H2O I2 + 2 thiosulphate ions --> 2 I- + tetrathionate ion $$Peroxide\ value = \frac{1000(S-B)N}{m}$$ Where sample and blank titres are in millilitres and sample mass is in grams. Hypothetical worked example: Sample titre 1.50 millilitres; blank titre 0.10 millilitre; thiosulphate normality 0.01; sample mass 5.0 grams. $$Peroxide\ value = \frac{1000(1.50-0.10)(0.01)}{5.0} = 2.8$$ Result: 2.8 milliequivalents per kilogram. Limitation: Formation and destruction occur simultaneously. A decreasing peroxide value during heating does not prove restoration of quality. D. Reichert–Meissl value Definition: Millilitres of 0.1 normal alkali needed to neutralise the steam-volatile, water-soluble fatty acids obtained from five grams of fat under the prescribed procedure. Principle: Saponify, acidify to release fatty acids, distil under specified conditions, separate the appropriate soluble fraction and titrate it. Principal teaching association: Butyric and caproic acids; useful in examination discussions of butter and ghee identity and purity. For a complete recovered fraction: $$Value = (S-B)\frac{N}{0.1}$$ If only an aliquot is titrated, multiply by the prescribed total-volume-to-aliquot factor. In a method using a 100- millilitre aliquot from 110 millilitres, that factor is 1.1. Do not insert this factor into every method indiscriminately. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 13

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY Qualification: This is an operationally defined distillation value, not an exhaustive measurement of every water-soluble fatty acid in the original fat. E. Polenske value Definition: Millilitres of 0.1 normal alkali needed to neutralise the steam-volatile, water-insoluble fatty acids obtained from five grams of fat under the prescribed procedure. Principle: Recover the insoluble volatile acid fraction, dissolve it in the specified solvent and titrate. Principal teaching association: Caprylic and capric acids, with contributions depending on the method; useful for recognising lauric-fat addition. For the complete recovered fraction: $$Value = (S-B)\frac{N}{0.1}$$ Important distinction: Coconut and palm-kernel fats are the relevant lauric-fat comparison. Plain palm oil should not be substituted for palm-kernel oil in a mechanistic explanation. F. Acid value: the essential companion measurement Definition: Milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to neutralise the free acids in one gram of sample. $$Acid\ value = \frac{56.1(S-B)N}{m}$$ Unlike saponification value, acid value does not deliberately count the alkali required to hydrolyse all ester bonds. If free fatty acids are reported as oleic acid: $$Free\ fatty\ acids\ (percent) = \frac{28.25(S-B)N}{m}$$ Approximately: $$Free\ fatty\ acids\ as\ oleic\ acid\ (percent) = \frac{Acid\ value}{1.99}$$ The conversion changes when a different reference fatty acid is used. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 3. Deep-Frying Dynamics DEEP-FAT FRYING: TRANSPORT, REACTION AND QUALITY CONTROL Core source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 9, printed pages 53–55. 1. First principle: frying is not merely heating food in oil A fryer is simultaneously a heat-transfer system, a water-removal system and a chemically reactive lipid environment. Food introduces moisture and solids; the oil supplies heat and becomes part of the finished product. The textbook describes frying at approximately 180 degrees Celsius. This is a representative operating temperature, not a legal requirement that every food must be fried at exactly that temperature. 2. Physical events at the food–oil interface Food enters hot oil | +--> Heat enters the food | +--> Water moves outward and becomes steam | | | +--> Agitation of oil | +--> Steam stripping of volatile compounds | +--> Water available for hydrolysis | +--> Crust and pore structure develop | +--> Oil is carried with or absorbed into the product | +--> Food lipids and solids may enter the frying medium Steam distillation of volatiles Water released by food sweeps some volatile oxidation products out of the oil. Their concentration may approach a plateau when formation is balanced by evaporation, stripping or further reaction. Critical inference: Removal of volatile compounds does not remove the entire nonvolatile degradation burden. Steam blanket The textbook notes that steam above the oil can reduce oxygen availability at the surface. This protective tendency does not eliminate oxidation throughout the fryer. Fat uptake Uploaded-source finding: Finished fried foods may contain approximately 5–40% fat by mass; potato chips are illustrated at approximately 35%. These are broad product examples. They are not a universal absorption fraction for every food, nor are they a legal maximum. Chemical interpretation: Product porosity, surface condition, drainage and cooling affect retained oil. The amount measured includes more than one possible uptake mechanism. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 15
