Polymerisation Intuitive opening When reactive lipid chains join, the average molecular size rises. Large molecules move less easily, so viscosity increases. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 10. Total Polar Compounds: interpretation and statutory boundary What the measurement means Chemical clarification: Total Polar Compounds represent a broad method-defined group of polar constituents in oil. These can include oxidised lipids, partial glycerides, free fatty acids and some degradation-related products. It is not another name for peroxide value and does not represent one single toxic chemical. A compositional expression is: $$Total\ polar\ compounds\ (percent) = \frac{Mass\ of\ polar\ fraction}{Mass\ of\ oil\ sample}\times100$$ Reference fractionation and rapid instrumental estimates are not automatically interchangeable without calibration and validation. Requested regulatory figures Requested figure Evidence status in the supplied corpus Fresh or unused frying oil: maximum 15% Not established by either upload Used frying oil: maximum 25% Not established by either upload These figures are therefore not cited here as verified provisions of the uploaded fortification compendium. Their exact governing regulation, wording, applicability and boundary rule require the relevant food-products or frying-oil notification. A maximum stated as “not more than 25%” and a prohibition stated as “25% or more” differ at the exact boundary. Do not decide that point without the actual legal text. 11. Defensible quality-control approach 1. Control time and temperature rather than relying only on appearance. 2. Remove accumulated food debris using appropriate operating procedures. 3. Minimise unnecessary idle heating and repeated thermal cycling. 4. Assess the oil with measurements appropriate to its history. 5. Interpret peroxide value cautiously in heated oil. 6. Apply the verified statutory discard criterion from the governing instrument. 7. Record oil use, replacement and disposal as required by the applicable framework. Answer-writing conclusion: Deep frying couples heat and mass transfer with hydrolysis, oxidation and polymerisation. Sensory defects are useful warnings, but analytical assessment and verified legal criteria determine a defensible safety decision. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 19

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 4. Module 6 — Enzymes & Kinetics MODULE 6: FOOD ENZYMES AND INDUSTRIAL KINETICS Core source: Food Chemistry, Lessons 6, 15 and 16. 6.1. First principle: an enzyme changes reaction speed, not the equilibrium destination An enzyme provides a lower-energy route to a chemical transformation. It does not supply unlimited energy, make an unfavourable process favourable by itself, or alter the equilibrium constant of the uncoupled reaction. The textbook treats enzymes as proteinaceous biological catalysts with an active centre. The active site includes regions important for substrate binding and catalysis. Chemical clarification: Most familiar food-processing enzymes are proteins, but the statement “all biological catalysts are proteins” is not universally true because catalytic ribonucleic acids exist. 6.2. Enzyme architecture Intuitive opening Some enzymes are complete as proteins alone. Others need an additional chemical component. Removing that necessary component leaves an incomplete catalytic system. Apoenzyme + required cofactor --> holoenzyme Protein part + nonprotein component --> complete functional enzyme system Term Meaning Important distinction Protein portion of a cofactor-dependent Apoenzyme Not the same as a zymogen enzyme Cofactor Required nonprotein component Can be a metal ion or organic molecule Defined primarily by its association Prosthetic group Tightly associated component with the protein Often loosely associated in the Coenzyme Organic catalytic partner textbook’s terminology Complete enzyme with its required Catalytically competent under suitable Holoenzyme component conditions Zymogen or proenzyme Inactive precursor requiring activation Often activated by limited proteolysis Examples of activation Pepsinogen --> pepsin Trypsinogen --> trypsin A zymogen is not necessarily inactive because it lacks a cofactor. Its peptide structure may prevent activity until an activation event occurs. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 20

Six textbook enzyme classes Intuitive opening Classify an enzyme by the reaction it catalyses, not by the food in which it is found. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “All pectin-degrading enzymes are hydrolases” is false. Pectate lyase belongs to the lyases. 6.4. Michaelis–Menten kinetics from first principles Intuitive opening Imagine a fixed number of catalytic workstations. When substrate is scarce, supplying more substrate increases the number of occupied workstations. When nearly every workstation is occupied, additional substrate cannot appreciably increase the rate. Elementary scheme E + S <--> ES --> E + P FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 21

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY Where: • E means free enzyme. • S means substrate. • ES means enzyme–substrate complex. • P means product. • k1 is the association rate constant. • k−1 is the dissociation rate constant. • kcat is the catalytic conversion rate constant in this simple model. Conditions for the elementary equation The derivation assumes initial-rate measurement, negligible reverse product reaction, substrate sufficiently in excess of enzyme, and an approximately steady concentration of the enzyme–substrate complex after the brief initial transient. Not every allosteric or multisubstrate enzyme follows this simple form. Derivation Formation of the enzyme–substrate complex approximately equals its disappearance: $$k_1[E][S] = (k{-1}+k{cat})[ES]$$ Define: $$K_m = \frac{k{-1}+k{cat}}{k_1}$$ The total enzyme concentration is: $$[E]_T = [E]+[ES]$$ Solving gives: $$[ES] = \frac{[E]T[S]}{K_m+[S]}$$ Because the initial rate is catalytic conversion of the complex: $$v_0 = k_{cat}[ES]$$ Therefore: $$v_0 = \frac{V{max}[S]}{K_m+[S]}$$ with: $$V{max} = k{cat}[E]_T$$ Evidence note: The upload describes saturation and gives the half-maximum relationship, but does not supply this full steady-state derivation. The derivation corrects its oversimplified description of the Michaelis constant as an equilibrium constant. The three substrate regimes Substrate concentration Approximate expression Order with respect to substrate Initial rate approximately equals maximum rate multiplied by substrate Much less than the Michaelis constant First order concentration divided by the Michaelis constant Full Michaelis–Menten equation is Comparable to the Michaelis constant Mixed or fractional order needed Much greater than the Michaelis Initial rate approaches maximum rate Approximately zero order constant Low substrate Intermediate substrate High substrate Many sites empty Occupancy increases Sites nearly saturated Rate tracks supply Curved response Rate approaches plateau FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 22

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY Michaelis constant: meaning and units At substrate concentration equal to the Michaelis constant: $$v_0 = \frac{V{max}K_m}{K_m+K_m} = \frac{V{max}}{2}$$ Thus the Michaelis constant is the substrate concentration producing half the maximum rate for the applicable model. Its units are concentration units, not rate units. Affinity: the qualified interpretation The binding dissociation constant is: $$K_d = \frac{k{-1}}{k_1}$$ If catalytic conversion is much slower than complex dissociation, the Michaelis constant approaches the dissociation constant. Otherwise, it incorporates catalysis as well as binding. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] A lower Michaelis constant often suggests greater apparent substrate affinity, but “the Michaelis constant always equals the enzyme–substrate binding constant” is incorrect. Hypothetical worked rate calculation Maximum rate: 100 micromoles per minute. Michaelis constant: 2 millimoles per litre. Substrate concentration, millimoles per litre Initial rate, micromoles per minute 0.2 9.09 2 50.00 20 90.91 At a substrate concentration ten times the Michaelis constant, the rate is approximately 90.9% of maximum, not exactly 100%. 6.5. Lineweaver–Burk double-reciprocal plot Intuitive opening The original saturation curve is curved. Taking reciprocals transforms the elementary equation into a straight- line form. $$\frac{1}{v_0} = \frac{K_m}{V{max}}\frac{1}{[S]} + \frac{1}{V{max}}$$ Plot feature Value Vertical axis Reciprocal of initial rate Horizontal axis Reciprocal of substrate concentration Slope Michaelis constant divided by maximum rate Vertical intercept Reciprocal of maximum rate Horizontal intercept Negative reciprocal of Michaelis constant Hypothetical example: With maximum rate 100 and Michaelis constant 2 in the preceding units: • Slope is 0.02 in the corresponding reciprocal-plot units. • Vertical intercept is 0.01. • Horizontal intercept is −0.5. It is useful for examination interpretation, but fitting the untransformed rate equation is generally preferable for accurate parameter estimation. 6.6. Reversible inhibition Intuitive opening An inhibitor may prevent substrate binding, disable catalytic turnover after binding, or bind preferentially to the enzyme–substrate complex. The kinetic effect depends on which enzyme forms it binds and how strongly. Apparent Michaelis Apparent maximum Effect of high Type Binding pattern constant rate substrate Binds free enzyme in a Inhibition can be manner mutually Competitive Increases Unchanged overcome in the exclusive with elementary model substrate binding Binds free enzyme and Cannot restore the enzyme–substrate Pure noncompetitive Unchanged Decreases original maximum complex with equal rate affinity Binds only enzyme– Does not overcome Uncompetitive Decreases Decreases substrate complex inhibition Binds free enzyme and Does not restore the enzyme–substrate May increase or Mixed Decreases original maximum complex with unequal decrease rate affinities General mathematical framework Let: $$\alpha = 1+\frac{[I]}{K_i}$$ $$\alpha' = 1+\frac{[I]}{K_i'}$$ Here I is inhibitor concentration, Ki describes binding to free enzyme, and Ki′ describes binding to the enzyme– substrate complex. Then: $$v_0 = \frac{V{max}[S]}{\alpha K_m+\alpha'[S]}$$ Consequently: $$V{max,app} = \frac{V{max}}{\alpha'}$$ $$K{m,app} = \frac{\alpha K_m}{\alpha'}$$ Competitive inhibition For competitive inhibition, alpha-prime equals one. • Apparent Michaelis constant increases by the factor alpha. • Maximum rate stays unchanged. • Reciprocal-plot lines share the vertical intercept. • Slope increases. • Horizontal intercept moves toward zero. Textbook example: Malonate competitively inhibits succinate dehydrogenase in the succinate comparison. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 24

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY Pure noncompetitive inhibition For pure noncompetitive inhibition, alpha equals alpha-prime. • Maximum rate decreases. • Michaelis constant remains unchanged. • Reciprocal-plot lines share the horizontal intercept. • Vertical intercept and slope increase. Binding away from the substrate-binding site is not enough, by itself, to prove these exact kinetic changes. Uncompetitive inhibition For uncompetitive inhibition, alpha equals one and alpha-prime exceeds one. • Maximum rate decreases. • Michaelis constant decreases by the same factor. • Their ratio, and therefore reciprocal-plot slope, remains unchanged. • Reciprocal-plot lines are parallel. A lower apparent Michaelis constant does not mean the inhibited enzyme processes substrate more successfully; the maximum rate is also lower. Hypothetical numerical comparison Starting values: Michaelis constant 2 millimoles per litre; maximum rate 100 micromoles per minute. Use an inhibition factor of two. Condition Apparent Michaelis constant Apparent maximum rate No inhibitor 2 100 Competitive 4 100 Pure noncompetitive 2 50 Uncompetitive 1 50 [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Competitive inhibition changes the apparent Michaelis constant. Do not claim that the inhibitor necessarily changes the intrinsic binding chemistry of every remaining unbound enzyme molecule. 6.7. Irreversible inhibition The textbook emphasises covalent attachment to an enzyme group and failure to restore activity through dilution or dialysis. Chemical clarification: Some effectively irreversible inhibitors act through exceptionally tight binding rather than a covalent bond. The operational feature is persistent loss of activity on the relevant timescale. Active enzyme + irreversible inhibitor --> persistently inactive enzyme Loss of active enzyme commonly lowers the observed maximum rate. The full kinetic pattern depends on mechanism and exposure history; irreversible inhibition should not automatically be equated with pure noncompetitive inhibition. Module 7 — Natural Pigments MODULE 7A: NATURAL FOOD PIGMENTS Evidence boundary The uploaded textbook directly treats anthocyanins, carotenoids, annatto and betalains in Lesson 20, and mentions chlorophyll degradation during ripening and tea processing. It does not provide a complete structural account of chlorophyll derivatives, anthoxanthins or meat pigments. Those requested topics are identified below as chemical clarifications rather than attributed to the missing Srilakshmi text. 7.1. First principle: colour comes from molecular electron behaviour Pigments absorb selected wavelengths of visible light. Conjugated systems, metal coordination and changes in molecular form determine the light absorbed and therefore the colour observed. A small chemical change can therefore create a large visible change. Replacing a coordinated metal, changing hydrogen ion concentration or oxidising iron may alter colour without removing the entire pigment molecule. 7.2. Flavour, Sweeteners & Colours MODULE 7B: FLAVOUR ENHANCERS, INTENSE SWEETENERS AND FOOD COLOURS Core source: Food Chemistry, Lessons 18–20, printed pages 99–110. 1. First principle: flavour is a combined sensory experience Taste is largely associated with compounds interacting with oral receptors. Aroma is associated with volatile compounds reaching the olfactory system. Texture also contributes to the overall experience called flavour. A flavour enhancer changes the perceived flavour of a food. It need not be chemically or sensorially identical to an aroma compound. Odour threshold and aroma contribution The textbook defines an aroma contribution ratio as the concentration of a compound divided by its odour threshold in the food. $$Aroma\ value = \frac{Concentration\ in\ food}{Odour\ threshold\ in\ that\ food}$$ A value above one supports the possibility of a detectable contribution, but interactions among compounds and the matrix still matter. 2. Monosodium glutamate Intuitive opening Glutamate provides a savoury taste rather than a fruity aroma. Its effect is especially useful in suitable soups, meat, vegetable and seafood systems. Uploaded-source findings: • Monosodium glutamate is associated with umami taste. • The L-form is the relevant flavour-active form in the textbook account. • Pure monosodium glutamate is odourless. • The textbook describes stronger effects around hydrogen ion concentration conditions corresponding to a pH of six to eight, with reduced effect at lower pH. Chemical clarification: Glutamate activates umami-related taste receptors. Describing it as having no taste of its own is incompatible with recognising umami as a primary taste. Synergy with 5-prime ribonucleotides Compound Main teaching association 5-prime inosinate Umami enhancement and synergy with glutamate 5-prime guanylate Umami enhancement and synergy with glutamate L-glutamate + suitable 5-prime ribonucleotide | v Greater perceived umami than a simple independent-addition model predicts The position of the phosphate matters. Do not assume that every nucleotide or every positional isomer has the same flavour-enhancing activity. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 35

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 8.3. Definitions under Regulation 2 Fortification Deliberately increasing the content of essential micronutrients in food to improve its nutritional quality and provide a public-health benefit with minimal risk to health. Fortificant A substance added to food to provide micronutrients; the definition excludes nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses. Fortified food A food specified under the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, that has undergone fortification according to these regulations. Fortified Processed Foods Processed foods altered from their natural state by industrial processing methods and fortified according to these regulations. They may use fortified staples as raw materials and/or be fortified with permitted micronutrients and additives under the referenced food-products and additives framework. Micronutrients Essential dietary nutrients, including vitamins, minerals and trace elements, required in very small quantities and important for development, disease prevention and well-being. Staple foods Foods intended for mass consumption on a daily basis, including rice, wheat, wheat flour, atta, maida, oil, salt, milk and other foods designated under the regulations. Government-funded programme A programme, policy, scheme or other provision through which Central or State Governments sell, distribute or otherwise make food available to the public. Quality assurance Systematic measures taken by manufacturers and packers throughout manufacturing or packing to ensure that the finished food complies with the Act and applicable standards and regulations. Terminology correction: The upload defines staple foods and fortified food separately. Do not invent a distinct quoted statutory definition of “fortified staple foods” where the supplied definition list does not provide one. 8.4. General principles under Regulation 3 Micronutrients may be appropriately added for: 1. Preventing, reducing the risk of, or correcting a demonstrated deficiency. 2. Reducing the risk of, or correcting, inadequate nutritional status. 3. Meeting requirements or recommended intakes. 4. Maintaining or improving health. 5. Maintaining or improving nutritional quality. Mandatory fortification Where fortification is made mandatory, it must be based on the severity and extent of public-health need demonstrated through generally accepted scientific evidence. The Food Authority may specify mandatory fortification of a staple food on the direction of the Government of India. FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 42

Fortified Processed Foods • May be prepared from fortified cereals and/or milk. • Shall provide 15–30% of the Indian adult recommended dietary allowance of micronutrients on the stated basis of approximately 600 kilocalories from processed foods, representing about one-third of adult daily energy requirements. • High Fat Sugar Salt foods are excluded from the Fortified Processed Foods category. • Their applicable micronutrient levels are in Schedule III. Compliance and tolerance under Regulation 4 The September 2021 amendment substitutes the earlier minimum-only formulation with requirements that: • Added micronutrients declared on the label fall within the Schedule I range. • A tolerance of minus ten percent of the declared total value may be allowed for compliance and analysis at any point in time. • The maximum added-micronutrient limit in Schedule I must still be complied with. What the tolerance does not mean • It is not an automatic plus-or-minus ten-percent allowance. • It does not authorise declaring an out-of-range added nutrient value. • It does not authorise exceeding the statutory maximum through an overage. • The compendium’s wording distinguishes added micronutrients from the declared total value; preserve that distinction. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 1. Physical alterations Moisture release and steam stripping: Water leaving the food becomes steam, agitates the oil and strips some volatile degradation products. Consequently, volatile-product concentrations may approach a plateau even while nonvolatile degradation continues. A steam blanket may reduce oxygen availability above the surface, but it does not eliminate oxidation. Oil uptake and lipid exchange: The textbook reports approximately 5–40% fat by mass in finished fried foods, with potato chips illustrated at approximately 35%. These are product-dependent examples, not universal absorption limits. Fat released from foods such as chicken can change the composition and oxidative stability of the frying medium. Increasing viscosity: Coupled and polymerised lipid products increase molecular size and viscosity. Oil may drain less effectively and the product may become greasy. Foaming, darkening and deposits: Polar degradation products and accumulated food material contribute to persistent foaming, darkening, gums and residues. Normal steam bubbling during frying must be distinguished from deterioration-associated persistent foam. Reduced smoke point: Accumulation of free fatty acids contributes to smoking at lower temperatures. Smoke point is nevertheless influenced by other oil constituents and cannot alone establish compliance. 2. Chemical alterations A. Hydrolysis Food-derived water promotes cleavage of triacylglycerol ester bonds under frying conditions: Triacylglycerol + water --> diacylglycerol + free fatty acid Diacylglycerol + water --> monoacylglycerol + free fatty acid Monoacylglycerol + water --> glycerol + free fatty acid Complete hydrolysis consumes three water molecules per triacylglycerol. The resulting free fatty acids increase acidity and contribute to a lower smoke point. This high-temperature hydrolysis does not require the original food lipase to remain active. B. Thermal oxidation Unsaturated lipid chains undergo oxygen-associated oxidation. A simplified chain mechanism is: Lipid radical + oxygen --> lipid peroxyl radical Lipid peroxyl radical + lipid --> hydroperoxide + new lipid radical Hydroperoxide --> reactive intermediates --> secondary products Hydroperoxide decomposition generates aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, acids and hydrocarbons. Volatile products contribute to flavour changes and may partly escape with steam. Oxygenated nonvolatile compounds remain in the oil. Temperature, oxygen exposure, metals, oil composition and heating duration govern the extent of deterioration. C. Polymerisation and thermal alteration Reactive lipid chains combine through carbon–carbon and oxygen-containing linkages. Cyclic monomers, dimers, trimers and higher polymers can form. Their accumulation increases viscosity, foaming, gum deposition and potentially oil retention by food. The textbook associates greater unsaturation and longer frying time with increased polymerisation under comparable conditions. 3. The ideal inverse relationship between saponification value and pure triacylglycerol molar mass cannot be applied mechanically to that mixture. 4. Why peroxide value alone is inadequate Peroxide value measures peroxide-related primary oxidation, conventionally expressed as milliequivalents of active oxygen per kilogram. It does not measure cumulative deterioration. The central kinetic distinction is: $$\frac{d[Hydroperoxides]}{dt}=Formation\ rate-Decomposition\ rate$$ If decomposition exceeds formation, hydroperoxide concentration falls despite continuing deterioration. High frying temperatures favour rapid decomposition, and the textbook explicitly describes peroxide content rising and later falling. Peroxide value alone is therefore inadequate for five reasons: 1. Hydroperoxides are unstable at frying temperatures. A small measured pool may reflect rapid destruction rather than little oxidation. 2. Secondary oxidation products are not comprehensively measured. Aldehydes, ketones and other products may accumulate after hydroperoxides disappear. 3. Hydrolysis is a different deterioration pathway. Free fatty acids can increase without a corresponding peroxide-value increase. 4. Polymerisation is not represented adequately. High-molecular-mass deterioration products can persist when peroxide value is low. 5. Thermal and sampling history matter. Cooling and oxygen exposure can alter the measured primary- oxidation pool. Oils with different histories cannot be ranked reliably by this index alone. Fresh oil ------------------------------> low peroxide value Severely heated oil with decomposition -> potentially low peroxide value Same index range does not imply the same quality history. 5. Integrated assessment and control Used frying oil should be assessed through a combination of processing history, acidity, appropriate primary- and secondary-oxidation measures, polar-product or polymer assessment, and physical observations. Conclusion Repeated frying produces interconnected hydrolytic, oxidative and polymerisation changes. Peroxide value is useful for primary oxidation, but its rise-and-fall behaviour makes it unreliable as a standalone used-oil quality test. A defensible decision combines complementary analytical measures with the verified applicable regulatory criterion. Worked analytical illustration This is a hypothetical calculation, not measured data from the uploads. For iodometric peroxide-value measurement: $$Peroxide\ value=\frac{1000(V_s-V_b)N_t}{m}$$ Where: • Vs is sample sodium-thiosulphate titre in millilitres. • Vb is blank titre in millilitres. • Nt is sodium-thiosulphate normality. • m is oil sample mass in grams. Assume sample titre 1.50 millilitres, blank titre 0.10 millilitre, normality 0.01 and sample mass 5.00 grams. $$V_s-V_b=1.50-0.10=1.40\ millilitres$$ $$1000\times1.40\times0.01=14$$ $$Peroxide\ value=14\div5.00=2.8\ milliequivalents\ per\ kilogram$$ Permissible inference: The assay detects the stated peroxide-related oxidation level under its conditions. Impermissible inference: The oil must be fresh, safe or legally suitable for further frying. Those conclusions require additional evidence. Legal caveat: Total Polar Compounds thresholds The requested revision targets are 15% for fresh oil and 25% for used frying oil. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 8.21. STAGE 2 DESCRIPTIVE MODEL ANSWER — 15 MARKS Question “Examine the statutory framework of Food Fortification under FSSAI Regulations. Detail the standards for fortified staple foods (Schedule I), mandatory label advisories, and the quality assurance obligations imposed on manufacturers.” Suggested marking breakdown This is a teaching allocation, not an official HPSC marking scheme. Component Suggested marks Definition, scope and general principles 2.0 Schedule I staple standards, permitted sources and units 6.0 Packaging, declarations, logo, exception and iron advisory 3.0 Quality assurance and general compliance obligations 2.0 Label tolerance, amendment distinctions and critical 1.5 evaluation Conclusion 0.5 Total 15.0 Complete model answer Introduction The Food Safety and Standards (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, 2018 establish a food-vehicle-specific framework for deliberately increasing essential micronutrients to improve nutritional quality and provide public-health benefit with minimal health risk. The uploaded 30 September 2021 compendium connects nutrient standards with permitted sources, packaging, labelling, quality assurance and generally applicable food law. Fortification is therefore not simply a nutrient-addition claim: it is a regulated process requiring suitable composition, reliable manufacturing control and appropriate consumer information. 1. Definitions and statutory scope Under Regulation 2: • Fortification means deliberately increasing the content of essential micronutrients in a food to improve its nutritional quality and provide public-health benefit with minimal health risk. • Fortificant means a substance added to food to provide micronutrients; the definition excludes nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses. • Fortified food is a food specified under the Food Products Standards and Food Additives Regulations, 2011 that has undergone fortification in accordance with these regulations. • Micronutrients include essential dietary vitamins, minerals and trace elements needed in very small quantities and important to development, disease prevention and wellbeing. • Staple foods are articles intended for daily mass consumption, including rice, wheat, wheat flour, atta, maida, oil, salt, milk and other designated staples. • Quality assurance means systematic measures throughout manufacturing or packing to ensure compliance of the finished fortified food. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | UNIT 3B • FOOD CHEMISTRY 6. Label range and analytical tolerance The September 2021 substitution of Regulation 4(1) requires the added micronutrients declared on the label to fall within Schedule I ranges. It allows a tolerance of minus 10% of the declared total value on the label for compliance and analysis at any point in time, while expressly requiring compliance with the Schedule I maximum for added micronutrients. The compendium states that this amendment was in force from 22 September 2021, with compliance by 1 April 2022. Three distinctions follow: • Declared added micronutrient levels must be within the applicable prescribed range. • A negative analytical tolerance is not an authorization for a ten-percent upward excess. • “Added micronutrients” and “declared total value” are different phrases in the provision and must not be silently treated as identical where intrinsic nutrients contribute. 7. Critical evaluation The framework combines public-health purpose with product-specific limits and consumer safeguards. Permitted-source restrictions address more than nutrient quantity: bioavailability, food compatibility and stability affect the suitability of the fortificant. The different iron-source ranges illustrate the importance of chemical form. Effective implementation nevertheless depends on manufacturing uniformity, appropriate mixing, representative sampling, nutrient retention, label accuracy and documented quality assurance. A compliant- looking logo is not a substitute for actual nutrient content or reliable process control. Fortified processed foods require separate Schedule III assessment, and High Fat Sugar Salt exclusion prevents nutrient addition from automatically converting a disqualified processed food into an eligible fortified processed product. Conclusion Fortification under the uploaded FSSAI framework is a coordinated system of public-health justification, vehicle- specific nutrient standards, permitted sources, packaging and labelling safeguards, and documented quality assurance. Strong compliance requires both accurate nutrient addition and continued verification of the food placed on the market. Worked statutory calculations Calculation 1 — Parts per million in double fortified salt For mass concentration: $$1\ part\ per\ million=1\ milligram\ per\ kilogram$$ Therefore, the prescribed iron range of 850–1100 parts per million as iron corresponds to: $$850–1100\ milligrams\ of\ iron\ per\ kilogram\ of\ salt$$ For a hypothetical 100-kilogram quantity assessed on the applicable mass basis: $$850\times100=85000\ milligrams=85\ grams$$ $$1100\times100=110000\ milligrams=110\ grams$$ The corresponding iron amount is 85–110 grams. It is not 85–110 grams of ferrous sulphate or ferrous fumarate: carrier mass depends on iron fraction, chemical form and purity. Calculation 2 — Oil vitamin units The schedule states: $$1\ international\ unit\ of\ vitamin\ A=0.3\ microgram\ retinol\ equivalent$$ FOOD LIPIDS • ENZYMES • FORTIFICATION | Page 67

It does not authorize a declaration outside the prescribed range, abolish the maximum added-nutrient limit, establish the treatment of every intrinsic-nutrient contribution, or create a universal Schedule III tolerance. Calculation 5 — Twice-yearly quality assurance undertaking $$1\ year\times2\ undertakings\ per\ year=2\ undertakings$$ “Twice a year” is the stated submission frequency. It does not mean that monitoring, inventory maintenance or testing occurs only twice a year. The listed controls include continuous inventory, stage-wise monitoring and regular audit. The examination logic of count-based pairs A count question asks how many pairs are correct, not necessarily which numbered pair is correct. For three pairs, assign 1 to a correct pair and 0 to an incorrect pair. $$N=c_1+c_2+c_3$$ Here, $N$ is the number of correct pairs, and each $c_i$ is either 0 or 1. • $N=0$: None. • $N=1$: Only 1 pair. • $N=2$: Only 2 pairs. • $N=3$: All 3 pairs. “Only 1 pair” does not mean “pair number 1 only.” The worked banks use this count convention consistently. Negative-marking calculation Under the user-supplied assumption of one mark for a correct answer, a loss of 0.25 mark for an incorrect answer and no loss for an unanswered question, the expected score from attempting a question is: $$E=q(1)+(1-q)(-0.25)=1.25q-0.25$$ The break-even probability is: $$q=0.20$$ This is a mathematical expectation, not a recommendation for indiscriminate guessing. It assumes exactly those scoring rules and does not account for omitted-answer penalties, time cost or errors in confidence estimation. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 3

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Module 1 — Water Dynamics MODULE 1 — WATER CHEMISTRY, MOISTURE SORPTION AND ANALYSIS 1. Foundational overview: amount of water is not its availability Imagine two foods containing the same mass of water. In one, much of that water is associated with dissolved salts or polymer surfaces; in the other, water behaves more like a continuous dilute aqueous phase. Their moisture percentages may be identical, yet their microbial and chemical stability may differ. Moisture content measures quantity; water activity describes an equilibrium property related to the tendency of water to escape. Water holding capacity asks a third question: can the structure prevent liquid from being expelled? These distinctions are the foundation of the entire module. Sources: Food Chemistry, Lessons 1–3, pages 5–29. 2. Molecular architecture of water 2.1 Why a small molecule produces a powerful liquid network Oxygen attracts the shared electrons of the oxygen–hydrogen bonds more strongly than hydrogen does. The resulting unequal electron distribution gives oxygen a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge. A water molecule is therefore electrically neutral overall but polar internally. The oxygen–hydrogen bonds are polar covalent bonds with partial ionic character. This does not mean that ordinary water molecules consist of fully separated oxide and hydrogen ions. The bond angle of an isolated water molecule in the vapour state is approximately 104.5 degrees. Oxygen: partial negative charge O / \ H H partial positive charges Vapour-state angle: 104.5 degrees A hydrogen attached to one oxygen can associate with a neighbouring oxygen through a hydrogen bond. The familiar tetrahedral picture allows one molecule to donate two hydrogen bonds and accept two through oxygen's available electron-pair directions. One water molecule | +--> Two hydrogen-bond donor directions | +--> Two hydrogen-bond acceptor directions | v Approximately tetrahedral local association | v Extended three-dimensional network Liquid water does not possess an immobile ice-like lattice. Hydrogen-bond relationships continually break and reform, allowing fluidity while retaining substantial intermolecular cohesion. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 6

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 3. Water holding, binding and solute interactions 3.1 Water holding capacity: immobilizing flow is not eliminating mobility A gel or tissue can prevent a large volume of liquid from flowing out while still allowing individual water molecules to move and act as solvent. Water holding capacity is therefore primarily a property of the matrix and its ability to retain liquid. Examples in the source include pectin gels, starch gels, plant tissues and animal tissues. Cutting a matrix does not necessarily cause its retained water to flow away. Nevertheless, this water can behave approximately like bulk water during freezing or drying. Syneresis is separation of liquid from a gel. Thawing exudate is another manifestation of impaired retention. Neither defect proves that all molecular hydration water has been removed. Source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 2, page 10. 3.2 Bound water: an operational category Water near strongly hydrophilic sites may have restricted mobility and properties different from those of the bulk aqueous phase. The source presents several operational indicators rather than one universally sharp boundary. These indicators include: • Restricted molecular mobility. • Little contribution to the measured bulk-like permittivity response. • Failure to freeze at a specified low temperature, with minus 40 degrees Celsius explicitly used in the sorption discussion. • Inability to dissolve additional solute in the usual bulk-water sense. • Association with a macromolecule during movement or sedimentation. In a high-moisture food, this strongly associated fraction is small compared with total water. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Bound water contributes absolutely nothing to permittivity” is not the source's careful formulation. The readable passage says it does not contribute significantly. Likewise, “unfreezable at minus 40 degrees Celsius” is an operational observation, not proof that freezing is impossible under every imaginable condition. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 8

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 3.3 Ion–dipole hydration Water orients differently around positive and negative ions. Its oxygen-rich negative end faces a sodium ion, whereas its hydrogen-rich positive ends face a chloride ion. Sodium ion: positive centre <-- oxygen ends of surrounding water molecules Chloride ion: negative centre <-- hydrogen ends of surrounding water molecules Ion–water interactions are described as stronger than ordinary water–water hydrogen bonding but much weaker than covalent bonds. Ionic composition can change mobility, permittivity, colloidal electrical surroundings and protein association. Salting-in and salting-out are consequences developed in Module 3. Source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 2, pages 11–12. 3.4 Hydrophilic nonionic solutes Hydroxyl-containing and other polar nonionic solutes can hydrogen-bond with water. Their interactions are generally weaker than ion–water interactions and comparable in kind to water–water hydrogen bonding. The source explicitly warns that hydrogen-bonding solutes do not all preserve water organization identically: urea is presented as a disruptive example. Therefore, a substance's ability to hydrogen-bond does not automatically establish identical effects on protein conformation or water structure. Source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 2, page 12. 3.5 Hydrophobic hydration and association Nonpolar surfaces are poorly accommodated by an aqueous environment. The source describes their mixing with water as thermodynamically unfavourable: $$\Delta G>0$$ Water reorganizes near an apolar surface. When two apolar regions associate, the total exposed water– apolar interface decreases. This tendency is called hydrophobic interaction in the source. Two exposed apolar regions in water | v Association of apolar regions | v Smaller water–apolar interfacial area | v Contribution to protein folding and association A clathrate hydrate is an inclusion structure in which hydrogen-bonded water forms a cage around a small guest molecule. The textbook uses such structures to introduce water organization around apolar entities. This should not be read as proof that every hydrophobic amino-acid side chain exists inside a rigid crystalline clathrate. Hydrophobic association is a major contributor to the tertiary structure of many proteins, directing numerous apolar residues toward the interior. Source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 2, pages 12–14. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Hydrophobic interaction is not a new covalent bond between nonpolar residues. It is an association tendency arising in the aqueous environment. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 9

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 4. Water activity and equilibrium humidity 4.1 Escape tendency gives an equilibrium measure A water molecule in a food does not have the same escaping tendency as one in pure water. The equilibrium comparison is expressed by water activity: $$a_w=\frac{f}{f_0}\approx\frac{p}{p_0}=\frac{\mathrm{ERH}}{100}$$ Here: • $f$ is the fugacity of water in the food system. • $f_0$ is the fugacity of pure water at the same temperature. • $p$ is the equilibrium water vapour pressure above the food. • $p_0$ is the vapour pressure above pure water at the same temperature. • $\mathrm{ERH}$ is equilibrium relative humidity expressed as a percentage. The vapour-pressure approximation applies under ordinary near-ambient pressure conditions. The temperature must be the same in numerator and denominator. Ambient humidity measured before equilibration is not automatically the food's equilibrium relative humidity. Source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 2, page 15; Lesson 31, page 176. Symbol placement has been normalized to remove the inconsistent wording in Lesson 2. 4.2 Worked calculation Hypothetical practice data: a food equilibrates with a headspace at 65 percent relative humidity. $$a_w=65/100=0.65$$ This result does not reveal the moisture percentage without the food's sorption relationship at the specified temperature. 4.3 Packaged and unpackaged foods Relative vapour pressure depends on temperature, and the extent of that dependence also depends on moisture content. In a moisture-tight package, a temperature change can alter water activity even though the total product moisture has not changed appreciably. An unpackaged product can additionally gain or lose moisture to the surrounding atmosphere. Thus, the two situations cannot be treated as identical temperature experiments. Situation Principal constraint Consequence Temperature can change water activity Product water is approximately Moisture-tight package without requiring external moisture retained exchange Moisture content and equilibrium state Unpackaged food Exchange with ambient air is possible can change together Source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 2, page 15. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Water activity always increases by the same amount when temperature rises” is unsupported. The source states dependence, not a universal direction or magnitude. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 5.3 Glass transition and plasticization A dry polymer-rich region can behave as a glassy solid with restricted segmental motion. Added water can act as a plasticizer, decreasing the glass transition temperature and permitting molecular movement at a lower temperature. It is not a universal 5-percent moisture-content boundary for all foods. 5.4 Hysteresis A dried sample taking up water need not follow the same equilibrium moisture relationship as a moist sample losing water. Failure of the adsorption or resorption curve to coincide with the desorption curve is sorption hysteresis. Moist sample --> water removal --> desorption curve Dry sample --> water addition --> adsorption curve Different histories can produce non-superimposable curves. The source lists food identity, structural changes during drying or hydration, temperature, desorption rate and extent of drying as influences. Accordingly, a hysteresis measurement requires a specified sample history and procedure. Verification required: the accessible text does not develop ink-bottle pore theory. Its detailed mechanism and any universal direction of temperature effects should not be attributed to this upload without inspecting the original relevant figure or another supplied passage. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] An isotherm is not a curve of moisture against time. An adsorption curve is also not automatically interchangeable with a desorption curve. 6. Food stability versus water activity 6.1 Why one curve cannot describe every deterioration mechanism Water can stabilize catalysts by hydration, mobilize reactants, plasticize a matrix or dilute reactants. The balance differs between lipid oxidation, enzyme reactions, browning and microbial growth. Therefore, reduced water activity does not suppress every reaction in the same way. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “All bacteria require above 0.91,” “no mould grows below 0.70,” and “water activity alone proves a food safe” are unjustified absolutes. Reduced water activity can prevent growth without necessarily destroying organisms or eliminating previously formed hazards. 7. Analytical moisture determination 7.1 Moisture content requires a measurement convention Analytical methods do not all measure water in exactly the same way. A drying method measures mass change; a distillation method recovers a separated water volume; a chemical method reacts with water. Matrix composition determines which biases matter. For a gravimetric drying measurement: • $m_0$: mass of empty dry dish. • $m_1$: mass of dish and sample before drying. • $m_2$: mass of dish and residue after drying. $$\text{Moisture percentage, wet basis}=100\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1-m_0}$$ $$\text{Moisture percentage, dry basis}=100\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_2-m_0}$$ These are derived mass-balance formulas. Wet basis uses initial sample mass; dry basis uses residual dry mass. Hypothetical example: dish 30 grams; dish plus initial sample 35 grams; dish plus dried residue 34 grams. Initial sample mass is 5 grams, apparent water loss is 1 gram and dry residue is 4 grams. $$\text{Wet-basis moisture}=100(1/5)=20\%$$ $$\text{Dry-basis moisture}=100(1/4)=25\%$$ 7.2 Thermal drying In oven drying, the sample is heated under a specified temperature and time programme, or to a defined near-constant mass. The source gives a broad method-dependent range of approximately 70–155 degrees Celsius; this is not one universal oven setting. Factors influencing the result include temperature, chamber humidity, air movement, vacuum, sample depth, particle size, container characteristics, oven construction and loading position. A shallow sample and greater exposed area generally favour moisture removal. Vacuum permits drying under reduced pressure and can allow a lower temperature for heat-sensitive matrices. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 5. Pectin chemistry and gel formation 5.1 A gel is a connected network, not simply high viscosity Pectin chains must associate at multiple junction regions to create a continuous network. Once that network spans the material, it can retain an aqueous phase. Charge, hydration, chain length and esterification control whether the chains can approach and form junctions. The principal structural unit is D-galacturonic acid. The course's enzyme discussion identifies alpha 1-to-4 linkages between galacturonic-acid units. Some carboxyl groups are methyl-esterified; others occur as free acid or salts. Sources: Food Chemistry, page 70, page 85 and pages 142–143. 5.2 Degree of esterification The distinction between high-methoxyl and low-methoxyl pectin concerns the fraction of carboxyl groups present as methyl esters. $$\text{Degree of esterification percentage}=100\frac{\text{methyl-esterified carboxyl groups}}{\text{total relevant carboxyl groups}}$$ This is a derived expression of the source definition. It is not the same quantity as methyl-group mass percentage. • High-methoxyl pectin: more than half of the relevant carboxyl groups are methyl-esterified. • Low-methoxyl pectin: fewer than half are methyl-esterified. Hypothetical practice example: 60 esterified groups among 100 relevant groups gives 60 percent esterification and the high-methoxyl category. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “50 percent esterification” does not mean that half the entire polymer mass consists of methoxyl groups. 5.3 High-methoxyl pectin: acidity and sugar reduce barriers to association In the course's mechanism, acidity changes the balance between ionized and unionized carboxyl groups. Reduced charge lowers repulsion between chains. Sugar competes for water and decreases pectin hydration, encouraging association involving methyl-ester regions. Junction regions connect chains into a network that traps the aqueous phase. Acid addition --> reduced carboxylate charge --> less repulsion Sugar addition --> reduced pectin hydration --> closer association Both effects --> junction regions --> continuous gel network The accessible text gives acidic gelation below approximately pH 3.5, an example optimum around pH 3.0 and formulations commonly around 65 percent sugar. It does not justify replacing “around 65 percent sugar” with a universal rule that every high-methoxyl pectin requires more than 65 percent total soluble solids. Verification required: the exact lower pH boundary of 2.8 is not established in the readable passage. 5.4 Low-methoxyl pectin: calcium bridges When more carboxyl groups remain available, divalent calcium ions can connect regions on neighbouring chains. Consequently, the source describes low-methoxyl gelation without requiring the high sugar concentration characteristic of the high-methoxyl system. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Module 3 — Protein Transformations MODULE 3 — FOOD PROTEINS AND PROCESSING TRANSFORMATIONS 1. Foundational overview: sequence, conformation and network are different levels A protein's peptide sequence is its covalent backbone. Folding organizes that backbone and its side chains into a particular conformation. Processing can unfold the chain without cutting peptide bonds; it can also produce aggregation, hydrolysis or new covalent cross-links. These are different transformations with different consequences. The examiner's first diagnostic question is therefore: Did processing change folding, peptide-chain continuity, side-chain chemistry or intermolecular networking? Sources: Food Chemistry, Lessons 4–7, pages 30–47; Food Science, pages 49–50, 98–107 and 125–127. 2. Physicochemical foundations 2.1 Charge depends on acidity Proteins contain groups that can accept or release protons. Their charge state therefore changes with acidity, affecting electrostatic repulsion, hydration, association and solubility. The isoelectric point is the acidity at which the average net charge is zero. The source gives approximately pH 4.6 for casein. At the isoelectric point, electrostatic repulsion between protein molecules is reduced. Protein–protein association becomes easier, so solubility is commonly minimal. The same reasoning can decrease water retention in many protein matrices, but minimum water holding should be treated as a tendency rather than an invariant law for every structured food. Acidity below isoelectric point --> predominantly positive net charge At isoelectric point --> zero average net charge Acidity above isoelectric point --> predominantly negative net charge Zero net charge does not mean absence of individual charged groups. Sources: Food Chemistry, pages 32–33; Food Science, pages 98 and 106. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “At the isoelectric point, every amino-acid side chain is uncharged” is false. Positive and negative contributions can cancel while ionized groups remain. 2.2 Amphoteric buffering A protein acts as an acid or a base because its functional groups can exchange protons. The course associates buffering below approximately pH 5 with carboxyl-containing groups and buffering above approximately pH 9 with lysine's epsilon-amino group, arginine's guanidinium group and tyrosine's phenolic group. The descriptive principle is that buffering is strongest in the acidity range where a relevant group changes protonation appreciably. The textbook's broad ranges should not be mistaken for universal titration curves for all proteins. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 34

A protein can be electrically neutral on average while still containing groups able to accept or release protons. 2.3 Salting-in and salting-out At suitable low salt concentrations, ions can reduce unfavourable protein–protein interactions and increase solubility. This is salting-in. At high salt concentrations, ion hydration and changes in solvent conditions reduce protein hydration and favour precipitation: salting-out. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 3. Processing-induced transformations 3.1 Denaturation: accessibility changes before sequence does Denaturation transforms a native conformation into a less ordered or unfolded state without requiring a change in primary structure. Buried regions can become exposed, altering association with water, other protein molecules and food constituents. The source describes many food proteins as susceptible to moderate treatments around 60–90 degrees Celsius for an hour or less, but this broad example is not a universal inactivation schedule. Native folded protein | Heat or another denaturing treatment | v Conformational disruption | +--> Greater enzyme access to some peptide regions | +--> Altered hydration and functionality | +--> Interchain association or aggregation Aggregation after unfolding can make the overall transformation effectively irreversible. Reversibility depends on whether a native state can reform and whether new associations stabilize the altered material. Sources: Food Chemistry, pages 35–36; Food Science, pages 103 and 126. Transformation Primary event Peptide cleavage required? Denaturation Conformational disruption No No, although chemical changes may Aggregation Association of molecules coexist Hydrolysis Peptide-bond cleavage Yes New covalent connection between No backbone cleavage is inherently Side-chain cross-linking residues required [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Denaturation is hydrolysis” is false. “All denaturation is irreversible” is false. “Heating always improves protein nutrition” is false. 3.2 Nutritional benefits and safety boundaries Moderate heating can improve digestive access to protein chains and inactivate some proteinaceous antinutritional factors, including susceptible trypsin inhibitors. The course also discusses enzyme inactivation and susceptible protein toxins. The benefit has limits. Extensive heating can reduce solubility, create cross-links, damage amino acids and promote carbonyl–amine reactions. For botulinum toxin, the examination distinction is between a susceptible toxin protein and the survival behaviour of the microorganism or its spores. The source's general toxin statement is not a validated time– temperature schedule for every product. The textbook also mentions enterotoxins in a broad list. Do not convert that list into a claim that all bacterial enterotoxins are destroyed by ordinary heating. Susceptibility is toxin-specific. Sources: Food Chemistry, pages 35–36 and 111; Food Science, page 76. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 36

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 3.3 Desulfuration and sulfur-containing volatiles Heating can alter sulfur-containing residues and generate volatile compounds contributing to cooked flavour. The source notes changes around 100 degrees Celsius and partial destruction of cysteine or cystine residues during more severe sterilization treatments above approximately 115 degrees Celsius. Hydrogen sulfide is among the products listed. The course also lists dimethyl sulfide and cysteic acid among heating-related compounds. Source caution: the passage mistakenly calls hydrogen sulfide “hydrogen disulphide.” Learn the chemical identity hydrogen sulfide, $\mathrm{H_2S}$. Verification required: the accessible passage does not establish that every listed sulfur product originates specifically from cysteine or cystine. Do not assign dimethyl sulfide a uniquely verified precursor from this wording alone. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] The appearance of a sulfur volatile does not prove that all protein sulfur residues have been destroyed. A temperature quoted for a noticeable reaction is not a sharp universal onset threshold. 3.4 Deamidation Asparagine and glutamine have side-chain amide groups. Their deamidation exposes carboxyl functionality and releases ammonia. The resulting charge-related changes can alter the isoelectric point and functional properties. Side-chain amide + water | v Carboxyl-containing side chain + ammonia The source discusses this during heating above approximately 100 degrees Celsius. The important mechanism is side-chain conversion, not obligatory peptide-backbone hydrolysis. Source: Food Chemistry, page 36. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Deamidation is not the same as removal of an amino group from every residue. A side- chain chemical change can alter protein charge without cutting the whole chain. 3.5 Racemization Racemization changes stereochemical configuration. The course associates partial conversion of L-amino- acid residues toward D configurations with severe heating, particularly above approximately 200 degrees Celsius, and alkaline processing. It also notes some conversion during other harsh treatments. Digestive proteases recognize local stereochemistry. D-configured residues can reduce efficient cleavage and impair nutritional utilization of the surrounding peptide. The textbook's statement of “50 percent loss” requires careful interpretation. It follows only from a particular limiting assumption: an originally all-L essential amino acid becomes an equal mixture, and the D fraction is counted as unavailable under the model. For an unavailable converted fraction $r$: $$\text{Remaining modeled available fraction}=1-r$$ If $r=0.50$, the modeled retained fraction is 0.50. Partial racemization of 10 percent would not mathematically imply a 50-percent loss. Source: Food Chemistry, pages 36–37. The equation is an explicit interpretation of the source shorthand, not a measured universal nutritional law. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Any racemization causes exactly 50 percent loss” is false. “D-configured peptide bonds can never be hydrolysed” is also stronger than the source's statement that hydrolysis is less efficient. Modification of lysine interferes with cleavage at the corresponding site. 2. The new connection creates steric restrictions that reduce enzyme access to neighbouring bonds. Texturized plant proteins 5.1 Creating anisotropy from globular starting proteins Many plant proteins begin as compact molecular assemblies. A meat-like material requires directional structure and mechanical resistance. Texturization unfolds or reorganizes the proteins, aligns chains or material domains, and stabilizes a structure capable of rehydration and subsequent processing. The course distinguishes true spun fibres from extrusion-generated hydratable laminar or porous masses. They should not be described as molecularly identical processes. What controls Maillard reaction rate? 4.1 Mobility, concentration and temperature interact A reaction requires molecular encounters. Too little hydration can restrict encounters; sufficient hydration permits mobility; extensive hydration can dilute reactants. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Module 4 — Complete Continuation MODULE 4 — BROWNING AND KINETICS Complete continuation: environmental regulation, Strecker chemistry, nutritional consequences, caramelization and enzymatic browning Source and scientific-integrity note This continuation develops the requested topics without replacing the existing handout. The accessible passages directly support the main Maillard sequence, its intermediate-water-activity optimum, heat and pH effects, Strecker flavour formation, lysine loss, phenolase oxidation and the use of sulfites against browning. The fuller molecular mechanisms and several requested numerical specifications are scientific elaborations not independently verified in the readable uploaded passages. These are identified where necessary rather than represented as quotations from missing textbook pages. Primary source anchors are Food Chemistry, Lesson 5, pages 39–42; Lesson 2, pages 20–23; Lessons 15–16, pages 88–93; Lesson 32, page 182; and B. Srilakshmi, Food Science, pages 103–104. No current additive permission or examination notification is inferred from these historical textbooks. 1. Environmental regulators of the Maillard reaction 1.1 First-principles explanation: reaction requires accessible carbonyl and amino groups Maillard chemistry begins when a chemically available amino group encounters a reactive carbonyl group. The rate depends on more than the total amounts of sugar and protein. The reacting groups must be accessible, the amino group must have sufficient nucleophilicity, and the matrix must permit movement or local contact. Three competing effects explain many processing observations: 1. Chemical activation: higher temperature and favourable ionization increase reaction probability. 2. Physical accessibility: hydration and plasticization allow reactants to encounter one another. 3. Dilution: excessive water lowers the concentrations of reacting groups. Consequently, a food containing abundant sugar and protein does not necessarily brown rapidly at low temperature or in a rigid dry matrix. 1.2 Temperature and processing time Molecular explanation Higher temperature generally accelerates carbonyl–amine condensation, rearrangement, fragmentation and subsequent pigment-forming reactions. Heating also changes the matrix by denaturing proteins, releasing or exposing amino groups, disrupting physical structure and modifying water distribution. The temperature dependence of an individual kinetically describable step can be represented by the Arrhenius relationship: FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 52

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER $$k=A\exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)$$ Here, $k$ is the rate constant, $A$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the apparent activation energy, $R$ is the gas constant and $T$ is absolute temperature in kelvin. For two temperatures: $$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right)=\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$ This equation explains why an increase in temperature can produce a disproportionately large increase in reaction rate. Numerical prediction requires an activation energy determined for the particular reaction indicator, food matrix and temperature interval. Why one rate constant is insufficient for the whole reaction The Maillard reaction is a network, not one elementary reaction. Early lysine blockage, formation of a specific aroma compound and accumulation of brown pigment need not have identical apparent activation energies or reaction orders. A simplified initial-rate expression is: $$r{\mathrm{initial}}=k{\mathrm{effective}}[\mathrm{reactive\ carbonyl}][\mathrm{available\ amino\ group}]$$ This is a conceptual approximation for an initial interaction, not a universal rate law for total browning. The effective rate constant incorporates temperature, ionization, matrix accessibility and other conditions. Industrial implications • Short, intense heating can generate substantial surface aroma and colour while leaving a moist interior comparatively pale. • Prolonged storage can cause Maillard damage at temperatures far below those required for conspicuous roasting. • Evaporated milk and milk powder can undergo unwanted colour development and loss of available lysine. • Bread crust, roasted coffee and cocoa develop desirable flavour through controlled carbonyl–amine chemistry. • A high oven temperature does not mean every part of the product immediately reaches that temperature. Textbook anchors: Food Chemistry, pages 39–42 and 126–127; Food Science, pages 103–104. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Maillard browning occurs only above 160 degrees Celsius” is false. That temperature is associated with conventional teaching descriptions of rapid sugar caramelization, not a minimum requirement for every Maillard reaction. 1.3 Water activity: why the maximum occurs at intermediate hydration Low-water-activity region At very low water activity, reactants may be concentrated but trapped within a rigid matrix. Limited molecular mobility and poor dissolution restrict effective encounters between carbonyl and amino groups. Intermediate-water-activity region Added water increases hydration, permits partial dissolution and plasticizes amorphous solids. Reactant mobility increases while concentrations remain appreciable. The uploaded course describes a maximum Maillard rate near: $$a_w=0.6\text{–}0.7$$ FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 53

Raising pH generally increases its fraction. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER The relevant acid-dissociation constant depends on the amino group and its molecular environment. A free amino acid, the terminal amino group of a peptide and the epsilon-amino group of a lysine residue need not behave identically. Acidic conditions Protonation generally suppresses initial amino-group attack. Nevertheless, acid-catalysed dehydration of sugar-derived intermediates can still occur. Acidic conditions can favour pathways associated with furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural formation. Neutral and alkaline conditions Greater amino-group nucleophilicity commonly accelerates the initial reaction. Fragmentation and formation of reactive carbonyl intermediates can also become important. The resulting pathway distribution can increase formation of reductones, dicarbonyl compounds and nitrogen-containing aroma compounds. The familiar association of acidic conditions with 1,2-enolization and of more alkaline conditions with 2,3- enolization is a useful pathway model, but does not imply that either route is exclusively permitted in one pH interval. Processing consequences • Alkaline formulation can increase surface browning. • Acidification can suppress initial carbonyl–amine interaction, although it does not eliminate every sugar-degradation pathway. • Heating can change pH and buffer equilibria, so the starting pH is not always the complete reaction environment. • Excessive alkalinity can simultaneously promote other protein damage, including racemization and lysinoalanine formation. Textbook anchor: Food Science, page 104, supports increasing browning with increasing pH in the cited model systems. The ionization equations are scientific elaboration. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Acid completely prevents every form of non-enzymatic browning” is false. Inhibiting amino-group attack does not prevent all acid-catalysed sugar dehydration or other browning pathways. 1.5 Sugar reactivity: pentoses, hexoses and disaccharides First principles A sugar must supply a reactive carbonyl under the reaction conditions. For many reducing sugars, this requires equilibrium access to an open-chain form. Reaction also depends on carbonyl accessibility, stereochemistry, sugar concentration and the identities of the amino reactant and intermediate products. The requested general examination order is: $$\text{Reducing pentoses}>\text{reducing hexoses}>\text{reducing disaccharides}$$ Typical examples are: • Pentoses: ribose and xylose. • Hexoses: glucose and galactose. • Reducing disaccharides: lactose and maltose. This is a useful broad trend, not a universal ranking of every sugar under every experimental condition. The accessible readable passages do not independently establish this complete class order; it is included as the requested qualified scientific elaboration. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 55

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Molecular oxygen is essential to polyphenol-oxidase browning but is not an obligatory reactant in the initial Maillard condensation. 2. Strecker degradation: molecular origin of important aroma compounds 2.1 First-principles overview Strecker degradation converts an amino acid into an aldehyde whose carbon skeleton contains one fewer carbon atom than the original amino acid. The removed carbon is released as carbon dioxide. A reactive alpha-dicarbonyl compound accepts nitrogen through the reaction sequence and becomes an alpha- aminocarbonyl product. The key concept is carbon-skeleton shortening coupled to nitrogen transfer. This is not simply ordinary thermal evaporation of an amino acid, nor is it identical to enzyme-catalysed transamination. The uploaded course identifies Strecker degradation in its pathway figure and associates Strecker aldehydes with flavour. The detailed elementary description below is scientific elaboration. 2.2 Reactants Amino acid A generic alpha-amino acid has the structure: $$\mathrm{R-CH(NH_2)-COOH}$$ Here, $R$ is the side chain. Its identity determines the resulting Strecker aldehyde. Alpha-dicarbonyl compound A generic adjacent dicarbonyl has the structure: $$\mathrm{R^1-CO-CO-R^2}$$ Adjacent carbonyl groups make these compounds particularly reactive. Maillard-derived sugar fragmentation supplies a pool of such intermediates. Examples include methylglyoxal, also called pyruvaldehyde, and diacetyl. 2.3 Step 1: nucleophilic attack and imine formation The amino group attacks one carbonyl carbon of the dicarbonyl compound, producing a carbinolamine-type intermediate. Elimination of water generates an imine, conventionally described as a Schiff-base intermediate. Alpha-amino acid plus alpha-dicarbonyl | v Amino nitrogen attacks a carbonyl carbon | v Carbinolamine-type addition intermediate | | Elimination of water FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 57

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER v Imine carrying the amino-acid carbon skeleton A representative condensation can be written: $$\mathrm{R^1COCOR^2+H_2NCH(R)COOH\rightleftharpoons R^1COC(R^2){=}NCH(R)COOH+H_2O}$$ Attack can occur at the alternative carbonyl in an unsymmetrical dicarbonyl, giving a different orientation of the subsequent aminocarbonyl product. 2.4 Step 2: decarboxylation The imine-containing intermediate facilitates loss of the amino-acid carboxyl carbon as carbon dioxide. Electron redistribution produces a resonance-stabilized intermediate, followed by proton transfer and imine–enamine-type rearrangement. Imine-linked amino-acid intermediate | | Decarboxylation v Carbon dioxide plus rearranged nitrogen-containing intermediate The essential examination point is the fate of the amino-acid carboxyl carbon: $$\mathrm{Amino\ acid\ carboxyl\ carbon\longrightarrow CO_2}$$ 2.5 Step 3: hydrolysis and product separation After decarboxylation and rearrangement, hydrolytic cleavage releases: 1. The Strecker aldehyde derived from the amino-acid side chain and alpha carbon. 2. An alpha-aminocarbonyl product derived from the dicarbonyl reactant. For a representative diketone orientation, the net transformation is: $$\mathrm{RCH(NH_2)COOH+R^1COCOR^2\longrightarrow RCHO+CO_2+R^1COCH(NH_2)R^2}$$ This is a net equation; the actual mechanism includes condensation, proton transfers, decarboxylation, rearrangement and hydrolysis. Water eliminated in condensation and used in hydrolysis cancels in this simplified overall representation. The alpha-aminocarbonyl product is an alpha-aminoketone when the retained carbonyl is a ketone. Other dicarbonyl structures can yield related aminoaldehyde or aminocarbonyl products. It is therefore more precise to describe the product class first and the aminoketone subclass second. 2.6 Carbon accounting If the amino acid contains $n$ carbon atoms, its Strecker aldehyde contains: $$n-1$$ The missing carbon appears in carbon dioxide. Caramelization: sugar degradation without a required amino reactant 4.1 First-principles overview Sugar can generate colour and aroma through heating even when no amino compound participates. Caramelization involves a network of sugar rearrangement, dehydration, fragmentation and condensation reactions. The decisive contrast is: • Maillard reaction: carbonyl–amine interaction is central. • Caramelization: sugar degradation does not require an amino reactant. “Without amino compounds” describes the mechanism and a pure-sugar model system. Real foods can contain amino compounds and undergo caramelization and Maillard chemistry simultaneously. 4.2 Temperature qualification The requested teaching threshold is above approximately 160 degrees Celsius for rapid conventional caramelization of some sugars. It must not be treated as a universal initiation temperature. The actual onset and rate depend on sugar identity, pH, water content, residence time and processing conditions. Sugar degradation can occur at lower temperatures during prolonged or catalysed treatment. The uploads themselves contain differing approximate temperature descriptions in their baking discussions. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Every sugar begins caramelizing only when its temperature exceeds exactly 160 degrees Celsius” is false. 4.3 Reaction sequence Step 1: structural rearrangement and enolization Heating promotes interconversion and rearrangement of sugar structures. Enolization generates intermediates susceptible to further dehydration and fragmentation. Step 2: dehydration Water is eliminated from sugar-derived intermediates. Furanic products, including hydroxymethylfurfural from hexose-related routes, can appear. Their presence is not unique to caramelization because related compounds can also arise in Maillard systems. Step 3: fragmentation Carbon-chain cleavage produces smaller carbonyls, organic acids and volatile compounds. These contribute characteristic aroma, acidity and, with excessive degradation, burnt notes. Step 4: condensation and accumulation of coloured material Reactive fragments condense into increasingly complex products with extended chromophoric structures. Continued treatment deepens colour and can increase bitterness and insoluble material. Enzymatic browning: polyphenol oxidase and quinone chemistry 5.1 First-principles overview: tissue damage brings the system together An intact plant tissue can keep phenolic substrates and enzymes in different cellular locations. Cutting, bruising, crushing or membrane damage permits contact. Oxygen reaching the damaged region allows enzymatic oxidation, followed by non-enzymatic reactions that produce colour. The practical triangle is: Active enzyme + Suitable phenolic substrate + Accessible molecular oxygen | v Quinone formation | v Pigment-forming secondary reactions Water supports the reaction environment and transport, but water alone does not provide the complete browning system. Textbook anchors: Food Chemistry, page 88 and the tea and cocoa processing lessons, pages 152–157 and 164–167. 5.2 Enzyme identity and terminology Polyphenol oxidase is the commonly used general name for copper-containing enzymes involved in oxidation of phenolic substrates. The familiar abbreviation is PPO. Phenolase is a broad traditional term. The names tyrosinase and catechol oxidase should not be treated as proof of identical catalytic capability: • Tyrosinase can possess both monophenol hydroxylation and ortho-diphenol oxidation activity. • Catechol oxidase primarily denotes ortho-diphenol oxidation activity. • Particular plant polyphenol-oxidase preparations may not display both activities to the same extent. The copper-containing active site participates in oxygen binding and redox transformations. Copper is a catalytic cofactor, not a substrate that is consumed in direct proportion to pigment formation. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Every enzyme called polyphenol oxidase necessarily hydroxylates every monophenol” is false. Activity and substrate specificity must be established for the particular enzyme. 5.3 Cresolase activity: monophenol hydroxylation Cresolase activity is the traditional name for monophenolase activity. A hydroxyl group is introduced at an ortho position relative to an existing phenolic hydroxyl group, producing an ortho-diphenol intermediate. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER The isolated hydroxylation step requires reducing equivalents within the coupled catalytic chemistry. It should not be written as an atom-balanced reaction in which one oxygen molecule simply becomes a second hydroxyl group without accounting for the other oxygen atom and electron transfers. A generic balanced hydroxylation representation is: $$\mathrm{Monophenol+O_2+2H^++2e^-\longrightarrow ortho!!\text{-}diphenol+H_2O}$$ This equation represents the redox accounting of hydroxylation; it does not prescribe the identity of the reducing species in every food system. 5.4 Catecholase activity: oxidation of ortho-diphenols Catecholase activity is ortho-diphenol oxidase activity. The two neighbouring hydroxyl-bearing ring positions are oxidized to the corresponding quinone carbonyl groups. For catechol as the model substrate: $$\mathrm{2C_6H_6O_2+O_2\longrightarrow 2C_6H_4O_2+2H_2O}$$ Equivalently: $$\mathrm{ortho!!\text{-}diphenol+\tfrac{1}{2}O_2\longrightarrow ortho!!\text{-}quinone+H_2O}$$ The oxidation removes two hydrogen equivalents from the diphenol. Oxygen is reduced and participates as the terminal electron acceptor in the catalytic cycle. The critical condition is exposure at the slowest-heating relevant location, not merely the nominal temperature of steam or water. A simple first-order inactivation model is: $$\frac{E_t}{E_0}=\exp(-k_dt)$$ Here, $E_0$ and $E_t$ represent initial and residual activity, $k_d$ is the inactivation rate constant at the specified temperature and $t$ is exposure time. Under a log-linear model: $$\log{10}\left(\frac{E_0}{E_t}\right)=\frac{t}{D}$$ The decimal-reduction time $D$ is the time needed for a tenfold activity decrease under those conditions. Some enzymes show non-log-linear behaviour or multiple activity fractions, so the model requires experimental validation. Ascorbic acid is oxidized, producing dehydroascorbic acid. A simplified coupled reaction is: $$\mathrm{ortho!!\text{-}quinone+ascorbic\ acid\longrightarrow ortho!!\text{-}diphenol+dehydroascorbic\ acid}$$ Polyphenol oxidase forms quinones | v Ascorbic acid reduces quinones | v Diphenols are regenerated before pigment accumulation | v Visible browning is delayed Why protection can be temporary Ascorbic acid is consumed. Once its reducing reserve is exhausted, quinones can accumulate and browning can resume if the enzyme, substrate and oxygen remain available. The observed induction period can therefore reflect antioxidant consumption rather than absence of enzymatic oxidation. Industrial use Ascorbic acid is often combined with acidification, cooling and oxygen management. Its concentration must be sufficient for the relevant oxidation burden, but arbitrary over-addition does not substitute for process validation. Quinone reduction is a central mechanism. 6.5 Oxygen exclusion Mechanism Because molecular oxygen is required for the initiating oxidation, reducing its availability can slow quinone generation. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER 6.7 Copper chelation Mechanism The catalytic copper centre is essential to the relevant polyphenol oxidase. Metal-binding agents can alter the availability or functionality of catalytic copper and thereby reduce activity in suitable conditions. Citric acid has metal-complexing capacity. Stronger chelators, such as ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, can be useful mechanistic examples, but this does not establish suitability or permission in every food. Critical qualification The active-site copper is protein-bound. The ability to chelate freely dissolved copper does not automatically mean that a reagent will rapidly remove or disable the copper centre of an intact enzyme.
