Stage 2 descriptive model answer — 10 marks Question Compare Maillard browning, caramelization and enzymatic browning with reference to reactants, mechanisms, conditions, products and industrial significance. Suggested structure and allocation • Introduction and classification: 1 mark. • Mechanisms of the three processes: 4 marks. • Diagnostic comparison: 3 marks. • Industrial significance and conclusion: 2 marks. The allocation is a study aid, not an official marking scheme. Complete model answer Introduction Food browning comprises chemically distinct processes that can produce similar visible colours. Maillard browning and caramelization are non-enzymatic processes, whereas polyphenol-oxidase browning begins with enzyme-catalysed oxidation of phenolic substrates. Correct identification requires examination of precursors and initiating reactions rather than colour alone. Maillard browning The Maillard reaction begins when an available amino group reacts with a carbonyl compound, commonly the open-chain form of a reducing sugar. Condensation produces an imine or glycosylamine-related intermediate. Aldose-derived products undergo Amadori rearrangement, while ketose-derived systems can undergo Heyns rearrangement. Subsequent dehydration, fragmentation and carbonyl chemistry generate reactive intermediates. Alpha-dicarbonyl compounds can react with amino acids through Strecker degradation, producing carbon dioxide, one-carbon-shorter aldehydes and aminocarbonyl products. These compounds contribute aroma directly or participate in further formation of roasted-flavour heterocycles. Later condensation generates heterogeneous brown melanoidins. The rate generally increases with temperature and favourable amino-group ionization. In the uploaded teaching schematic it reaches an intermediate-water-activity maximum near 0.6–0.7; restricted mobility limits reaction at very low hydration, while dilution can reduce the rate at high hydration. Controlled reaction provides desirable crust colour and roasted aroma. Excessive reaction can block lysine, reduce digestibility and contribute selected processing contaminants. Caramelization Caramelization involves sugar degradation without a required amino reactant. Heating promotes rearrangement, enolization, dehydration, fragmentation and condensation. Volatile carbonyl compounds and furanic products contribute aroma, while complex condensation products contribute colour. Rapid conventional caramelization is often associated with temperatures above approximately 160 degrees Celsius, but this is not a universal threshold for every sugar or condition. The traditional designations caramelans, caramelens and caramelins are associated respectively with the empirical formulas $ \mathrm{C{12}H{18}O_9}$, $\mathrm{C{36}H{50}O{25}}$ and $\mathrm{C{125}H{188}O{80}}$. Enzymatic browning Cutting or bruising plant tissue brings phenolic substrates, active polyphenol oxidase and oxygen into contact. In enzymes possessing monophenolase activity, a suitable monophenol is hydroxylated to an ortho- diphenol. Diphenolase activity oxidizes ortho-diphenols to ortho-quinones. Subsequent largely non- enzymatic coupling and condensation produce melanin-like pigments. This process can occur in hydrated tissues without intense heating. It is generally undesirable in fresh-cut produce but contributes to characteristic processing changes in products such as black tea. Enzymatic browning is controlled by disabling the enzyme, restricting oxygen, changing reaction conditions or reducing and trapping quinones. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Suggested structure and allocation • Definition and tissue context: 2 marks. • Enzyme chemistry and pigment formation: 5 marks. • Industrial prevention: 6 marks. • Process validation and conclusion: 2 marks. The allocation is a study aid, not an official marking scheme. Complete model answer Introduction and tissue context Enzymatic browning is colour development initiated by oxidation of suitable phenolic substrates in the presence of active enzyme and molecular oxygen. In many plant tissues, cellular compartmentation restricts enzyme–substrate contact. Cutting, bruising, crushing or membrane disruption removes this protection and increases access to oxygen. The principal requirements are therefore active polyphenol oxidase, a suitable phenolic substrate and accessible molecular oxygen. Their coexistence explains rapid discoloration of damaged produce. Enzyme identity Polyphenol oxidase is a copper-containing oxidoreductase. Phenolase is a broad traditional name. Tyrosinase can exhibit both monophenolase and diphenolase activity, whereas catechol oxidase primarily denotes diphenol oxidation. These terms should not be assumed to describe identical substrate specificity in every preparation. Monophenolase or cresolase activity Where the enzyme possesses this activity, a hydroxyl group is introduced at an ortho position of a suitable monophenol, generating an ortho-diphenol intermediate. The reaction is oxygen-dependent and involves electron-transfer chemistry at the copper-containing catalytic centre. Diphenolase or catecholase activity Ortho-diphenols are oxidized to ortho-quinones. The balanced model reaction is: $$\mathrm{2C_6H_6O_2+O_2\longrightarrow 2C_6H_4O_2+2H_2O}$$ Oxygen acts as the terminal electron acceptor. The resulting quinones are more reactive than the original phenolic substrates. Secondary pigment formation Quinones participate in coupling, addition and further oxidation reactions. They can react with other phenolics and with amino or thiol groups. Accumulation of complex coloured oligomers and polymers generates brown or dark melanin-like material. The enzyme initiates precursor formation, but many later pigment-forming reactions are non-enzymatic. text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | v Reactive ortho-quinones | v Coupling, addition and condensation | v Brown melanin-like pigments Control by blanching A validated thermal treatment inactivates polyphenol oxidase by disrupting its catalytic structure. The process must deliver adequate exposure throughout the relevant product volume. Product size, heating method and matrix-dependent enzyme resistance influence the required treatment. Blanching is powerful because it targets the enzyme rather than merely delaying visible pigmentation. However, excessive treatment can soften tissue, alter flavour and cause nutrient leaching. Residual activity should be measured or assessed through a validated indicator system. Blanching must not be confused with complete sterilization. Control by acidification Lowering pH alters catalytic-group and substrate ionization and can suppress productive reaction. Citric acid is useful because it acidifies the food and can also contribute metal-complexing effects. A target below approximately pH 3.0 is a practical teaching condition for strong suppression in many systems, not a universal irreversible inactivation limit. Buffering capacity and incomplete acid penetration must be considered. Excess acid can create unacceptable sourness or alter texture and pigment stability. Control by reducing agents Ascorbic acid reduces quinones back to diphenols and is oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid. This prevents or delays accumulation of the pigment precursors while reducing capacity remains available. $$\mathrm{Quinone+ascorbic\ acid\longrightarrow diphenol+dehydroascorbic\ acid}$$ Protection is often temporary because the reducing agent is consumed. Browning can resume after depletion if enzyme activity and oxygen access persist. This mechanism differs from permanent thermal enzyme inactivation. Control by oxygen restriction Deaeration, suitable barrier packaging, inert-gas handling and immersion can reduce oxygen transfer to the reactive surface. These approaches directly target a required oxidation reactant. However, dissolved oxygen, packaging leakage and subsequent exposure can permit renewed browning. Oxygen restriction must be integrated with microbiological safety requirements rather than treated as a complete preservation method. Control by sulfites Sulfites and potassium metabisulfite supply reactive sulfur species that can intercept quinones and form sulfonated products, reducing their participation in pigment formation. They can also inhibit other oxidation-related processes. Their application must account for sensitive consumers, legal permissions, residual limits and labelling requirements. Antibrowning effectiveness does not establish universal permission. FOOD CHEMISTRY — UNIT 3A • PAGE 78

text: FOODSAFE | HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER Control by copper chelation Chelating agents can interfere with catalytic-metal availability or functionality. Citric acid provides a relevant food-processing example, while stronger chelators illustrate the underlying mechanism. Because catalytic copper is protein-bound, binding freely dissolved copper does not guarantee complete inhibition of the intact enzyme. Chelator access, concentration, pH, competing ions and contact time determine effectiveness. Combined control and validation Industrial systems frequently combine acidification, ascorbic acid, cooling and oxygen management where fresh texture must be retained. Where the product tolerates heating, blanching can provide stronger residual-activity control before freezing or dehydration. Validation should assess residual enzyme activity, colour stability during intended storage, antioxidant depletion where relevant, sensory quality and microbiological safety. A method that suppresses colour briefly at the laboratory surface may not protect the full product throughout distribution. Conclusion Polyphenol-oxidase browning is an oxygen-dependent enzymatic generation of quinones followed by largely non-enzymatic pigment chemistry. Effective prevention targets the enzyme, oxygen supply, catalytic environment or quinone intermediates. The best industrial approach combines mechanistic understanding with product-specific validation rather than reliance on an absolute temperature, pH or additive rule. 10. Final examination consolidation Ten distinctions to retain 1. Maillard initiation: carbonyl–amine reaction; no enzyme is required. 2. Intermediate hydration: the textbook schematic places maximum Maillard browning near water activity 0.6–0.7. 3. pH: higher pH generally increases the nucleophilic unprotonated amino-group fraction. 4. Sugar order: reducing pentoses generally react faster than reducing hexoses, which generally react faster than reducing disaccharides; this is not universal. 5. Strecker accounting: the amino-acid carboxyl carbon becomes carbon dioxide; the aldehyde has one fewer carbon. 6. Lysine damage: blockage can occur before visible brown pigment. 7. Acrylamide precursor: free asparagine, not principally the epsilon-amino group of lysine. 8. Caramelization: sugar degradation does not require an amino reactant; 160 degrees Celsius is not an invariant onset temperature. 9. Enzymatic browning: phenolic substrate plus active copper enzyme plus oxygen produces quinones, followed by secondary pigment reactions. 10. Ascorbic acid: quinone reduction provides reserve-dependent protection; it is not equivalent to permanent enzyme destruction. FOUNDATIONAL BACTERIAL PHYSIOLOGY 2.1 Gram reaction: a cell-envelope phenomenon Mental model The Gram stain is a differential staining procedure reflecting how the cell envelope retains a crystal-violet–iodine complex during decolourisation. It is not a direct assay of pathogenicity, spore formation or oxygen requirement. Procedure and mechanism Step Reagent Principal event 1 Crystal violet Initially stains both major groups 2 Iodine Forms a crystal-violet–iodine complex 3 Alcohol/acetone decolouriser Produces differential retention 4 Counterstain, commonly safranin Colours decolourised cells pink/red Gram-positive envelope • Thick peptidoglycan. • Usually contains teichoic and lipoteichoic acids. • Lacks the characteristic Gram-negative outer membrane. • Retains the primary stain under correctly controlled conditions. Gram-negative envelope • Relatively thin peptidoglycan. • An outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide in typical Gram-negative bacteria. • A periplasmic compartment. • Decolourisation permits subsequent counterstaining. Why errors occur • Old cultures may become Gram-variable. • Excessive decolourisation can make Gram-positive organisms appear Gram-negative. • Insufficient decolourisation can produce the opposite error. • Damaged cells may stain atypically. • Food debris can obscure morphology. The specific growth rate, (\mu), is related to generation time by: [ \mu=\frac{\ln 2}{g} ] and: [ N_t=N_0e^{\mu t} ] Example If a population has an 8-minute generation time under favourable conditions: [ n=\frac{80}{8}=10\text{ generations} ] [ N{80}=N_0\,2^{10}=1024N_0 ] This does not imply that all food populations maintain an 8-minute generation time. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 5. STAGE 1 — COUNT-BASED OBJECTIVE SCREENING BANK For every question, use the same options: • A. Only 1 statement is correct • B. Only 2 statements are correct • C. All 3 statements are correct • D. None of the statements is correct The explanations identify both the count and the specific error. Question 1 — Gram reaction and spores 86. A Gram-positive reaction establishes that the bacterium forms endospores. 87. Old cultures of some Gram-positive organisms can appear Gram-variable. 88. The Gram-negative outer membrane contributes to envelope differences relevant to decolourisation. Answer: B — Only statements 2 and 3 are correct. • 1: Incorrect. Many Gram-positive food organisms are non-spore-formers. • 2: Correct. Age and envelope damage can alter staining. • 3: Correct. Gram staining reflects envelope structure and decolourisation behaviour. Question 2 — Catalase and oxidase 89. Catalase produces oxygen during hydrogen-peroxide decomposition. 90. Every obligate aerobe must be oxidase-positive. 91. Oxidase-negative Acinetobacter can still possess respiratory metabolism. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 3 are correct. • 1: Correct. (2H_2O_2\rightarrow2H_2O+O_2). • 2: Incorrect. The oxidase test detects particular respiratory components, not all respiration. • 3: Correct. Its oxidase result does not preclude aerobic metabolism. Question 3 — Oxygen relationships 92. Facultative anaerobes may grow both with and without oxygen. 93. Aerotolerant anaerobes must use oxygen as their terminal electron acceptor. 94. Vacuum packaging kills all anaerobic bacteria. Answer: A — Only statement 1 is correct. • 1: Correct. Alternative metabolic routes support growth. • 2: Incorrect. Oxygen tolerance is not equivalent to oxygen-dependent respiration. • 3: Incorrect. Vacuum is not a sterilising treatment. Question 4 — Endospores 95. A bacterial endospore is primarily a reproductive structure. 96. Sporulation necessarily produces multiple daughter spores from one cell. 97. Endospores multiply by binary fission while dormant. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Answer: D — None is correct. All three statements confuse survival with reproduction. Ordinary endospore formation produces a dormant survival structure; multiplication occurs after germination and outgrowth. Question 5 — Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas 98. Acinetobacter is typically oxidase-negative. 99. Most familiar food-spoilage pseudomonads possess flagellar motility. 100.Both genera form heat-resistant bacterial endospores. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 2 are correct. • 1: Correct. • 2: Correct, with species-level exceptions. • 3: Incorrect. Neither genus is an endospore-forming genus. Question 6 — B. cereus toxins 101.Cereulide is a cyclic depsipeptide. 102.Nhe and Hbl are identical names for cereulide. 103.Emetic illness principally follows ingestion of preformed toxin. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 3 are correct. • 1: Correct. • 2: Incorrect. Nhe and Hbl are protein enterotoxin systems. • 3: Correct. This defines the emetic intoxication model. Question 7 — B. cereus disease differentiation 104.Every B. cereus strain produces cereulide. 105.Diarrhoeal B. cereus illness and emetic illness have the same toxin chemistry. 106.Reheating that kills vegetative cells invariably destroys cereulide. Answer: D — None is correct. • Cereulide production is strain-specific. • Diarrhoeal toxins are proteins; cereulide is a depsipeptide. • Cereulide can persist after a cell-lethal reheating treatment. Question 8 — Bread rope 107.Subtilisin is a serine protease. 108.Bacillary spores can survive a baking process in the bread crumb. 109.Rope spoilage is attributable exclusively to one species and one polysaccharide. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 2 are correct. • 1: Correct. • 2: Correct. The food interior has its own thermal history. • 3: Incorrect. Related bacilli, enzymes and polymers can participate. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 39

text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Question 9 — Carnobacterium 110.Some strains produce anti-listerial bacteriocins. 111.Some strains can form tyramine through tyrosine decarboxylation. 112.Vacuum packaging can provide conditions compatible with their growth. Answer: C — All 3 are correct. The statements describe compatible capabilities, not contradictory ones. A strain may offer antimicrobial potential while also requiring assessment for undesirable metabolites. Question 10 — Diphtheria toxin 113.Fragment A mediates the principal catalytic activity. 114.Fragment B contributes to binding and translocation. 115.The toxin inhibits protein synthesis through eEF2 modification. Answer: C — All 3 are correct. The key reaction is ADP-ribosylation of eEF2. Do not reverse the functions of A and B. Question 11 — Toxin-target confusion 116.Diphtheria toxin depurinates 28S rRNA as its defining mechanism. 117.Shiga toxin primarily ADP-ribosylates eEF2. 118.Botulinum neurotoxin causes paralysis principally by activating acetylcholine release. Answer: D — None is correct. • Diphtheria toxin modifies eEF2. • Shiga toxin depurinates 28S rRNA. • Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release through SNARE cleavage. Question 12 — C. perfringens 119.Ordinary food poisoning is classically associated with intestinal CPE production. 120.CPE and beta toxin are the same protein. 121.Generation time can be below 10 minutes under favourable conditions. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 3 are correct. • 1: Correct. • 2: Incorrect. Beta toxin is distinct and important in type C necrotic enteritis. • 3: Correct. It is an optimum-condition result, not a universal rate. Question 13 — C. perfringens classification and control 122.Many strains historically described as enterotoxigenic type A are designated type F in the expanded system. 123.Cooking that kills vegetative cells necessarily kills all spores. 124.Slow cooling of bulk meat dishes can permit extensive growth. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 3 are correct. The error in statement 2 is the word necessarily. Spores require separate consideration. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 40

text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Question 14 — Botulism 125.Food-borne botulism usually follows ingestion of preformed neurotoxin. 126.Infant botulism can follow ingestion of spores. 127.Botulinum toxin light chains cleave components of the SNARE machinery. Answer: D — None is correct. • Acidity inhibits growth; it does not prove spore destruction. • Non-proteolytic strains can grow near 3°C. • Sensory normality does not prove safety. Question 16 — Listeria 131.L. monocytogenes is an endospore-forming psychrophile. 132.Listeriolysin O contributes to vacuolar escape. 133.ActA contributes to actin-based intracellular movement. Answer: B — Only statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 contains two errors: the organism is non-spore-forming and is better described as psychrotrophic, with a substantially warmer optimum. Answer: B — Only statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is the reverse of the typical pattern: most salmonellae are motile, with notable exceptions. doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 1. FIRST-PRINCIPLES MODEL: WHY MOULDS GROW AND WHY MYCOTOXINS APPEAR 1.1 Ecological niche of filamentous fungi Filamentous fungi are favoured where oxygen is available, bacterial growth is restricted by low pH or low aw, substrates are rich in carbohydrates or lipids, and storage is warm, humid or poorly ventilated. The principal sequence is: Spore deposition → germination → hyphal extension → mycelial colonisation → sporulation and/or toxin production However: Growth does not imply toxin production in every strain. Absence of visible growth does not imply absence of toxin. 1.2 Spoilage versus mycotoxigenesis Mould spoilage may cause visible mycelium, pigmentation, softening, dehydration, musty odours, lipolysis, pectin degradation and structural collapse. Mycotoxigenesis is the formation of biologically active secondary metabolites by selected fungal strains under particular environmental and nutritional conditions. A practical model is: Mycotoxin risk = f(toxigenic strain, aw, temperature, oxygen, substrate, time, stress and competition) 1.3 Primary and secondary metabolism Primary metabolism supports growth, energy generation, biosynthesis and reproduction. Secondary metabolism produces compounds not essential for immediate biomass formation but potentially important in ecological competition, defence or stress responses. Many mycotoxins are secondary metabolites. Their formation may increase during drought stress, insect damage, nutrient limitation, temperature shifts or microbial competition. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Secondary metabolite does not mean unimportant; it means not directly required for basic multiplication under ordinary conditions. 2. MORPHOLOGY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF FOOD MOULDS 2.1 Hyphae and mycelium A hypha is a tubular fungal filament. A network of hyphae forms a mycelium. Hyphae may be septate or sparsely septate depending on the group. Growth occurs mainly at the hyphal tip. Tip growth requires membrane synthesis, cell-wall assembly, vesicle trafficking and polarised cytoskeletal transport. This enables moulds to penetrate cracks, pores and damaged plant tissue. 2.2 Asexual spores: conidia The common asexual spores of Aspergillus and Penicillium are conidia. They are produced externally on specialised structures, assist dissemination, and often tolerate drying. Conidia are not bacterial endospores. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 61

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Conidium → germ tube → hypha → mycelium 2.3 Sexual spores Some food moulds produce sexual spores such as ascospores. These may be more heat-resistant than vegetative hyphae or conidia in certain species. A sexual stage is not required for spoilage or mycotoxin production. 2.4 Conidiophore architecture Aspergillus Typical architecture: Foot cell → conidiophore → vesicle → phialides → conidia Species differ in stalk morphology, vesicle size, phialide arrangement, conidial colour and sclerotium formation. Penicillium The conidiophore branches into a brush-like penicillus containing branches, metulae, phialides and conidia. Arrangements may be monoverticillate, biverticillate or more complex. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] The brush-like conidiophore is characteristic of Penicillium. Aspergillus typically forms a vesicle-based conidial head. 3. WATER ACTIVITY, OXYGEN AND MOULD GROWTH 3.1 Water activity Water activity is: aw = p / p0 where p is the vapour pressure of water above the food and p0 is the vapour pressure of pure water at the same temperature. At equilibrium: ERH (%) ≈ 100aw Therefore, aw = 0.80 corresponds approximately to 80% equilibrium relative humidity. Total moisture percentage is insufficient because water may be bound to proteins, salts, sugars or the food matrix. Microorganisms respond more directly to available water than to total moisture. 3.2 Approximate lower aw values Group Approximate lower aw for growth Many Gram-negative bacteria About 0.95 Many Gram-positive bacteria About 0.90–0.92 Staphylococcus aureus Approximately 0.83–0.86, depending on conditions Ordinary yeasts About 0.88 Most filamentous moulds About 0.80 Xerophilic moulds Approximately 0.61–0.65 under favourable conditions These are approximate physiological values, not legal product limits. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 62

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES For aflatoxigenic strains, the aw required for toxin formation may be higher than the aw required for visible growth. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Mould growth at aw 0.80 does not establish aflatoxin production at aw 0.80. 3.3 Obligate aerobic character Food-associated filamentous moulds are generally obligately aerobic. They are favoured by oxygenated surfaces, headspace oxygen, cracks, insect channels and inadequately sealed packages. Vacuum packaging can suppress mould growth only if oxygen is sufficiently removed and maintained at a low level. Leaks, oxygen ingress or surface exposure can restore the aerobic niche. Reduced oxygen may inhibit moulds but select for yeasts or anaerobic bacteria. It changes the hazard profile rather than eliminating all hazards. 4. ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS CONTROLLING MYCOTOXIN PRODUCTION 4.1 Temperature Each species has minimum, optimum and maximum growth temperatures. The optimum for toxin production may differ from the optimum for biomass formation. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Maximum biomass and maximum toxin concentration are not necessarily obtained at the same temperature. 4.2 pH Moulds commonly tolerate a wider pH range than many bacteria and can grow in acidic foods. Many food moulds grow in approximately pH 3–6, although species vary. Low pH suppresses many bacterial competitors and may give moulds a competitive advantage. 4.3 Oxygen and redox potential Fungal growth and many oxidative biosynthetic reactions require oxygen. Oxygen limitation may reduce hyphal growth, sporulation and toxin biosynthesis. Oxygen may nevertheless vary greatly within a food particle or package. 4.4 Substrate Mycotoxin production depends on carbon source, nitrogen source, lipids, trace minerals, plant defence compounds and available precursors. A substrate that supports growth does not necessarily support the same toxin profile. 4.5 Crop stress and insect damage Pre-harvest risk factors include drought, high temperature, insect feeding, plant disease, delayed harvest and mechanical injury. Damaged kernels permit easier fungal penetration and provide more available nutrients. 4.6 Post-harvest storage Risk rises with inadequate drying, moisture migration, condensation, warm storage, poor aeration, insect activity, prolonged storage and mixing of old and new lots. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 63

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES The central control principle is: Rapid drying + uniform moisture + cool, clean storage + lot monitoring 5. ASPERGILLUS FLAVUS, ASPERGILLUS PARASITICUS AND AFLATOXINS 5.1 Taxonomic and ecological position A. flavus and A. parasiticus belong to Aspergillus section Flavi. A. flavus commonly produces B-series aflatoxins. A. parasiticus commonly produces B- and G-series aflatoxins. Some section Flavi species also produce aflatoxins, and many strains are non-toxigenic. Species identification by colony appearance alone is insufficient to predict toxin production. 5.2 Morphological profile A. flavus may show yellow-green to olive-green conidial masses, globose or subglobose vesicles, one or two layers of phialides and, in some strains, sclerotia. A. parasiticus is often associated with darker green conidial masses, commonly biseriate conidial heads and production of both B- and G-series aflatoxins. These are tendencies, not definitive diagnostic criteria. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Conidial colour is not an aflatoxin assay. 5.3 Aflatoxin types • Aflatoxin B1 — AFB1. • Aflatoxin B2 — AFB2. • Aflatoxin G1 — AFG1. • Aflatoxin G2 — AFG2. The historical letters refer to fluorescence: B for blue and G for green. AFB1 is generally the most important toxicologically. 5.4 Biosynthetic pathway A simplified pathway is: Acetate → polyketide chain → norsolorinic acid → averantin → averufin → versicolorin → sterigmatocystin → O- methylsterigmatocystin → aflatoxin The pathway is controlled by a biosynthetic gene cluster containing genes for polyketide synthesis, oxidation, reduction, methylation, transport and regulation. 5.5 Metabolic activation of AFB1 Aflatoxin B1 is activated principally by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. AFB1 → CYP450 → AFB1-8,9-exo-epoxide The terminal 8,9 double bond in the terminal furan ring is central to this activation. The reactive epoxide forms DNA adducts: AFB1-8,9-epoxide + DNA guanine → AFB1-N7-guanine adduct Further rearrangement can generate AFB1–formamidopyrimidine adducts. These may cause misreplication, mutations, hepatocellular injury and hepatocellular carcinoma risk. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 64

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES A characteristic TP53 codon-249 mutation is strongly associated with AFB1 exposure in relevant settings. Detoxification routes include hydroxylation, glutathione conjugation and urinary excretion of metabolites. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] AFB1 is not simply directly mutagenic in its original form; metabolic activation is central to its genotoxicity. 5.6 Aflatoxin M1 and M2 AFB1 → hepatic hydroxylation → AFM1 AFB2 metabolism is associated with AFM2. Food-chain pathway: Contaminated feed → animal ingestion → hepatic metabolism → AFM1 in milk → human exposure AFM1 is a milk metabolite, not usually the result of Aspergillus growing in milk. It is relatively resistant to pasteurisation, boiling and ordinary dairy processing. Feed control is therefore a primary milk-safety intervention. 5.7 Commodity associations Aflatoxins may occur in groundnuts, maize, tree nuts, oilseeds, cottonseed, spices, dried fruits, cereals and animal feed. Risk is influenced by crop variety, climate, insect damage, harvest timing, drying, storage and sorting. 5.8 Prevention and control Pre-harvest • Resistant cultivars. • Appropriate irrigation. • Insect management. • Reduction of drought stress. • Timely harvesting. • Approved biological control with selected non-toxigenic A. flavus strains. Post-harvest • Rapid drying. • Removal of damaged kernels. • Optical, density or colour sorting. • Pest control. • Moisture monitoring. • Aerated storage. • Prevention of condensation. • Lot segregation. • Representative sampling. Aflatoxins are comparatively stable and may survive baking, frying, roasting and ordinary cooking. Physical removal, adsorption, alkaline treatment or validated detoxification may reduce exposure, but degradation products must also be assessed. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 65

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 6. OCHRATOXIN A 6.1 Principal producers Important producers include selected strains of: • Aspergillus ochraceus sensu lato. • A. westerdijkiae. • A. steynii. • A. carbonarius. • Some A. niger-group strains. • Penicillium verrucosum. • Penicillium nordicum. Warmer environments commonly favour relevant Aspergillus species, whereas P. verrucosum is important in temperate storage. 6.2 Chemical nature OTA is a chlorinated isocoumarin linked to L-phenylalanine. 6.3 Toxicological effects OTA has been associated with nephrotoxicity, immunotoxicity, oxidative stress, developmental toxicity and possible carcinogenicity. 6.4 Food sources Potential sources include cereals, coffee, cocoa, dried fruits, wine, grapes, spices, nuts and animal products indirectly exposed through contaminated feed. 6.5 Control • Rapid drying. • Low and uniform storage moisture. • Prevention of temperature fluctuations. • Insect and rodent control. • Sorting and monitoring. • Prevention of cross-contamination. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] OTA is produced by selected Aspergillus and Penicillium species; it is not exclusively an Aspergillus toxin. 7. PENICILLIUM MOULDS AND THEIR TOXINS Penicillium species may function as starter cultures, surface-ripening moulds, spoilage organisms or mycotoxin producers. Genus-level identification does not predict toxin production. 7.1 Patulin The principal food-associated producer is Penicillium expansum, especially in bruised or rotten apples and pears, apple pomace, apple juice, cider and fruit purees. Other fungi, including selected Aspergillus, Byssochlamys and Paecilomyces species, may produce patulin. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 66

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Patulin is an unsaturated lactone. Its reactive structure permits interaction with sulfhydryl groups in proteins and enzymes. Patulin + protein sulfhydryl groups → enzyme dysfunction Potential effects include gastrointestinal irritation, oxidative stress, cellular toxicity and immunotoxicity. Apple risk factors • Bruising. • Fallen fruit. • Rotten cores. • Inadequate sorting. • Mixing damaged and sound fruit. • Insufficient removal of mouldy tissue. Patulin can diffuse beyond visible mould. Removing surface mould alone does not guarantee safety. Processing Patulin is not reliably eliminated by ordinary pasteurisation. Reduction may depend on pH, heat, sulphur dioxide where legally permitted, ascorbic acid, fermentation, clarification and adsorption. A commonly encountered international benchmark for patulin in apple juice is approximately 50 micrograms/kg, with lower limits sometimes applying to products for infants and young children. The current applicable national limit must be verified. 7.2 Other Penicillium toxins Toxin Important associations P. verrucosum, P. nordicum; cereals, coffee, dried foods and Ochratoxin A meat Citrinin P. citrinum and others; cereals, rice and stored commodities Patulin P. expansum; apples and apple juice Roquefortine C P. roqueforti and related mould-ripened products Mycophenolic acid Selected Penicillium species Cyclopiazonic acid Selected Penicillium and Aspergillus species PR toxin P. roqueforti under some conditions [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Presence of one Penicillium species does not establish production of every toxin listed above. 8. FUSARIUM MYCOTOXINS 8.1 Field infection and storage evolution Fusarium toxins are commonly associated with pre-harvest crop infection: Plant infection → fungal colonisation → toxin formation in the field → harvest → persistence or redistribution during storage The absence of visible mould after cleaning does not prove absence of a Fusarium toxin. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 67

doc: Food Microbiology, Spoilage & Preservation — Master Study Manual
text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 8.2 Trichothecenes Major trichothecenes include deoxynivalenol, nivalenol, T-2 toxin, HT-2 toxin and diacetoxyscirpenol. Many trichothecenes interact with the 60S ribosomal subunit and inhibit protein synthesis. DON DON is also called vomitoxin. It is associated with Fusarium graminearum species complex, F. culmorum, wheat, barley, maize and other cereals. Possible effects include nausea, vomiting, feed refusal, reduced growth, intestinal injury and immune modulation. T-2 and HT-2 toxins These may cause protein-synthesis inhibition, gastrointestinal injury, haematological effects, immunotoxicity and mucosal injury. 8.3 Zearalenone Important producers include Fusarium graminearum species complex, F. culmorum and F. equiseti-related species. Zearalenone is a resorcylic acid lactone with estrogenic activity: Zearalenone + estrogen receptor → abnormal estrogenic signalling Effects may include altered oestrus, infertility, reproductive disturbance, vulvar swelling and hyperestrogenism, particularly in pigs. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Zearalenone is principally an estrogenic/reproductive toxin, not an aflatoxin analogue. 8.4 Fumonisins Important producers include Fusarium verticillioides and Fusarium proliferatum. They are strongly associated with maize. Principal compounds include fumonisins B1, B2 and B3, with FB1 commonly the principal concern. Fumonisins resemble sphingoid-base intermediates and inhibit ceramide synthase: Fumonisin → decreased ceramide synthase → increased sphinganine/sphingosine → disrupted sphingolipid metabolism Possible effects include liver and kidney injury, equine leukoencephalomalacia, porcine pulmonary oedema and developmental or carcinogenic concerns. Milling may redistribute fumonisins among bran, germ and endosperm. Alkaline processing may reduce extractable parent fumonisins but can form hydrolysed products. 8.5 Other Fusarium metabolites • Moniliformin. • Beauvericin. • Enniatins. • Fusaric acid. • Modified or masked mycotoxins. Cereal lots may contain several toxins simultaneously. Co-occurrence may produce additive or interactive effects. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Compliance with a limit for one mycotoxin does not establish freedom from all other mycotoxins. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 68

MYCOTOXIN SAMPLING AND ANALYTICAL CONTROL 10.1 Heterogeneous distribution Mycotoxins are often unevenly distributed. Analytical uncertainty is: Sampling error + subsampling error + laboratory error 10.2 Correct sampling logic Define the lot. Collect incremental samples across locations. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Flexible membrane composition. Efficient osmotic-stress responses. Compatible-solute accumulation, especially glycerol. Fermentative metabolism without oxygen. Acid-stress adaptation. Extracellular enzyme secretion. Biofilm or surface-film formation. Resistance to selected preservatives. The food-selection sequence is therefore: Preservation hurdle → bacterial inhibition → ecological release of yeasts → yeast growth → fermentation, gas, turbidity or off-flavour 3.2 Morphology and structure Food yeasts are unicellular fungi, usually oval, spherical, cylindrical or elongated. Important structures include: • Cell wall containing glucans, mannoproteins and chitin. • Plasma membrane rich in sterols, principally ergosterol. • Nucleus and other eukaryotic organelles. • Vacuoles for storage and stress physiology. • Mitochondria for respiration. • Bud scars after asexual budding. Reproduction Most food yeasts multiply by multilateral or polar budding: Mother cell → bud formation → nuclear division → bud separation Some form pseudohyphae or true hyphae. Filamentation should not automatically be interpreted as a bacterial contamination. Sexual forms Some yeasts produce ascospores. These are fungal sexual spores and are distinct from bacterial endospores. Ascospore formation can increase persistence under environmental stress in some species. 3.3 Respiration and fermentation Aerobic respiration When oxygen is available: Glucose → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → TCA cycle → electron transport → CO₂ + H₂O + high ATP yield Alcoholic fermentation Under oxygen limitation or in strongly fermentative conditions: Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO₂ → 2 ethanol The overall reaction is: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + energy The simplified net yield is approximately 2 ATP per glucose. Mechanism of osmotolerance High external solute concentration lowers water activity and creates an outward osmotic gradient. The yeast responds by: Accumulating glycerol and other compatible solutes. Maintaining intracellular turgor. Modifying membrane transport. Reducing loss of cytoplasmic water. Repairing osmotic damage. A simplified water-stress relationship is: High external solute → low aw → water efflux → cell stress → glycerol accumulation → partial restoration of turgor Control • Lower (a_w) sufficiently and uniformly. • Combine sugar with pH control, heat treatment and hygienic packaging. • Prevent dilution by condensation or wash-water carryover. • Monitor concentrated products during storage. 3.7 Debaryomyces hansenii Basic significance D. hansenii is a halotolerant yeast associated with: • Salted meats. • Dry-cured products. • Cheese surfaces. • Brines. • High-salt fish products. • Protein-rich foods stored under reduced water activity. Functional traits • Strong salt tolerance. • Ability to grow at low water activity. • Surface-film formation. • Lipolytic activity. • Proteolytic activity in some strains. • Contribution to ripening aroma in selected controlled fermentations. Cells may differ in: • Age. • Physiological state. • Spore maturity. • Location in the food. • Access to heat. • Protective matrix exposure. • Stress history. A thermal process therefore produces a probability distribution of survival, not an instantaneous universal kill. Under the ideal logarithmic model: N_t = N_0 × 10^(−t/D) where (N_0) is the initial population, (N_t) is the survivors after time (t), and (D) is the decimal reduction time. Taking logarithms: log₁₀N_t = log₁₀N_0 − t/D The survivor curve is linear when log survivors are plotted against time. 4.2 D-value Definition The D-value is the time at a specified temperature and in a specified food matrix required to reduce the surviving population by 90%, or one decimal logarithm. For a constant temperature: F_T = D_T × number of decimal reductions For a changing temperature process, lethality is integrated over time. 4.6 Reference lethality and F₀ The conventional reference for F₀ is: • Reference temperature = 121.1°C. • z-value = 10°C. Instantaneous lethality at temperature T is: L = 10^[(T − 121.1)/z] For z = 10°C: F₀ = ∫ L dt For constant temperature: F₀ = t × 10^[(T − 121.1)/10] Example A product is held at 111.1°C for 10 min. L = 10^[(111.1 − 121.1)/10] = 10⁻¹ = 0.1 F₀ = 10 × 0.1 = 1 min The same lethality can be obtained through different time–temperature combinations, provided the reference model is valid. 4.7 12D botulinum cook The classical low-acid canned-food concept uses: • A reference temperature of 121.1°C. • A z-value of 10°C. It is a theoretical or highly stringent laboratory concept and is difficult to demonstrate directly. Commercial sterility A condition in which the food is free from microorganisms capable of growing under normal non-refrigerated storage and distribution conditions and is safe and stable for its intended use. Commercial sterility depends on: • Product pH. • Water activity. • Container hermeticity. • Process severity. • Storage temperature. • Target organisms. A commercially sterile food may not be absolutely sterile in the philosophical sense. 4.9 Shoulder and tailing effects Shoulder A delay in measurable inactivation at the start of treatment. It changes the physical state and availability of water. For growth, a lower temperature generally reduces metabolic rate and increases lag time. For freezing, water changes from liquid to ice, concentrating solutes in the remaining unfrozen phase. The central sequence is: Chilling → slower metabolism and longer lag → extended shelf life Freezing → ice formation and freeze concentration → growth inhibition plus possible structural damage 5.2 Chilling Chilling usually means storage above the product freezing point and commonly near 0–5°C for many foods. Effects on microorganisms • Slower enzyme activity. • Reduced membrane transport. • Longer lag phase. • Lower specific growth rate. • Delayed toxin formation. • Selection for psychrotrophic organisms. Mathematically, if the specific growth rate falls from μ₁ to μ₂: N_t = N₀e^(μt) A lower μ gives a smaller population after the same storage time, but does not necessarily give zero growth. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES Group Growth capability Approximate optimum Psychrotrophs Grow at refrigeration temperatures Often approximately 20–30°C Mesophiles Prefer moderate temperatures Often 30–40°C The exact definitions vary by textbook and experimental method. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Psychrotrophic threshold and optimum temperature are not the same parameter. Chilling injury in produce Some fruits and vegetables suffer physiological chilling injury above their freezing point. Effects may include: • Pitting. • Surface browning. • Failure to ripen normally. • Water-soaked tissue. • Increased decay susceptibility. • Membrane leakage. Thus the lowest temperature is not always the best storage temperature. 5.3 Freezing-point depression Pure water freezes at 0°C at standard pressure. Dissolved solutes lower the freezing point. The first ice forms when the liquid phase reaches its product-specific freezing point. As ice forms, solutes remain in the unfrozen phase, raising its concentration and further lowering its freezing point. The sequence is: Cooling → nucleation → ice growth → solute concentration → lower remaining-phase freezing point 5.4 Ice nucleation and crystal growth Nucleation The formation of a stable microscopic ice nucleus. It may be: • Homogeneous. • Heterogeneous, promoted by surfaces, particles or impurities. Crystal growth Once nuclei form, water molecules add to the crystal lattice. The final crystal size depends on: • Cooling rate. • Product composition. • Nucleation temperature. • Solute concentration. • Tissue structure. • Thermal conductivity. • Package geometry. 5.5 Slow freezing Slow freezing generally results in: • Fewer nuclei. • More time for crystal growth. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES • Larger ice crystals. • Greater extracellular concentration gradients. • More mechanical disruption of tissues. • Greater drip loss on thawing. Large extracellular crystals can compress cells and damage membranes. Water migrates out of cells, increasing shrinkage and solute concentration. 5.6 Quick freezing Rapid freezing generally results in: • Greater nucleation. • Smaller crystals. • More uniform crystal distribution. • Less time for solute migration. • Better retention of texture after thawing. The common course statement that quick freezing produces numerous small intracellular crystals is an oversimplification. The location of ice depends on freezing rate and cell dimensions. Very rapid freezing can generate intracellular ice; such ice may be lethal to cells, although small crystals generally produce less structural damage in food tissues than large crystals. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] The scientifically safe comparison is large, damaging crystals in slow freezing versus generally smaller crystals and less structural damage in rapid freezing—not an absolute extracellular-versus- intracellular rule. 5.7 Freeze concentration When pure water crystallises as ice, solutes remain in the unfrozen liquid. Thus the unfrozen phase becomes concentrated in: • Sugars. • Salts. • Organic acids. • Proteins. • Minerals. • Preservatives. Consequences include: • Lower water activity. • Increased ionic strength. • Local pH shifts. • Protein denaturation. • Membrane stress. • Greater concentration of reactive solutes. 5.8 Cryohydric point The cryohydric point is the eutectic temperature at which ice and a concentrated solute phase can coexist at equilibrium for a particular aqueous solution. Foods contain multiple solutes, so they generally have a complex range of phase transitions rather than one simple universal point. At or below a eutectic condition, solutes may crystallise rather than remain in a concentrated liquid phase. This affects: • Texture. • Chemical stability. • Solute distribution. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES • Recrystallisation. • Freeze-drying behaviour. 5.9 Freeze-thaw damage Repeated freezing and thawing causes: • Recrystallisation. • Membrane rupture. • Drip loss. • Protein denaturation. • Emulsion destabilisation. • Pigment migration. • Texture softening. • Increased microbial opportunity during thawing. Recrystallisation Small crystals can melt partially and feed larger crystals during temperature fluctuation. Therefore stable low- temperature storage is essential. 5.10 Microbial behaviour during freezing Freezing may: • Kill a fraction of vegetative cells. • Injure membranes. • Select resistant subpopulations. • Preserve surviving pathogens for long periods. • Prevent multiplication while frozen. Survival is enhanced by: • Sugar. • Fat. • Protein. • High initial population. • Protective food matrices. A thawed food can support rapid growth if held in the danger zone. 5.11 Freezing process sequence Selection and preparation. Washing and trimming. Blanching where required. Rapid heat removal. Freezing through the zone of maximum ice-crystal formation. Completion of freezing. Packaging with moisture and oxygen control. Storage at stable temperature. Controlled thawing or direct cooking. 5.12 Packaging and freezer burn Freezer burn is a dehydration and oxidation defect caused by moisture migration from the food to the package environment. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 6.3 Pasteurisation Pasteurisation is a relatively mild thermal treatment designed to destroy specified vegetative pathogens and reduce spoilage organisms while preserving product quality. Milk reference schedules LTLT or batch method 62.8°C for 30 minutes This is historically equivalent to 145°F for 30 minutes. HTST method 71.7°C for 15 seconds This is historically equivalent to 161°F for 15 seconds. These are classic milk values. Current legal standards may include additional methods such as higher-temperature short-time or ultra-pasteurisation schedules. Pasteurisation does not destroy • All bacterial spores. • All heat-stable toxins. • All post-process contaminants. • All enzymes. 6.4 Alkaline phosphatase test Principle Alkaline phosphatase is naturally present in raw milk and is more heat-resistant than many milk-borne vegetative pathogens. Proper pasteurisation should inactivate it below the validated detection threshold. A substrate is hydrolysed by residual phosphatase to produce a measurable colour or fluorescence. Interpretation Result Possible interpretation Consistent with adequate pasteurisation, assuming test Negative validity Inadequate heating, raw-milk contamination, phosphatase Positive from another source or analytical interference A negative result does not prove absence of post-pasteurisation contamination. Factors causing interpretation errors • Incorrect incubation temperature. • Reagent deterioration. • Inadequate cleaning. • Microbial phosphatases. • Product composition. • Excessive dilution. • Improper sampling. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Alkaline phosphatase is a process indicator, not a direct pathogen assay. 6.5 UHT processing Correct definition Ultra-high-temperature processing applies a very high temperature for a short period, commonly approximately 135–150°C for a few seconds, followed by aseptic packaging. A typical operational range may be approximately 135–140°C for 1–10 seconds, but the actual scheduled process is product-specific. Correction of the 93.4°C/3-second statement A treatment at 93.4°C for 3 seconds is not a general definition of UHT commercial processing. It may describe another high-temperature treatment or a course-material misprint, but it should not be quoted as the authentic UHT standard without qualification. Direct systems • Steam injection. • Steam infusion. Advantages: • Very rapid heating. • Short residence time. • Reduced quality damage if steam quality is controlled. Indirect systems • Plate heat exchangers. • Tubular heat exchangers. • Scraped-surface exchangers for viscous products. UHT sequence Preheating → UHT heating → holding → flash cooling or regenerative cooling → aseptic filling Aseptic packaging requirements • Commercially sterile product. • Sterilised packaging material. • Sterile filling zone. • Hermetic closure. • Validated sterilisation of product-contact surfaces. • Environmental monitoring. Shelf stability UHT products are shelf-stable at room temperature only when commercial sterility and package integrity are maintained. After opening, refrigeration is normally required. 6.6 Retorting and commercial canning Product categories • Low-acid foods: equilibrium pH greater than 4.6. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES • Acidified or acid foods: equilibrium pH at or below 4.6, subject to regulatory definitions and product controls. Low-acid foods require particular attention to proteolytic C. botulinum spores. Retort sequence Container preparation and filling. Headspace control. Exhausting or air removal. Seaming or hermetic closure. Loading into the retort. Venting and come-up period. Holding at the scheduled process. Cooling under controlled conditions. Drying and inspection. Incubation or verification where required. Cold spot The cold spot is the location in the container receiving the least lethal treatment. It depends on: • Container geometry. • Product viscosity. • Solid-to-liquid ratio. • Convection or conduction heating. • Fill weight. • Headspace. • Agitation. The cold spot is not automatically the geometric centre in every product. Heat transfer modes Conduction-heating foods Viscous or solid foods transfer heat mainly by conduction. The cold spot is often near the geometric centre, but this must be verified. Convection-heating foods Liquids circulate and transfer heat by convection. The cold spot may be displaced and changes with viscosity and particle content. Container defects • Flipper: one end becomes convex but returns on pressure release. • Springer: one end remains convex after the other is depressed. • Swell: both ends bulge due to gas or pressure. • Leaker: loss of hermetic integrity. • Buckled seam. • Paneling. • Rust and corrosion. A swollen can is unsafe to taste or open casually. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 100

text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 7.2 Bound water and free water Free or relatively mobile water • Supports dissolution. • Participates in biochemical reactions. • Can migrate during drying or freezing. • More available to microorganisms. Bound water • Associated with proteins, polysaccharides, salts or surfaces. • Has reduced mobility. • Has lower vapour pressure. • Is less available for microbial metabolism. Food water exists on a continuum; the terms free and bound are useful models rather than two perfectly separate pools. 7.3 Thermodynamic definition of aw aw = p/p₀ where p is water vapour pressure above the food and p₀ is vapour pressure above pure water at the same temperature. Water chemical potential is related to aw: μw = μw⁰ + RT ln aw For aw less than 1, the chemical potential of water is lower than that of pure water. Relative humidity relationship At equilibrium: ERH (%) ≈ 100 × aw 7.4 Effect of solutes Dissolved solutes reduce aw by binding water and lowering vapour pressure. Important humectants include: • Sodium chloride. • Sucrose. • Glucose syrup. • Fructose. • Glycerol. • Sorbitol. • Propylene glycol where permitted. The antimicrobial effect depends on: • Solute identity. • Concentration. • Ionic versus non-ionic nature. • Food pH. • Temperature. • Organism. Equal moisture content does not imply equal aw if solutes differ. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 103

text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 7.5 Moisture sorption isotherms A moisture sorption isotherm plots equilibrium moisture content against aw at a fixed temperature. Adsorption Moisture is added to a dry product. Desorption Moisture is removed from a wet product. Hysteresis The adsorption and desorption curves do not coincide. At the same aw, a food may contain different moisture levels depending on whether it is gaining or losing water. Causes include: • Capillary condensation. • Swelling. • Structural collapse. • Solute crystallisation. • Glass transition. • Irreversible matrix changes. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] A sorption isotherm is temperature-specific. The curve shifts when temperature changes. 7.6 Regions of a sorption isotherm Monolayer region Water is strongly associated with polar sites. Mobility is low. Multilayer region Additional layers form with increasing mobility. Capillary-condensation region More mobile water accumulates in pores and can support chemical reactions and microbial growth. The monolayer moisture content is important for predicting stability, but it is not itself a universal microbial- growth boundary. 7.7 Approximate lower growth boundary A practical food-microbiology teaching boundary is: aw ≈ 0.60 Below approximately 0.60, multiplication of ordinary food-associated microorganisms is generally prevented. Xerophilic moulds can grow near 0.61–0.65 under favourable conditions; some highly adapted organisms may approach this range. This does not imply: • Immediate cell death. • Toxin destruction. • Spore destruction. • Elimination of viruses or prions. FOOD MICROBIOLOGY, SPOILAGE & PRESERVATION | 104

text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES • Absence of chemical deterioration. 7.8 Intermediate Moisture Foods Intermediate Moisture Foods commonly have: • Moisture content often approximately 15–40%, depending on definition. • aw approximately 0.60–0.85. • Sufficient plasticity or softness for direct consumption. • Shelf stability without full refrigeration when properly formulated. Examples may include: • Fruit bars. • Soft dried fruits. • Meat products. • Confectionery. • Bakery fillings. • Semi-moist pet foods. IMF preservation system Reduced aw + pH control + preservatives + packaging + heat + hygienic manufacture Humectant mechanism Humectants bind water and reduce aw without necessarily removing all moisture: Food water + humectant → lower vapour pressure → lower aw IMF limitations • Surface moisture migration. • Localised high-aw pockets. • Mould growth at the surface. • Preservative redistribution. • Texture changes. • Chemical browning. 7.9 Hurdle technology Hurdle technology applies several preservation factors, each targeting a different homeostatic system. Major hurdles: • Temperature. • pH. • aw. • Redox potential. • Preservatives. • Organic acids. • Competitive flora. • Modified atmosphere. • Packaging integrity. • Heat treatment. • Irradiation. • High pressure where applicable. For example: • Acidification before heating may increase heat sensitivity. • Salt may alter preservative partitioning. • Low aw may increase heat resistance while reducing growth. • Packaging may prevent recontamination but also create anaerobic conditions. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 8.3.1 Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship For a weak acid HA: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) The undissociated fraction is approximately: Fraction HA = 1 / [1 + 10^(pH − pKa)] As pH decreases below pKa, the undissociated fraction increases. Approximate pKa values: Acid Approximate pKa Benzoic acid 4.2 Sorbic acid 4.76 Propionic acid 4.87 Acetic acid 4.76 Lactic acid 3.86 Values vary slightly with temperature and ionic environment. 8.3.2 Mechanism Undissociated acid crosses the microbial membrane. Intracellular pH is higher than the external acidic environment. The acid dissociates inside the cell. Protons lower intracellular pH. Anions accumulate. ATP is consumed for proton extrusion. Enzymes and transport systems are disrupted. Growth is inhibited or the cell dies. External HA → membrane penetration → intracellular dissociation → proton stress + anion accumulation → metabolic failure 8.3.3 Benzoates Most effective in acidic foods, especially beverages, pickles, sauces and fruit products where legally permitted. Limitations: • Reduced activity at higher pH. • Partitioning into food components. • Strain adaptation. • Possible benzene formation under particular conditions involving benzoate, ascorbate, metals and heat/light; risk management is product-specific. 8.3.4 Sorbates Sorbic acid is particularly useful against: • Yeasts. • Moulds. • Some bacteria. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 8.5 Nitrites and nitrates Technological functions • Cured-meat colour. • Characteristic cured flavour. • Control of selected spoilage organisms. • Inhibition of C. botulinum growth and toxin formation. • Antioxidant effects in some cured systems. Nitrate-to-nitrite pathway Nitrate → nitrite → nitric oxide → nitrosylated haem pigment Nitric oxide binds myoglobin and contributes to the cured pink colour after heating. Safety concerns • Methemoglobinemia from excessive nitrite exposure. • Formation of nitrosamines under suitable conditions. • Need for strict formulation and process control. • Interaction with antioxidants such as ascorbate or erythorbate in cured-meat systems. A historical statement that nitrites are permitted up to 2000 ppm in all cured meats should not be used as a current universal legal value. Current limits are food-category-specific and may be much lower. 8.6 Biological antimicrobials 8.6.1 Nisin Nisin is a lantibiotic peptide produced by selected strains of Lactococcus lactis. Mechanism Nisin binds lipid II. Cell-wall precursor transport is disrupted. Nisin–lipid II complexes form membrane pores. Ion gradients collapse. The susceptible Gram-positive cell dies. Nisin + lipid II → pore formation + cell-wall inhibition → Gram-positive cell death Spectrum Nisin is mainly active against Gram-positive bacteria, including selected clostridia and bacilli. Gram-negative organisms are often protected by their outer membrane. Applications • Processed cheese. • Dairy products. • Selected canned or heat-processed foods. • Control of clostridial outgrowth in permitted products. Mechanism Natamycin binds ergosterol in fungal membranes and disrupts membrane function. It has limited penetration into many food matrices and is therefore useful primarily as a surface treatment. Applications • Surface treatment of cheese. • Selected cured meats. • Other permitted surface applications. Unit correction A surface limit is an area-based quantity, for example mg/dm² where specified. mg/dm³ expresses a volume concentration and should not be substituted for an area loading. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Natamycin is antifungal, whereas nisin is principally antibacterial against Gram-positive organisms. 8.7 Food irradiation 8.7.1 Physical principle Ionising radiation transfers sufficient energy to remove electrons or produce reactive chemical species. Food irradiation can produce: • Direct DNA damage. • Water radiolysis. • Hydroxyl radicals. • Hydrogen atoms. • Hydrated electrons. • Oxidative injury to membranes and proteins. Water radiolysis H₂O + radiation → •OH + •H + e⁻aq + H₂O₂ + molecular products The actual product spectrum depends on oxygen, solutes, dose rate and food composition. 8.7.2 Radiation sources Gamma radiation • Cobalt-60, Co-60. D10 = dose for 1-log reduction It is analogous conceptually to a thermal D-value but is not numerically interchangeable with it. text: FOOD SAFETY • HPSC FSO STUDY SERIES 8.7.5 Historical process terminology Radurisation Low-dose irradiation intended to extend shelf life by reducing spoilage flora, broadly analogous to mild pasteurisation. Radicidation Dose intended to reduce specific non-spore-forming pathogens to a defined level. Radappertisation High-dose treatment intended to achieve commercial sterility-like stability by reducing viable organisms, including more resistant forms, to a very low level. These terms are historical or descriptive process terminology. Current regulations may use different legal language. 8.7.6 Indicative technical dose bands The following are commonly taught or operational ranges, not a replacement for current Indian legal schedules: Objective Commonly encountered dose range Important qualification Sprout inhibition in potatoes, onions Approximately 0.05–0.15 kGy Commodity and notification specific and garlic Insect disinfestation of grains and pulses Approximately 0.25–1.0 kGy Insect species and commodity matter Specific pest and importing-country Quarantine insect treatment of fruits Approximately 0.15–1.0 kGy requirement matter Variety and physiological maturity Delay of ripening or senescence Approximately 0.3–1.0 kGy matter Reduction of vegetative pathogens in Product temperature and sensory Approximately 1–5 kGy meat or seafood quality matter Dose must comply with current Spice and dry-herb decontamination Approximately 5–10 kGy schedule High-dose commercial-sterility-like Approximately 25–45 kGy or higher in Food quality and regulatory treatment selected systems authorisation are critical Statutory caution Exact approved dose clearances in India must be taken from the current FSSAI regulations, relevant Department of Atomic Energy or AERB requirements, irradiation-plant licence conditions and commodity-specific notifications. A historical textbook band must not be presented as a current universal statutory limit. 8.7.7 Food irradiation does not make food radioactive Approved irradiation uses energy that passes through or is absorbed by the product. It does not leave a radioactive source in the food. The distinction is between: • Irradiation: exposure to ionising energy. • Radioactive contamination: unwanted radioactive material deposited in the food. These are not the same event. doc: Food Safety Law & HACCP — Master Study Manual
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP HPSC Food Safety Officer — Master Study Manual (FSN 421 High-Yield Modules) Module 1: Hazards & Foodborne Illness MODULE 1: FOOD HAZARDS & FOODBORNE ILLNESSES 1.1 First-Principles: Why does this module exist? Before memorising definitions, build the mental model. Every food safety question ultimately reduces to one chain: SOURCE (raw material / environment / handler) ↓ HAZARD enters food (biological / chemical / physical) ↓ HAZARD survives processing / storage ↓ HAZARD reaches consumer in a dose sufficient to harm ↓ ADVERSE HEALTH EFFECT (illness, injury, chronic disease) Food safety science is simply the discipline of breaking this chain at the earliest possible point. Everything in this module — definitions, hazard classes, infection vs intoxication, the WHO Five Keys — is organised around where in this chain you intervene. 1.2 Codified Definitions (verbatim-grade, exam-ready) Term Definition (exam-ready) Conceptual Anchor Assurance that food will not cause harm to the consumer when prepared Food Safety Outcome-based guarantee and/or eaten according to its intended use. The capacity of a substance to produce Toxicity harm or injury of any kind, under any Intrinsic property of the substance condition of exposure. "A biological, chemical or physical agent in, or condition of, food with the Hazard (Codex Alimentarius) Potential, not certainty potential to cause an adverse health effect." Presence of harmful or objectionable foreign substances (chemicals, micro- Contamination organisms, dilutants) in food, Unintended presence before/during/after processing or storage. FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 1

doc: Food Safety Law & HACCP — Master Study Manual
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Term Definition (exam-ready) Conceptual Anchor Intentional or accidental addition of impure, cheap, or unnecessary Adulteration ingredients to cheat, cheapen, or falsify Deliberate or negligent degradation a preparation, altering composition/quality. Attributes that influence a product's value to the consumer — negative Quality ⊃ Safety (quality is the wider Food Quality (spoilage, contamination, adulteration, umbrella) safety hazards) AND positive (colour, flavour, texture). Toxicity vs Hazard — the single most tested distinction. Toxicity is a fixed intrinsic property (e.g., cyanide is always toxic). Hazard is a contextual probability — it depends on dose, exposure route, and whether the substance is "not used in the prescribed manner and quantity." A substance can be toxic but pose negligible hazard if controlled (e.g., nitrite at legal ppm levels). [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier alert: A question may state "Toxicity and Hazard are synonymous terms under Codex." This is FALSE. Toxicity = capacity to cause harm (static). Hazard = probability of harm occurring given actual use conditions (dynamic/contextual). Never conflate the two on MCQ elimination logic. 1.3 Tripartite Classification of Hazards FOOD SAFETY HAZARDS | ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ BIOLOGICAL CHEMICAL PHYSICAL | | | ┌────┴────┐ ┌───────┼────────┐ extraneous matter / Macro- Micro- Agri- Pollution Food foreign bodies biological biological chemicals (heavy chemicals/ (visible) (invisible: (pesticides, metals: naturally bacteria, hormones, Pb,Hg,As, occurring yeast,mold, antibiotics) Cd) toxicants protozoa, viruses) (A) Biological Hazards Intuition: Micro-organisms are everywhere; they only become a "hazard" the moment they are (i) pathogenic to humans AND (ii) present in food in numbers/toxin-load sufficient to cause illness. Spoilage organisms ≠ pathogenic organisms — a food can look/smell fine and still carry a biological hazard (classic trap). • Macro-biological hazards: visible pests and insects — larvae, adult insects, rodent droppings/hair — detectable by the naked eye. • Micro-biological hazards (invisible without magnification): ◦ Bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Clostridium botulinum, Staphylococcus aureus) ◦ Yeasts and moulds (spoilage + some mycotoxin producers) ◦ Protozoa (parasitic) ◦ Viruses (do not multiply in food, but survive and transmit via faecal-oral route) FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 2

Soybeans These are protein-derived hazards — the allergenic potential resides in specific proteins, not the whole food matrix. This is why highly refined oils (e.g., refined soybean/peanut oil, protein largely removed) carry much lower allergenic risk than the whole legume, though labelling precaution still applies. 1.4 Food Infection vs Food Intoxication — THE definitive distinction First-Principles Intuition Ask: "Is the live organism itself the problem, or is a pre-formed poison the problem?" • Infection = you swallow a living army (pathogen) that invades and multiplies inside you. Damage accrues over hours–days as the population builds up. Think: slow siege. • Intoxication = you swallow a poison that is already made (toxin), whether or not the organism that made it is still alive. Damage can begin almost immediately. Think: instant poisoning. doc: Food Safety Law & HACCP — Master Study Manual
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP [HPSC EXAM TRAP] "Fever" is a high-yield discriminator. Infections more typically present WITH fever (active immune battle against live organisms); intoxications more typically present WITHOUT fever (no active infection, pure toxin effect) but WITH neurological signs. If an MCQ gives a symptom set with double vision + respiratory failure + NO fever → answer is intoxication (think botulism). If it gives fever + cramps + multi-day onset → answer is infection (think Salmonella). [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Food intoxication is ALWAYS communicable." — FALSE. By definition, intoxication is not communicable person-to-person; only infections carry the faecal-oral transmission risk. 1.5 Food-Borne Disease: Classification & Transmission Routes Food-borne disease outbreak (definition): occurrence of 2 or more cases of similar illness from a common food source, OR observed cases exceeding the expected baseline number for that illness. Transmission Pathways (chain-of-custody view) Infected food handler ──faecal-oral / nasal flora──► ready-to-eat food │ Cross-contamination ──shared utensils/surfaces──► uninfected food │ Inadequate cooking ──survives heat-stable toxins──► consumer │ Improper storage (10–50°C "danger zone") ──pathogen multiplication──► consumer Route Mechanism Prevention Point Pathogens shed in faeces; transferred via faecal-oral route; infected skin Infected individuals Personnel health screening, hygiene lesions/nasal flora transferred to ready-to-eat food Same equipment/utensils used across Cross-contamination raw and ready-to-eat food without Separate equipment, cleaning SOPs washing/disinfecting Insufficient heat allows multiplication; Inadequate cooking many bacterial toxins are heat-stable Validated cook temperatures and survive cooking Holding food at 10–50°C (danger zone) Improper storage Time-temperature control permits pathogen multiplication 1.6 WHO Five Keys to Safer Food (complete operational framework) KEY 1 KEY 2 KEY 3 KEY 4 KEY 5 Keep Clean Separate Raw Cook Thoroughly Keep at Safe Use Safe Water & Cooked Temperatures & Raw Materials FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 5

Keep clean for food preparation; protect kitchen areas and food from insects, pests, and other animals. Separate raw meat, poultry, and seafood from other foods; use separate equipment and utensils (cutting boards, knives) 2. Separate raw and cooked for handling raw foods; store food in containers to avoid contact between raw and prepared foods. Cook food thoroughly, especially meat, poultry, eggs, and seafood; bring foods like soups and stews to boiling to 3. Cook thoroughly ensure pathogen destruction; reheat cooked food thoroughly. Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours; refrigerate promptly (preferably below 5°C); 4. Keep food at safe temperatures keep cooked food hot (above 60°C) prior to serving; do not store food too long even in the refrigerator; do not thaw frozen food at room temperature. Use safe water or treat it to make it safe; select fresh and wholesome foods; choose foods processed for safety (e.g., 5. Use safe water and raw materials pasteurized milk); wash fruits and vegetables, especially if eaten raw; do not use food beyond its expiry date. Mnemonic: C-S-C-T-W → Clean, Separate, Cook, Temperature, Water. 1.7 Stage 2 Model Answer Framework (10 Marks) Question: "Differentiate between Food Infection and Food Intoxication with appropriate examples. Comparison table (4 marks): Reproduce the master table above — cause, mechanism, incubation, symptoms, transmissibility, examples. Examiners award marks per correctly matched parameter. 3. Worked examples (2 marks): Salmonella typhimurium infection (incubation 12–72 hrs, fever + diarrhoea) vs Staphylococcus aureus intoxication (incubation 1–6 hrs, vomiting without fever, heat- stable enterotoxin survives cooking). 4. (iii) Infection incubation period is typically shorter than intoxication's incubation period. Answer: Only 1 is correct (statement ii). • (i) FALSE — fever is a more typical marker of infection, not necessarily intoxication. • (ii) TRUE. • (iii) FALSE — it is the REVERSE: infection has a longer incubation (hours-days) vs intoxication's shorter one (minutes-hours). Q3. On WHO Five Keys to Safer Food: (i) The five keys include "Keep Clean," "Separate Raw and Cooked," and "Cook Thoroughly." (ii) "Use Safe Water and Raw Materials" is one of the five keys. (iii) The WHO Five Keys mandate refrigeration below 0°C for all cooked food. Answer: Only 2 are correct (statements i and ii). • (i) TRUE. • (ii) TRUE. • (iii) FALSE — the guidance is to refrigerate promptly, preferably below 5°C, not 0°C; the "always/mandate" framing with an incorrect numeric threshold is a classic absolute-qualifier trap. (ii) Insects can constitute both a macro-biological hazard AND a physical hazard depending on context. (iii) Physical hazards are defined as materials normally found in food in small amounts. Answer: Only 2 are correct (statements i and ii). • (i) TRUE — all four appear in the standard physical hazard table. • (ii) TRUE — insects are listed under both macro-biological hazards and as a physical hazard source (contamination/extraneous matter), a nuance often tested. • (iii) FALSE — physical hazards are explicitly defined as materials NOT normally found in food. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Module 2: Additives & Plant Toxicants MODULE 2: FOOD ADDITIVES & PLANT-ORIGIN TOXICANTS 2.1 First-Principles: Why classify additives at all? Regulators do not ban "chemicals" per se — they distinguish between substances whose safety is self-evident from long traditional use and low toxicity even unrestricted (Class I) versus substances that are effective but carry a dose-dependent risk profile requiring a legal ceiling (Class II). This single idea — unrestricted vs quantity-capped — is the organizing logic behind nearly every additive question HPSC asks. FOOD PRESERVATIVES | ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ CLASS I CLASS II (natural, NOT restricted (chemical, RESTRICTED to in any food unless Rules specified foods, concentration say otherwise) capped per Rules) | | Common salt, sugar, Benzoic acid & salts, dextrose/glucose syrup, Sulphurous acid & sulphites, wood smoke, spices, Nitrites & nitrates, vinegar/acetic acid, honey Sorbic acid & salts [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Class I preservatives are permitted in UNLIMITED quantity in ALL foods." — Partially FALSE. Class I is "not restricted unless otherwise provided in the Rules" — a conditional, not an absolute, exemption. Always flag "unlimited/unrestricted/all" wording against the actual legal phrasing. 2.2 Additive Categories — Mechanism-First Walkthrough (a) Antioxidants Intuition: Fats and oils undergo autoxidation — a free-radical chain reaction with atmospheric oxygen that converts unsaturated fatty acids into aldehydes/ketones, producing rancid off-flavours, loss of colour, and destruction of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E) and essential fatty acids (e.g., linoleic acid). Unsaturated fatty acid + O2 (catalyzed by light, heat, metal, pigment) ↓ Lipid free radical (R•) ↓ (chain propagation) Peroxide → Aldehydes + Ketones → RANCID OFF-FLAVOUR An antioxidant works by donating a hydrogen atom to the lipid free radical, terminating the chain reaction before it propagates (free radical scavenging). FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 8
