text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Type Examples Notes Found in plant tissues; heat-labile — Natural Tocopherols (Vitamin E family) lost during refining, deodorizing, processing BHA is more effective in animal fats than vegetable oils; very effective for Synthetic BHA, BHT short-chain fatty acids (coconut, palm kernel oil) used in cereals/confectionery (b) Emulsifiers & Stabilizers Intuition: Oil and water naturally separate because they are chemically incompatible (one polar, one non- polar). An emulsifier is amphiphilic — it has both a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and a lipophilic (fat-loving) tail — allowing it to sit at the oil-water interface and stabilize what is naturally an unstable two-phase system. • HLB (Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance): a numeric scale describing the relative strength of hydrophilic vs lipophilic portions of an emulsifier molecule; determines whether the emulsifier favours oil-in-water or water-in-oil emulsions. • Most widely used emulsifier: monoglycerides; lecithin is another key natural emulsifier. (c) Clarifying Agents Used to remove chill haze (from tannins/proanthocyanidins/polyphenols) in beverages like beer, wine, fruit juices. • Gelatin — commonly used to clarify beverages. • PVP (polyvinylpyrrolidone) — synthetic resin with selective affinity for polyphenols. (d) Colorants FOOD COLORANTS ┌───────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ NATURAL NATURE-IDENTICAL ARTIFICIAL INORGANIC (carotenoid, SYNTHETIC (coal-tar dyes, (PROHIBITED except annatto, (lab-synthesized e.g. Indigocarmine) Titanium Dioxide, paprika, replicas of capped at 1% in saffron, natural colors) CHEWING GUM only) anthocyanin, caramel, chlorophyll, turmeric/curcumin) [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Titanium dioxide — 1% — chewing gum ONLY. This is a frequently tested exact numeric + exact food- category pair. Any MCQ substituting a different percentage (e.g., 2%) or a different food (e.g., "permitted in all confectionery") is a trap. The rule is narrowly scoped: PFA prohibits inorganic colors except titanium dioxide, and only in chewing gum, maximum 1%. (e) Flavour Enhancers & Sweeteners • MSG (Monosodium Glutamate): sodium salt of glutamic acid; does not itself possess a primary flavour but intensifies/synergizes flavours of other foods. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 5′-ribonucleotides (from yeast): possess roughly 10× the flavour-enhancing property of MSG, and act synergistically with it (umami synergy). • Non-nutritive sweeteners: Saccharin (~300× sweeter than sucrose), cyclamate, aspartame, acesulfame-K — none perfectly replicates full sucrose taste profile. (f) Anticaking Agents • Function: absorb excess moisture, coat particles for water repellency, or act as an insoluble particulate diluent to maintain free-flow of hygroscopic powders. • Calcium silicate: used in baking powder and table salt, up to 2%. • Microcrystalline cellulose: prevents grated/shredded cheese from clumping. • Other agents: sodium silicon aluminate, tri-calcium phosphate, magnesium silicate, magnesium carbonate. (g) Antibiotics in Food — Nisin • Nisin: a polypeptide antibiotic produced by streptococci. • Permitted use: prevents outgrowth of Clostridium botulinum in high-moisture processed cheese. • Spectrum: active against Gram-positive organisms (spore-formers in particular). • Also used to prevent spoilage of condensed milk. Nisin's narrow Gram-positive spectrum is the key testable nuance — it does NOT control Gram-negative spoilage/pathogenic organisms. (h) Nitrites & Nitrates • Function: stabilize colour of cured meat after cooking (prevent green-brown discoloration of lean meat), impart flavour, and critically act as inhibitors of Clostridium botulinum (anti-botulism preservative function). • Lethal dose for humans is of the order of 1 gram. • US Code of Federal Regulations cap: nitrites permitted as preservatives in cured meat/poultry not exceeding 2000 ppm. 2.3 Class I vs Class II Preservatives — Master Table Class I (Natural, unrestricted*) Class II (Chemical, legally capped) Common salt Benzoic acid & its salts Sugar, dextrose/glucose syrup Sulphurous acid & its sulphites Wood smoke Nitrites & nitrates Spices Sorbic acid & its salts Vinegar / acetic acid Honey *unless otherwise provided in the Rules FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 10

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP 2.4 Endogenous Plant Toxicants & Anti-Nutrients — Deep Mechanistic Treatment (a) Glycoalkaloids — α-Chaconine & α-Solanine First principles: These are steroidal glycoalkaloids produced by Solanaceae plants (potato, tomato, nightshade) as a natural chemical defence against pests. They act on humans via cholinesterase inhibition and cell membrane disruption (saponin-like action). Parameter Detail All Solanaceous plants — potatoes most significant staple Source exposure Key compounds α-chaconine + α-solanine (summed) 200 mg/kg (potatoes), based on an estimated 300 g/day Maximum safety limit intake Variety, light exposure, irradiation, mechanical injury, Variability factors storage conditions Largely unaffected by common processing — baking, Thermal stability cooking, frying do NOT significantly reduce glycoalkaloid content Peeling is the most efficient method — outer layers are Detoxification richest in toxin; manual peeling can remove up to 60% of total content (varies with tuber size/variety) Tomatine (α-tomatine + dehydrotomatine mixture) is largely degraded as the fruit ripens — tomatoes are Tomato-specific note therefore much safer than potatoes regarding glycoalkaloid exposure [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Cooking/boiling/frying completely detoxifies glycoalkaloids." — FALSE. Glycoalkaloids are thermally stable; peeling (not heat) is the primary mitigation, and even peeling removes only up to ~60%, not 100%. (b) Cyanogenic Glycosides Mechanism — enzymatic HCN release: Cyanogenic glycoside (intact, non-toxic while compartmentalized) │ tissue damage (chopping/chewing/grinding) brings │ substrate and enzyme into contact ▼ β-glycosidase (endogenous plant enzyme) ▼ Hydrolysis releases cyanohydrin → spontaneously decomposes ▼ Hydrogen Cyanide (HCN) — the toxic agent Source Crop Cyanogenic Glycoside Cassava Linamarin (main cyanogen) FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 11

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Source Crop Cyanogenic Glycoside Stone fruit pits (e.g., apricot, peach, almond kernels) Amygdalin Traditional detoxification practices (cassava, Africa/South America): chopping, grinding, soaking in running water, fermentation, cooking — these physically disrupt plant tissue, allow HCN to volatilize/leach out, and denature enzymes. Amygdalin risk specifically arises when heat-processed products made from stone fruits retain the seeds/pits — consumers may be unknowingly exposed to HCN from unremoved seeds. (c) Lectins (Haemagglutinins) • Chemical nature: carbohydrate-binding glycoproteins, ubiquitous in nature. • Dietary relevance: present in most commonly eaten plant foods, especially legumes — consumed daily in appreciable quantities. • Key toxicological feature: high stability — survive gastrointestinal digestion, binding to gut mucosal carbohydrate receptors and causing gastric upset / mucosal damage via disruption of nutrient absorption and gut lining integrity. (d) Pyrrolizidine Alkaloids • Large group — ~350 distinct chemicals. • Toxicological classification: shown carcinogenic in animals; classified as potential human carcinogens (hepatotoxic mechanism — liver injury). • Exposure routes: (i) contamination of food supply by seeds containing these alkaloids, (ii) presence in traditional remedies/dietary supplements. (e) Anti-Nutrient Overview Table Toxicant Plant Family Glucosinolates Cruciferae (cabbage family) Cucurbitacins Cucurbitaceae (gourd family) Proteinase inhibitors Leguminosae Coumarins Leguminosae, Rubiaceae, Umbelliferae Cyanogenic glycosides Leguminosae, Gramineae, Rosaceae Glycoalkaloids Solanaceae Lectins Leguminosae Furocoumarins Umbelliferae, Rutaceae Family-mnemonic: Solanaceae → Glyco-ALKALoids (potato/tomato); Cruciferae → GlucoSINOlates (cabbage/mustard); Cucurbitaceae → CucurbitaCINS (gourds); Leguminosae → Lectins + Proteinase inhibitors + Coumarins (legumes carry the heaviest anti-nutrient burden). text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Module 3: Microbiology & Spoilage MODULE 3: MICROBIOLOGICAL PRINCIPLES & SPOILAGE CRITERIA 3.1 First-Principles: The Three-Lever Control Model Every microorganism needs three things to grow: suitable temperature, suitable pH, and available water. Food preservation technology is fundamentally the science of pushing one or more of these three levers outside the microbial comfort zone. This module is organized around those three levers, in the exact order the syllabus tests them: Temperature → pH → Water Activity. MICROBIAL GROWTH REQUIRES: ┌─────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┐ │ TEMPERATURE │ pH │ WATER ACTIVITY│ │ (°C) │ (H+ conc.) │ (aw) │ └─────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘ Push any lever outside tolerance → growth slows/stops 3.2 Cardinal Parameter 1: Temperature Domains Microbial Group Growth Range Optimal Growth Temperature Psychrotrophs Grow well at ≤7°C 20–30°C Mesophiles Grow well between 20–45°C 30–40°C Thermophiles Grow well at ≥45°C 55–65°C Key nuance: Psychrotrophs' optimal growth is NOT at refrigeration temperature — it is at 20–30°C. Their defining feature is that they can still grow, albeit slowly, at 7°C or below — this is precisely why refrigeration only extends shelf life (by increasing lag phase) rather than fully halting spoilage. Reducing temperature increases microbial lag time, which is the biochemical basis for chilling as a preservation method. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Refrigeration completely stops microbial growth." — FALSE. It only slows growth (extended lag phase) — psychrotrophs remain active at chill temperatures, hence refrigerated shelf life is finite, not infinite. 3.3 Cardinal Parameter 2: pH (Hydrogen-Ion Activity) Intuition Most microorganisms are physiologically "happiest" near neutral pH (~7.0). As the environment becomes more acidic, enzymatic machinery inside the cell is disrupted, and most pathogens cannot sustain growth. But not all FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 15

doc: Food Safety Law & HACCP — Master Study Manual
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP organisms have the same acid tolerance — this differential tolerance is exploited for both food safety classification and spoilage control. Organism / Food Type pH Tolerance Most microorganisms (general optimum) Close to pH 7.0 A few organisms Can grow below pH 4.0 Lactic acid bacteria (spoilage group) Can grow as low as pH 2.0 Clostridium botulinum Cannot grow below pH 4.6 THE Critical Public Health Threshold: pH 4.6 pH 4.6 is THE single most important numeric threshold in this entire module. Because of Clostridium botulinum's pathogenic potential (producer of the lethal botulinum neurotoxin) and its inability to grow/sporulate-outgrow below pH 4.6, this value is used as the universal legal/technical cutoff differentiating: - Low-acid foods: pH > 4.6 (require more stringent thermal processing — e.g., full retort sterilization — because C. botulinum CAN grow) - Acid / high-acid foods: pH ≤ 4.6 (safer from C. botulinum outgrowth; can often be processed with milder heat treatments) Nuance: The minimum pH tolerated by a given organism also depends on which acid is used — citric, hydrochloric, phosphoric, and tartaric acids permit growth of certain lactobacilli at lower pH values than acetic and lactic acids. This means pH value alone is not the complete story — the identity of the acidulant modulates antimicrobial efficacy (undissociated acid molecules of weaker organic acids like acetic/lactic penetrate cell membranes more effectively, giving them superior antimicrobial action at a given pH compared to strong mineral acids). [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "All bacteria are more pH-sensitive than filamentous fungi and yeasts." — Broadly TRUE as a generalization (bacteria tend to be more pH-sensitive than fungi/yeasts), but the trap variant "pathogenic bacteria tolerate LOWER pH than spoilage bacteria" is FALSE — it is the reverse: pathogenic bacteria are MORE pH-sensitive (narrower tolerance) than spoilage organisms like lactic acid bacteria. 3.4 Cardinal Parameter 3: Water Activity (aw) Intuition Total moisture content is not what matters to a microbial cell — what matters is how much of that water is metabolically available (not bound to solutes/structures). Water activity (aw) quantifies this available fraction, scaled 0 (no available water) to 1.0 (pure water). Food / Organism Type Water Activity Threshold Fresh produce aw exceeds 0.99 Spoilage bacteria (most) Grow at aw above 0.91 Filamentous fungi / moulds Can grow at aw as low as 0.80 FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 16

doc: Food Safety Law & HACCP — Master Study Manual
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Gram-positive vs Gram-negative generalization: Bacteria generally need HIGHER water activity than fungi; Gram-negative bacteria need higher aw than Gram-positive bacteria. This ordering (Gram-negative bacteria > Gram-positive bacteria > fungi, in terms of minimum aw required) is a testable hierarchy. Mechanism of control: Lowering aw below the organism's optimum increases lag phase and reduces growth rate — this induced stress is called osmotic stress. This is the biochemical basis for preservation by salting, sugaring, and drying. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Numeric trap: Do not swap the thresholds. Spoilage bacteria: >0.91. Filamentous fungi: as low as 0.80. Fresh produce: >0.99. If an MCQ states "most filamentous fungi require aw above 0.91 to grow," this is FALSE — fungi are notably MORE tolerant of low water activity than bacteria, growing down to 0.80. 3.5 Microbiological Spoilage Patterns (a) Bacterial Spoilage • Only specific bacterial groups cause spoilage despite many bacteria being capable of growing in food. • Governing factors: storage temperature, oxygen availability, food composition, pH, thermal treatment, competing microbiota. • Classic manifestation in horticultural produce: bacterial soft rot. (b) Yeast Spoilage • Yeasts are unicellular eukaryotic organisms. • They gain a competitive advantage over bacteria specifically in foods with: high sugar or salt content, low pH, or other selective conditions. • Mechanism: produce extracellular enzymes (proteases, lipases, amylases, pectinases) and volatile/non- volatile metabolites that spoil flavour and texture. • Key genera: Saccharomyces, Candida, Zygosaccharomyces, Debaryomyces, Rhodotorula, Pichia. • Especially important in fruit/vegetable spoilage due to environmental exposure and minimal processing; low pH of these foods also limits competing bacterial growth, giving yeasts a competitive field. (c) Filamentous Fungi Spoilage • Grow on a very wide range of foods: grains, meats, milk, fruits, vegetables, seeds, high-fat products. • Manifestations: discoloration, off-flavours, loss of structure/texture, visible mycelium formation, volatile compound production. • Fungi are obligate aerobes, capable of growing across a WIDE range of pH, temperature, and water activity — their metabolic flexibility is precisely why they are the dominant spoilage organism at low aw (0.80) where bacteria cannot compete. Spoilage Comparison Summary Organism Group Cell Type Competitive Niche Key Genera/Examples Neutral pH, moderate-high Bacteria Prokaryote Soft rot bacteria aw FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 17

Why is pH 4.6 universally designated as a critical food safety threshold?" Answer architecture (~10 marks, 2 pages): 1. Intrinsic vs extrinsic factors (1 mark): Define intrinsic (food-inherent: pH, aw, redox potential, nutrient composition) vs extrinsic (environment-imposed: storage temperature, atmosphere, packaging). 2. pH section (3 marks): General microbial optimum near 7.0; differential tolerance (lactic acid bacteria down to pH 2.0 vs C. botulinum blocked below 4.6); acid-identity nuance (citric/HCl/phosphoric/tartaric vs acetic/lactic). 3. Why pH 4.6 (3 marks): Explicit explanation — Clostridium botulinum cannot grow/produce toxin below this threshold; hence pH 4.6 is used worldwide to classify foods as low-acid (>4.6, requiring full retort sterilization to destroy C. botulinum spores) vs acid/high-acid (≤4.6, safer, can use milder thermal processing). Link to practical canning regulation (e.g., GMP requirement that acid/acidified foods be monitored and maintained at pH 4.6 or below). 4. Water activity section (2 marks): Define aw; give thresholds for fresh produce (>0.99), spoilage bacteria (>0.91), fungi (0.80); explain osmotic stress mechanism. 5. Integration/Conclusion (1 mark): Both factors are manipulated together industrially (e.g., pickling = low pH + reduced aw) for synergistic pathogen control — hurdle technology concept. 3.8 Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Bank Q1. Regarding temperature domains: (i) Psychrotrophs have an optimal growth temperature range of 20–30°C. (ii) Mesophiles grow well between 20–45°C with optimum at 30–40°C. (iii) Thermophiles have optimal growth below 45°C. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 18

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • (iii) FALSE — thermophiles grow well AT OR ABOVE 45°C, with optimum 55–65°C; the statement reverses the threshold direction. Q2. On pH and Clostridium botulinum: (i) C. botulinum cannot grow below pH 4.6. (ii) pH 4.6 is used to differentiate low-acid from high-acid/acid foods. (iii) Lactic acid bacteria can tolerate pH as low as 2.0. Answer: All 3 are correct. • All three statements are directly supported by the source material. Q3. On water activity thresholds: (i) Most spoilage bacteria require aw above 0.91. (ii) Filamentous fungi can grow at aw as low as 0.80. (iii) Fresh fruits and vegetables typically have aw below 0.80. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — fresh produce has aw exceeding 0.99, not below 0.80; this is a scope-reversal trap. Q4. On spoilage organisms: (i) Yeasts gain competitive advantage in high-sugar, low-pH foods. (ii) Zygosaccharomyces and Candida are key spoilage yeast genera. (iii) Filamentous fungi are strict anaerobes. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — filamentous fungi are obligate aerobes, the exact opposite. Q5. On acid identity and microbial growth: (i) Citric, hydrochloric, phosphoric and tartaric acids enable lactobacilli growth at lower pH than acetic/lactic acid. (ii) All acids have identical antimicrobial efficacy at the same pH value. (iii) Acetic and lactic acids are generally MORE inhibitory per unit pH than mineral acids due to undissociated acid effects. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and iii — note these are consistent, not contradictory; ii is false). • (ii) FALSE — different acids have different antimicrobial efficacy at the same measured pH, which is precisely why this nuance is tested. text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Module 4: Post-Harvest Adulteration MODULE 4: POST-HARVEST ADULTERATION & CHEMICAL TREATMENTS 4.1 First-Principles: Why does post-harvest malpractice exist? Consumers judge produce primarily by appearance — colour, size, shine, perceived ripeness/sweetness — at the point of purchase, before any taste or safety assessment is possible. This appearance-based buying heuristic creates a profit incentive for unscrupulous traders to manipulate the visible signal without manipulating the underlying quality — i.e., fake the signal (colour, size, apparent ripeness) rather than deliver the substance (genuine nutrient/flavour maturity). Every malpractice in this module follows this exact logic: cheap chemical trick → false visual/sensory signal → consumer deception → health risk. True quality driver (slow, costly, requires time) ──X── bypassed by trader │ Fast/cheap chemical shortcut │ False visual/sensory signal │ Consumer deceived + potential health hazard 4.2 Artificial Ripening Agents (a) Calcium Carbide ("Masala") — STRICTLY BANNED Reaction mechanism: Calcium Carbide (CaC2) + Moisture (H2O) ↓ Acetylene gas (C2H2) + Calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2) ↓ Acetylene is structurally/functionally ANALOGOUS to ethylene (C2H4) ↓ Triggers surface-level ripening signalling in fruit Why it is banned under FSSA, 2006 — multi-factor reasoning (exam gold): 1. Acidic nature of the compound/by-products — contributes to tissue damage; chronic consumption linked to ulcers, kidney and liver damage. 2. Trace contamination with arsenic and phosphorus hydride — industrial-grade calcium carbide (the commonly available/cheap form) is contaminated with arsenic and phosphorus compounds, which are themselves toxic. 3. Superficial colouration without internal ripening — acetylene changes ONLY the surface colour of the fruit; the interior remains unripened — a cosmetic fraud rather than genuine ripening. This is functionally and texturally inferior to ethylene-based ripening. 4. Carcinogenic property attributed to calcium carbide with prolonged exposure. FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 20

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP 4.4 Food-Grade Waxing Regulations Approved Waxes (under GMP) Wax Source Carnauba wax Carnauba palm tree Beeswax (white and yellow) Bee secretion Shellac wax Secretion of the lac insect/beetle Rationale for waxing: replaces natural wax lost during primary processing (washing etc.), reduces water loss, surface abrasion, controls internal gas composition, provides shiny/attractive appearance, extends shelf life. Preferred over: petroleum-based waxes (which may contain wood rosins or solvent residues). Typical waxed commodities: breadfruit, passion fruit, coconut, carambola, grapefruit, guava, mango, lime, lemon, orange, papaya, avocado, tangerine, pineapple (fruits); melon, bitter gourd, cassava, eggplant, peppers, sweet potato, tomato, pumpkin, yam, cucumber, asparagus, turnip, brinjal, okra, parsnip, sweet peppers (vegetables). Mandatory Label Declarations for Waxed Produce Under FSSA, 2006, fresh fruits/vegetables coated with wax (bees or carnauba) MUST have a clear label declaration stating: 1. Origin of the wax — animal-based (e.g., beeswax, shellac) vs vegetable-based (e.g., carnauba) — with food-grade certification. 2. Presence of known allergens that may be present in coating ingredients — e.g., milk, soybeans, fish, peanuts, nuts, wheat. 3. Post-harvest antimicrobial coatings/substances — their application must be indicated on each shipping container. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "All waxes and mineral oils are permitted on fruits and vegetables under GMP." — FALSE. No mineral oil and no colour is permitted at all on fresh fruits/vegetables per Indian regulatory bodies; only the THREE named food-grade waxes (carnauba, beeswax, shellac) are permitted, strictly under GMP, with mandatory labelling. Nutrient absorption caveat: Wax coating can form an insoluble layer that reduces nutrient absorption in the intestine — hence the practical consumer advice to wash fruits thoroughly / boil vegetables briefly before consumption, acknowledging that negative impact cannot be fully eliminated by washing alone. 4.5 Regulatory Residue/Tolerance Summary Substance Tolerance/Limit Status Permitted per GMP as food additives, with mandatory label Approved waxes (carnauba/beeswax/shellac) declaration Strictly prohibited — NO tolerance limit at all under Calcium carbide (ripening agent) FSSA, 2006 FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 23

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Module 5: Packaging & Labelling Law MODULE 5: PACKAGING & LABELLING STATUTORY STANDARDS 5.1 First-Principles: Why does the label matter legally? A food label is a legally binding representation to the consumer — it is the primary (often only) information bridge between a manufacturer's internal quality/safety processes and the buyer's informed choice. Every mandatory declaration exists to answer one of three consumer questions: (1) Is this food safe for me right now? (2) What exactly am I eating? (3) Who is accountable if something goes wrong? Organize your memorization around these three questions. LABEL ANSWERS THREE QUESTIONS: ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────┐ │ IS IT SAFE NOW? │ WHAT AM I EATING? │ WHO IS ACCOUNTABLE? │ │ (dates, veg/non- │ (ingredients, │ (manufacturer │ │ veg, allergens) │ nutrition facts) │ address, batch, │ │ │ │ country of origin)│ └─────────────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────┘ 5.2 Statutory Date Markings — Precise Definitions "Date of Manufacture" vs "Date of Packaging" Term Definition The date on which the food becomes the product as Date of manufacture described (i.e., the food's identity/composition is finalized) The date on which the food is placed in the immediate Date of packaging container in which it will ultimately be sold These are conceptually distinct steps — a food can be manufactured on Day 1 and packaged on Day 3; both dates may be legally relevant depending on the product category. "Best Before" vs "Use By / Expiry Date" — THE critical distinction PRODUCT TIMELINE Manufacture ──► "Best Before" ──► "Use By / Expiry" (quality marker) (safety marker) │ │ Food MAY still be Food shall NOT perfectly safe to be sold — safety consume past this threshold passed date, though quality may have diminished (BUT: food shall not be sold if it becomes unsafe at ANY stage) FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 26

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Term Full Definition Key Legal Effect Signifies the end of the period, under stated storage conditions, during which the food remains fully marketable and retains claimed qualities. Beyond Quality guarantee, NOT an absolute "Best before" this date, food MAY still be perfectly safety cutoff safe to consume, though quality may have diminished. HOWEVER — the food shall NOT be sold if at any stage it becomes unsafe. Signifies the end of the estimated period, under stated storage "Use-by date" / "Recommended last conditions, after which the food The food SHALL NOT be sold after consumption date" / "Expiry date" probably will not have the quality this date — absolute safety/sale cutoff and safety attributes normally expected. [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Absolute qualifier: "Food past its 'best before' date is always unsafe and must never be sold." — FALSE. "Best before" is a quality marker — food MAY remain safe and even saleable past this date UNLESS it has independently become unsafe. Do not confuse this with "use by/expiry," which IS an absolute sale prohibition threshold. This exact confusion (best-before = safety cutoff) is the single most common trap in this sub-topic. Other Statutory Definitions Term Definition Numerals/alphabets/combination, preceded by words like Lot number / Code number / Batch number "Lot No," "Code," "Batch No," by which the food can be traced in manufacture and identified in distribution Food placed in a package of any nature such that the Prepackaged / Pre-packed food contents cannot be changed without tampering, and which is ready for sale to the consumer That part of the container/package intended/likely to be displayed, presented, shown, or examined by the Principal Display Panel (PDP) customer under normal/customary conditions of display, sale, or purchase A package containing two or more individually packaged/labelled pieces of the same commodity of Multipiece package identical quantity, intended for retail either as individual pieces or as a whole A package containing a number of retail packages (intended for sale to an intermediary, NOT a single Wholesale package consumer) OR a bulk commodity sold to an intermediary for repackaging/resale in smaller quantities Infant A child not more than twelve (12) months of age FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 27

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Vegetarian vs Non-Vegetarian Food — THE statutory exclusion trap Term Definition An article of food which contains whole or part of any animal including birds, fresh water or marine animals, or "Non-Vegetarian Food" eggs, or products of any animal origin, BUT EXCLUDING MILK OR MILK PRODUCTS, as an ingredient "Vegetarian Food" Any article of food OTHER THAN Non-Vegetarian Food [HPSC EXAM TRAP] This is one of the single highest-yield statutory traps in the entire syllabus. Milk and milk products are statutorily EXCLUDED from the definition of "Non-Vegetarian Food" — meaning milk/milk products are classified as VEGETARIAN under this specific legal definition, DESPITE being an animal product. A question stating "milk and milk products are classified as non-vegetarian food because they are of animal origin" is FALSE under this statutory scheme — eggs ARE non-vegetarian, milk is NOT. 5.3 Mandatory Package Label Declarations — Complete Checklist MANDATORY LABEL ELEMENTS ┌───────────┬────────────┬─────────────┬────────────┬───────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Name of Ingredient Nutritional Veg/Non-Veg Manufacturer Net Qty/ Food List Facts Logo Name+Address Batch/ (trade (descending (per 100g/ (specific Date/ name/ order by 100ml: dimensions/ Origin/ descrip) weight/vol) Energy kcal, geometry) Use Protein,CHO, Instructions Fat in g) Element Detail Name of food Trade name or description of the food contained Title "Ingredients"; listed in descending order of List of ingredients composition by weight or volume, as at time of manufacture (except single-ingredient foods) Energy value in Kcal; amounts of Protein, Carbohydrate, Nutritional information (per 100g/100ml or per serving) and Fat in grams; amount of any nutrient for which a nutrition/health claim is made Mandatory symbolic logo with specific dimensions and Veg/Non-veg differentiation geometry Manufacturer details Name and complete address of the manufacturer Net quantity Of the product Lot/Code/Batch identification For traceability Date of manufacture or packing As defined above Best before and use-by date As defined above Country of origin Mandatory for imported foods FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 28

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Module 6: HACCP System MODULE 6: THE HACCP SYSTEM & QUALITY ASSURANCE 6.1 First-Principles: Why HACCP replaced end-product testing The core insight that birthed HACCP: if you only test the FINISHED product for safety, you can never achieve near-100% assurance, because (a) you'd have to destructively test almost every unit to be statistically confident, leaving nothing left to sell, and (b) by the time a defect is found, the unsafe batch may already be shipped. HACCP's genius is to shift control upstream, into the process itself — identify exactly WHERE in the process a hazard could enter or fail to be controlled, and build real-time monitoring AT THAT POINT, so you catch failures before the product is even finished, let alone shipped. OLD MODEL: Raw material → Process → Process → Process → [TEST FINISHED PRODUCT] (if contaminated, discovered too late / insufficient sampling) HACCP MODEL: Raw material → [MONITOR CCP1] → Process → [MONITOR CCP2] → Process → Product (hazard caught in real time, AT the exact point of risk) 6.2 Historical Foundations Milestone Detail Pillsbury Company, pioneered application of HACCP Origin concept to food production in the early 1960s Supplying food for the U.S. space program (NASA) — existing QC (end-product testing) could not provide Driving need adequate contamination assurance; extensive end-testing would consume so much product that little food would remain available for space flights 1985 — NACMCF (National Advisory Committee on Formalization Microbiological Criteria for Foods) formulated the HACCP principles [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Date-pairing trap: Pillsbury origin = early 1960s (the practical invention); NACMCF formal principles = 1985 (the codification). Do not swap these two dates — a question may ask "In which year were the 7 HACCP principles formulated?" and offer "1960s" as a distractor; the correct year for the formal 7-principle codification is 1985. 6.3 Hazard vs Undesirable Defect — THE scope-defining distinction In HACCP terminology, "hazard" has a narrower, more precise meaning than in everyday food safety usage. It refers ONLY to conditions/contaminants that can cause illness or injury. FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 32

text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP 6.4 The 7 Core HACCP Principles — Full Treatment PRINCIPLE 1 PRINCIPLE 2 PRINCIPLE 3 PRINCIPLE 4 Conduct Hazard ──► Determine ──► Establish ──► Establish CCP Analysis CCPs Critical Monitoring (decision tree) Limits Procedures │ ▼ PRINCIPLE 7 PRINCIPLE 6 PRINCIPLE 5 Establish ◄── Establish ◄── Establish Documentation & Verification Corrective Record-Keeping Procedures Actions Principle 1: Conduct Hazard Analysis • HACCP team bears initial responsibility to decide which hazards are significant and must be addressed. • Safety concerns must be explicitly differentiated from quality concerns (quality issues are NOT the subject of HACCP control). • Tool: hazard identification and evaluation worksheet — organizes the process step (Column 1), identified hazard (Column 2), hazard evaluation result (Column 3), and justification for accepting/rejecting the hazard (Column 4). Principle 2: Determine Critical Control Points (CCPs) • For every significant hazard identified in Principle 1, there must be one or more CCPs where the hazard is controlled. • A CCP = a specific point in the process flow where applying a control measure effectively prevents, eliminates, or reduces the hazard to an acceptable level. • Determined using decision tree logic — a structured sequence of questions applied at each process step to test whether that step qualifies as a CCP. Principle 3: Establish Critical Limits • A critical limit = the boundary/boundaries used to ensure a process produces safe product at a given CCP. • Each CCP may require one or more critical limits, one per associated food-safety hazard. • Deviation from a critical limit → mandatory corrective action. • If exact critical limit data is unavailable: gather from scientific publications, regulatory guidelines, experts, or experimental studies; if still unavailable, select a conservative value. The rationale/reference becomes part of the HACCP plan's support documentation. Principle 4: Establish CCP Monitoring Procedures Monitoring must define four elements: Element Meaning What characteristic will be monitored (e.g., temperature, What pH, line speed) How How the critical limit/control measure will be measured Frequency How often monitoring is performed Who Who is responsible for performing the monitoring FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP • 34

doc: Food Safety Law & HACCP — Master Study Manual
text: HPSC FOOD SAFETY OFFICER | FOOD SAFETY LAW & HACCP Purpose: accurate monitoring reveals loss of control at a CCP and deviation from a critical limit in real time; also creates records proving compliant production (feeds into Principle 7 and Principle 6 verification). Principle 5: Establish Corrective Actions When a critical limit is violated, pre-determined, documented corrective actions must be instituted. Effective corrective action plans must: 1. Correct and eliminate the cause of non-compliance, restoring the CCP to control. 2. Segregate, assess, and determine disposition of the non-compliant product. Options: isolate/hold product for safety evaluation; divert affected product to a non-critical line; reprocess; destroy product. Principle 6: Establish Verification Procedures • Verification = collecting and evaluating scientific/technical information to confirm the HACCP plan, if properly implemented, will effectively control hazards. • Validation = a component of verification performed BEFORE the plan is implemented — substantiates that the plan, if followed, is sufficient to control the likely food-safety hazards; provides objective evidence that all elements have a scientific basis. • Approaches to validation: incorporation of fundamental scientific principles, use of scientific data, reliance on expert opinion, or in-plant observation/testing. Validation vs ongoing verification: Validation happens once, UP FRONT (before operation). Verification (in the broader sense, including scheduled audits) is ongoing, confirming the system continues to function as validated. Principle 7: Establish Documentation and Record-Keeping Procedures Accurate record-keeping is essential — provides documentation that critical limits were met OR appropriate corrective action was taken when exceeded. Four record categories: 1. HACCP-plan support documents 2. Monitoring records 3. Corrective action records 4. CCP determination via decision tree (3 marks): Explain the sequential logic — is control necessary? is the hazard likely to occur/increase? will a later step eliminate it? — concluding in CCP designation only when all conditions align. 4. CCP vs PRP distinction (2 marks): Reproduce the comparison table — CCP is hazard-specific and point- specific with a measurable critical limit; PRP is a general plant-wide foundational practice (GMP/GHP) that enables the HACCP system to function, but is not itself tied to a single measurable critical limit at a single process point. 6.7 Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Bank Q1. On HACCP origins: (i) HACCP originated at the Pillsbury Company in connection with the NASA space programme. (ii) The 7 HACCP principles were formulated by NACMCF in 1985. (iii) HACCP was developed in the early 1960s as a reactive, end-product-testing-based system. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — HACCP was developed specifically because end-product testing (reactive) was found inadequate; HACCP is explicitly a preventive, not reactive, system — the exact reverse characterization. Q2. On HACCP hazard scope: (i) Hair and filth are automatically classified as HACCP hazards. (ii) Economic fraud is excluded from the HACCP hazard definition unless directly tied to illness/injury. (iii) A hazard in HACCP terms must have the potential to cause an adverse health effect. Answer: Only 2 are correct (ii and iii). • (i) FALSE — hair and filth are "undesirable defects," not automatically HACCP hazards, unless a direct injury/illness link is shown. Q3. On the 7 principles, consider this set relating to Principle 4 (Monitoring): (i) Monitoring must specify "what," "how," "frequency," and "who." (ii) Monitoring is only required at the END of the production line. (iii) Monitoring records support verification under Principle 6. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and iii). • (ii) FALSE — monitoring occurs AT each CCP throughout the process, not solely at the end; this contradicts HACCP's core preventive, real-time logic. Q4. On CCP vs PRP: (i) A CCP is always hazard-specific and tied to a measurable critical limit. (ii) A PRP (e.g., GMP/GHP/sanitation programme) is plant-wide and foundational, not hazard-point-specific. (iii) Every PRP failure automatically qualifies as a critical-limit deviation requiring product disposition under Principle 5. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and ii). • (iii) FALSE — PRP failures are generally managed through general corrective maintenance, not necessarily triggering the formal CCP critical-limit deviation/product-disposition process (unless the PRP failure is severe enough to compromise an actual CCP). Q5. On validation vs verification: (i) Validation occurs before the HACCP plan is implemented. (ii) Verification is the same process as validation and occurs only once. (iii) Verification includes collecting and evaluating scientific/technical information to confirm the plan will effectively control hazards. Answer: Only 2 are correct (i and iii). • (ii) FALSE — validation is a one-time, pre-implementation component; verification (in the broader sense) is an ONGOING activity, not identical to or synonymous with a single one-time validation event.
